title: Are you tweaking on your partner? From secret boob jobs to Botox on the sly, people explain why they keep their cosmetic procedures hidden | Cosmetic surgery | The Guardian
description: Daniel’s boyfriend thinks his youthful complexion is down to fancy skincare, and Jessica’s nearest and dearest still don’t know she’s had a breast enhancement …
Author: Rhiannon Evans
Headline: Daniel’s boyfriend thinks his youthful complexion is down to fancy skincare, and Jessica’s nearest and dearest still don’t know she’s had a breast enhancement …
Content: Illustration: Jacquie Boyd/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Jacquie Boyd/The GuardianCosmetic surgeryAre you tweaking on your partner? From secret boob jobs to Botox on the sly, people explain why they keep their cosmetic procedures hiddenDaniel’s boyfriend thinks his youthful complexion is down to fancy skincare, and Jessica’s nearest and dearest still don’t know she’s had a breast enhancement …Rhiannon EvansSat 15 Aug 2026 06.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJessica was at a spa with her friends of more than 20 years when she noticed one stare at her bikini, lock eyes with her and laugh, before asking: “Wait, have you …?” The game was up – eight months after she’d had a secret breast enhancement, she’d been rumbled. Fearing judgment from even her closest circle, she had only spoken to two people who’d had the procedure, for advice, and told a neighbour in case she was unwell after the surgery. “My family still don’t know – most people don’t,” the 42-year-old from London says, including her two children who live between her and her ex-husband. “I’m not alone; I’ve since learned winter is the most popular time for people to get things done, then they can just hide under jumpers while everything settles in, so no one notices.”For years, celebrities have endured public speculation about their tweakments and surgeries – but as procedures become more commonplace, “civilian” patients are facing the same questions from family and friends. And many of them are choosing to go incognito; somesurgeons estimate up to 70%of their clients aren’t telling others about their aesthetic procedures. But what are the practicalities of disguising everything from breast augmentation to filler to hair transplants from your closest circle? And why are so many people spending thousands of pounds to alter their appearance – only to hope that no one notices?“I am definitely seeing more patients who prefer not to tell friends, family, or even colleagues that they’ve had aesthetic treatments,” saysAllergan Aesthetics’Dr Sophie Shotter. She has seen a “noticeable shift” from 10 or 15 years ago when procedures such as dramatic boob jobs or big lips were a status symbol intended to be seen. Things have changed. “Today, many patients tell me that the best compliment they can receive is not, ‘Have you had something done?’ but, ‘You look well’ or, ‘You look refreshed’,” she says.It’s not just a case of wanting subtle work, or not broadcasting your business to the world; many are keeping enhancements even from the partners with whom they share homes, bank accounts and their deepest secrets. This is especially the case when the tweakment involves little recovery time, such as with Botox injections, often used to decrease visible facial lines. It hasbeen estimatedthere are more than 900,000 Botox injections done a year in the UK, across 5,589 clinics. Despite its popularity, there still remains some stigma about the injections, which block the nerve signals that tell muscles to move. But, with costs starting from £150, if there’s no bruising or nerve damage, the injections can remain fairly undetectable both on the face and in the joint bank account.View image in fullscreenLaura had Botox twice a year for two years before her partner found out. “One day he was looking at me across the dinner table, and said: ‘Why aren’t you scowling?’ And I was like: ‘What?’ He said: ‘Why aren’t you scowling at me? Frown!’ And I tried to frown, and he was like: ‘No, you’ve had Botox.’”It was the stigma that kept her quiet for so long. “He has always been adamant that he likes women who are really natural,” says Laura. “For years, he’s said: ‘Promise me you’ll never get any of that done because everyone looks so fake.’ Also it’s financial as well, because it feels like it’s a waste of money, with the kids.”His objections did matter to her. “I definitely didn’t do it for a while when he said that,” she admits. “Then I started to look at myself in photos and just saw my 11 lines” – the vertical creases between your eyebrows that look like the number 11. “I’ve always hated them, and because of my job being very expressive, being a drama teacher, I think my lines are way worse. Everyone’s always said to me: ‘You’re scowling!’ I did hold off for a little while, but then thought, ‘Sod it. It’s not about what he wants, it’s about what’s going to make me happy.’ So I went for it, and I’ve never looked back.”Her husband was upset about the deception. “He couldn’t believe I’d done that and lied about it. He was cross about me spending the money on it, and that I wasn’t ageing naturally. And then I showed him pictures of me with the scowl and without it. He looked at them and was like: ‘OK, I get why you want it done.’ I did appreciate why he was angry and apologised. But also, it’s my body. I’m going to do what I want.”She jokes about the way her husband rarely notices when she has her hair done and that she had justified the cost of the Botox by not having facials, massages or manicures. Her behaviour chimes with an assertion by Dr Ahmed El Houssieny, a doctor with Allergan Aesthetics, who posits that fewer patients are telling loved ones about aesthetic treatments not “because they’re ashamed; it’s more that, for many people, it’s become part of their self-care routine, much like getting a facial or going to the gym. Many patients simply don’t feel the need to share it.”Daniel, 42, from Kent works in corporate banking and has been having £280 worth of Botox, twice a year for four years without telling his partner of 19 years. He takes careful steps to avoid any bruising by “having it done at a reputable skin clinic and making sure they have digital visibility of any nerves in my face to avoid any potential calamities”. He adds: “I always make sure I get it done when he’s working in London and I’m working from home,” he adds.“I’ve always been into skincare, so I think he assumes that all of the designer anti-ageing moisturisers actually work,” he says. “It doesn’t – it’s certainly nowhere near as effective as Botox.” He’s not shy about anyone else knowing he’s having injections, just his partner. “If anyone compliments my appearance or says that I look younger than my years I literally just go, ‘Botox.’ It takes all the credit,” he says.Daniel says he hasn’t told his partner because they disapprove of the whole aesthetics industry. “He has a complete misconception about what Botox actually is and gets it confused with filler,” says Daniel. Whereas Botox is a solution that relaxes muscle, fillers involves inserting a gel-like substance under the skin to plump up areas. “People don’t seem to realise that you can have the two things done independently and that they aren’t remotely the same thing.”Daniel maintains he doesn’t feel guilty about keeping the secret. “Really, it bears no real relevance to our relationship. It’s a bit like: ‘What he doesn’t know, can’t hurt.’” He thinks eventually his partner will find out. “Probably when he moans about someone looking like they have a trout pout. He’ll say: ‘Look at her with all that Botox,’ and my guard will be down and I’ll defend the needle and educate him.”View image in fullscreenDaniel doesn’t think it will be relationship-ruining when that moment comes. “What can he say? I think he’ll be a bit sulky for a very short time and then realise nothing’s actually changed and just move on. He will definitely ask where I’m getting it done, to validate that it’s being done professionally and not in the back of a car or something.”Still, though, Daniel admits it does sometimes niggle that he’s never noticed. “But I do think I get more compliments from him about six weeks after I’ve had it done,” he adds. “Just at the point where you have the smoothness but a little bit of flex and more expression without all the wrinkles.”The idea of “so-subtle-you-can’t-tell” is taking over the industry, with the art of “undetectable treatments” being marketed more than ever. “I often say that the best aesthetic treatment is one nobody notices,” says El Houssieny, begging the question: if a tree falls in the forest and no one is around to see it … then what’s the point of the Botox anyway?“People might ask if you’ve been on holiday, rather than asking if you’ve had something done,” he says. “I think there’s been a real shift away from transformation and towards maintenance. Patients want to look like themselves on a really good day.” Aesthetics, then, is no longer about ugly ducklings being transformed. It’s about swans, looking effortlessly unchanged above the water and desperately kicking to maintain that appearance below.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Jacquie Boyd/The GuardianFor those not indulging, it can feel like a betrayal of trust knowing friends have not revealed their aesthetic procedures. “It sometimes feels like people are trying to catch you out,” said Rebecca, 41. “I’ve had friends say: ‘I wanted to see if you noticed!’ when they have had tweakments, and it’s hard to know what they want the response to be. It’s a strange feeling – some of these women, we’ve shared every intimate detail of our lives and bodies since we were teenagers and now there are things they’re actively hiding.”Claire, 42, agrees: “Although many of my friends have clearly had Botox and filler, they don’t own up to it. I often feel a bit left behind, like a bit of a mug. I panic it’s too late, before worrying about the cost and then parking the idea. The envy has never been enough to push me into it. I actually don’t have that many lines yet, but then I wish I had that  glossy perfect skin that everyone seems to have.”View image in fullscreenBecca, a project manager from Manchester, finally told her husband of seven years about having Botox six weeks after her treatment. “He wasn’t like: ‘Why didn’t you tell me?’ It was just more: ‘What have you done that for? You don’t need it.’” She says she didn’t feel it was a betrayal. “I think it’s something quite personal and you’re doing a test in some way by not telling people. You want to know: is it obvious? Is it not?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘So destructive’: women are paying for face scans that tell them what cosmetic procedures to getRead moreIt is a complex issue for Becca, who admits that after having a microneedling facial, she was nervous her primary-school-aged daughter would see the redness on her face. “I really didn’t want my daughter to pick up on that,” she says. “I didn’t want her knowing I was having needles poked into my face to make my skin better. So I spoke to my husband and said, ‘If she comments, I’m going to say: It’s this cream. And I’ve had a funny reaction to it.’ I didn’t want that to be in her head, that you mess around with your face.”Keeping things from your family can backfire, of course. “I had fillers done in my lips about three years ago and genuinely thought I’d be able to get away with it without anyone noticing,” says Victoria. “I didn’t tell anyone as I guess I was a bit embarrassed to admit to it as I was approaching my 40s and saw it as a tweakment rather than a drastic blowing up of the lips.“Everything was fine immediately afterwards, but about 24 hours later my lips blew up. Obviously, my partner clocked immediately and I had to fess up, but my mum was due to visit. I did everything I could to bring the swelling down. But as soon as she saw me, she told me I looked like Katie Price.“The swelling went down after a few days and I was happy with the overall result, but haven’t plucked up the courage to get it done again,” she says. “Lesson learned – it’s best to be open and honest when it comes to certain treatments, as it’s pretty impossible to get away with.”Shane lives in New York and shaved his head before he underwent a hair transplant. He also paid a premium to have it close to home rather than travelling to Turkey, to avoid raising any suspicion. “NYC came at a price, almost $13,000 [£9,600] for 1,500 grafts,” he says. “He’s a well-regarded doctor who gives natural results, and that was what I wanted. I’m 47 and wanted to look 47, not 27. If I had an unnatural result, I’d look ridiculous.”View image in fullscreenWeekendPulls for online2Shane had battled thinning hair since he was 24 and had tried every medication available before opting to get grafts, mostly filling in his temples and the top front hairline. From the beginning, he worked to keep things under wraps from everyone but his wife and young kids (although his parents later noticed and brought it up with him). “I can wear hats at work, so I pre-emptively wore one for about six months before my procedure, so that no one would be surprised when I wore one afterwards,” he explained. “It took about a week of recovery at home with noticeable blood and redness. Then I looked like I just had a short haircut done. No one could see the grafts on the top of my head. The worst part was that because I have Irish heritage and pale skin, the donor area [at the back of my head] was red for at least six months. Sixlongmonths.” A slight irritation in his donor area caused pimples, too, he adds.“I don’t tell friends, co-workers or strangers about other medical surgeries, so I didn’t see the point in broadcasting this one. Once I took off the hat, it was almost two years since they had seen me without it. I assume people forgot what my hair looked like. If anyone asks me if I did something to my hair, I just say that it was hair meds. For some reason, that’s easier to explain and less taboo than a transplant.“This new hairline makes me feel less self-conscious in photos,” he adds. “My wife loves it. It’s a bit vain, but I want to enjoy the next 10 years looking better.”Shane has found himself posting on Reddit boards where men ask for reassurance about whether they can keep their transplants unnoticed by friends and family. His advice? “Don’t tell people if you don’t want to; tell people if you do. If you wouldn’t share your other medical history with others, why this?”Jessica thought about all of this before getting her £7k breast enhancement, which took her from a B/C cup to a D cup, choosing to have the implants under the muscle where the placement looks more natural. She planned ahead for months, choosing a week to take annual leave when she wouldn’t have her children.For her, it’s the case that, “I’ve just always wanted bigger boobs, but I didn’t want to do anything that would impact breastfeeding – then after two kids they didn’t look great,” she says. “I knew more people who’d had it done and it felt more mainstream, but I needed the money to do it. So when my divorce and house sale came through, it was my present to myself.”Outside the few people she told, it remained her secret for months. “I didn’t tell my family as I think boobs are kind of a sexual thing, so it draws attention to that,” she says. “It’s not like a nose job; it’s personal. With my friends, I think I worried about the judgment. Some people do think: ‘Why have you done that? You were fine the way you were.’ With my good friends it felt like everyone had lots going on, and it’s hard to throw into conversation. It just doesn’t come up, then time passes. Now I’ve got friends who’ve commented: ‘Have you got a new bra?’ and I think I’m too far down the line and it’s awkward to go back on it.”She’s glad now, after months of worry, that her close friends found out at that spa. “We just laughed about it and then spent all weekend talking about them,” she says. “It felt so nice to realise they weren’t going to judge me – mostly it was good not to have to hide things and to watch what I was saying.”Despite the welcome surprise of her friends’ reaction, she doesn’t think she’ll tell more people, and is resolute she’ll continue to keep the truth from her children. “I’ve done everything I can to avoid them knowing.” She even told them she’d hurt her back to explain the brace she wore during recovery. “I didn’t want to tell my daughter as I didn’t want her to feel like she needs to do anything like that. Her body is perfect the way it is.”Some names have been changedExplore more on these topicsCosmetic surgeryBeautyFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: It’s the SUV tyranny: where have all the normal family cars gone? | Coco Khan | The Guardian
description: They rule the roads and, in their wake, even old-style saloons have been supersized. It’s an illusion of consumer choice, says writer and podcaster Coco Khan
Author: Coco Khan
Headline: They rule the roads and, in their wake, even old-style saloons have been supersized. It’s an illusion of consumer choice, says writer and podcaster Coco Khan
Content: ‘Traditional car body styles have been modified into taller, wider frames.’Photograph: Crispin/Crispin Hughes/Clean Cities Campaign/Climate VisualsView image in fullscreen‘Traditional car body styles have been modified into taller, wider frames.’Photograph: Crispin/Crispin Hughes/Clean Cities Campaign/Climate VisualsOpinionMotoringIt’s the SUV tyranny: where have all the normal family cars gone?Coco KhanThey rule the roads and, in their wake, even old-style saloons have been supersized. It’s an illusion of consumer choiceSat 15 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.40 EDTShareRecently, while traipsing from showroom to showroom in search of a used car for my growing clan, the iconic line from Christopher Nolan’s seminal Batman movie The Dark Knightcame to mind: “You either die a hero, or live long enough to see yourself become the villain.” And by villain, of course, I mean an SUV driver.Because, if you haven’t shopped for a secondhand family car recently, I’ll save you the shock: wherever you look, it’s SUVs.It’s no surprise when these giant cars now makeup 30% of all carson the road and were50% of all new car salesin rich countries in 2023. The look has been so popular that traditional body styles have been modified into taller, wider frames. Even Volvo, the defining family car brand,now only offers SUVsin the UK. All of which means that if, like me, you want a car under 10 years old, hoping it lasts another five, your options are “tank” and “tank-ette”.Britain’s cars and SUVs are growing bigger – but there is a way to stop this deadly ‘carspreading’  | Christian WolmarRead moreDriving the same small city car for nearly 10 years has felt, overall, like a net good. Cheap to run and clean-air-zone-compliant, the compact car is the sociable motor. The people pleaser of the road, at this size a tight parking spot is rarely a worry. Even its horn, a pipsqueak of a beep, conveys more “toodles” than threat. Yes, fine, on a windy motorway it can feel like it might become airborne. But this precious little donkey is reliable and humble. Unlike the flashy warhorse, the SUV, with its ever-widening size (0.5cm wider each year) intimidating other drivers and pedestrians, causing chaos on narrow roads andreducing parking spaceswhen lines are redrawn to accommodate them. Also, a special mention of the branding: so much military language (the JeepCommanderor Land Rover’sDefender, apparently “built toconquer”)– for a vehicle whose main enemy is the roundabout outside Sainsbury’s.So when it came to buying my first family car I figured I’d find an estate, a saloon or a hatchback: something that was safe, since it would carry the most precious cargo of all, children; fuel efficient; wipe-down seats; and a big boot big enough for strollers and bikes, and all the hopes and dreams for a happy family life. But my dreams would soon be dashed.One thing’s for sure, it has been a memorable month hunting for a “normal” family car. The experience of saying “I’m not interested in an SUV” and still being shown one … then a small one … and then one that justlookslike one, but technically isn’t because it can’t go off-road, is the closest thing I’ve experienced to performance art in some years.How can I forget the forecourt so dominated by these cars that the best on offer was a black “mid-size” SUV, a Lexus RX450H, so huge that I genuinely mistook it for a hearse. Or the gentle, sympathetic nature of the used-car salesman showing me a grey and dowdy people carrier. “But, but … I’m in my 30s. I’m still young, I can’t drive this,” I protested, as he gave me a smile conveying “this is all that’s left for you, my friend”.View image in fullscreenWhen smaller was beautiful … children look out from their family’s hatchback.Photograph: FG Trade Latin/Getty ImagesYet,I’m not sure what it is about this that deflates me. Is it the illusion of consumer choice, and how we are funnelled into the same purchases and lifestyles even when we don’t really want them? Or the corrosive quality of fear: against your neighbour’s SUV, your regular car looks flimsy, so you arm up, too. The car lobby has pushed the message that these vehicles are fortresses to keep your children safe inside, with no care for how unsafe they may be outside. The increased height of these bonnets means a child is three times more likely to be killed if hit by an SUV rather than by a conventional vehicle –and, as transport writer Christian Wolmar observes, more likely to be hit at all, since the driving position is often too high to see a child ahead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut mostly I suspect it’s to do with our modern parenting culture, where everything – buggies, cars, technology for baby socks to monitor their breathing – has scaled up to capitalise on our need for safety in a precarious world. Yet the best thing to keep us safe will always be one another, collectivism over individualism. But here we are, driving around in Batmobiles, thinking ourselves heroes, blithely unaware we just might be the baddies.Needless to say, I still haven’t found the right family car. I do (reluctantly) have an SUV test drive booked, though. Perhaps I should embrace the chaos. It could be my Joker moment.Coco Khan is a freelance writer and co-host of the politics podcast Pod Save the UKExplore more on these topicsMotoringOpinionRoad safetyChildrenAutomotive industryTransport policyTravel and transportTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s archaic’: the struggle to heat poorly insulated homes let by royal estates | Housing | The Guardian
description: A number of idyllic-looking homes in estates owned by King Charles and Prince William do not meet energy standards for rentals
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A number of idyllic-looking homes in estates owned by King Charles and Prince William do not meet energy standards for rentals
Content: RoyalLandlord-CoalstoveIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenRoyalLandlord-CoalstoveIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyHousing‘It’s archaic’: the struggle to heat poorly insulated homes let by royal estatesA number of idyllic-looking homes in estates owned by King Charles and Prince William do not meet energy standards for rentalsRoyal estates rent out homes that fail to meet legal energy efficiency standardsNick SommerladSat 15 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis summer, the duchy of Cornwall got a new-look website with a bold statement of intent at the top: “We’re on a mission to become a world-leading impact organisation.”Updating the website will have been the easiest part of that mission. Upgrading hundreds of ageing, mostly rural, rented cottages, farmhouses and country houses will be one of the hardest.For many tenants, it will be long overdue. One, who is in failing health and struggling to heat a mostly uninsulated home where the only source of warmth is coal-fired stoves, said: “This place is not up to the standards of the 20th century, let alone the 21st. It’s archaic. It needs to be upgraded but I don’t think they want to spend the money.”There is money. Established in 1337 to provide an income to male heirs to the throne, the duchy of Cornwall is unburdened by many of the taxes faced by other landlords, such as corporation tax, capital gains tax and inheritance tax. It enjoys profit margins of about 60% and pays out more than £20m a year to the monarch’s eldest son.View image in fullscreenKing Charles with his eldest son, Prince William.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesChanges are afoot: the duchy announced earlier this year that it would be selling off 20% of the estate over the next decade and investing £500m in local communities, housing and environmental projects.Prince William, four years into his tenure as the 25th duke of Cornwall, has promised to transform his inheritance: “There is so much good we can do. I’m trying to make sure I’m prioritising stuff that’s going to make people’s lives, living in those areas, better.”However, the same tenant is not convinced he will benefit. “I’m sure this is one of the properties that he will sell and I don’t know what will happen to me after that,” he said. “Will they have to find somewhere else for me or will I just be turfed out?”It is the dilemma facing many duchy tenants, most of whom are reluctant to speak out, in parts of the country where the housing crisis is being keenly felt.Many properties in these areas – including those owned by the duchies – have been turned into holiday lets. Combined with an abundance of second homes, there are few other rental properties available for tenants.At first glance, some of the duchy cottages look idyllic. But many were built cheaply, over the centuries, for the agricultural working poor. The older ones are stone, the relatively newer ones typically a single skin of brick. They are often clustered around farms, but some are the towns and villages dotted throughout the duchy’s heartlands in Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and Dartmoor.View image in fullscreenA former Duchy of Lancaster property sold last year, which was rated G in 2020.Photograph: Nick SommerladTime and again the same complaints surface – the duchy doesn’t like to spend money, repairs take an age, friends are envious, but the homes are cold, winters hard.They are not the kind of properties that make it into the duchy’s glossy annual reports, which under William have been renamed “impact reports”. The homes that feature tend to be the newer-built developments at Poundbury in Dorset and Nansledan in Cornwall.Commercial investments now make up over half of the duchy’s income, but the homes it owns will only become a bigger headache as standards for rental properties are raised.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Geoffrey Swaine/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPoundbury and the surrounding fields.Photograph: Adrian Dennis/AFP/Getty ImagesIn response to the Guardian’s investigation, the duchy of Cornwall said it had a “unique portfolio, including many historic buildings located in isolated rural and island locations.”“Whilst this confers a special character, it also brings some unique challenges which we have started to address systematically through our retrofit programme,” a spokesperson said.“We recognise that these challenges mean work does not always happen as fast as we would like, but we will continue to work closely with our tenants to identify effective and practical energy-efficiency improvements as quickly as possible.”On top of the previously announced £500m investment over the next decade, the duchy of Cornwall told the Guardian that “an additional £50m is planned for improving the condition and efficiency of our existing properties”.The duchy added that it had spent £11m on home improvements since 2022, and in the past year had delivered 150 “modern, energy-efficient homes, all of which are EPC A or B”.However, in response to follow-up questions from the Guardian, it confirmed that only six of the new properties were duchy private rents, with most having been sold.Similar problems face the duchy of Lancaster, established a century later and which covers 18,000 hectares (44,000 acres), stretching from northern England down to Northamptonshire and into parts of London.The king inherited this duchy on Queen Elizabeth II’s death in 2022, along with the smaller and more recent Sandringham estate, acquired by the royal family in the 19th century. Sandringham does not publish its accounts.The duchy of Lancaster said it placed great importance on “being a responsible landlord”. “Any tenant with concerns is encouraged to contact us directly and can be assured we will address these issues promptly and constructively,” a spokesperson added.“Over the last year, the duchy of Lancaster has invested more than £3m in residential property repairs and upgrades as part of our ongoing commitment to provide well-maintained homes compliant with all legislation.“Whilst improving the energy efficiency of some historic buildings is challenging, we continue to work to improve their EPC ratings.”View image in fullscreenCrumbling brickwork at the former duchy of Lancaster property.Photograph: Nick SommerladView image in fullscreenBlack mould on the ceiling at the property.Photograph: Nick SommerladA spokesperson said Sandringham “has a mixture of property and tenancy types, which are fully compliant with MEES regulations”.“We continue to invest significantly in an ongoing programme of maintenance and improvement works on all properties, including those out of scope of the regulations, to upgrade energy efficiency across the estate,” they added.“While we do not comment on individual cases, these regulations do not apply to every property on the estate and exemptions are necessary on a small number of properties.”The three estates, collectively worth well over £2bn, are among the nation’s biggest and highest-profile landlords, with more than 1,000 rental homes between them.Elizabeth Earle, a knowledge lawyer at Farrer & Co, which acts for the duchies of Cornwall and Lancaster, recently wrote about changes in legislation that “may feel unduly hard on owners of older, rural and often energy-inefficient properties”.Earle was not talking of the royals, but said: “The irony is that, while these are precisely the sort of properties in which people dream of living, it is becoming increasingly hard to let them – and nigh-on impossible to make them comply with modern standards.”A duchy of Cornwall spokesperson said it was unable to confirm the accuracy of our findings because the Guardian did not provide the estate with a list of properties we had inspected. Such details were not provided in order to protect the tenants who spoke to us on condition of anonymity.Explore more on these topicsHousingMonarchyKing Charles IIIPrince WilliamDuchy of CornwallDuchy of LancasterEnergy efficiencyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t even drink whisky’: Scotland reels in visitors as much of Europe swelters  | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: More direct flights from North America and, say tourism chiefs, Highland warriors and Tartan Army have helped
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: More direct flights from North America and, say tourism chiefs, Highland warriors and Tartan Army have helped
Content: Tourists throng Edinburgh’s Royal Mile during the festival. VisitBritain figures show a 15% rise in flight bookings to Scottish airports in June and July.Photograph: Athanasios Gioumpasis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTourists throng Edinburgh’s Royal Mile during the festival. VisitBritain figures show a 15% rise in flight bookings to Scottish airports in June and July.Photograph: Athanasios Gioumpasis/Getty ImagesTravel & leisure‘I don’t even drink whisky’: Scotland reels in visitors as much of Europe sweltersMore direct flights from North America and, say tourism chiefs, Highland warriors and Tartan Army have helpedGwyn TophamandRobyn VinterSat 15 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the tourist industry, 2026 has been a rocky year, with war, EU border delays, climate and economic woes gnawing away at holiday plans. But while much of Britain is feeling the loss of visitors from the Middle East and beyond, one part is thriving.Scotland is reeling in ever more visitors, with strong annual growth and a 15% rise in flight bookings to Scottish airports in June and July, compared with a drop in bookings to London and the rest of England in recent months, according to VisitBritain figures.With heatwaves gripping much of Europe, the hope of finding cooler climes farther north may have increased Scotland’s allure – although tourism chiefs saydashing Highland warriorsand kilted football fans may have more to do with it.Long-term plans to increase direct flights from North America have come to fruition in the last two years, bolstering the traditional US-led foreign tourist base.A rise in visitors from continental Europe, possibly looking to escape the heat, has added to the mix. And more Britons have chosen to holiday at home rather than face theborder confusion and delaysunder the EU’s entry-exit system.In Edinburgh, where August has long been the busiest time of the year, Princes Street was this week particularly teeming with tourists, gathered around bagpipers and being targeted with leaflets by cheery fringe promoters.View image in fullscreenThe Gilded Balloon, one of the main venues during the Edinburgh fringe.Photograph: PAFestival sales are up 30%, according to Marc Crothall, the chief executive of the Scottish Tourism Alliance. “Edinburgh is jumping, which is great. And that’s a massive draw for international visitors,” he said.Not all were here for theworld’s biggest arts festival: Zanet Garcia, from Mexico City and on her second day in the country, had no idea it was on. “I was really confused by it all. I had never heard of the fringe and I didn’t know what it was,” she said with a laugh. “But everyone has been so friendly.”Garcia chose Scotland because of her interest in Scottish mythology, sparked by books and TV shows that were huge UK exports, such as Harry Potter and Outlander, and had visited locations connected with them. She was taking in traditional national attractions too, fresh from the Johnnie Walker Experience – “I don’t even drink whisky” – and with tickets to the military tattoo.View image in fullscreenAn earlier visitor to the Johnnie Walker Experience in Edinburgh, the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe majority of tourists are from the UK. But it is the big-spending foreigners who are more likely to stay longer, chalk up the visitor attractions and pack in the experiences. An average overseas visitor to Scotland spent just over £900 in a week in 2024, compared with just over £300 in three nights for a British holidaymaker.According to data from the Moffat Centre for travel and tourism at Glasgow Caledonian University the biggest jump this year has been in visitors touring by campervan rather than staying in hotels.Numbers are up but spending per head is down, Crothall said, describing the overall picture as “healthy but by no means booming”.The holidaying Briton is more likely, he said, to be pursuing free visits to museums and walking in the countryside, with the cost of living still a big issue. “Instead of the three course meal, it’s the one. The5% VAT and free travelhelps, but it’s not magic,” Crothall said.View image in fullscreenA scene from an earlier series of the TV show Outlander has helped spark an interest in Scottish mythology among visitors.Photograph: Starz! Movie Channel/CourtesyAlthough Scotland has suffered its own heatwaves, and devastatingwildfires in the Cairngorms, it remains cooler than the southern UK. “We hope and suspect that we’ll see more European visitors given the climate conditions,” Crothall added.Conclusive data linking the heat to changing tourism habits is not yet available, said Vicki Miller, the chief executive of VisitScotland. “But certainly we’ve seen this year strong demand from Europe including Spain and Italy, which is potentially the climate impact,” she added.What the research does show, however, is just how many visits, such as Garcia’s, were inspired by the screen. Online searches spiked on the back of reality TV hit The Traitors, although Ardross Castle – the main location for the UK and US versions of the show – is not open to visit. Castles that have featured in Outlander – a long-running hit in the US and parts of Europe – have also become big draws.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenArdross Castle, where The Traitors is filmed, is not open to visitors, but castles that have featured in Outlander have been big draws.Photograph: Peter Jolly/Shutterstock“We know that 36%-37% of international visitors are inspired by film or TV,” said Miller. “And people’s memories are long: they remember Braveheart or Local Hero as well.”Sport has also pulled in visitors, from this year’s Commonwealth Games in Glasgow to big golf tournaments, along with the reflected glory from travelling Scottish football fans.Interest from Germany increased after it hosted Euro 2024, when the Tartan Army were voted the best supporters at the football tournament: a mixture of “friendliness, banter, and donations to local charities – they capture hearts, they’ve been fantastic ambassadors”, Miller said.View image in fullscreenScotland fans cheer in the stands before their team’s World Cup match against Morocco at Boston stadium in June.Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty ImagesAt this year’s World Cup, when Scotland played in the US, VisitScotland “painted Boston tartan” to capitalise, she said, prompting local online searches for Scottish holidays to double.While Scotland hopes to reap the fruits of a long-term strategic approach, including more direct flights – 100,000 more seats annually from the US alone – and promoting visits in all seasons, many are still feeling the pinch from reduced spending.On the streets of the Scottish capital, Dexter, working at Edinburgh Bus Tours, was rueful. “I’ve been here seven years and the crowd is going down. Tips have gone, big time. I used to be able to go on vacation just on my tips, now that’s not the case,” said the tour guide, who is originally from Nevada, US.He said the tourist tax – a 5% levy introduced in July on accommodation in Edinburgh – “has hurt”, on top of the cost of living: “People have got no money.”Leon Thompson, the executive director of the trade body UKHospitality Scotland, concurred. “People are in their cost of living crisis and that is a challenge,” he said.Thompson added that companies were feeling the impact of business rates, national insurance contributions and VAT, and were anxiously awaiting tourist levies to be introduced by other Scottish local authorities after Edinburgh.“Scotland will always be a popular destination, but we can’t be complacent. We can’t allow ourselves to be priced out of what is the global visitor market,” he said.Explore more on these topicsTravel & leisureScotlandHospitality industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to buy a ‘mega-dinghy’: the perilous new model of Channel crossing | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Boats carrying hundreds of people are a clear and alarming trend. But where do such large vessels come from?
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Boats carrying hundreds of people are a clear and alarming trend. But where do such large vessels come from?
Content: The average number of people travelling on each Channel-crossing dinghy has sharply increased in recent years.Photograph: SNMS Berck sur Mer/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe average number of people travelling on each Channel-crossing dinghy has sharply increased in recent years.Photograph: SNMS Berck sur Mer/AFP/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumHow to buy a ‘mega-dinghy’: the perilous new model of Channel crossingBoats carrying hundreds of people are a clear and alarming trend. But where do such large vessels come from?Daniel BoffeyChief reporterSat 15 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProviding a large dinghy for use in the choppy seas of western Europe was not a problem, as long as the order was for more than 20 vessels, they said. The sales manager at the Chinese company even had an online brochure for an undercover Guardian reporter, posing as a prospective client, to peruse.They had a production capacity of 500 boats a month and, yes, it was possible to get even bigger ones for the right price. They could do a seven or even an eight-metre military-style dinghy for $1,678 (£1,238) a boat, without the engines, but that would be lacking CE certification, the mandatory mark that shows a product meets EU health and safety requirements.“We can sell this big boat toChinawarehouse only,” wrote the sales manager on the Made in China messaging platform. From there, it was up to the client to export it and get the right certification.In the early hours of Monday morning, a full-to-the-brim dinghy of a type similar to that being offered by the Chinese salesperson arrived in the UK after crossing the Channelwith a record 230 people onboard. French authorities say there have been 11 such “mega-dinghy” crossings of the Channel so far this year. Last week one of those carrying 173 people capsized after its engine caught fire.It is a clear and perilous trend. An analysis by theMigrationObservatory at the University of Oxford, based on Home Office figures, shows how the number of people travelling on a dinghy has sharply increased since the crossings first began nearly a decade ago.In 2018, there would be an average of seven people per small boat. That ticked up to 13 by 2020. The number shifted up to 27 by the following year and by 2022 it was 41. The average number of people on a dinghy crossing is up to 66.5 people in the first six months of 2026. These are often no longer small boats. The length of the dinghy that arrived this week was 15 metres.Graph: average number of people per dinghy each year since 2018Where are the “mega-dinghies” coming from? The sales manager offering boats to an undercover Guardian reporter worked for a company called Wuxi Funsor Marine Equipment that is described on its own website as a subsidiary of the Weihai Yamar Outdoors Product Co Ltd.Weihai Yamar, which is headquartered in an industrial park inWenquan Town in Weihai, in the eastern Chinese province of Shandong, was put under economic sanctions by the UK in July last year for offering rigid inflatable boats for sale on online retail platforms to organised crime gangs smuggling people across the Channel. Weihai’s largest shareholder at the time is now the main shareholder of Wuxi Funsor Marine Equipment. Weihai Yamar has denied advertising lifeboats and boats for migrants online.The likely onward journey of dinghies from eastern China can be traced thanks to the recent trial ofAdem Savas, a Turkish national identified by the National Crime Agency (NCA) as one of the key enablers of small boat crossings.Between 2019 and 2024, Savas was said by the NCA to have supplied inflatable boats, outboard engines and equipment to gangs across Europe, enabling thousands of crossings, including around half of all Channel crossings in 2023, generating millions of pounds in profit.Savas was the primary equipment supplier toa Kurdish smuggler, Hewa Rahimpur.The boats and engines were sourced largely from China, transported from Turkey through Bulgaria, and stored in Germany before onward distribution to smuggling networks in Belgium and France.A Netherlands-based haulage firm facilitated the logistics. A raid coordinated by Europol in December 2024 resulted in 25 searches in Germany and the seizure of equipment and cash.Savas pleaded guilty in a court in Bruges to people-smuggling and being a member of an organised crime group and was sentenced to 11 years’ imprisonment and a €400,000 (£340,000) fine. Savas’s co-defendants received combined sentences of 38 years.A spokesperson for Europol said the shift to larger boats was plausibly an indication that the gangs were getting desperate.“I can confirm that Europol – and within our agency specifically the experts forming theEuropean Centre Against Migrant Smuggling (ECAMS)– is aware of this development,” the spokesperson said.“We are in constant exchange with the appropriate authorities in both France and the United Kingdom on this phenomenon and also have a dedicated operational taskforce running that concentrates on smuggling of migrants with boats (no matter if relatively small boats or, as of recently, larger boats) across the Channel.“As with any criminal phenomenon, a change of tactics used by criminal networks may be the result of law enforcement pressure.”Mihnea Cuibus, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory, said the mega-dinghy phenomenon made economic sense for the gangs as they faced pressures on their supply chains from the authorities.“It’s simply much more efficient, much more profitable for gangs to pack as many people as possible on one boat,” he said. “What we’ve seen in the last few weeks with some of these so-called mega-dinghies is an acceleration of this longstanding trend.“It’s very likely to do with increased enforcement in and around the French coast in particular. We’ve seen the authorities work, quite differently, targeting the supply chains and making it hard to get hold of the small boats in the first place.”Weihai Yamar did not respond to a request for comment.Additional reporting by Lyndon LiExplore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumMigrationChinafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is the US ready for President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez? | Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez | The Guardian
description: The New York congresswoman’s power is in the spotlight as people wonder if the stars are finally aligning for her to run for US president in 2028
Author: David Smith
Headline: The New York congresswoman’s power is in the spotlight as people wonder if the stars are finally aligning for her to run for US president in 2028
Content: Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesThe Saturday readAlexandria Ocasio-CortezIs the US ready for President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez?The New York congresswoman’s power is in the spotlight as people wonder if the stars are finally aligning for her to run for US president in 2028David Smithin WashingtonSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 01.01 EDTShare“They assume that my ambition is positional. They assume that my ambition is a title or a seat. And my ambition is way bigger than that. My ambition is to change this country.”The words were delivered slowly, deliberately and with some steeliness byCongresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Her audience, crammed into the pews of Rockefeller Memorial chapelat the University of Chicago, burst into spontaneous applause. That was in May. In the three months since, the speculation around Ocasio-Cortez’s ambitions – for herself and for America – has only grown louder.Friends and foes alike wonder if the stars are aligning for the New York congresswoman to run for US president in 2028. They point to voters raging against the machine – including the ageing Democratic party establishment – and hungry for change. They note how progressives pushing for economic justice and universal healthcare have won astring of impressive victoriesin mayoral elections and congressional primaries over the past year.Then there are the opinion polls. Last month aGranite State Pollfrom the University of New Hampshire found Ocasio-Cortez leading a potential Democratic field in that crucial state. She has the kind of name recognition that money can’t buy, nearly 10m followerson Instagram aloneand fans ranging from the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) to Nancy Pelosi, the former speaker of the House of Representatives.As Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden showed, presidential elections have a habit of finding the right person at the right time in the right place. Ocasio-Cortez, a 36-year-old with a progressive agenda and can’t-be-taught social media smarts, could meet the moment for a nation eager for a fresh start after a decade of Trumpism.If modern politics is about pendulum swings, it is hard to imagine anyone who better personifies a rebuke of the octogenarian Trump and his nativist “Make America great again” (Maga) movement. This week aZogby Strategies national pollfound that a generic democratic socialist candidate leads generic Maga candidate 45% to 33%.Ashik Siddique, a co-chair of the DSA, of which Ocasio-Cortez is a member, said: “If she were to throw her hat in the ring, there would be a lot of excitement for it from members of Democratic Socialists of America. We definitely want to see a strong working class voice in the 2028 presidential primary.”Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a run for president and her actions have done nothing to quell the notion of a campaign in stealth mode. Last year she joined her mentor, the independent senator Bernie Sanders,on a “Fighting Oligarchy” tourthat drew huge crowds. More recently she has crisscrossed the country to support progressive candidates, further enhancing her national profile.In the past week alone she made two moves that intensified political pundits’ chatter. First Ocasio-Cortez used Instagram toannounce that she is freezing her eggs, a decision she described as a move to “feel more in control of my life”. She acknowledged the “political risk” in sharing personal family planning details but stated her goal is to normalise conversations about the professional and personal challenges women face. The internet quickly became awash in speculation that Ocasio-Cortez ended her relationship with and engagement to long-time partner Riley Roberts , driven by reports from Puck News and others noting she had long since stopped appearing with him in public and mentioning his name.Then, when asked by ABC interviewer Jonathan Karl about the cultural battles of the 2020 pandemic era – including calls from some on the left to defund the police – she laughed and, quoting a New York city council ally,remarked: “Woke One was crazy” – apparently trying to draw a strategic line between hard-fought struggles for racial justice and the performative excesses of lockdown isolation that became an easy target for the right.Unlike many would-be presidents of the time, Ocasio-Cortez does not appear to be driven by personal ego, according to those who knew her, which may prove to be her political superpower. She was a volunteer organiser for Sanders’ 2016 campaign, his first presidential run and one that built a national movement around his vision of democratic socialism, even as he lost to former secretary of state Hillary Clinton.View image in fullscreenOcasio-Cortez during her victory celebration New York City in 2018.Photograph: Rick Loomis/Getty ImagesWhen she decided to run for office herself, the former bartender and waitress had virtually no money but was assisted by progressive organisations such as Brand New Congress and Justice Democrats. In 2018 she beat10-term incumbentcongressman Joe Crowley, a member of the Democratic leadership and potential future speaker, in a New York primary.Corbin Trent, her first communications director in the House of Representatives and the co-founder of Justice Democrats, was there on the night she ousted Crowley. He recalls that the political industrial complex began trying to map her career path before the ink on the ballots was even dry.“Primary night, she beats Joe Crowley,” he recalled. “I get phone calls from elected officials and other people and their question is, what’s next? What’s the pathway here? What’s she going to run for? What higher office would she seek? This is literally a few hours after the polls close in the primary. That’s the way DC thinks. Not, hey, what can we do with Medicare for all or this or that or any of the other things?”As Ocasio-Cortez’s national profile exploded – bringing in $15m in her first electoral cycle and attracting unprecedented demands from foreign heads of state – Trent tried to lay out a long-term strategic map. He suggested upstate New York events to prepare for a statewide Senate run. But she resisted the logic of political careerism.“To my chagrin and frustration that never was a way in which she could plan or operate. She did not have an idea in her head of this ultimate prize of president or governor or senator.”Instead, Trent argues, her appeal lies in a rare authenticity – an ability to validate the deep-seated economic anxiety of Americans. “Alexandria has two things going for her. She’s genuinely curious about other people. It’s not like she has to pretend to be. I’ve had politicians ask me, ‘How can I be more genuine?’ Well, that’s probably not going to help if you have to fucking ask me that.“Two, she is genuinely open about herself. Some people believe that nobody cares what they think or who they are and then other people don’t want you to know who they are. She doesn’t suffer from either of those failings.”Other observers agree that Ocasio-Cortez has that X factor missing from so many professional politicians: relatability.Chris Scott, a political strategist who served as the coalition director for Kamala Harris’s 2024 presidential campaign, said: “When you talk about AOC’s humble beginnings being a bartender that’s a lived experience story that resonates, especially with millennials, with their upbringing.“What you are starting to see – whether it’s conservative or progressive - is people are leaning more and more towards candidates with lived experience that they feel they relate to as politics gets more polarising.”That said, Ocasio-Cortez has now been in Washington long enough to draw accusations of going from outsider to insider. The activist who critiqued the establishment and championed the Green New Deal has spent recent years working closely with Democratic leadership. This week she received warm praise from Pelosi,who told a Politico summitin Sacramento, California: “I think that she has been so operational, and it’s just wonderful. I know it’s a joy to work with her.”The transition has caused some on the far left to wonder if the system has simply co-opted its most dangerous critic.Cenk Uygur, a controversial political commentator and co-founder of the online progressive news show The Young Turks, watches Ocasio-Cortez’s recent evolution with a mixture of policy agreement and tactical despair.Ocasio-Cortez has described Israel’s actions in Gazaas a “genocide”and last month voted to block US military aid to the country. But Uygur has not forgotten herhigh-profile appearanceat the 2024 Democratic National Convention, where she delivered a rousing speech praising vice-president Harris’s efforts to secure a ceasefire in Gaza — a claim that many leftwing activists viewed as a dishonest whitewashing of the administration’s complicity in the conflict.View image in fullscreenOcasio-Cortez speaks during the Democratic national convention in August 2024.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images“Why did she basically fib on Kamala Harris’s behalf during the DNC and pretend that Kamala Harris cared about Palestinians and was trying to keep the Israelis in check?” he said. “Because she secretly loves Israel? No, it’s because she wanted to prove to mommy and daddy that she’s a good girl. If you’re a good girl you support Kamala Harris and, if you need to, you fudge her record.“Then you go tell Jonathan Karl that your side is ‘crazy’ and you changed and you can’t explain what you changed into or how you changed or why you changed. But the message is super clear both for the establishment and progressives: ‘I’m not going to challenge the system so establishment, you can rest easy, I’m not a threat.’ And they have rested easy. That’s why she’s getting enormously positive coverage.”The 2028 Democratic presidential primary election is expected to be crowded and noisy. If Ocasio-Cortez runs, she might face challenges from fellow progressive Congressman Ro Khanna of California along with heavyweights including Harris, Pete Buttigieg, Gavin Newsom and Jon Ossoff. Some Democrats, scarred by Clinton and Harris’s defeats in 2016 and 2024, might be reluctant to nominate Ocasio-Cortez out of perceived expediency if they believe the US is still not ready to elect its first female president, a fearexpressed by former first lady Michelle Obamaamong others.The congresswoman faces another potentially formidable hurdle. CentristDemocratshave long argued that the democratic socialist wing of the party might succeed with white, college-educated voters but struggles to connect with African American communities, pointing to primary races where progressive insurgents have hit a wall. That could prove decisive in an early primary state such as South Carolina.Nina Turner, a national co-chair of Sanders’ 2020 campaign, who has just been travelling in South Carolina, said: “There are some rumblings in some segments of the Black community that DSA and progressives in general are not doing what it takes to court Black voters and in some ways are leaving us behind for other people who are of colour but not Black.“That’s real and so DSA as well as progressives are going to have to do something to say, no, we understand the Black plight and we understand that the survival of working-class people comes through Black liberation. They have not done a good job of doing that. I’m hoping that they will.”Antjuan Seawright, a Democratic strategist in South Carolina, suggests that Ocasio-Cortez’s national viability depends on her remaining a disciplined team player who addresses universal, kitchen-table concerns. He said: “I would love her to run as far away as she can from being any sort of liability in places where we know we have to win in November where we’ve lost before because people have been used as a weapon of mass political destruction and distraction.“If she continues to talk about health care in such a way that is accessible and affordable for all Americans without burning down the system, but making some alterations to the system, she will be a positive voice to the conversation.”If she runs, Ocasio-Cortez can also expect a crude onslaught from Republicans and a rightwing media machine that has spent years demonising her as a radical communist who threatens the essence of America. Her “Woke One was crazy,” comment has been seen as an attempt to assuage the concern.Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, said: “That was a very interesting strategic decision to do that and that’s her way of trying to moderate. But she’s palling around with Bernie Sanders and hasn’t completely, as far as I’m aware, repudiated [the influencer] Hasan Piker and some of those leftwing folks. People are not going to forget that and, in this day and age of the internet, it lives forever.”Setmayer, cofounder ofthe Seneca Project, a women-led, bipartisan political super political action committee, argues that, instead of campaigning for the White House, Ocasio-Cortez could seek to cement her legislative power by challenging Chuck Schumer for his New York Senate seat.“If I were advising her, given the failures, unfortunately, of women candidates for the Democrats over the last two election cycles, it would behoove her to run for Senate,” Setmayer said. “She’s almost guaranteed to win that Senate seat.View image in fullscreenOcasio Cortez outsie the US Capitol in January 2023.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images“It would provide her more gravitas and she’s young enough that she could do a term or two – or a term and a half like Barack Obama – and then run for president. I don’t think that she can go from being a congresswoman to a serious presidential candidate without some time in the Senate.”History, however, is littered with examples of White House aspirants who waited their turn and missed their moment. There are others, such as Obama, who said “carpe diem” and rode a wave all the way into the Oval Office.Ocasio-Cortez, who would beat Theodore Roosevelt and John F Kennedy to become the youngest US president in history, has said her ambition is way bigger than that. The calling to change America may prove irresistible.Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said: “When you look at the current trajectory of the Democratic party, she is the natural successor to the Bernie Sanders-Elizabeth Warren coalition. She is one of the most gifted communicators in all of politics.“She is someone who engenders a tremendous amount of passion, either for or against. She does possess the unique quality of: people give a shit. She’s got a lot more going for her than most people. She never has to worry about standing out. The attention vacuum that we live in, and the way that content works, she is in a league of her own.”

title: Royal estates rent out homes that fail to meet legal energy efficiency standards | Housing | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: More than 100 homes on King Charles and Prince William’s inherited estates have EPC ratings of F or G
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Exclusive: More than 100 homes on King Charles and Prince William’s inherited estates have EPC ratings of F or G
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyHousingRoyal estates rent out homes that fail to meet legal energy efficiency standardsExclusive: More than 100 homes on King Charles and Prince William’s inherited estates have EPC ratings of F or G‘It’s archaic’: the struggle to heat poorly insulated homes let by royal estatesNick SommerladSat 15 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 100 homes on the inherited royal estates of King Charles andPrince Williamfail to meet the legal minimum energy standards for landlords, the Guardian can reveal.An analysis of a large sample of domestic lets on the duchies of Lancaster and Cornwall and the Sandringham estate found that one in five haveEnergyPerformance Certificate (EPC) ratings of F or G.EPCs are documents that provide an energy efficiency score for properties, in relation to their running costs. Introduced in England and Wales in 2007 as concern grew about carbon emissions, they help to estimate energy bills and environmental impact. The most energy-efficient properties are awarded an A rating and the worst are given a G.The revelations are likely to be embarrassing for Charles and William, both of whom have cultivated reputations as environmental advocates. Since 2020, it has been illegal to rent out properties with EPC ratings below E, unless the landlord can demonstrate that it is exempt. In the majority of failing royal rentals, no formal exemption has been cited.However, in some cases, the royal estates appear to be using gaps in the regulations to continue letting properties out.This includes the homes of dozens of farmers, who are living in poorly insulated and hard-to-heat farmhouses they lease from the two duchies. Some farmhouses are not subject to current regulations, depending on the type of tenancy in place.View image in fullscreenA former duchy of Lancaster property sold last year, which was rated G in 2020.Photograph: Nick SommerladOther homes rented out by the royals are not covered by the rules, as they apply only to tenancies that began after October 2008. These older tenancies often house elderly and vulnerable people with health conditions, with some living without central heating and reliant on unhealthy coal fires or expensive electric heaters.The Guardian has visited a number of the worst F and G-rated duchy properties, and found many were affected by black mould, with draughty single-glazed windows.The pressure group Fuel Poverty Action said the conditions in some properties were “Dickensian”. It accused the royals of “putting profits above the health and welfare of their tenants”.It is not known how much money the king receives from his private Sandringham estate, which was bought by Queen Victoria in 1862 and is set over 8,000 hectares (19,000 acres) in Norfolk.However, the duchies of Lancaster and Cornwall, sprawling property portfolios that date back to feudal times, are exempt from most business taxes, allowing them to maximise their profits. They have paid out more than £400m to the king and his family since 2018.View image in fullscreenMembers of the royal family stand on the Buckingham Palace balcony after King Charles and Queen Camilla’s coronation ceremony in 2023.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/ReutersThat is when the minimum energy efficiency standards (MEES) regulations came into force, designed to ensure a minimum EPC rating of E for all new private tenancies, which was extended to existing tenancies from 2020.Landlords must spend up to £3,500 on each property to bring them up to standard or cite one of the exemptions allowed under the rules. If they fail to do so, but continue to rent out the property, they can be fined up to £5,000.Fewer than one in 12 of the F and G-rated properties on the royal estates that the Guardian analysed had registered exemptions. The duchy of Lancaster had recorded exemptions for eight properties, while the duchy of Cornwall had logged four and the Sandringham estate five.The most common exemption, used in nine royal-owned properties, is that consent to improve the property “has been refused, or given conditions that cannot reasonably be met”. In four other properties, it is stated that “wall insulation is not appropriate for the property”.In three properties, improvements that would help obtain an E rating have not been carried out as they would exceed the £3,500 cap. None of those three properties have central heating or full double glazing. All rely on electric heaters rated “very poor” by the energy assessors and solid-fuel fires or burners.The estates do not publish lists of their land holdings, meaning it is difficult to conduct a comprehensive analysis of all of their rental properties. In the case of the two duchies, aides have gone to great lengths in the past to obscure their property portfolios, withholding the information even from parliament.However, the Guardian has examined the EPCs of more than 700 domestic properties listed as being owned by one of the three royal estates on the Land Registry. This audit found that about one-fifth have been rated F or G.View image in fullscreenBlack mould at the former duchy of Lancaster property.Photograph: Nick SommerladThe analysis excluded properties that had been converted into holiday lets, where the MEES regulations do not apply. It also disregarded those with leasehold titles recorded by the Land Registry where the landlord’s responsibility is less straightforward.It is unclear how many of the 143 properties rated F or G are unoccupied while they are being renovated or sold. However, the Guardian spoke to the tenants living in a significant number of them.The duchy of Lancaster, established in 1265 to provide the monarch with a private income, is the only royal estate to publish details of how it is complying with the MEES regulations.There are more than 300 rental properties on the 18,000-hectare (44,000-acre) estate, which stretches from the north of England to London. Most of its domestic lets are in the north-west and the Midlands.In its most recent annual report, it said: “The duchy continues to invest in improving energy efficiency across its rental properties, with 97% of the let properties for which minimum energy efficiency standards are applicable being rated A+ to E.”It added: “Making improvements can often be challenging due to the listed or historical status of some of our buildings; of the 10 properties that are rated F and G (12 in 2025), seven meet the criteria for registered exemptions and three have ongoing works to improve the EPCs.”However, the problem is far more extensive. Of more than 200 duchy of Lancaster properties identified, nearly 40 have domestic EPC ratings of F or G.View image in fullscreenThe new owner of the former duchy of Lancaster property said the previous occupant had been a man in his 90s.Photograph: Nick SommerladAbout half of the substandard properties are farmhouses, which, depending on the type of agricultural tenancy in place, could be considered exempt from the MEES regulations. Of these, 15 were rated F and another six were rated G, including two with the lowest possible EPC score of one point.The duchy’s own lawyers, Farrer & Co, have argued that landowners should do more. Elizabeth Earle, Farrer’s “knowledge lawyer” for rural property, wrote on the firm’s website: “Farmhouses are not referred to in the MEES regulations and this causes a problem.“Although it might be tempting to try and exploit what may look like a loophole now, the more prudent position is to treat farmhouses as though they must comply with MEES. Doing so will be consistent with the overall intention of public policy and less likely to create a problem for the future.”One duchy of Lancaster tenant farmer, whose home was given a very low EPC score, said: “When I’m at the post office and they see my council tax, they think: you must live in a nice house. But I wouldn’t live here unless I had to.“We have no central heating and almost no double glazing. Our only heating is from coal fires. It’s very cold in the winter and very hot in the summer.“When they came to do the EPC, the man said we were one of the worst he had ever done. They would need to spend a lot of money on this place but the duchy told us we are exempt. It doesn’t seem fair that we don’t get anything.”When EPCs were introduced in England and Wales in 2007, they initially applied only to homes with more than four bedrooms. The rules were extended the next year to cover rental properties.However, the regulations do not apply to tenancies that started before this point. In these cases, an EPC is only required if there is a change of tenant, or if a property is sold.In these cases, if a landlord carries out an EPC without a change of tenant, it is considered “voluntary” and does not trigger the regulations. The Guardian has spoken to duchy tenants in this situation, finding a terrace of duchy of Lancaster cottages in Cheshire where several were rated F and G.A local parish councillor said: “The tenants are all elderly and have been there for many decades. They complain about the duchy. They don’t like to spend any money on repairs.“Because they have been there so long they have low rents compared to the market locally. If they complain too much they are reminded that the duchy can put up their rent. They are terrified of that and keep quiet.”The Guardian visited another cottage that had, according to the new owner, been home to a man in his 90s before it was sold by the duchy.It was rated G and, according to the estate agent, required “a full programme of renovation, modernisation and extension”. The decrepit property had single-glazed windows, little insulation and an oil-fired boiler. It had black mould spots, crumbling paintwork from apparent damp and peeling wallpaper.View image in fullscreenBlack mould on the ceiling of a former duchy of Lancaster property sold last year.Photograph: Nick SommerladView image in fullscreenCrumbling brickwork at the property.Photograph: Nick Sommerlad“Poor man, he lived there for more than 60 years and barely moved for the last 20,” the new owner said. “The conditions were appalling. I wouldn’t let my dog stay in there, let alone a 90-year-old.”Another duchy of Lancaster tenant, who has lived for decades in a property that is now rated F, said: “They do no repairs. My windows are so rotten I am scared they will fall out.“I can’t believe how bad it is, it really gets me down. I do complain but nothing ever gets done. I need to step away from it. Hearing how much money they have makes me sick. People are scared to take them on.”The duchy of Lancaster said it placed “great importance” on “being a responsible landlord”. “Any tenant with concerns is encouraged to contact us directly and can be assured we will address these issues promptly and constructively,” a spokesperson added.“Over the last year, the duchy of Lancaster has invested more than £3m in residential property repairs and upgrades as part of our ongoing commitment to provide well-maintained homes compliant with all legislation.“Whilst improving the energy efficiency of some historic buildings is challenging, we continue to work to improve their EPC ratings.”King Charles inherited the duchy of Lancaster and the Sandringham estate from his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, after her death in 2022. Assets transferred from one monarch to another are exempt from inheritance tax. On the Sandringham estate, 18 out of nearly 170 properties with EPCs were rated F or G.A spokesperson said Sandringham “has a mixture of property and tenancy types, which are fully compliant with MEES regulations”.“We continue to invest significantly in an ongoing programme of maintenance and improvement works on all properties, including those out of scope of the regulations, to upgrade energy efficiency across the estate,” they added.“While we do not comment on individual cases, these regulations do not apply to every property on the estate and exemptions are necessary on a small number of properties.”For many years, the king controlled the duchy of Cornwall, a vast royal estate concentrated mainly in the south-west of England, covering about 55,000 hectares (135,000 acres). When he ascended the throne, responsibility for the estate was passed to Prince William.View image in fullscreenPrince William speaking to staff during his visit to Nansledan, a sustainable community development led and managed by the duchy of Cornwall, in the suburbs of Newquay.Photograph: Hugh Hastings/ReutersIt recently announced it would sell 20% of its property in the next 10 years and invest £500m in local communities. On top of the £500m investment, the duchy of Cornwall told the Guardian that “an additional £50m is planned for improving the condition and efficiency of our existing properties”.The Guardian found that the estate, founded in 1337 to provide an income for male heirs to the throne, owned about 340 domestic properties with EPCs. More than 80 received F or G ratings on their most recent assessments.This includes more than 20 farms and numerous properties with longstanding tenants where the EPCs were done “voluntarily”. However, in some cases, the rules appear not to have been followed.One tenant, who did not want to be identified, moved into her duchy of Cornwall property after the rules requiring EPCs came into force. Her property was never advertised on the open market, where an estate agent would ask for a valid EPC, and there is no evidence that one was done at the time. A subsequent EPC has given the property an F, and no exemption from MEES regulations has been registered.“It can be cold,” she said. “We are in the middle of nowhere. We have oil central heating but we don’t like to use it because it is so expensive. We use the log burners but they are hard work. We are both pensioners.“The duchy doesn’t like to spend money on these properties but the rent is expensive and goes up every couple of years.”The duchy of Cornwall said it had a “unique portfolio, including many historic buildings located in isolated rural and island locations”.“Whilst this confers a special character, it also brings some unique challenges which we have started to address systematically through our retrofit programme,” a spokesperson said.“We recognise that these challenges mean work does not always happen as fast as we would like, but we will continue to work closely with our tenants to identify effective and practical energy efficiency improvements as quickly as possible.”The duchy added that it had spent £11m on home improvements since 2022, and in the past year had delivered 150 “modern, energy-efficient homes, all of which are EPC A or B”.However, in response to follow-up questions from the Guardian, it confirmed that only six of the new properties were duchy private rents, with most having been sold.Jonathan Bean, of Fuel Poverty Action, said: “Vulnerable people are suffering in Dickensian conditions while the royals enjoy vast profits from the duchies.“Using loopholes instead of making these homes safe is immoral and negligent, especially given the age and vulnerabilities of many of the tenants. Mould and damp can seriously damage their health and potentially be fatal.“Forcing elderly residents with health conditions to rely on coal burners for heating endangers their health and damages the environment. Wealthy royal estates are putting profits above the health and welfare of their tenants.”A duchy of Cornwall spokesperson said it was unable to confirm the accuracy of our findings as the Guardian did not provide the estate with a list of properties we had inspected, to protect the tenants who spoke to us on condition of anonymity.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsHousingMonarchyDuchy of CornwallDuchy of LancasterKing Charles IIIPrince WilliamEnergy efficiencynewsShareReuse this content

title: Tributes paid to Jason Arday after former Cambridge professor’s death | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham calls for reflection after ‘a tragedy on so many levels’ in comments echoed by London mayor Sadiq Khan
Author: Aneesa Ahmed
Headline: Andy Burnham calls for reflection after ‘a tragedy on so many levels’ in comments echoed by London mayor Sadiq Khan
