Content: Jason Arday was found dead at his home in south London on Friday.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday was found dead at his home in south London on Friday.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianJason ArdayTributes paid to Jason Arday after former Cambridge professor’s deathAndy Burnham calls for reflection after ‘tragedy on so many levels’ in comments echoed by London mayor Sadiq KhanAneesa AhmedSat 15 Aug 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 18.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has called the death ofJason Arday, whose body was found at his home in south London on Friday, a “tragedy on so many levels”.Arday resigned as a professor at the University of Cambridge last week after allegations of plagiarism, which he denied.He was pronounced dead just after 3pm on Friday.In a statement issued via his publisher, Simon & Schuster UK, the former academic’s family said they were “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.Speaking to broadcasters during a visit to Cornwall on Saturday, the prime minister said: “It’s a tragedy on so many levels, but particularly just for everybody who knew Jason, his family obviously, his friends. We think of them today.“It’s not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It’s a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this. A really sad, sad and sorry state of affairs and I think we all today think of Jason, his contribution and his family and friends.”More than £20,000 has been raised for the family of Arday after the Windrush campaigner Sir Patrick Vernon launched a fundraising drive via GoFundMe in his memory.Other leading figures to pay tribute included the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, and the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy.Khan said: “I’m devastated for the family and friends of Jason Arday. He faced an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse. I know many Londoners will be angry and upset this evening.“Jason Arday was the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn’t have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake-up call for all of us.”Speaking on Newsnight, Ribeiro-Addy read out a list of names including William O’Reilly, Ross Holmes, David Lachman, and Nicola Morrison. “These are all people that have actually proven to have been plagiarists, or people that have manipulated their data, and people that have been proven to have lifted whole pages from students’ papers or published work that they had to withdraw,” she said.Ribeiro-Addy said there had been a media witch-hunt which was cruel because “it didn’t aim to just target him”.“It aimed to target anybody that supported him, trying to isolate him as much as possible, going after people who had signed up to statements,” she said. “The difference between them and him was they were white, and he was not.”The Conservative MP James Cleverly expressed his anger over Arday’s death. In a statement on X, he wrote that a number of people at academic institutions “have serious questions to answer”.“They put him into positions he was clearly not qualified for so they could have a black wunderkind to show off, they pushed him into the spotlight for their own benefit,” they said. “His exposure was inevitable, a case of when, not if. His whole world fell apart.”Simon Baron-Cohen, a clinical psychologist and the director of the Autism Research Centre, who was a friend of Arday’s, told Radio 4’s Today programme that he contacted him Friday morning and said that he felt he was unable to go on.“He used those words in voice notes,” Baron-Cohen said. “At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.“He was a vulnerable child, a vulnerable teenager and a vulnerable adult, so he needed and deserved safeguarding and support and reasonable adjustment every step of the way.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArday was initially accused ofplagiarising another person’s workin his PhD thesis, but denied all allegations. A review conducted by Liverpool John Moores University, where he completed his doctorate, upheld its decision to award him a PhD earlier this year.In recent weeks, otherelements of his life story were increasingly questioned, including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running. He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal as a child.The National Education Union general secretary, Daniel Kebede, said Arday had been subjected to “a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism”.“I don’t believe this was ever simply about ‘professional conduct’ or ‘plagiarism’,” he said.“There is a profound difference between scrutiny and a sustained public campaign that turns an individual into a symbol of everything the right believes is wrong with DEI.“The effect has been chilling. It tells Black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target.“A target not only for criticism of your work, but for a much broader political and cultural backlash.”The Metropolitan police said his death was being treated as unexpected, but not believed to be suspicious.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsJason ArdayUniversity of CambridgeAcademicsHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Moroccan police arrest more than 100 people as they attempt to enter Ceuta | Morocco | The Guardian
description: Border security tightened after social media posts call for another mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Border security tightened after social media posts call for another mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory
Content: Moroccan police were seen monitoring dozens of migrants on the outskirts of the border town of Fnideq on Saturday.Photograph: Mohamed Siali/EPAView image in fullscreenMoroccan police were seen monitoring dozens of migrants on the outskirts of the border town of Fnideq on Saturday.Photograph: Mohamed Siali/EPAMoroccoMoroccan police arrest more than 100 people as they attempt to enter CeutaBorder security tightened after social media posts call for another mass crossing into Spain’s north African territoryReutersSat 15 Aug 2026 14.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMoroccan police have arrested 111 people as they tried to enter Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, amid ⁠tightened security on both sides after social media posts ​called for another mass crossing.The attempted crossing on Saturday came two weeks after more than72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta, causingtensions within the EUand prompting anti-immigration rhetoric among far-right parties worldwide. At least 96 people died trying to ⁠reach European soil.A source in Morocco’s interior ministry told news agency Reuters that those detained included 109 migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and two Moroccan citizens arrested in or around Fnideq, the Moroccan city near Ceuta.Moroccan police used teargas to disperse groups of migrants ⁠gathered on hills about 1.9 miles (3km) from the border, according to Spanish news agency EFE. Reuters later saw hundreds of police officers, some in riot gear and others in plainclothes, returning from the hills outside ​Fnideq.EFE and Spanish state broadcaster TVE said Morocco’s interior ministry ordered their journalists ‌to leave Fnideq immediately, without providing an explanation.View image in fullscreenWitnesses said they saw teargas being fired at migrants on hills near the border.Photograph: Jalal Morchidi/EPAIn Ceuta, ‌Spanish soldiers guarded supermarkets while police patrolled the main streets. The city was calmer than in the days after thedeadly crossing attempton 30 July.Madrid has ‌since installed a maritime barrier and deployed more than 500 additional police officers from mainlandSpain, raising the total in Ceuta to more than 1,600. The interior ministry said the reinforcements would remain for as long as needed.“We’ll continue to deploy whatever personnel are necessary to restore normality as soon as possible and prevent events like those of 30 July from happening again,” Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said on Thursday.About 5,000 migrantsremained in Ceuta, the minister added. Reuters saw hundreds sheltering from scorching heat under makeshift bamboo shelters on the urban beach of El Trampolin.View image in fullscreenMigrants seen sheltering from the sun on El Trampolin beach in Ceuta.Photograph: Jorge Guerrero/AFP/Getty ImagesGrande-Marlaska said migrants who entered irregularly would not be allowed to stay in the territory, travel to mainland Spain or ‌obtain legal status, except in rare cases involving extreme vulnerability. Those without a right to remain would be returned to Morocco, he added.Earlier this week, Rabat said it was monitoring “the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin” calling for a mass crossing ​on 15 August, warning it would prosecute organisers and participants.A Reuters witness saw reinforced security near the border, including police vans with wire shields and road checkpoints. Local media reported similar measures near Melilla, another Spanish territory in north Africa.Authorities prevented several groups from boarding trains and buses to northern Morocco in cities such as Casablanca, Fez and Kenitra. However, witnesses told Reuters that some migrants from sub-Saharan Africa were bypassing security checkpoints by taking mountain routes towards Fnideq.One witness said the schools in Fnideq had been turned into accommodation for security forces deployed near the ⁠border.Explore more on these topicsMoroccoSpainAfricaMigrationRefugeesEuropeMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans gather to pay respects as coffin brought home | Bonnie Tyler | The Guardian
description: Fans line streets singing Total Eclipse of the Heart ahead of Welsh singer’s Swansea funeral
Author: Aneesa Ahmed
Headline: Fans line streets singing Total Eclipse of the Heart ahead of Welsh singer’s Swansea funeral
Content: Fans of singer Bonnie Tyler line the streets as her coffin is taken back to her former home ahead of her funeral, in Mumbles, Wales.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APView image in fullscreenFans of singer Bonnie Tyler line the streets as her coffin is taken back to her former home ahead of her funeral, in Mumbles, Wales.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APBonnie TylerThousands of Bonnie Tyler fans gather to pay respects as coffin brought homeFans line streets, singing Total Eclipse of the Heart ahead of Welsh singer’s Swansea funeralAneesa AhmedSat 15 Aug 2026 14.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands ofBonnie Tylerfans lined the streets of her home town in south Wales to pay respects to the singer as her coffin was brought back to her former home.The singer, whose real name was Gaynor Sullivan, died unexpectedly on 8 July in Portugal at the age of 75.Many fans stood along Newton Road in Mumbles,Swansea, to watch the procession as her coffin was brought back. The coffin was draped in the Welsh flag and accompanied by a framed photograph of the singer.View image in fullscreenFans pay their respects by placing flowers on the hearse carrying Welsh singer Bonnie Tyler as it travels along Newton Road to her home in Llwynderw, Mumbles, Wales.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/EPAFans threw flowers on to the hearse, and the crowd erupted into applause and broke out into a rendition of Total Eclipse of the Heart.Mumbles was Tyler’s part-time home, as she split her time between Algarve in Portugal and a large Victorian house in Blackpill, near Mumbles, overlooking Swansea Bay.Tyler became renowned globally for her pop music hits, including Total Eclipse of the Heart and I Need a Hero.View image in fullscreenBonnie Tyler fans (left-right) Melanie Smith, Melissa Smith and Carys Edwards in the Mumbles, Swansea, ahead of paying their respects to the late singer and watching the procession as she is transported back to her former home.Photograph: Eleanor Storey/PAAmong those waiting to pay their respects to Tyler was Carys Edwards, 18, who said the singer was “an inspiration to everybody”.She told PA Media: “Her music touched a lot of people, especially me. I’m quite surprised how many people came here today, but then not as well, because she was such an icon.“She was always coming home and making sure that she came back to her fans inWales.“Her songs really did touch a lot of people here in Wales, we loved her a lot. When we found out she passed away, it was such a heartbreak to all of us. We cried and everything.”View image in fullscreenA Welsh flag draped over the coffin of Bonnie Tyler.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesMichael Bone, 58, and his partner Alan Hawkins, 54, travelled from Derby to watch the procession.“We thought it’d be nice to pay our respects,” said Bone. “For me personally, it’s because in my teens, her music was quite prolific. For me, it was her most iconic period in the 1980s.”Others were reported to have travelled from as far as Austria to witness the procession of Tyler’s coffin.Her other hits included It’s a Heartache and If You Were a Woman (And I Was a Man). She represented the UK in the 2013 Eurovision song contest in Malmö, Sweden, with the song Believe in Me, finishing in 19th place.A celebration of Tyler’s life is set to take place at Swansea Minster (Church of St Mary’s) on Monday 17 August. Only those with invitations will be allowed inside, but the service will be shown on a large screen in nearby St David’s Square – and members of the public can pay their respects.View image in fullscreenBonnie Tyler.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAAfter the service, Tyler’s coffin will make a final journey through her home village of Skewen – followed by a private gathering strictly for family and friends.Tyler grew up in a council house in Skewen with five older siblings. “I class myself as a working-class girl, and I’ve never stopped working,” she told the Guardian in 2013. “I do an awful lot [of performances] because I feel other people would love to be offered what I’m offered.”In her memoir, she wrote fondly of Wales: “I may have done some extraordinary things … but in so many ways, I’m still that young girl from Wales, dancing around the piano with her family, and I always will be.”At the time of her death, then prime minister, Keir Starmer, said Tyler was an “iconic figure” and “one of Britain’s greatest recording artists”. Others who paid tribute to her included Catherine Zeta-Jones and Cliff Richard.Explore more on these topicsBonnie TylerSwanseaWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alarmed by the alarm: people react to ‘severe alert’ on phones over UK wildfires | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Many complained online that piercingly loud tone was ‘overreach’ while others lamented lack of action on decarbonisation
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Many complained online that piercingly loud tone was ‘overreach’ while others lamented lack of action on decarbonisation
Content: The severe alert sent by the UK government on Friday warned of a ‘very high risk of wildfires’.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe severe alert sent by the UK government on Friday warned of a ‘very high risk of wildfires’.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesWildfiresAlarmed by the alarm: people react to ‘severe alert’ on phones over UK wildfiresMany complained online that piercingly loud tone was ‘overreach’ while others lamented lack of action on decarbonisationSammy GecsoylerSat 15 Aug 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 17.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Friday at 7pm, Thérèse Coffey was nine miles away from a nuclear power station when her phone made a loud, piercing and very worrying sound: it was a“severe” emergency alert. “Was expecting [a] much more specific alert, not a generic message on wildfires,” the former Conservative cabinet ministersaidon X.She wasn’t alone in being alarmed by the alarm sent to phones in England and Wales. In the aftermath, thousands of social media users expressed their shock at alert. Some sharedfunny memesand others lamented what they viewed aslack of government actionon decarbonisation. Academic John Ritzemacalled ita “massive overreach” and said the alert system should be “be for ‘drop everything and prepare for something terrible’ situations”, something Coffey echoed, saying alerts should not become commonplace to avoid “Peter cries wolf situations”.Even broadcasters were taken by surprise. The alert sounded live on the BBC’s The One Show, with host Ronan Kempsaying: “We’ve got some form of fire alarm going on.”Chris Packham used the alertto plug a parliamentary petitioncalling for a UK-wide briefing on climate and nature risks.The alert on Friday night came as Andy Burnham spent time in Stourbridge in the West Midlands earlier that day afterhomes were destroyed and residents were left injuredby a series of fires. The prime ministerwarnedthat Britain “is a tinderbox right now”, with the public set for a “difficult weekend”.It has been a record year of wildfires inEnglandand Wales: the number so far has passed the 1,017 recorded in 2025. Fire services declared 11 major incidents in a 24-hour period starting on Thursday.People have been urged not to light barbecues, campfires, fireworks or anything else that could spark a blaze while the wildfire risk remains high. They have also been urged to call 999 immediately if they spot a fire.Hot topic: why is Burnham so reluctant to talk about the climate crisis?Read moreThe wildfires have also prompted calls within the Labour party to accelerate action against the climate crisis. Sadiq Khan warned Burnham not to “slow down on net zero” and said the heatwave and wildfires showed the need for action on climate change. The London mayor described the planet as being in a “deeply precarious position”.“We need reassurance from the government that they won’t slow down on net zero or reducing our reliance on oil and gas and that they’ll continue accelerating the green investment we need to get our country and planet back on track,” he said.Burnham announced a temporary nationalban on the sale of disposable barbecues, to be enforced immediately. The ban will remain in place as long as the risk of wildfires remains high.The military was called in to assist stretched emergency services in southWales. About 100 personnel were deployed, with about 100 more due to arrive to distribute water and provide logistical support.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSoldiers digging out fire breaks in south Wales.Photograph: Cpl Christian P Delice/MoD Crown copyright/PABurnham also announced £65m of extra ⁠funding for ⁠farmers ​hit by a drought. He said on X: “Today we’re putting £65m more into ⁠supporting farmers through this drought and preparing ​for the ‌summers ahead. They’re ‌on the frontline of a ‌changing climate and they shouldn’t be left to face it alone.“The ability to grow our own food is ‌national security. I’ll treat it that way,” he said.Britain’s cereal harvest ​is on track to be ​the ‌worst since comparable ​records ​began in 1984, according to an analysis published earlier this month.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresEnglandWalesClimate crisisExtreme heatnewsShareReuse this content

title: Concerns grow over increased global ties with Taliban in Afghanistan | Taliban | The Guardian
description: Campaigners fear deeper diplomatic contacts are undermining demands for improvements in human rights
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Campaigners fear deeper diplomatic contacts are undermining demands for improvements in human rights
Content: The UN described Taliban-run Afghanistan as a ‘human rights graveyard’.Photograph: Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe UN described Taliban-run Afghanistan as a ‘human rights graveyard’.Photograph: Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty ImagesTalibanConcerns grow over increased global ties with Taliban in AfghanistanCampaigners fear deeper diplomatic contacts are undermining demands for improvements in human rightsJason BurkeSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 16.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Taliban inAfghanistanhave launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement inhuman rightsin return for any diplomatic concessions.‘When she turns eight they will take her’: rising number of Afghan girls being sold into child marriageRead moreThe United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a“graveyard for human rights,”the UN said in March.India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels aboutreturning failed asylum-seekersto Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even withEuropeand the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.4:33The promises the Taliban made to women, then broke – video explainer“TheTalibansee any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggestedmore countries recognisethe regime. Others want intensified“back channel”engagement.“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.View image in fullscreenAn Afghan woman walks among Taliban soldiers at a checkpoint in Mazar-i-Sharif.Photograph: Ali Khara/ReutersThe European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towardsregularising consular relationswith EU countries.The meeting prompted outrage.“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.‘Her face was beaten in’: how Taliban rule ushered in a new era of women being killedRead moreThis year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes andpipelinedeals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.View image in fullscreenTaliban security personnel take part in a parade in front of the former US embassy in Kabul to celebrate the fifth anniversary of their return to powerPhotograph: Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty ImagesAfghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through theUK Mission to Afghanistanbased at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.View image in fullscreenA convoy of Taliban fighters in the days after the fall of Kabul in 2021.Photograph: Aamir Qureshi/AFP/Getty ImagesTaliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.The Taliban are split, withdeep disagreementson the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent.Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.View image in fullscreenAfghanistan’s foreign minister Mawlawi Amir Khan Muttaqi was criticised for not allowing female journalists into his press conference while visiting India.Photograph: Elke Scholiers/Getty Images“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.Explore more on these topicsTalibanAfghanistanIndiaRussiaEuropeWomenSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Body found in Romania believed to be missing British hiker George Smyth | Romania | The Guardian
description: Family paid tribute to Bristol University geology student, 18, after being notified by Avon and Somerset police
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Family paid tribute to Bristol University geology student, 18, after being notified by Avon and Somerset police
Content: His family said Smyth ‘was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends’,Photograph: Family handout via Salvamont BrașovHis family said Smyth ‘was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends’,Photograph: Family handout via Salvamont BrașovRomaniaBody found in Romania believed to be missing British hiker George SmythFamily paid tribute to Bristol University geology student, 18, after being notified by Avon and Somerset policeNadeem BadshahSat 15 Aug 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA body has been found in the search for an 18-year-old British man who went missing last year while hiking inRomania, UK police said.George Smyth, a geology student at theUniversity of Bristol, went missing in November.On Saturday, Avon and Somerset police said a body found in the region of the country is believed to be that of Smyth.His family have been informed and are being supported by a family liaison officer, the force added.Smyth’s family said: “We are all devastated by George’s death.“He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends.“We want to thank Salvamont mountain rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George, despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions.“They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time.”Efforts will be made to return Smyth’s body to the UK once formal identification has taken place.The family’s statement added: “We would also like to thank Avon and Somerset police and University of Bristol, who have gone above and beyond to try and find George, and to support us as a family.“Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye.“We would appreciate privacy while we continue to come to terms with this loss.”On Wednesday, mountain rescue teams said they had resumed their search in “previously indicated areas, under rock walls, in grates and in the hard-to-reach sectors” but without success.The student, from Newport in Shropshire, is believed to have left Poiana Brașov heading to Bran. He reached Țigănești, where he made an emergency call for help.At the time, rescuers said he was in a “very isolated and hard to access mountain area” and the weather conditions were extremely severe with strong winds, heavy snowfall and dense fog.The search and rescue operation also involved a canine unit, drones and helicopters being deployed.Sebastian Marinescu, from the area’s mountain rescue service, previously told the BBC the 18-year-old “was disoriented, physically exhausted, and already showing signs of hypothermia” when they received the emergency call.Explore more on these topicsRomaniaEuropeUniversity of BristolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Safety check calls after Irish teenager electrocuted taking shower in Greece | Greece | The Guardian
description: Alex McKee killed when picking up showerhead in ‘outdoor and rudimentary’ bathroom on Kimolos
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Alex McKee killed when picking up showerhead in ‘outdoor and rudimentary’ bathroom on Kimolos
Content: The  incident happened on the small  Greek island of Kimolos, the birthplace of Alex McKee’s mother.Photograph: Ralf Adler/Getty/imageBroker RFView image in fullscreenThe  incident happened on the small  Greek island of Kimolos, the birthplace of Alex McKee’s mother.Photograph: Ralf Adler/Getty/imageBroker RFGreeceSafety check calls after Irish teenager electrocuted taking shower in GreeceAlex McKee died when picking up showerhead in ‘outdoor and rudimentary’ bathroom on KimolosHelena Smithin AthensSat 15 Aug 2026 10.26 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe death of an Irish teenager, electrocuted while taking a shower in a holiday home inGreece, has led to calls for tighter checks on appliances at tourist accommodation.Alex McKee, 17, is said to have died instantly when picking up the showerhead in a bathroom described as “outdoor and rudimentary” on Kimolos.“We are lucky there weren’t two deaths as a result of electrocution,” Agapitos Xanthis, a doctor on the island told Greek TV, recounting how the boy’s mother had described feeling a similar surge when she called him for help. “I told her to immediately turn off the mains.”Alex McKee.Photograph: Stripe Young Scientist & Technology ExhibitionMcKee, from Cork, had been on the island barely three days when the tragedy occurred on 9 August. As the birthplace of his mother, Iphigenia, he and his family visited regularly, staying in the same stone house built more than 50 years ago.Greek police told the Guardian an inquiry was now focused on the building’s water heater and a possible fault in the wiring. “The house has been cordoned off and we have requested an independent expert to come and inspect the wiring,” said an officer based in Syros with oversight of the Aegean. “It is thought the fusebox may not have had a safety valve.”The teenager’s body was transported to the mainland where a postmortem conducted at a hospital in Piraeus had attributed the cause of death to electrocution.McKee, a fifth-year student in Cork, had won plaudits inIrelandfor developing an innovative communication system, with two of his classmates, for people suffering from nonverbal autism.Colm Burke, the Irish Fine Gael politician for Cork North-Central paid tribute to the teenager saying: “It is extremely sad to hear that someone so young has died so tragically. He was a really talented young person with his whole life and huge career ahead of him. Earlier this year, he put a huge effort into getting to that stage in the Young Scientist and Technology Exhibition and was awarded for his efforts.”In a nation so dependent on tourism – and with visitor numbers expected to, once again, soar this year – the incident has also shone a light on electrical standards in accommodation rented out seasonally on the Greek islands.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe mayor of Kimolos, Konstantinos Vendouris, expressed profound shock over the tragedy saying it had plunged the less than 1,000-strong island into mourning.It later emerged, however, that as a professional electrician he had signed off on the property’s electrical installation certificate in 2024 – a document that police said was also being investigated.The family signalled it would be pressing charges. “The current mayor faces huge criminal responsibility,” their lawyer Stelios Voudouris told Open TV.Explore more on these topicsGreeceEuropeIrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Amy Hunt claims third European Championships gold in relay triumph for ‘fantastic four’ | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Amy Hunt sealed a hat-trick of golds at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham as the women’s and men’s British teams won the 4x100 relays
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Amy Hunt sealed a hat-trick of golds at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham as the women’s and men’s British teams won the 4x100 relays
Content: The victorious British teams: back row (from left): Success Eduan, Zharnel Hughes, Dina Asher-Smith  and Louie Hinchliffe. Front row (from left) Romell Glave, Imani Lansiquot, Jeremiah Azu and Amy Hunt.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe victorious British teams: back row (from left): Success Eduan, Zharnel Hughes, Dina Asher-Smith  and Louie Hinchliffe. Front row (from left) Romell Glave, Imani Lansiquot, Jeremiah Azu and Amy Hunt.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAmy Hunt claims third European Championships gold in relay triumph for ‘fantastic four’Men’s and women’s 4x100 teams complete wins in styleHunt will aim for fourth gold in mixed relay on SundaySean Ingleat the Alexander Stadium, BirminghamSat 15 Aug 2026 18.36 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 19.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo sooner had Amy Hunt won a staggering third European gold medal in five days than she pointed at the superwomen guiding her closer to history. “We’re the fantastic four,” she said.It was hard to argue with that, especially after watching Britain’s 4x100m women power to glory in 42.05secs, more than 10 metres clear of Switzerland and Poland.“It’s such a privilege to be able to step on the track with these ladies, and the individual superpowers that we bring,” said Hunt. “It’s no joke. We’re all superwomen together out there.”European Athletics Championships: Double gold for Great Britain in 4x100m relays – live reactionRead moreFirst she addressed Dina Asher-Smith, who ran the first leg and whose gold equalled the Polish sprinter Irena Szewinska’s overall record tally of 10 medals at the championships. “I’m stood next to Dina, she’s the most decorated European athlete in history,” she said. “She has got thousands of medals.”Then Hunt turned to the emerging 21-year-old star Success Eduan, who is three weeks from completing a degree in midwifery. “This girl, Success, is a midwife,” said Hunt. “She brings new babies into the world.”Finally, Hunt pointed to Imani-Lara Lansiquot, who had brilliantly carried the baton home. In 2021 she had also written a play, Armour of Gaza, about growing up in Peckham. “Imani, that girl wrote a play,” said Hunt, clearly deeply impressed.The overall message was clear. On Sunday, Hunt will attempt to become the first athlete to win four gold medals at a single edition of a European championships in the mixed 4x100m relay. But she wanted this night to be about her teammates most of all.And that included praise for Britain’s new relay coach, Richard Kilty, who told the women a simple message before they stepped out on to the track: “Go out and break their hearts.”The British team certainly did that. Everyone played their parts, including the newcomer Eduan, who is now intending to become a full-time sprinter. “I finish in three weeks and I graduate in November, hopefully,” she said.Is it harder to deliver a baby or a baton, she was asked. “A baby! Someone’s life is in my hands,” she said smiling.It was a great night overall for Britain’s relay teams given that 15 minutes earlier the men’s quartet of Jeremiah Azu, Louie Hinchliffe, Zharnel Hughes and Romell Glave also took gold, in 38.45secs, ahead of Germany and Belgium.Before the drama of the relays there were a series of extraordinary performances across the night. The best of them? That surely came in the triple jump, where Italy’s Andy Díaz’s stunning leap of 18.15m – the fourth furthest in history – brought him gold by 39cm from Portugal’s Pedro Pichardo.View image in fullscreenAndy Díaz won triple jump gold with the fourth longest jump of all time.Photograph: Maja Hitij/Getty Images for European AthleticsBut not far behind was Sweden’s Andreas Almgren’s destructive display in the men’s 10,000m. After a dawdling first kilometre, Almgren gradually broke the resistance of all his rivals and lapped most of the field, to win by nearly 20 seconds in a championship record 27mins 23.44secs.“If someone is going to beat me, they are going to have to suffer for it,” said Almgren. “I’m in the best 10k shape of my life.”The Swiss athlete Dominic Lobalu took silver, while the world champion Jimmy Gressier won bronze in a sprint finish from Italy’s Yeman Crippa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSoon afterwards, Germany’s Julian Weber broke Steve Backley’s javelin championship record with a monster 90.40m final round throw to beat his compatriot Nick Thumm.“I’m delighted for him,” said Backley. “Julian Weber is my favourite thrower. A brilliant athlete. He has thrown ridiculously far tonight. Records are there to be broken and it is why we love Championships. Medals are for keeps, records are to borrow.”In the women’s 400m, Norway’s Henriette Jaeger was just as impressive as she took gold in 49.04, a second clear of Natalia Bukowiecka of Poland with Lieke Klaver of the Netherlands winning bronze.It was also a great night for Ireland as Kate O’Connor took gold in the women’s heptathlon with a score of 6751. Behind her were two Dutch athletes, Emma Oosterwegel and Sofie Dokter, who scored 6712 and 6664 points respectively.Afterwards, O’Connor dedicated her gold medal to her father and coach, Michael. “He still turns up to training, day in, day out, because this is my dream – but it is also his dream too,” she said.However, Katarina Johnson-Thompson vowed to fight on despite finishing 23rd. “I’ve had a really difficult season behind the scenes, and I didn’t know what form I was going to come here in,” she said. She is reported to have been battling a calf injury. “I obviously trusted myself to perform in major championships. I just didn’t have the preparation that I truly needed to be competitive.”The biggest surprise of the night, meanwhile, came in the men’s 1500m. Most had expected the world champion and silver medallist from 2025, Isaac Nader and Jake Wightman, to be battling it out for gold. But Nader faded to tenth, and Wightman found nothing when leading with 100m to go.And that left Stefan Nillessen, a 6ft 4in 23-year-old, to weave his way through for a shock success in 3:35.70. “The smile won’t go off my face for a long time,” said Nillesen, who runs a bit like Forrest Gump.Finally, in the women’s high jump, Yaroslava Mahuchikh cleared 1.97m to take gold from Poland’s Maria Zodzik and Montenegro’s Marija Vukovic.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Strategic change and grasping nettles’: where now for John Lewis as boss exits? | John Lewis | The Guardian
description: Peter Ruis appeared ‘to be doing a good job in difficult circumstances’ at department store chain, says analyst
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Peter Ruis appeared ‘to be doing a good job in difficult circumstances’ at department store chain, says analyst
Content: Peter Ruis said he was leaving John Lewis with the business on a ‘stronger footing’.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeter Ruis said he was leaving John Lewis with the business on a ‘stronger footing’.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianJohn Lewis‘Strategic change and grasping nettles’: where now for John Lewis as boss exits?Peter Ruis appeared ‘to be doing a good job in difficult circumstances’ at department store chain, says analystSarah ButlerSat 15 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 16.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Going up?” After a tough week for department stores it feels as if that sales aspiration is as dated as the singsong phrase in the opening credits of Are You Being Served? Simpsons of Piccadilly, which inspired the fictional Grace Brothers department store in which the 1970s TV sitcom was set, islong gone, and several of its modern equivalents are now fighting oblivion.The boss of John Lewis, Peter Ruis, clearly decided it was time to exit the elevator this week, announcinghis abrupt departurefrom the UK’s biggest department store chain in a surprise statement. Days later, Harvey Nichols, the luxury Knightsbridge store that was once a byword for 1990s chic, wasbought out of administrationfor a knock-down price by the owner of Sports Direct, Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group.It was only nine months ago that Ruis wastalking about possible expansionof the 36-store chain and a burst of investment was seen to have revived sales. Since then, trading has been tough, not helped by blistering summer weather during which shops on hothigh streets have lost outto online specialists, while the high cost of living has put spending on big-ticket items such as sofas and beds on hold.John Lewis said Ruis had decided to step down to “pursue new projects”. Ruis said he was leaving with the business on a “stronger footing”.Insiders suggest he had been discussing an exit for months. However, this was greeted with scepticism by those who know the company well, given that John Lewis recently organised a media briefing led by Ruis on 3 September, just three days before he is due to step down. It is understood he will still hold the briefing, days before the group announces half-year results.View image in fullscreenPeter Ruis oversaw the renovation of major John Lewis stores including those in Oxford Street (pictured), Bluewater and Glasgow.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianRuis is to be replaced by Will Kernan, a non-executive board member of the employee-owned John Lewis Partnership, which also runs the Waitrose supermarket chain. Those close to Ruis suggest he was leaving “on his own terms”, may have personal reasons for moving on, and did not appear to have a new job lined up.Sources close to John Lewis who have worked with Ruis, a fashion veteran, say he and Jason Tarry, the chair of the department store’s parent group, have notably different career backgrounds and management styles, and were always unlikely to gel. Ruis returned to the business in 2024 after a decade away running retailers including Jigsaw and Anthropologie, while Tarry, a former Tesco executive,took the top jobshortly after.“I am surprised Peter has lasted as long as he has,” one source said. However, Tarry said Ruis had done a “fantastic job”.Nick Bubb, an independent retail analyst, said the sudden exit came despite Ruis “appearing to be doing a good job in difficult circumstances”. He said it was “hard not to link the news with the recent Jason Tarry comments about tough trading at John Lewis” but noted the company’s line that it had arranged an “orderly succession to Kernan”.Ruis led therevivalof the group’s 100-year-old “never knowingly undersold” promise, which helped deliver a decent festive season. He also oversaw the renovation of large stores including those in Oxford Street, Bluewater and now Glasgow, and spearheaded the launch of buzzy collaborations including bringing Topshop, Waterstones and the Jamie Oliver brand into stores.Last year, the department store chain increased sales by 3% to £4.9bn, with underlying profit up 29% to £58m in a “subdued market”. Staff across the partnershipreceived their first annual bonus in four years.Richard Hyman, a retail analyst, said Ruis might have been prone to big investments but “for a department store to work, it has got to be a really strong brand. It is about handwriting and that is something Peter Ruis is good at.”Another industry source said Ruis was “getting the best tune out of it on trading that was possible, but the issue is more strategic change and grasping nettles”.Some industry watchers believe the business will have to reduce its space further after closing 16 department stores during the Covid pandemic.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe now closed John Lewis store in Sheffield city centre. The chain closed 16 stores during the Covid pandemic.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianIt is possible that Ruis and Tarry fell out over strategy, with Tarry potentially wanting to keep a tighter rein on investment than Ruis was prepared to accept. However, it is unlikely Tarry would have pushed out Ruis in favour of Kernan, who does not have experience with handling relationships with big brands or running department stores. Kernan has served as the chief executive of River Island, The White Company and the cycling retailer Wiggle after more than a decade rising through the ranks at New Look.Hyman said Tarry was also unlikely to have wanted to make a big change just months after a management changeover at John Lewis’s sister group Waitrose.The top job at the group’s department store arm is starting to appear among the hardest in retail. The role has been stuck in the revolving doors since 2016 whenAndy Street leftafter a decade. His immediate successor, Paula Nickolds, did four years, Pippa Wicks less than three, and then the former Hovis boss Nish Kankiwala was brought into the new role of chief executive for two years before hiring Ruis as managing director in January 2024.The multiple changes are no surprise given the pressure that department stores are under. Once the only places where consumers can compare and buy a wide range of brands under one roof, department stores now face heavy competition from the internet, which can host an almost inexhaustible array of products.View image in fullscreenRival department store chain Harvey Nichols was described as being in a ‘death spiral’ by Frasers Group boss Mike Ashley.Photograph: James Willoughby/SOPA Images/ShutterstockLarge sites have become a burden, attracting bills for huge business rates and hefty costs to keep them updated and in tune with the latest trends. One moment stores are adding cafes and bars, the next gyms, massage rooms and beauty parlours. Homewares may boom in sales one year and technology the next, but flexing a large store to accommodate the latest tastes can take many months and millions of pounds while websites can adjust in the beat of an algorithm.The John Lewis estate is almost the last national department store chain standing after the closure of Debenhams and Beales. In recent years the family-owned Fenwick chain has closed its London flagship store on Bond Street, theWeston family sold off Selfridges in 2022, and the Harvey Nichols deal came after Ashley described it as in a “death spiral”.House of Fraser has been reduced by two-thirds since 2018 to just 20 outlets under Ashley. He has nevertheless gained five new sites in the UK in landing Harvey Nichols, including the Knightsbridge flagship and potentially another in Dublin.Ashley is an expert in property development, and can no doubt see a chance to make more of these sites with a mix of his brands and potentially other services such as hotels or gyms. Kernan has his work cut out to keep the tills ringing at John Lewis, or this may be the next chain Ashley has his sights set on.Explore more on these topicsJohn LewisRetail industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaign | Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva | The Guardian
description: Brazil’s president was union chief who led metalworkers’ strikes of 1979-80 that paved the way for return of democracy
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Brazil’s president was union chief who led metalworkers’ strikes of 1979-80 that paved the way for return of democracy
Content: Union chief Lula speaking at the Vila Euclides stadium in de São Bernardo do Campo in 1979.Photograph: Jesus Carlos/ImagensView image in fullscreenUnion chief Lula speaking at the Vila Euclides stadium in de São Bernardo do Campo in 1979.Photograph: Jesus Carlos/ImagensLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaignBrazil’s president was union chief who led metalworkers’ strikes of 1979-80 that paved the way for return of democracyTom Phillipsin São Bernardo do CampoSat 15 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDay after day, tens of thousands of metalworkers would cram on to the football pitch in São Paulo’s industrial suburbs to demand higher wages and, perhaps unwittingly, transform the destiny ofBrazil.“You weren’t just documenting a fact – you were documenting history,” said photographer Jesus Carlos, who immortalised the now legendary strikes of 1979 and 1980 with his 24mm lens.As Carlos snapped the sea of downtrodden but tenacious labourers, he remembers sensing the momentous nature of their challenge to Brazil’s military dictatorship, whose foot soldiers would surround the Vila Euclides stadium wielding truncheons and guns.“I was a photographer – but before being a photographer I was a leftie,” recalled the former Communist party activist, now 75. “So I was fully aware what all it meant … [and] that the whole situation would be really important for the future.”Carlos’s instincts were right. The strikes in the industrial city of São Bernardo do Campo – a bold act of defiance against a regime that ruled with an iron fist – were subsequently credited with helping to pave the way for Brazil’s 1985 return to democracy and spawning one of the most influential and enduringpoliticians in modern Latin American history.For one of the key architects of those walkouts wasLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a bushy-bearded, heavy-smoking 33-year-old union chief who became a household name in Brazil and a global icon as a result.View image in fullscreenBrazil’s future president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, aged 33, speaking at the Vila Euclides stadium.Photograph: Fernando FerreiraThe New York Timeshailed himas “the continent’s leading working-class hero” and“a Brazilian equivalent of Poland’s Lech Walesa”, the activist who became the European country’s first democratically elected president after the fall of communism.In 1980, Lula helped found what became one of Latin America’s biggest leftwing political movements, the Workers’ party (PT), and in 2002, he was finally elected Brazil’s first working-class president after three unsuccessful attempts. The former lathe operator was re-elected in 2006 and won a historic third term in 2022,helping thwart an attempted coupled by his far-right opponent, the outgoing president Jair Bolsonaro.João de Deus Martinez, a metalworker who came to know Lula during the São Bernardo strikes, said his leadership potential had been obvious to those who saw him charm the throng in Vila Euclides. “There was no one who could beat him up there on the podium … He had this magnetism. People cried [when he spoke] – tears of hope,” recalled the scraggly haired 85-year-old whom Lula calls “Cabeludo” (Shaggy).View image in fullscreenMetalworkers at the Vila Euclides stadium in 1980 voting to continue their strike.Photograph: Foto: Jesus Carlos/ImagensNearly 50 years after the São Bernardo strikes catapulted him to fame, Lula, now 80, is preparing to make an emotional return to Vila Euclides to launch the seventh – and final – presidential campaign of a storied life that began in rural poverty and took him to the highest job in the land.On Sunday, thousands of PT supporters are expected to fill the football ground in the city where Lula’s astonishing rise began to watch him fire the starting gun on October’s election. “Vila Euclides is more than a stadium. It’s a symbol of democracy. A cradle of change,” reads the invitation urging party activists to travel to “where it all began” to make their voices heard.Like 2022’s election, when Lula beat Bolsonaro by a whisker, this year’s contest is expected to be tight. Bolsonaro cannot run, after receivinga 27-year jail sentencefor plotting to stop Lula taking power. His senator son, Flávio Bolsonaro, will stand in his place, with polls giving Lula a modest lead.“I don’t think it’s going to be a walkaway,” said Lula’s American biographer, John D French, who has charted the leftist’s trajectory since first visiting the ABC Paulista – the industrial region of which São Bernardo is part – in 1980.View image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva speaking after winning the presidential run-off election in October 2022.Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty ImagesFrench called the factory strikes “a unique effervescence”of disgruntlement against worker exploitation and the “ignorant military men” who seized power in 1964 but suddenly found themselves on the back foot. “Nobody knew what was going to happen, which is what made it dramatic, because there were a number of moments when it could have turned into a massacre,” recalled the academic, whose next book focuses on the reporters and photojournalists who chronicled the workers’ rebellion in the heartlands of Brazil’s automotive industry.Memories of that mobilisation, in which famous musicians, intellectuals, film-makers and politicians flocked to the region to champion the metalworkers and demand democracy, remain fresh to this day.“There was an awakening,” said Fernando Ferreira, 67, another photographer who covered the Vila Euclides assemblies. “Brazil is only what it is today because of the ABC.”Ademir Medici, a former newspaper editor who often interviewed Lula for the regional Diário do Grande ABC, said: “It was more exciting than a local derby between Corinthians and Palmeiras. It was thrilling. You thought: can this really be happening in my city? It gave you goose bumps.”Back then, Medici said the buzz around Lula was such that locals would boast of ties to the union boss, however tenuous. “It was cool to go around saying: ‘I’m Lula’s friend! I know Lula! I used to play football with Lula!’”Lula’s newfound fame even earned him a flattering profile in the Brazilian edition of Playboy, in which the interviewer asked the union leader if he would consider posing nude. (Lula declined.)Brazil’s Lula, 80, livestreams workouts before election against rival half his ageRead moreBut the ABC has changed dramatically since those heady days of people power, amidfactory closures, sociodemographic shifts, union splits, public anger at PT corruption scandals, and a lurch to the right driven by social media and the evangelical church.Once known as the “red belt” – Brazil’s version of the Labour party’s “red wall” in the UK, or a smaller version of the US Democratic party’s “blue wall” – much of the regionbacked Bolsonarowhen he won power in 2018. Today, only one of the seven cities in the ABC has a PT mayor. São Paulo state is governed by Tarcísio de Freitas, a close Bolsonaro ally who looks likely to be re-elected. “If Lula turned up on Marechal Deodoro [São Bernardo’s main street] he’d be booed,” Medici claimed.View image in fullscreenFlavio Bolsonaro at a Liberal party ceremony in Brasília in August 2026.Photograph: André Borges/EPADalila Teles Veras, a PT-voting poet and cultural activist who also witnessed the strikes, lamented the rightward drift of an area so crucial to the history of Brazil’s left. “Today, the sons of those [1979] union leaders are grown men who subscribe to fascist ideas,” she said of their support for the Bolsonaros. “How do you switch sides just like that? I keep thinking about those old workers. What if they were still around? They’d die of heartbreak, no doubt.”Veras, 80, had kept faith with Lula, calling him the “kind of leader [who] only comes along once every 100 years or more – if that”. She feared Brazil was facing its “most dangerous year” because of Donald Trump’s efforts to swing the election in favour of Flávio Bolsonaro, byslapping tariffson Brazilian imports,revoking the visaof Brazil’s US ambassador and championing Lula’s rival as “a smart young man who loves his country”. But Veras was trying to remain upbeat, insisting: “We have to believe – otherwise we’d go mad.”Martinez was also sticking with Lula, despite feeling frustrated that his octogenarian union comrade had failed to nurture an heir. “Lula has one flaw: he never bloody wants anyone to upstage him,” the former Volkswagen factory employee grumbled.As he prepared to return to Vila Euclides’ yellow and black stands on Sunday to witness another historic day, Martinez vowed to vote for Lula, almost certainly for the last time. “I can’t betray my way of thinking,” he said. “He showed us the path.”Explore more on these topicsLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaBrazilPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: I heard her beautiful laugh again, and all my emotions came flooding back | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Eddie Botha felt an easy connection with Jennifer. But when she went away for a trip, he thought that was the end of their growing romance
Author: James Norman
Headline: Eddie Botha felt an easy connection with Jennifer. But when she went away for a trip, he thought that was the end of their growing romance
Content: Eddie Botha and Jennifer at their wedding in Kuala Kubu Bharu, Malaysia, in 2007View image in fullscreenEddie Botha and Jennifer at their wedding in Kuala Kubu Bharu, Malaysia, in 2007The moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: I heard her beautiful laugh again, and all my emotions came flooding backEddie Bothafelt an easy connection with Jennifer. But when she went away for a trip, he thought that was the end of their growing romanceFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesEddie Botha, as told toJames NormanSat 15 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 20.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImet Jennifer at a Guy Sebastian concert in Kuala Lumpur in 2005. It was strange I was there because I’m kind of anti-pop music, but we were introduced there by a mutual friend. We didn’t talk that much but I immediately liked Jen and invited her to dinner the following week.That first date wasn’t in a fancy restaurant and we sat in the corner and talked for over an hour. I liked that she wasn’t at all bothered by the simplicity of the dining room. Being a foreigner inMalaysia, I immediately felt with Jen that there wasn’t as much of a culture gap as I’d felt with others. I could talk to her easily and was struck by her warmth and openness. And it was there that I first heard her laugh beaming out across the room, a pure, joyous sound.A few weeks later I organised a weekend getaway to Kuantan with my friend Ivan, who had introduced us, and invited Jen along. I remember she was sort of jumping into the waves and fell backwards, and I caught her in my arms. I didn’t let go immediately and then I felt her hand on my shoulder, and then I heard that laugh again. It was a moment of unexpected intimacy that didn’t feel forced or contrived – almost as if nature pushed us towards each other.View image in fullscreen‘I didn’t know if I was going to hear from her again’: Eddie Botha and Jennifer in Malaysia in 2006After that trip she went away with a girlfriend of hers to Bali and I thought maybe that was the end of things for us. Partly because her friend was a bit butch, I really wondered for a moment whether maybe they had gotten together on that trip – which of course I would have accepted.Then one day I was just getting home from work when, out of the blue, I saw her name appear on my phone. I was a bit surprised but very excited – we hadn’t spoken for two or three weeks. I hadn’t known I was going to hear from her again.The moment I knew: As I packed, our future looked uncertain – then he gave me his fluffy pyjamasRead moreShe told me she’d had a wonderful trip away and had been thinking about me a lot. I expressed how happy I was to hear from her; that I had been thinking about her a lot as well and would love to see her again soon. In my nervousness I made some silly jokes. When I heard her beautiful, pure laugh again, and all my emotions came flooding back, I was certain she was the one for me. It was only a short call but it was enough to tell me everything I needed to know.After that we started spending more time together and would speak to each other on the phone for hours in the evenings. She stayed over at my place a few times.I knew Jen was always worried about how any guy would deal with meeting her eccentric father. When I met him, he was very flamboyant – brightly coloured clothes with lots of jewellery and bling. But I really liked him because I’m a bit eccentric myself.After three or four months, I asked Jen to marry me. She said no at first. She was only 21 at the time and I was 30. But a few months later, as we spent even more time together, she finally said yes, with her dad’s approval.View image in fullscreen‘She still has that beautiful, free flowing laugh, which brings our whole family so much joy’: Eddie Botha and Jennifer with their children in Melbourne, 2026.We’ve been together for almost 20 years now, have two kidsand live in Melbourne. Not to say we haven’t had any troubles. I’m the risk-taker and she’s very risk-averse. I think she is the voice of reason whereas I shoot from the hip. But I think she generally trusts my instincts. We have a healthy, balanced relationship.I love that she’s always believed in me as an artist. When we met in Malaysia I was working as a landscape architect. When we moved to Australia that fell to the wayside, so she encouraged me to venture more into the arts. She brings her business sense to my arts career.I admire her career as a CFO for a software company – I’ve had to let go of my old-fashioned instinct that the man should be the bread-winner. I am quite paternal and love spending more time with the kids. Our relationship is based on love and caring for each other – but I think our friendship is the real core that keeps us going. And she still has that beautiful, free flowing laugh, which brings our whole family so much joy.Eddie Botha’s work will feature as part of theScotch Foundation Art Show, 10-13 September at James Forbes Academy, Scotch College MelbourneTell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share? title: Mission review – dangerous quest to mend a broken childhood | Movies | The Guardian
description: George MacKay plays a troubled restaurant worker embarking on bleak inner and outer journeys reflecting the pressures on young men
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: George MacKay plays a troubled restaurant worker embarking on bleak inner and outer journeys reflecting the pressures on young men
Content: Tunnel vision … George MacKay in Mission.Photograph: EIFFView image in fullscreenTunnel vision … George MacKay in Mission.Photograph: EIFFMoviesReviewMission review – dangerous quest to mend a broken childhoodEdinburgh film festivalGeorge MacKay plays a troubled restaurant worker embarking on bleak inner and outer journeys reflecting the pressures on young menPeter BradshawSat 15 Aug 2026 18.23 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePaul Wright has created a moodscape of loneliness in this seriously intended, strenuously performed movie, a followup tohis 2013 debut feature For Those in Peril. As before, Wright is working with lead actor George MacKay, who here plays Dylan, a troubled restaurant worker embarking on inner and outer journeys of wretchedness, desperate to make sense of a passionately remembered past and heading for the cliff-edge. As before, I think Wright has intelligently absorbed the influence of Terrence Malick in the emphasis on non-narrative ideas of mood and moment, foregrounding fleeting images and perceptions. Wright often intersperses the action with a barrage of millisecond-clips from TV and online, migraine rushes of sensory overload showing us how the world is just somehow too much.To be honest, Mission is flawed. Some of the action is a bit drama-school-improv; the film’s ambient poetic realism can be shapeless; and in screenwriting terms, suddenly and miraculously finding a pistol out of the blue is borderline preposterous – although on this point Wright does find a way of (almost) subverting Chekhov’s rule about what happens to a gun produced in act one. But Mission is a serious film about a serious, relevant subject: the mental health of young men.Dylan, played by MacKay, is an intense, lonely, vulnerable guy who has found a job working in an upscale hotel restaurant. He’s doing his best, nursing a crush on co-worker Becky (Emma Naomi), but simmering like a pressure cooker with unexpressed pain. He is tormented with memories of a childhood in which he thinks he was happy for the only time in his life, hanging out with his sister Claire (played as an adult by Rosy McEwen). When he was seven years old, he says, he died for four minutes, and realised what existence was all about.But did that really happen? Or has Dylan just imagined or misremembered it? It’s not explicitly shown in any of the analogue home-video flashbacks of his childhood with Claire. And the fact/fiction borderline is where many of Dylan’s many violent confrontations with strangers appear to take place: shoving a cop, or threatening a guy at a party with knives, things don’t seem to have any consequences. But if they are only happening in his head, then that is where the consequences are accumulating.Dylan’s crisis moment – and the film’s best moment – arrives when the hotel’s smarmy, creepy CEO James (Emun Elliott) calls in the staff one by one for a performance-assessment interview and Dylan, though clearly uncomfortable, tries his hardest to go along with this workplace pantomime and tell the boss what he thinks he wants to hear. Dylan is however honest and the calamity of this interview actually made me (bleakly) laugh out loud. But the awful truth is that it was the wrong move; MacKay’s performance shows us how Dylan’s inability to go along with the interview is symptomatic of his estrangement from the world. This revelation starts him off on the violent road to nowhere.In anguish, he tries to reconnect with Claire (McEwen) who is deeply concerned, but also scared and bewildered by his pointless, self-harming fetishisation of the past. She herself has grown up. She has made accommodations with what needs to be done to get along in life. Why can’t Dylan? It’s a mystery. Dylan feels the burden of manhood and the combination of sensitivity and success that is expected of young men. At one point, he yells: “I want a world where the dreamers and the freaks and the good guys win!” Fair point. But Dylan is shouting this at someone whose house he has broken into, while wearing scary goth makeup. His putative victim is entitled to think that Dylan is not one of the good guys. The irony is semi-intentional.If Dylan is on a mission, it is perhaps not simply to recapture the past, but to force Claire to recapture it alongside him, to confirm that he is right, to provide some company in his loneliness. The film’s interestingly ambiguous and hallucinatory embrace between the siblings leaves unanswered the question of how much his mission can ever succeed.Mission screened at the Edinburgh film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsGeorge MacKayMenEdinburgh film festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kabul review – this thriller about Afghanistan’s abandonment is every bit as gripping as it is horrifying | Television | The Guardian
description: This tense, powerful six-parter starkly captures the nation’s slide into oppressive terror. Its capturing of a shameful moment in history is hugely vivid
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: This tense, powerful six-parter starkly captures the nation’s slide into oppressive terror. Its capturing of a shameful moment in history is hugely vivid
Content: ‘Wrenching and terrifying’ … Kabul.Photograph: BBC/© Cinétévé - 24 25 Films - France Télévisions/Domniki MitropoulouView image in fullscreen‘Wrenching and terrifying’ … Kabul.Photograph: BBC/© Cinétévé - 24 25 Films - France Télévisions/Domniki MitropoulouTV reviewTelevisionReviewKabul review – this thriller about Afghanistan’s abandonment is every bit as gripping as it is horrifyingThis tense, powerful six-parter starkly captures the nation’s slide into oppressive terror. Its capturing of a shameful moment in history is hugely vividJack SealeSat 15 Aug 2026 16.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe final episode of Kabul pointedly soundtracks its opening scene with a speech given by George W Bush when America invaded Afghanistan in 2001. “The oppressed people of Afghanistan will know the generosity of America and our allies,” Bush’s teleprompter tells him to say. “The United States of America is a friend to the Afghan people.”This taut six-part thriller, a pan-European co-production, is set in Afghanistan’s capital in August 2021, at the end of a 20-year western intervention that has, ultimately, not delivered the stated goal of freeing the country’s people from the fundamentalist authoritarianism of the Taliban regime. To the contrary, the Taliban are ready to install a more fearsome version of their old government as soon as the scheduled withdrawal of the Americans and their European allies takes place.The series sketches how, for the vast majority of ordinary Afghans, living under oppressive terror is now their only possible future: the foreigners who arrived in the wake of President Bush’s announcement are about to become absent friends, if indeed friends is what they ever were. But for the purposes of the drama, we are with the fortunate few who have a ticket out. Their connection to the visitors from Nato has given them the paperwork necessary to be evacuated to new lives in the west.Kabul’s first episode starkly captures the slow-dawning realisation, among citizens and the last few diplomats in the French and Italian embassies, that those visas might just be one final batch of broken promises. The Taliban have entered the city and are not sticking to the agreed timetable: a piece of paper will offer no protection from being imprisoned, killed or just physically prevented from accessing the increasingly besieged airport.The drama uses the old but powerful trick of focusing on a single family, headed by matriarch Zahara (Darina Al Joundi). Her work as a prosecutor has seen her imprison countless Taliban fighters as terrorists, so she will be shot on sight if recognised by the forces storming into Kabul. Her husband Baqir (Vassilis Koukalani) is in the middle of trying to persuade her she should leave everything behind immediately when he is proven right by gunfire on their street. A wrenching, terrifying scene sees Zahara abandon a beloved elderly colleague who isn’t fit enough to dash to the French embassy. Everywhere, impossible decisions are hurriedly being made.View image in fullscreenFazal (Shervin Alenabi), in search of his old CIA handlers.Photograph: BBC/© Cinétévé - 24 25 Films - France Télévisions/Domniki MitropoulouAs Zahara and Baqir flee, they are forever on the phone to their adult children, neither of whom can be trusted to prioritise their own safety. We meet Fazal (Shervin Alenabi) as he mans a rural checkpoint on behalf of the Afghan army. Having been forced to abandon it by the Taliban’s overwhelming numbers, instead of heading to the city he moves further out into the country in search of his old CIA handlers; thus becoming our way of seeing the situation in the nation outside Kabul, and assessing the role of the last remaining Americans.Providing an insight into what dealing with the Taliban close-up is like, meanwhile, is the family’s daughter Amina (Hannah Abdoh), a hospital doctor for whom starting again in Europe holds no appeal. She has trained to help sick and injured Afghans and is determined to keep doing that. But when the Taliban enter the hospital, she (and we) see that their psychopathic aggression and stupid dogma cannot be reasoned with or resisted. One is reminded of Margaret Atwood’s warning that everything in The Handmaid’s Tale has already happened, somewhere.The Taliban immediately set about building a crude cinder-block wall to split the hospital building in two, enforcing their strict separation of men and women with no regard for patients’ health. On the ward, Amina has bonded with a girl of primary-school age who benefits greatly from the calming distraction of songs on her iPod - until a Taliban soldier charges in and rips the device from the girl’s hands, because “music is haram”.Will Zahara’s family be reunited, and can the good-hearted westerners – including Giovanni (Gianmarco Saurino), a hesitant, nerdy administrator who suddenly becomes the Italian consul and has to rapidly transform himself into a steely and proactive diplomat – save all the people they promised to protect? The answer to the latter question is a doom-laden no, but as Kabul establishes itself as an efficient, empathic drama, infused with political rage without being slowed down by it, we care about the struggle.It’s not perfect – it has weaknesses for speechified dialogue, and for characters’ journeys converging in unlikely ways – but its thriller tropes, of a race against time and of risks taken under the gaze of an implacable enemy, are utilised effectively to make the story as compelling as it is appalling. August 2021 in Kabul was an awful, shameful moment in history; this show vividly re-lives it.Kabul aired on BBC Four and is available on iPlayer in the UK and on SBS On Demand in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Once I started zooming in, I never stopped’: the mesmerising art of macro photography | Insects | The Guardian
