description: Coverts describe a demanding form of capturing nature very close up that has grown in popularity in last few years
Author: Safeerah Ahmed
Headline: Coverts describe a demanding form of capturing nature very close up that has grown in popularity in last few years
Content: A walker’s moth by Dara Ojo, who started photographing insects a few years ago after a suggestion from a friend.Photograph: Dara OjoView image in fullscreenA walker’s moth by Dara Ojo, who started photographing insects a few years ago after a suggestion from a friend.Photograph: Dara OjoInvertebrate of the year 2026Insects‘Once I started zooming in, I never stopped’: the mesmerising art of macro photographyConverts describe a demanding form of capturing nature very close up that has grown in popularity in last few yearsVote here for your favourite invertebrate of the yearLauren Lees andSafeerah AhmedSat 15 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Ialways just pray ‘please don’t fly away’,” says Dara Ojo. As a wildlife photographer, he can handle spending minutes, hours and sometimes days waiting for the shot, but insects are not always very cooperative.Ojo is one of an increasing number of photographers turning their lenses towards something smaller: macro photography. This refers to photographing the natural world at an extremely close range, close enough to see the facets of a fly’s eye, or the geometry of a spider’s face.This discipline has quietly evolved in popularity over the past few years, driven by a wave of macro influencers, more affordable lenses and the coronavirus pandemic, which left a lot of photographers with nowhere to go but their own back gardens.It is a demanding form. Photographers rely on “focus stacking”, a technique that combines multiple images taken at slightly different focus distances to create one final frame. That is difficult enough with a still subject. However, insects, by nature, are not often static subjects. Add in wind, and a creature that can simply fly away mid-shoot, and a single successful image can represent hours, or even days, of failed attempts.Macro photography is also an increasingly viable career, with more routes to income than people may expect. A well-run account can generate income through monetisation, alongside the production of print sales and books. Brand partnerships can also play a significant role, with camera and lens manufacturers seeking to work with macro specialists for content.View image in fullscreenDara Ojo says he fell in love with insects when he saw the intricate design of their faces.Photograph: Dara OjoOjo, 35, grew up in Lagos, Nigeria. He recalls planting yam, corn, tomatoes and beans with his late father. “I was just fascinated about putting something so tiny in the ground and coming back in a few days time and it’s starting to grow out. It was like magic to me,” Ojo says.That sense of wonder resurfaced later. Ojo developed a love for photography during the pandemic, initially photographing birds in China, where he was based at the time. “I never want to be on the other side of the camera. If there’s a group photo, I will always volunteer to take it,” he says, joking. Feeling stagnant in his photography around this time, a friend suggested Ojo try capturing insects.“When I started taking photos of them, when I’d never seen them that close up before, I was just fascinated by the design of their faces. It’s very intricate and it made me fall in love with them. I think people that live in tropical countries don’t appreciate [insects] as much because of the amount of times you get bitten by mosquitoes, stung by ants and wasps and whatnot,” Ojo says.View image in fullscreen‘I tried for two or three years to capture that moment,’ Dara Ojo says of his favourite thing he has capture: a damselfly grooming itself.Photograph: Dara OjoHis favourite thing that he has ever captured is a video of a damselfly grooming itself. “I tried for two or three years to capture that moment,” he says. Ojo found it in an 8-hectare (20-acre) botanical garden, a large space to manage in macro photography.He arrived there just as the sun was coming up, his research telling him that a damselfly would be most likely to clean itself at this time. After finding one, Ojo focused on it: “I waited for an hour and 30 minutes for it to do it. I always tell people if you’re doing macro, you’re not going to get your steps in.”There is something meditative in how Ojo describes his photography process. On a trip, he likes to initially connect with nature first, often going out for a walk without a camera. “Sometimes when I’m looking for a particular species, I just say it out loud into nature and seven out of 10 times I find them. Or, I picture what I want to find in my head and eight out of 10 times I find it in the same way that I pictured it,” he says.View image in fullscreenA ladybug by Marit van Ekelenburg. It was while photographing flowers that she found herself distracted by what was happening inside them.Photograph: Marit van EkelenburgOjo macro beginnings are echoed by other photographers. For Marit van Ekelenburg, who photographs as Macro by Marit from the Netherlands, it started with a favour for her mother eight years ago.“My mum asked me if I could take some photos of her beautiful garden in the Netherlands, as she wanted it for her website,” she says. “I had never held a professional camera, and at that time my knowledge ended at recognising the difference between a wasp and a bee.”View image in fullscreenMarit van Ekelenburg began with equipment far too complicated for a beginner, and taught herself the hard way. ‘I messed up a lot,’ she says.Photograph: Cristian KochWhile photographing flowers, van Ekelenburg found herself distracted by what was happening inside them: “It started with a bee, then a weevil, and before I knew it I was so mesmerised.” She began with equipment far too complicated for a beginner, and taught herself the hard way. “I messed up a lot. But I’m stubborn, so after many hours of practice, I learned. Once I started zooming in, I think I just never stopped,” she says.What hooked her was the same thing that hooked Ojo: “I could finally see details that I couldn’t with the naked eye. Once you start really looking, it’s like, wow, what on earth is that? What are those colours, structures, and details that you just can’t see otherwise?”And crucially, van Ekelenburg adds, you do not have to travel to find it: “They’re right by you and you walk past them every day.”View image in fullscreenA longhorn beetle by Dara Ojo.Photograph: Dara OjoIn France, biologists-turned-photographers Maceo and Andrea Grammatico (who post their work together on Instagram as TwinWildLens) came to macro from a more scientific angle. They discovered the genre through YouTube tutorials about two years ago before saving up for their first dedicated lens.What drew them in, they say, was diversity: “We chose insects because there is so much difference in their shapes, colours and behaviours. We can find them very close to us, in our garden or in the forest nearby. We wanted to show people all of the incredible details you can see when you look closely.”View image in fullscreenA pearly tree frog (Nyctixalus margaritifer).Photograph: Maceo and Andrea GrammaticoTheir most memorable shoot took persistence. They spent three days searching an area of Mediterranean scrubland for a conehead mantis, which was found only in the final hours. A trip to Costa Rica also delivered fascinating discoveries, spanning frogs to snakes, and a moth with markings that they nicknamed “the Dobby moth”.View image in fullscreenThe conehead mantis (Empusa pennata).Photograph: Maceo and Andrea GrammaticoThese photographers say they photograph insects as most people have simply never been shown that they can be beautiful at all. Van Ekelenburg says that she enjoys “capturing common insects in a way in which people can think: ‘Oh my gosh, that’s so cute,’ instead of having an initially negative reaction. I never kill them and always keep them alive.”Ojo says: “I want to appreciate [insects]. Lions, tigers and giraffes get all the PR. Insect decline is at about 45% to 47% right now, and they are such a fundamental part of the ecosystem. They’re the foundation of it.”View image in fullscreenA polydrusus weevil by Marit van Ekelenburg. ‘The power of macro photography is that the curiosity you had as a kid still sparks,’ she says.Photograph: Marit van EkelenburgThat mission extends well beyond Instagram. Ojo also runs workshops with children in schools, hoping to instil a love for invertebrates in children. Van Ekelenburg has built out a similar strand of teaching, running group workshops from Olgarden on the outskirts of the Dutch village of Deurningen.As she puts it: “The power of macro photography is that the curiosity you had as a kid still sparks. It’s like a whole new world, and you don’t even have to go that far for it. These are creatures that we live with. Maybe we should treat them better.”It’s invertebrate of the year!Vote here for your favouriteExplore more on these topicsInsectsInvertebrate of the year 2026Photography (Technology)Photography (Art and design)AnimalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Atsuko Okatsuka: ‘Fans have cut their hair to look like mine, which is a huge commitment’ | Culture | The Guardian
description: The comedian and actor on her love for White Chicks, getting a bad Yelp review as a dog walker and doing stand-up during an earthquake
Author: Dee Jefferson
Headline: The comedian and actor on her love for White Chicks, getting a bad Yelp review as a dog walker and doing stand-up during an earthquake
Content: Atsuko Okatsuka: ‘I think people think I’m more wholesome than I am.’ The comedian and actor wears an outfit made of pink hair rollers.Photograph: Lee JamersonView image in fullscreenAtsuko Okatsuka: ‘I think people think I’m more wholesome than I am.’ The comedian and actor wears an outfit made of pink hair rollers.Photograph: Lee Jamerson10 Chaotic QuestionsCultureAtsuko Okatsuka: ‘Fans have cut their hair to look like mine, which is a huge commitment’The comedian and actor on her love for White Chicks, getting a bad Yelp review as a dog walker and doing stand-up during an earthquakeDee JeffersonSat 15 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 21.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou went to film school, what movie do you rewatch or return to most?This would not be an answer that my film school would respect, or expect: White Chicks by the Wayans brothers. It’s about two brothers who are pretending to be rich white girls from the Hamptons. I love when something’s super stupid and silly, and there’s ascenewhere this group of [white] girls is in the car singing, and the two brothers have to pretend to know Vanessa Carlton’s A Thousand Miles, and I was like, “Oh my god, I’ve been there!”I think I was 16 when I watched it for the first time, and I finally knew enough English and also slang, and it also had physical humour, which I grew up watching a lot in Japan. So it was the perfect blend of “Oh, I’m an Asian American now”.What’s the strangest job you’ve ever had?I used to walk dogs in LA, and there’s a bad Yelp review about me, saying that I only walked Charlie the terrier mix for 10 minutes instead of the full 30. And I did do that. But it was a rainy day and the dog didn’t want to keep walking, and it was shaking, so I brought it back to the house. But turns out the owner of the dog had a friend spying on me and timing me from the moment I let the dog out and back in. I guess it’s not a weird job, but it’s a memorable one.What’s the best thing you learned from someone you worked with?Chelsea Handler is a good friend of mine, and she says about jealousy: just keep in mind that there is room for everyone. You may go, “I wanted first place, like that person”. But you have a role in life in whatever field you’re in. So never compare yourself to others – we’re all made so different.What’s the most chaotic thing that’s happened to you on stage?I was doing a stand-up set in Pasadena [California] and a 7.1 magnitude earthquake hit as I was walking on stage. You cansee iton YouTube. I was freaked out because I have no skills to help in an earthquake. I went to art school! But I am quick on my feet, I’m funny, and I do care about people. I think having a mom with schizophrenia, and living in the US as an undocumented migrant for seven years – I was like, I can deal with anything. What’s a 7.1 earthquake? This is like the chillest heckler in my life.When you get to a hotel, what’s the first thing you do?Every time, I’m genuinely so stoked that I’m not in my house, in my mess. Thank goodness I’m away from my dishes, I’m away from my dirty underwear. I only have clean ones because that’s all I brought.Is there anything you do to make it feel like home?Oh no, I never really feel at home anywhere. Even in my own home, sometimes I feel like a stranger. Maybe it’s because I moved around a lot as a kid – I still don’t settle down easily. I’m always like, “Gotta be ready to leave at any point!” Maybe it’s from being undocumented for so long? Or living in a garage for seven years. But I’m always like, we’re gonna get kicked out soon, somehow!What video is guaranteed to make you laugh?There’s thisvideoa woman made for her husband, pointing out all the messes he’s made around the house – using a stick with a tiny hand with a pointing index finger. And she does it really aggressively sometimes. It makes me laugh so hard.What’s been your most memorable interaction with a fan?A couple of people have cut their hair to look like mine, which is a huge commitment. There was another fan who came to my show wearing a wig of my bowl cut. Her name was Atsuko too. She said, “People used to have a hard time pronouncing my name, and it was always an insecurity of mine – I even wanted to change my name at one point in my life. But because of you, people are able to say my name, and I feel less alone and more seen because of it.” That was cool.John Cameron Mitchell: ‘It’s punk to turn off your phone – you’re walking away from the herd’Read moreWhat are you secretly really good at?I’m really good at physical therapy, especially for senior citizens. Like, if my grandma’s knees are hurting or my mom’s knees are hurting, I know the right exercise to strengthen the muscles around there. I think it’s from my days teaching dance fitness. I got really into fitness in junior high, and studied it a lot on my own – and I was a cheerleader too. So I know how to rehabilitate if someone’s injured.If you had to appear on a reality TV show, which one would it be?I want to go on one of the love shows, even though I’m married. Maybe me and my husband could do it. They’ve never had a married couple on Love Island, and they need antagonists, they need villains.You seem very wholesome, I’m not confident you’d be a great villain …Well, thank you. I do tend to be positive. But there’s a surprising edge to me. I think people think I’m more wholesome than I am.If you could plan a fantasy dinner party of people – living or dead, real or fictional – who’s on your list?Lucille Ball, Stitch [from Lilo and Stitch]. Charlie Chaplin. I want to meet Hachiko, the akita dog that everyone in Japan loves because he loyally waited for his owner at the same train station for years. Maybe Sia, because I’m friends with Kathy Griffin, and she’s really close to her, and so Sia and I see each other sometimes, and I want to invite someone I don’t usually see. And Paddington [Bear].What a totally normal, natural mix of guests.I don’t know. I feel like fights will break out. Maybe put Mary, Jesus’s mother, in there too. I have questions.What would you ask her?Any regrets?Atsuko Okatsuka’sThe Big Bowl Touris in Brisbane on 16 August; Adelaide on 18 August; Perth on 19 August; Sydney on 21 August; and Melbourne on 22and 23 AugustExplore more on these topicsCulture10 Chaotic QuestionsComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)TV comedyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Tony to Jungle: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Dominic Sessa plays Anthony Bourdain in a fun biopic, and the ever-danceable UK funksters are back with a sun-dappled new album
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dominic Sessa plays Anthony Bourdain in a fun biopic, and the ever-danceable UK funksters are back with a sun-dappled new album
Content: Kitchen nightmares … Dominic Sessa in Tony.Photograph: Seacia PavaoView image in fullscreenKitchen nightmares … Dominic Sessa in Tony.Photograph: Seacia PavaoGoing out, staying inCultureFrom Tony to Jungle: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadDominic Sessa plays Anthony Bourdain in a fun biopic, and the ever-danceable UK funksters are back with a sun-dappled new albumSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out: CinemaTonyOut nowThis comic biopic of Anthony Bourdain focuses on the celebrity chef and documentarian’s late adolescence, as he gets a summer job at a restaurant in Cape Cod at the age of 19. Dominic Sessa (The Holdovers) plays Bourdain, with Matt Johnson directing. Rich Sommer, Leo Woodall and Antonio Banderas also star.The End of Oak StreetOut nowDavid Robert Mitchell (It Follows) is back, writing and directing a sci-fi mystery in which prehistoric creatures start to make appearances in suburbia. Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor play members of a family who find themselves trying to survive.Sunny DancerOut nowBella Ramsey, James Norton and Neil Patrick Harris, among many others, make up the ensemble cast of a breezy comedy about a decidedly unbreezy subject: a summer camp for kids suffering from cancer. George Jacques directs this UK indie.Holy DaysOut nowThe year is 1974. The country is New Zealand. Three nuns, played by three legends of stage and screen – Judy Davis, Miriam Margolyes and Jacki Weaver – are going on a road trip in order to save their convent, in a broad comedy from Nat Boltt based on the book by Joy Cowley.Catherine BrayGoing out: GigsView image in fullscreenLeader of the pack … Chelsea Wolfe.Photograph: Magdalena WosinskaArcTanGentFernhill Farm, Bristol, 19 to 22 AugustIf you prefer your rock to come with a prefix, perhaps post-, or math-, or noise-, this Bristol festival is for you. Celebrating alternative music, this year’s lineup features funk-metal pioneers Primus, hotly tipped sludge purveyors Chat Pile and the distinctly gothic Chelsea Wolfe.Michael CraggLenny KravitzCrystal Palace Park, London, 16 AugustSexy hitmaker and unfeasibly large scarf experimentalist Lenny Kravitz heads to south London to headline his own mini-festival (support comes from Leon Thomas and Joss Stone). Expect a smattering of recent singles, but hold out for Fly Away, It Ain’t Over ’Til It’s Over and Are You Gonna Go My Way.MCUkrainian Freedom OrchestraSt Paul’s Cathedral, London, 18 AugustFormed by the Canadian-Ukrainian conductor Keri-Lynn Wilson in 2022 following Russia’s invasion, this remarkable ensemble continues its cultural fightback. The UK stop on its latest tour pairs new music by Ukrainian composer Bohdana Frolyak with Verdi’s Requiem. Heavyweight international soloists include Ailyn Pérez and Solomon Howard.Flora WillsonColtrane and Hartman on Impulse! ft Marvin Muoneké and Mark LockheartWatermill Jazz, Dorking, 18 AugustGifted founder member of cutting-edge UK jazz bands Loose Tubes and Polar Bear performs with former Britain’s Got Talent vocal contestant? Saxophonist Mark Lockheart’s partnership with young singer Marvin Muoneké shows how illuminating that rare conjunction can be, as they sensitively celebrate John Coltrane’s classic 1963 album with jazz balladeer Johnny Hartman.John FordhamGoing out: ArtView image in fullscreenSquare space … Hurvin Anderson’s Jersey.Photograph: Hurvin AndersonHurvin AndersonTate Britain, London, to 23 AugustFrom inner-city Birmingham to lush, tropical Trinidad, this British artist’s hazy, haunted take on barbershops and Caribbean landscapes features some of the best figurative painting you’ll see this year.Edinburgh art festivalVarious venues, to 30 AugustThe UK’s biggest annual art festival returns, taking over pretty much every space in the Scottish capital with a raft of diverse exhibitions. Among this year’s highlights are promising Japanese fetish paintings and queer images of Edinburgh’s graveyards.Lawrence Abu HamdanThe Common Guild, Glasgow, 20 August to 17 OctoberLawrence Abu Hamdan’s work is based on the idea of “forensic listening”, which uses sonic recording techniques to investigate global injustices. Here, he combines sound, video and installation to look at the Israeli occupation of the Golan Heights.David HockneySerpentine North, London, to 23 AugustThe world lost one of its great modern artists when David Hockney died this year, but not before he pulled together one last exhibition at the Serpentine, featuring a single vast digital painting of his beloved Normandy.Eddy FrankelGoing out: StageView image in fullscreenFringe concern … Ele McKenzie.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearEle McKenzieBunker at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, to 30 AugustHaving showcased her comic chops in the exceptional sitcom Funboys (she plays the eccentric, libidinous girlfriend of one of the leads), McKenzie brings her debut standup hour about constipation and moving back in with her parents to the fringe.Rachel AroestiHow the Other Half LovesThe Old Vic, London, to 19 SeptemberA comedy caper starring Roger Allam and Dorothy Atkinson. In Alan Ayckbourn’s domestic farce, an affair prompts cascading mayhem – played out amid a chaotic set.Miriam GillinsonMayfliesBrown’s of Leith Warehouse, Edinburgh, to 30 AugustAndrew O’Hagan’s moving novel has been adapted for the fringe – and will be staged by Grid IronTheatreCompany in a former metalworks. It’s a story about mortality and middle age, as a group of teenagers embark on a riotous weekend.MG360General Gordon Square, London, 21 AugustThe opening of the Greenwich+Docklands international festival is a free outdoor spectacle from choreographer Mehdi Kerkouche, which turns a town square into a pumping dancefloor. Kerkouche’s YouTube videos went viral in lockdown; now he’s an energetic force in contemporary dance.Lyndsey Winshipskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in: StreamingView image in fullscreenThe sleuth is out there … Ludwig.Photograph: BBC/Big Talk Studios/Colin HuttonLudwigiPlayer & BBC One, 20 August, 9pmAmateur detectives are middlebrow TV’s bread and butter, but few are as charmingly reluctant as David Mitchell’s reclusive puzzle-setter, who returns to resume the extraordinarily difficult search for his missing detective brother. Mark Bonnar and Sian Clifford join the cast for series two.Sunny NightsITVX, 16 AugustWill Forte (The Four Seasons) and D’Arcy Carden (The Good Place) are two squabbling siblings who travel down under to launch their spray-tan business in a new Australian series that soon descends into a gangland conspiracy thriller.LanternsHBO Max, 17 AugustThis DC comics adaptation centres on an intergalactic peacekeeping cop and his protege, who investigate a murder while navigating alien forces. The tone is dark and the cast is decent: Kyle Chandler, Aaron Pierre, Kelly Macdonald and Laura Linney co-star.Little BirdNow & Sky Atlantic, 18 August, 9pmIt may have aired in Canada more than three years ago, but rave reviews mean this miniseries about a First Nations girl from Saskatchewan who is forcibly removed from her parents and adopted by a Jewish family in the 1960s is very much still worth a look.RAStaying in: GamesView image in fullscreenLife and Souls … Mortal Shell 2.Photograph: Cold SymmetryMortal Shell 2PC, Xbox Series X/S, PS5, out 20 AugustAction RPGs tend to blur into one another, but this sequel looks to be rather a step up from its predecessor. Expect deeper, more exciting combat, along with a more intricate, interconnected world. A weapons upgrade should excite the Soulslike fans.The Sinking City 2PC, Xbox Series X/S, PS5, out 18 AugustArriving seven years after the original, this Frogwares-developed sequel based on the work of HP Lovecraft again unfolds in a supernaturally flooded city. In this semi open-world game, you must discover what’s going on in the city of Arkham while defending yourself against monstrous enemies by using 1920s-era weapons.Tom OrryStaying in: AlbumsView image in fullscreenJungle boogie … Tom McFarland, Lydia Kitto and Joshua Lloyd-Watson AKA Jungle.Photograph: MasonJungle – SunshineOut nowMore than a decade into their career, Jungle’s brand of sleek dance-pop recently hit a commercial peak. After the chart success of Volcano in 2023, the UK trio won a Brit award and upgraded their live shows to arenas. This fifth album, self-produced as ever, looks set to continue the hot streak, and will see them touring round the world into 2027.Benny Blanco – HermosoOut nowSuper-producer Benny Blanco, who’s worked with the likes of Justin Bieber, Rihanna and his wife, Selena Gomez, returns with his follow-up to his 2018 solo debut, Friends Keep Secrets. Hermoso is his celebration of Latin American and Spanish pop and features guest spots from Becky G and Bb Trickz.Carly Simon – Comes in WavesOut nowThe much-loved singer-songwriter returns with her first album of new material since 2009’s Never Been Gone. On lead single Howl, Simon – who recently revealed she’s been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease – turns a quiet storm of anger into an ode to joy and forgiveness.Phoebe Bridgers – Lost WeekendOut nowAfter teasing the album via a short run of phone-free pop-up shows, the increasingly influential Bridgers finally releases this third album, her first since 2020. Collaborators assisting with Bridgers’ heart-lifting indie-folk this time around include Alex G, Jack Antonoff and Bo Burnham.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreenSax machine … Joe Lovano.Photograph: Bianca de Vilar/Getty ImagesECM RecordsPodcastTh revered European jazz label ECM publishes this fascinating audio series featuring its roster of artists discussing new releases and the nature of improvisation. Recent highlights include saxophonist Joe Lovano on the nature of creative trust.The Bittman ProjectSubstackWriter Mark Bittman’s newsletter explores the social and political impacts of the modern food industry, from the recent US cyclospora outbreak, which caused shoppers to re-examine the source of their vegetables, to the joys of cooking alone.Saving Young Men from Murder: The Homeboy StoryRadio 4, 18 August, 8pmPsychiatrist Dr Gwen Adshead has spent three decades working with perpetrators of violence. Visiting the gang rehabilitation programme Homeboy Industries in Los Angeles, she analyses how its psychological model could be applied to the UK.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From My Brilliant Career to Chelsea Wolfe: the week in rave reviews | Culture | The Guardian
description: A young woman battles social strictures in 1890s Australia in a charming period drama series, while the sonic experimentalist drops the drone metal for goth rock. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A young woman battles social strictures in 1890s Australia in a charming period drama series, while the sonic experimentalist drops the drone metal for goth rock. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
Content: Dress to impress … Genevieve O'Reilly and Phillipa Northeast in My Brilliant Career.Photograph: Ian Routledge/NetflixView image in fullscreenDress to impress … Genevieve O'Reilly and Phillipa Northeast in My Brilliant Career.Photograph: Ian Routledge/NetflixThe week in reviewsCultureFrom My Brilliant Career to Chelsea Wolfe: the week in rave reviewsA young woman battles social strictures in 1890s Australia in a charming period drama series,  while the sonic experimentalist drops the drone metal for goth rock. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviewsSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTVIf you only watch one, make it …My Brilliant CareerNetflix; available nowSummed up in a sentenceA joyous, witty and beautiful adaptation of the classic feminist novel about a young woman in 1890s Australia who rebels against society’s expectations.What our reviewer said“Sybylla, the charmingly irrepressible and irrepressibly charming heroine, is played utterly convincingly and with vim, vigour and joy by Philippa Northeast. Creator Liz Doran must have wept with happiness when they found an actor capable of bringing so much to an already glorious script – and who embodies the joie de vivre upon which so much of the plot, as everyone she meets becomes part of her orbit, depends.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewPick of the restThe Schoolgirl Terrorist?Channel 4; out nowView image in fullscreenThe Schoolgirl Terrorist?.Photograph: Rhianan RuddSummed up in a sentenceA documentary that speaks to the family of Rhianan Rudd, a teenager who was the youngest girl ever charged with terror offences in the UK, and who later died by suicide after the charge was dropped.What our reviewer said“By the end of the hour you feel like you have sat through a nightmare, watching [her mother] Emily and others who loved Rhianan shout into voids that were supposedly filled with people trained and ready to help those in exactly their situation.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewYou may have missed …PossessionSky Atlantic/Now TV; available nowSummed up in a sentenceGugu Mbatha-Raw is a lawyer who has a nightmarish experience when she is sent to a Jamaican plantation to get to the bottom of a mystery about an inheritance.What our reviewer said“Possession is a well-textured, evocative tale touching on many important questions, if never quite digging down far enough into any of them to be truly satisfying.’”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewFurther reading‘You can’t paper over the cracks of history. It will haunt you’: Gugu Mbatha-Raw on her race-horror thrillerFilmIf you only watch one, make it …LadyOut nowView image in fullscreenLady.Summed up in a sentenceFleabag’s Sian Clifford plays delusional Lady Isabella Ravenhyde, who fancies herself “the aristocracy’s answer to the Kardashians” and invites a documentary-maker into her stately pile with comically calamitous results.What our reviewer said“A scuzzier, shroomier B-side to Saltburn. An outrageous barnstormer. But there are laughs and unexpected tenderness in this very peculiar sentimental education.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewPick of the restSteal this Story, Please!Out nowView image in fullscreenSteal This Story, Please!.Summed up in a sentenceA documentary about the life and times of campaigning US political journalist and talk radio host Amy Goodman, whose scoops range from oil giants and Bill Clinton to East Timor.What our reviewer said“On the air since 1996, Goodman is flying the flag for journalism of the unfashionably homespun progressive left, while America’s corporate news media are sheepishly capitulating to their tech oligarch owners.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewFurther reading‘They slammed their M16s against his skull’: inside the film about Amy Goodman’s fearless reportingTonyOut nowSummed up in a sentenceDominic Sessa puts on the chefs whites in this 70s-set origin story of TV star Anthony Bourdain, adapted from his bestselling memoir Kitchen Confidential.What our reviewer said“For all the drugs and punch-ups, this is an unexpectedly sentimental coming-of-age story. And it is entertaining but its feelgood trajectory is compromised by what we know of the author.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewFurther reading‘These cooks ripped each other apart’: Dominic Sessa on playing Anthony Bourdain, kitchen bullies and the joys of being a 70s barflyJames: Getting Away With ItOut nowSummed up in a sentenceA charming and funny documentary about the Manchester indie music stalwarts.What our reviewer said“The interpersonal dynamics of this band are fascinating. They’re a mixture of hippies and hardnuts, dreamers and pragmatists, united by music. And quite deliberately, it seems, they have maintained a position on the brink of implosion, always dancing on the edge of chaos.”Laurence PhelanRead the full reviewNow streamingMiss You, Love YouHBOView image in fullscreenMiss You, Love You.Photograph: HBOSummed up in a sentenceOscar winner Alison Janney and Andrew Rannells (Elijah from TV’s Girls) star in this grownup drama about a woman grieving the death of her husband with the help of her son’s personal assistant.What our reviewer said“The script allows for more depth and darkness than we often get to see from Janney, leading to one of her finest turns to date. I admired its willingness to allow characters to be selfish or exhausting or hypocritical even until the very end.”Benjamin LeeRead the full reviewFurther reading‘It was fun to get pushed around’: Andrew Rannells on ‘razzle dazzle’, kissing co-stars and being a better friend to Lena DunhamBooksIf you only read one, make it …A History of the Novel in Britain by Philip HensherReviewed by Kathryn HughesSummed up in a sentenceA rollicking literary adventure across 300 years.What our reviewer said“There is nothing dreary here; no sense of being back in the seminar room taking notes. Instead it is an excuse to revisit old literary loves and be reminded of ones that have slipped from view.”Read the full reviewPick of the restView image in fullscreenI Give You My Silence by Mario Vargas Llosa, translated by Adrian Nathan WestReviewed by Marcel TherouxSummed up in a sentenceThe late Nobel laureate’s final novel is an eccentric love letter to the music of Peru.What our reviewer said“By the novel’s end, I had followed Toño up the Pacific coast of Peru on Google Maps, made avalsplaylist on Spotify and searched the prices of return flights to Lima.”Read the full reviewCan Nothing Save Us? by Irvine WelshReviewed by Jake ArnottSummed up in a sentenceGun culture and generational conflict in an explosive American family saga.What our reviewer said“This late-career tour-de-forceexplores a collective emotional malaise at the heart of a great power in decline.”Read the full reviewThe Beverly Hills Housewife by James CahillReviewed by Ben EsthamSummed up in a sentenceAn exploration of David Hockney’s milieu via a painting of his muse, Betty Freeman.What our reviewer said“Rather than digging up the painting’s glossy surface, he glances off it into anecdotal histories of vanguard American music, the mythologised Los Angeles art scene, and much else besides.”Read the full reviewJohn Berger: From Life by Tom OvertonReviewed by Xan BrooksSummed up in a sentenceA multi-faceted biography of the pioneering critic.What our reviewer said“His exuberant biography is thick with detail and lit by wonder. It strains to paint the whole canvas and give us the man in full, warts and all.”Read the full reviewYou may have missed …View image in fullscreenAll Them Dogs by Djamel White reviewReviewed by Jack ArnottSummed up in a sentenceA homoerotic dance of desire and betrayal, longlisted for the Booker prize.What our reviewer said“White’s ability to conjure a downbeat world of rundown estates, boxing gyms and tattoo parlours is truly compelling, and there’s a real dynamism to his prose that combines street slang with poetic simile.”Read the full reviewFurther readingThis Booker longlist may have two previous winners, but it’s keen to experimentAlbumsIf you only listen to one, make it …Chelsea Wolfe: The DarkOut 21 AugustView image in fullscreenChelsea Wolfe.Photograph: Magdalena WosinskaSummed up in a sentenceThe Californian sonic experimentalist dabbles in various genres, from folk to windswept goth-rock a la Evanescence, on this expansive ninth album.What our reviewer said“Drone and doom metal has almost entirely made way for brooding bass lines, wailing guitars, dramatic dynamic shifts and subtle orchestrations.”Dave SimpsonRead the full reviewPick of the restHenry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto: FifteenOut nowView image in fullscreenDafnis Prieto, Vijay Iyer and Henry Threadgill.Photograph: Michael WilsonSummed up in a sentencePianist/composer Vijay Iyer and Cuban percussionist Dafnis Prieto join forces with 82-year-old Pulitzer prize-winning flautist on this dizzying, improv-heavy opus.What our reviewer said“Hearteningly delightful contemporary music-making.”John FordhamRead the full reviewOpen Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal: Doomed!Out nowSummed up in a sentenceAdding to the canon of breakup albums, Doomed! picks over the bones of US rapper Open Mike Eagle’s five-year relationship, aided by producer Segal’s glistening beats.What our reviewer said‘“It’s the sound of Open Mike Eagle replaying every row and coming up with the ideal comeback just a few months too late.”Will PritchardRead the full reviewExplore more on these topicsCultureThe week in reviewsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Community Shield offers insight into Arsenal’s desire and Maresca’s Manchester City impact | Community Shield | The Guardian
description: Wembley curtain-raiser can offer clues but it is no reliable pointer to a season – its winners have not landed the title since 2018
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: Wembley curtain-raiser can offer clues but it is no reliable pointer to a season – its winners have not landed the title since 2018
Content: Mikel Arteta and Enzo Maresca come head to head at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Sunday.Composite: Guardian Design; Tyler Miller/Sportsfile via Getty Images; Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta and Enzo Maresca come head to head at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Sunday.Composite: Guardian Design; Tyler Miller/Sportsfile via Getty Images; Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty ImagesCommunity ShieldCommunity Shield offers insight into Arsenal’s desire and Maresca’s Manchester City impactJonathan WilsonWembley curtain-raiser can offer clues but it is no reliable pointer to a season – its winners have not landed the title since 2018Sat 15 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTShareThe doubt for anyone when a long-strived-for goal has been achieved is hunger. Arsenal waited 22 years for their 14th league title and, compounding the yearning, finished second three times in a row before finally lifting the Premier League trophy in May. The physical exertions of last season were immense – as seen by Declan Rice’s clear exhaustion and Bukayo Saka’s intermittent contributions at the World Cup, where William Salibapicked up a back injury– but so too was the emotional strain.The first weeks of a new season after a major tournament, especially the World Cup, are often a little erratic anyway, but this feels like a particularly unpredictable start to a campaign. Nine of the 20 Premier League clubs have changed manager this summer. For the first time in 40 years, none of the five big managerial beasts of the Premier League era – Sir Alex Ferguson, Arsène Wenger, José Mourinho, Jürgen Klopp and Pep Guardiola – will be in charge of a club. There are unknowns and uncertainty everywhere, even atArsenal. Mikel Arteta may be the longest-serving manager in the league but there are questions even there; it would be no great surprise if Arsenal were to start slowly.Enzo Maresca says Manchester City will not meet Chelsea’s deadline for FernándezRead moreManchester City are at the other end of the scale, after two seasons that were disappointing by their extremely elevated recent standards, and with a new manager after a decade under Guardiola. Enzo Maresca may look like his predecessor and his football may look like a version of his predecessor’s – notably from that period when he was his assistant manager – but he arrives at City surrounded by questions. He led Leicester to promotion and won the Europa Conference League and Club World Cup with Chelsea, but fans of those clubs seemed unconvinced by the style of play. And while Chelsea clearly had problems with the balance of their squad, and got dramatically worse after he left, it wasn’t entirely clear he was making the best of the resources he had.The Community Shield is a first opportunity to make some kind of assessment of whether Arsenal’s hunger is as sharp as it was last season, and of how City’s squad are adapting to their new manager. It is, though, a largely ceremonial occasion, any lessons drawn to be taken with extreme caution. Notsince 2018have the winners of the Community Shield gone on to win the Premier League; in that sense, it’s a sort of anti-bellwether. Where it can give indicators as to the season ahead tends to be less in showcasing the strengths of a potential champion than in exposing the flaws that might bring a side low.View image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca looks like his predecessor, and his football can resemble some of Pep Guardiola’s, but he has challenges to overcome.Photograph: Lee Jin-man/APThis year is unlikely to bring a repeat of 1974, when the scrap between Kevin Keegan and Billy Bremner exposed both the Liverpool forward’s unease at the retirement of Bill Shankly and, more consequentially, the general loss of morale at Leeds after Brian Clough had succeeded Don Revie. Often the significance of the Community Shield is properly recognised only in retrospect. José Mourinho was clearly in a strange mood when he turned up for the 2015-16 game unshaven and in tracksuit bottoms and a baggy T-shirt before suffering hisfirst ever defeat to Arsène Wenger. Few suspected, though, the chaos that was about to unspool at Chelsea, culminating with Mourinho’s dismissal that December.Last season, asCrystal Palace beat Liverpool on penaltiesafter a 2-2 draw, there were abundant indications of what was to come, especially about Arne Slot’s side. Mohamed Salah seemed disconnected from the rest of the forward line. The defence was a mess. Twice they conceded equalisers. Whether they were recognised at the time is another matter; the difficulty is separating teething problems or a team being only partway through their preparation for the new season from longer-term issues that could still be undermining a team two or three months into the season.There are few obvious questions to which Sunday’s meeting could begin to offer answers. Bruno Guimarães came off the bench for Arsenal in Wednesday’s friendly against Como and could be involved, probably alongside Myles Lewis-Skelly in midfield. The 19-year-old has been prominent in pre-season after Declan Rice, Martín Zubimendi and Martin Ødegaard were given extended breaks after the World Cup, but he has been linked with a move. In that context, his celebration after scoring against Como, making a heart sign with his hands and tapping the badge, felt significant.After thesale of Leandro Trossard, the left side of Arsenal’s attack is in need of strengthening. Morgan Rogers went to Chelsea and Vinícius Júnior stayed at Real Madrid, but they did sign the24-year-old Greece international Christos Tzolisfrom Club Brugge. Sunday offers an opportunity to see how he fits in, and whether Arsenal still need another option on that flank.For City, the biggest personnel issue probably surrounds the future of Rodri, whoseproposed move to Barcelonais yet to materialise, which in turn leaves City hanging on a potential replacement. Enzo Fernández appears the preferred candidate but whether his comparative lack of physicality can be accommodated deep in midfield, even after the signing of the robust Elliot Anderson, remains to be seen.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPhil Foden, pictured in action against Atlético Madrid during their recent friendly, has a chance to reassert himself.Photograph: Chung Sung-Jun/Getty ImagesTijjani Reijnders started friendlies against Inter and Atlético but is on his way to Al-Qadsiah while Bernardo Silva has joined Real Madrid, meaning a significant overhaul of midfield. Whether that includes Phil Foden in the long term is unclear. Since being named player of the year in 2024, he has struggled for form, but started the Inter and Atlético games. As others recover from the World Cup, the next few weeks offer an opportunity to reassert himself.Given he started only 11 games over the past two seasons, thedeparture of John Stonesprobably matters less from a footballing point of view than in the loss of a dressing-room leader. Without Stones and Silva – and Guardiola – the character of the squad cannot but be different.Sunday constitutes an opportunity to see both what the new City may look like, and how Arsenal have adapted, having at last won the title. But it’s only the Community Shield; any conclusions should be treated with appropriate caution.Explore more on these topicsCommunity ShieldArsenalManchester CityFriendliescommentShareReuse this content

title: Novak Djokovic suffers in Cincinnati heat as Thiago Agustín Tirante inflicts shock defeat | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Novak Djokovic toiled in the heat and humidity as he lost his opening game at the Cincinnati Masters to Argentina’s Thiago Agustín Tirante
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Novak Djokovic toiled in the heat and humidity as he lost his opening game at the Cincinnati Masters to Argentina’s Thiago Agustín Tirante
Content: Novak Djokovic reacts during his defeat by Thiago Tirante at the Cincinnati Open.Photograph: Shaina Benhiyoun/SPP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic reacts during his defeat by Thiago Tirante at the Cincinnati Open.Photograph: Shaina Benhiyoun/SPP/ShutterstockTennisNovak Djokovic suffers in Cincinnati heat as Thiago Agustín Tirante inflicts shock defeatArgentinian powers to 2-6, 6-4, 6-4 victoryHeat and humidity take toll on DjokovicFery holds off Duckworth  6-4, 2-6 7-6(4)Tumaini Carayolat the Lindner Family Tennis CenterSat 15 Aug 2026 18.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 20.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe scoreboard did not yet indicate that anything was awry, but even asNovak Djokovicled by a set in his opening match at the Cincinnati Open, he was already struggling badly.From the second set onwards, he spent much of his time between points squatting and bending over as he desperately tried to catch his breath in the notorious Ohioan humidity. He was eventually dispatched 2-6, 6-4, 6-4 by Thiago Agustín Tirante of Argentina, who took this golden opportunity to register the biggest win of his career.After more than a decade of dominating his sport regardless of terrain, early losses for Djokovic at the non-slam events have become increasingly familiar. The 39-year-old has long insisted that, at such an advanced age, the grand slam tournaments and Olympics are his priority. His results have reflected this reality.While Djokovic reached the final at Roland Garros and he returned to thesemi-final of Wimbledon last month, this was just his third non-grand slam tournament of the season. He has failed to reach the quarter-finals in any of those tournaments, compiling a 2-3 record across his appearances at Indian Wells, Rome and Cincinnati.View image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic was seen struggling in the heat and humidity.Photograph: Shaina Benhiyoun/SPP/ShutterstockEarly on, Djokovic seemed to be well on his way to a straightforward win as he rolled through the opening set without a problem. However, he began to wilt in the humidity from early in the second set. He called for the physio and doctor while leading 6-2, 2-1, where he vomited into a towel before having his blood pressure checked. He continued to move at half-speed for most of the match. “It was not an enjoyable match for me, for sure, the way I felt,” Djokovic said. “Not the first, I guess, not the last time, but it is what it is.”While Djokovic crumbled, Tirante remained strong throughout. The 25-year-old Argentinian is one of the biggest servers in the world, and he used his serve and potent forehand well to force an already uncomfortable Djokovic behind the baseline before closing out a victory. Incredibly, the world No 50 now holds a 4-1 record against top 10 opponents.After his defeat, Djokovic walked directly from the court to his media conference, where he briefly explained his struggles with humidity. “It’s just the condition that I have health-wise,” he said. “It’s been bothering me for the last couple of years. And a lot of issues, especially when it’s humid and hot. Yeah.”Djokovic said he had anticipated a difficult day but tension and pressure of matchplay had naturally made things worse. “Yeah, I did, but it is all these things … nerves and everything involved makes it worse. So that’s what happened.”View image in fullscreenThiago Agustín Tirante took full advantage of Novak Djokovic’s struggles.Photograph: Wally Nell/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockAsked if he believes he will return to Cincinnati, Djokovic responded: “I certainly hope so, but it looks more likely not, unfortunately. But let’s see what the future brings.”Djokovic’s preparation for this tournament had been preceded by a promotional tour for his upcoming Amazon Prime documentary, with the Serb spending time in the United States during the World Cup before setting his sights on the final weeks of the North American hard court swing.He explained before the tournament that he had decided to compete in Cincinnati in order to give himself some matches before the US Open. Instead, he again faces the challenge of finding his feet quickly in New York as he attempts to continue his excellent results at the grand slam tournaments, where he has reached the semi-final or better in six of his last seven appearances.Elsewhere, Arthur Fery made a positive start to his first ever appearance in the Cincinnati Open main draw as he held his nerve at the end of an incredibly tight tussle to defeat James Duckworth 6-4, 2-6 7-6(4) and reach the third round.Fery had opted to take four weeks off after Wimbledon, meaning this was his first match since his run to the semi-finals at the All England Club, a result that has changed the trajectory of his career. He had never previously won a Masters 1000 main draw match and this was his first ever direct appearance at a Masters 1000 despite being seeded.It required an immense fight for the 32nd seed to drag himself over the line. He began well, taking the ball early dictating from inside the baseline, before his level dropped and he quickly found himself in a final set. Both players comfortably held serve in set three until the final set tiebreak, where Duckworth made the first move to lead *4-3 with a mini-break. Fery responded brilliantly, lasering two excellent, deep returns in succession to reach 5-4 before serving extremely well to close out the match.An even greater challenge awaits Fery in round three as he faces the fifth seed Alex de Minaur. De Minaur, who has been struggling to find his form recently, recovered from a set down to defeat the qualifier Quentin Halys 1-6, 6-3, 7-6(4).Explore more on these topicsTennisNovak DjokovicnewsShareReuse this content

title: Championship roundup: Middlesbrough seal comeback win; West Brom beat Norwich | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Will Lankshear scored a second-half double on his debut as Middlesbrough fought back to start their Championship campaign with a 2-1 victory over Lincoln
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Will Lankshear scored a second-half double on his debut as Middlesbrough fought back to start their Championship campaign with a 2-1 victory over Lincoln
Content: Middlesbrough's Will Lankshear celebrates scoring their winner against Lincoln.Photograph: Bruce Rollinson/PAView image in fullscreenMiddlesbrough's Will Lankshear celebrates scoring their winner against Lincoln.Photograph: Bruce Rollinson/PASoccerChampionship roundup: Middlesbrough seal comeback win; West Brom beat NorwichLankshear ends Lincoln’s nine-month unbeaten runMillwall start with 2-0 win over 10-man Bristol CityPA MediaSat 15 Aug 2026 12.37 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWill Lankshear scored a second-half double on his debut asMiddlesbroughfought back to kick off their Championship campaign with a hard-fought 2-1 victory, ending promotedLincoln’sremarkable nine-month unbeaten run.The Imps – playing their first second-tier match in 65 years – made a strong start and opened the scoring in the 12th minute through Adam Reach. But the former Tottenham forward Lankshear marked his first league appearance since his move to the Riverside by equalising just after the hour and then stabbing in a stoppage-time winner.It was a devastating end for Lincoln as a run of 29 games undefeated in all competitions since early December was brought to a halt in their first league match since their new joint head coach partnership of Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw stepped up to take over after the departure of Michael Skubala toBristol Cityin May.Philippe Clement was left feeling extremely hard done by after watching hisNorwichside lose 2-1 at home toWest Brom. Clement felt his side should have won the game comfortably with the number of chances they created – and also felt Aune Heggebø’s opener, which came against the run of play, should have been ruled out for handball.“It was clearly with the arm that the player scores – we could see that from where we were watching, 50 yards away,” he said. “It was the decisive moment in the game and should have been spotted. There are four officials and one of them should have seen it. Maybe the referee didn’t have the best view – but the linesman on our side needs to see that. Missing game-changing moments like this shouldn’t happen – it has cost us at least two, maybe three points.”View image in fullscreenAune Heggebø (right) appeared to score West Brom’s opener against Norwich with his arm.Photograph: Paul Chesterton/Focus Images Ltd/ShutterstockNorwich were on the front foot for most of the game but could not find a way past a resolute defence, and were made to pay for failing to take their chances as Albion scored two late goals to make it a dream start to the new season.The visitors went in front on 75 minutes when Callum Styles played in Jimmy-Jay Morgan, whose cross was bundled over the line by Heggebø. With three minutes remaining, Morgan made it two with his third goal since joining the Baggies in the summer, racing clear and working his way into the box before blasting the ball home. Mathias Kvistgaarden nodded home a loose ball as the game entered added time.Ilias Chair scored twice asQPRcame from behind to beatPortsmouth3-1 and claim their first win at Fratton Park in 26 years. Pompey dominated the opening half an hour and took the lead through Terry Devlin’s long-range screamer. But Rangers scored three times in 15 minutes before half-time.Quick GuideLeague One: Lowe penalty gives Wednesday winning startShowJamal Lowe converted a second-half penalty asSheffield Wednesdaymade a winning start in  League One following relegation with a 2-1 victory atLeyton Orient. The Owls, under new ownership since succumbing to the earliest relegation in English Football League history in February, went ahead through Callum Slattery’s debut goal before Joseph Olowu levelled before the break. But Lowe picked himself up after being fouled in the area by James Morris to fire home from the spot in the 66th minute.Former Premier League championsLeicesterwere denied victory atNotts Countyin their first match since relegation as they were held 1-1. Conor Grant’s late strike cancelled out Jayden Joseph’s second-half opener for Leicester and salvaged a deserved point for the home side.Ciaron Brown’s stoppage-time equaliser rescued another relegated side,Oxford, earning them a 2-2 draw at newly-promotedMK Dons. Charlie Goode and Aaron Collins gave the Dons a 2-1 half-time lead after Mark Harris had fired the U’s in front before Brown turned home a cross in the fifth minute of added time.Substitute Gideon Kodua scrambled a stoppage-time winner to sealLutona 4-3 win atReading, for whom Jack Marriott scored a first-half hat-trick.Huddersfield’ssummer signing Derensili Sanches Fernandes struck twice as they beatAFC Wimbledon3-0 at home despite the first-half dismissal of Bali Mumba.Victor Adeboyejo fired a second-half winner asBromleywon 1-0 atBarnsleyfor their first-ever win in the third tier following promotion.CambridgeUnitedheld off a fightback to beatWigan3-2 on the U’s return to League One.Goals from Kell Watts, Louis Appere and Isaac Heath put the hosts in control but Wigan  made a game of it in the last 20 minutes when Sonny Perkins and Akeel Higgins set up a nervy finish.BlackpoolandWycombeshared the points in an opening day 1-1 draw.The visitors led for long periods at Bloomfield Road, following an early opener from Fred Onyedinma. This was cancelled out by substitute Finley Munroe, who made an instant impact following his loan move from Middlesbrough last week.Bradfordmade a winning start  with a comfortable 2-0 victory overPeterborough, who finished with 10 men after David Okagbue’s red card.Second-half goals from Macaulay Gillesphey and Nick Powell were enough for last season’s play-off semi-finalists to secure three points.Stockporteased to a sparkling 3-1 win at Plymouth as Jack Diamond scored their opener, helped set up a second for Kyle Wootton and a third for Ryan Glover before Xavier Amaechi gave Argyle a late consolation.Mansfieldmade a winning start with a hard-fought 2-1 victory overDoncaster.Rhys Oates swept home the opener but Rovers levelled four minutes after the break when through Jack Senior before Mansfield deservedly won it in the 74th minute with a free-kick from Louis Reed.Olly Sanderson bundled home in stoppage time to snatchStevenagea point in a 1-1 draw atBurton. The former Fulham youngster came off the bench to cancel out Jack Armer’s second-half strike for the Brewers.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Josh Coburn scored twice asMillwallkicked off their campaign with a comfortable 2-0 win over 10-manBristol Cityat Ashton Gate. The home side went a man down after 36 minutes when midfielder Adam Randell was shown a second yellow card for a foul to prevent a counterattack.Five minutes later, Coburn converted a low Ryan Leonard cross from the right with a near-post volley. Coburn then doubled the advantage after 50 minutes, taking advantage of poor defending to score unchallenged with a downward header from 10 yards.The result meant that Skubala’s reign as City manager has begun with two home defeats, after the shock Carabao Cup exit at the hands of League Two Walsall, and without his side scoring a goal.View image in fullscreenJosh Coburn scores Millwall’s second against Bristol City.Photograph: Alex Pantling/Getty ImagesSteven Schumacher celebratedBolton’sfirstChampionshipwin for seven years after surviving a late scare againstPreston. Sam Dalby and Thierry Gale put Bolton in command with first-half goals, but the Preston substitute Jusef Erabi ensured a nervy ending by pulling a goal back in the 86th minute. Liam Lindsay passed up a chance to equalise, heading over in added time, to leave Schumacher a relieved man.“That’s what this division is all about,” he said. “From being in control of the game we’re happy they missed a sitter at the end not to take away our three points. It’s going to be an exciting ride so strap in.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTyreece Campbell’s impressive start to the new season continued as his 80th-minute goal earnedCharltona 2-1 victory overDerbyat The Valley. It capped off a week to forget for the Rams after the takeover by the Saudi government official Turki Alalshikh collapsed on Monday.Sammie Szmodics, who scored in the EFL Cup loss to Lincoln, put Derby into a lead at the halfway point. But Lloyd Jones, who signed a new two-year contract on Friday, headed the Addicks level before Campbell produced an excellent finish to seal maximum points for the home side.Quick GuideLeague Two: York return with victoryShowYorkdebutant Harry Boyes bagged a brace to mark the club’s EFL return after a 10-year absence with a thrilling 3-2 home triumph overBristol Rovers.Boyes – a summer signing from Southend – netted the first EFL goals of his career and was joined on the Minstermen scoresheet by Alex Newby.Clinton Mola had given Steve Evans’ visitors a first-half lead and substitute Tommy Leigh later levelled from the penalty spot, but Boyes had the last say.Newportand new manager Hayden Mullins enjoyed a dream start to their League Two campaign with a 3-0 home win over newly-promotedRochdale.First-half goals from summer signings Kyle Cameron and Shaquille Gwengwe put the Exiles in charge at a sun-baked Rodney Parade.Calum Kavanagh’s second-half double gaveOldhama 2-0 home win against relegatedPort Vale.Kavanagh, who scored twice in 10 games last season after arriving from Bradford in January, struck twice in the space of 15 minutes to earn the Latics an opening-day victory.Charlie Caton scored twice butAccringtonhad to settle for a point in a 2-2 draw withColchester.Colchester who broke the deadlock after 24 minutes when Ellis Iandolo headed home. Stanley levelled five minutes later when Shaun Whalley’s cross was headed into the far corner by Caton. The Reds took the lead in the first minute of added time at the end of the first half as Caton in the box and he fired home.Colchester equalised on the hour when Rob Hunt’s high cross dipped straight into the top corner of the net.Goals from Oisin Gallagher, Charlie Lakin and Kabongo Tshimanga earnedBarneta 3-1 opening-day win overSalford.The trio struck to put the Bees in full control before Adebola Oluwo’s last-minute consolation.A debut strike from Leicester loanee Jake Evans sealed a 2-1 home win forCheltenhamoverRotherham.The Robins led through Charlie McCann’s first-half strike before Jili Buyabu levelled for the Millers in the 62nd minute. But Evans, who turns 18 on Friday, went on from the bench and sealed the points for Steve Cotterill’s side.Veteran striker Ched Evans scored the only goal of the game, finding the net against one of his former clubs to giveFleetwoodan opening day 1-0 victory atChesterfield.Josh March headed the winner in the fifth minute of stoppage time as 10-manCrewegot the better of nine-manCrawleyat the Broadfield Stadium.Late goals from Isaac Moore, James Connolly and Aaron Pressley did the damage asWalsallsecured a fine 3-0 away win overGillingham.Grimsbygot off to a winning start at the expense of newly-relegatedExeterwith a tightly-contested 1-0 triumph at Blundell Park.Harvey Rodgers gave the hosts the lead 36 minutes in as he got on the end of a corner from Charles Vernam, with the linesman calling it over the line before it was cleared.Tranmerecompleted a 2-0 victory overShrewsbury.Jordan Davies’ first league goal for the club and a Charlie Whitaker wonder strike secured the points in an entertaining opening-day clash at Prenton Park.NorthamptonandSwindonplayed out a goalless draw at Sixfields.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Charlton’s manager, Nathan Jones, said later that he was hoping to secure Campbell on a new contract. His current deal expires next summer. “TC gets in those positions all the time and one-v-one he is a threat. We just want the outcomes from him. We are in really advanced negotiations with him. We’re hoping we can get that done.”Adam Idah snatched the winner with his first touch asSwanseabattled back from a goal down to beatStoke2-1. The Republic of Ireland international had been on the pitch for barely 60 seconds when he scored in the 66th minute as the Swans claimed their first win at Stoke for more than five years. Eric Bocat had fired Stoke into a 10th-minute lead and Joseph Opoku hit a 23rd-minute equaliser for the Swans, powering in with a sweet right-foot shot after some poor defending.Sheffield UnitedandBirminghammade an underwhelming start to the season in a goalless draw at Bramall Lane. Both sides have ambitions of mounting promotion challenges but there was not too much to get excited about.The only action of note in the opening half came just before the half-hour. The Blades went first as Patrick Bamford hooked Femi Seriki’s deflected cross just wide. Birmingham responded straight away and Alex Cochrane’s cross was perfect for Paik Seung-ho but the South Korean could not get enough on his header.Birmingham had a big moment in the 58th minute when Carlos Vicente was played through on goal but his attempted pass was cut out by Japhet Tanganga when the better option was to shoot. The visitors produced the first shot on target in the 62nd minute when Jay Stansfield’s low show was kept out by Michael Cooper.Explore more on these topicsFootballChampionshipMiddlesbroughLincoln CityNorwich CityWest Bromwich AlbionMillwallShareReuse this content

title: Scotland hope to name 39-year-old Pocognoli as successor to Clarke in fresh approach | Scotland | The Guardian
description: The Belgian, sacked by Monaco in June, would become Scotland’s first foreign manager since Berti Vogts from 2002-04
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The Belgian, sacked by Monaco in June, would become Scotland’s first foreign manager since Berti Vogts from 2002-04
Content: Former Monaco manager Sébastien Pocognoli led Union Saint-Gilloise to their first title in 90 years in 2025.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAView image in fullscreenFormer Monaco manager Sébastien Pocognoli led Union Saint-Gilloise to their first title in 90 years in 2025.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAScotlandScotland hope to name 39-year-old Pocognoli as successor to Clarke in fresh approachBelgian would be first non-Scot in role since Berti VogtsScotland face Slovenia on 26 September in Nations LeagueEwan MurraySat 15 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Scottish Football Association hopes to name the Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke as manager early next week. The 39-year-old, who was sacked by Monaco in June, will become the country’s first non-Scottish manager since Berti Vogts, who was in charge from 2002-04.Clarke’s abrupt departurecame asScotland exited the World Cupat the group stage. He had signed a four-year contract extension immediately before the tournament. It quickly became clear the SFA would turn towards a foreign manager; Jon Dahl Tomasson and Kasper Hjulmand were linked with the position.Pocognoli will probably be welcomed byScotlandfans in respect of a fresh approach. Clarke was in position for a generally successful seven years, but was often criticised for a pragmatic style.After a period in youth coaching, Pocognoli enjoyed a successful time in charge of Union Saint-Gilloise in his homeland. Under Pocognoli, Union won their first title in 90 years in 2025. A move to Monaco followed, but Pocognoli lasted eight months and 38 games in France.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland begin their Nations League campaign with the visit to Slovenia on 26 September. Pocognoli’s first home game in charge will be Switzerland’s visit to Glasgow three days later.Explore more on these topicsScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Finlay Tarling’s NSN team withdraw from Volta a Portugal day after his death | Cycling | The Guardian
description: NSN Development has said: ‘We will continue to hold Fin in our hearts,’ as they announced their withdrawal from the Volta a Portugal
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: NSN Development has said: ‘We will continue to hold Fin in our hearts,’ as they announced their withdrawal from the Volta a Portugal
Content: Finlay Tarling was reportedly involved in a head-on collision.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPAView image in fullscreenFinlay Tarling was reportedly involved in a head-on collision.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPACyclingFinlay Tarling’s NSN team withdraw from Volta a Portugal day after his death19-year-old killed on Friday by collision with van‘We will continue to hold Fin in our hearts’Agence France-PresseSat 15 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinlay Tarling’s NSN Development team withdrew from the Volta a Portugal on Saturday, the day afterthe death of the 19-year-old British riderin an accident during the race.Tarling, the younger brother of the Ineos rider Josh, was reportedly involved in a head-on collision with a vehicle unconnected with the event that was travelling in the opposite direction.“Following Fin Tarling’s tragic passing, the NSN Development Team has withdrawn from the remaining Volta a Portugal stages,” NSN said. “With the full support of Fin’s parents, the World Tour team will race on at Czech Tour and the Arctic Race of Norway.“We will continue to hold Fin in our hearts as we race in his honour, doing what he loved most.”Friday’s eighth stage was suspended with about 20km remaining and the podium ceremony was cancelled.A spokesperson for Portugal’s national republican guard said there had been a collision between a cyclist and a light vehicle towards the back of the peloton. “We do not yet know exactly the circumstances in which it unfolded. We will investigate.”The race resumed on Saturday with the leader, Alex Guerin, wearing a black jersey and riders wearing black armbands on the penultimate stage.“The ninth stage of the Volta a Portugal set off in an atmosphere of mourning,” said organisers on social media. “Before the symbolic start, a minute of silence was observed in memory of Finlay Tarling.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOrganisers said sponsors had cancelled planned activities this weekend out of respect. “The race continues. There will be a sporting competition but not a party,” they said in a statement. “This Saturday, the Tour cycles for Finlay.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s U20 World Cup boycott may hurt in short term but can send Fifa a vital message | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Women’s football has much to gain from the kind of reforms that threats to snub upcoming tournaments might prompt. Infantino should be taken on
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Women’s football has much to gain from the kind of reforms that threats to snub upcoming tournaments might prompt. Infantino should be taken on
Content: Gianni Infantino congratulates Spain’s players after their 2023 Women’s World Cup win. Some progress has been made under Fifa’s president but it remains heavily male-dominated.Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino congratulates Spain’s players after their 2023 Women’s World Cup win. Some progress has been made under Fifa’s president but it remains heavily male-dominated.Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty ImagesFifaWomen’s U20 World Cup boycott may hurt in short term but can send Fifa a vital messageTom GarryWomen’s football has much to gain from the kind of reforms that threats to snub upcoming tournaments might prompt. Infantino should be taken onSat 15 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTShare“And I say to all the women … Pick the right battles. Pick the right fights. You have the power to change. You have the power to convince us men what we have to do and what we don’t have to do. You do it. Just do it. With men, withFifa, you will find open doors. Just push the doors. They are open.”Those werethe condescending words of Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, three years ago during a tone-deaf speech in Sydney, which left his audience, including some of the most senior women in the game, exasperated. It is a damning indictment of Infantino’s tenure that his patronising monologue on the eve of the Women’s World Cup final now barely even creeps into the top 10 of the most controversial moments since his latest re-election, in March 2023.Europe’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsedRead moreYet, with the Swiss administrator’s future hanging finely in the balance, the power to enforce once-in-a-generation change at Fifa may well be in the hands of women’s teams after all, as the threat of a boycott lingers over September’s Women’s Under-20 World Cup, the Women’s Under-17 World Cup, which gets under way in October, and that month’s senior World Cup playoff ties for next summer’s major showpiece, the Women’s World Cup in Brazil.This week Lisa Nandy told the BBC that Infantino “should go” and, overall, the culture secretary spoke well on the matter, but she added that she would not support a boycott of the U20 World Cup and said she was “not generally in favour of sporting boycotts full stop – because they unfairly penalise athletes and competitors who are not responsible for the reason that these boycotts take place”. On that specific element, it is important to respectfully disagree with Nandy and the many others who share that view.Yes, it would feel deeply unjust for football’s political turmoil to have an adverse impact on the development of the world’s best young women footballers through no fault of their own, but that is why any participating countries being prepared to boycott the upcoming under-20 tournament would send such a powerful message.It is tempting to follow the stance that many working within the women’s game are taking privately, which is that it would be a travesty if women’s football, having been neglected and let down by the authorities for generations, was harmed again by disruption to such a significant tournament, but the painful reality is that the young generation of women’s stars stand to be most affected by the decisions that are made by governing bodies in the days, weeks and months ahead.View image in fullscreenNorth Korea celebrate winning the most recent Women’s U20 World Cup, in 2024.Photograph: Julian Medina/SPP/ShutterstockAnd yes, is it unfair for women’s teams, and young women’s teams in particular, to shoulder the responsibility of taking a stance against the now-scrapped vision of selling off a stake in Fifa tournaments – which, we should remember, would include all Fifa’s women’s tournaments too – through the murky concept of the Fifa Forward Enterprise subsidiary, but it is their futures, and the organisation of the World Cups finals that will come to define their careers, which are at stake.And the future of the governance of the sport, and decisions about who runs the game, is a debate that women’s football players, coaches and fans all deserve a much more vocal say in, on far more deep-rooted injustices than those that have dominated the news in recent weeks.Is it fair that, for example, there are only two women – Paola López of Mexico and Vietnam’s Thi My Dung Nguyen – among the 18 members of Fifa’s disciplinary committee, which hit the headlines amid the farcical Folarin Balogun scandal this summer? Or that all 10 of the members of Fifa’s Future of Football committee are men?Is it fair that, of the 37 members of Fifa’s council, the organisation’s strategic and oversight body, 29 are men and only eight are women? Or that seven of the eight vice-presidents are men?Is it fair that the 2023 Women’s World Cup prize money totalled $110m and this summer’s men’s World Cup’s prize pot was around eight times larger, at a record-breaking $871m?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt would be wrong to say that there have not been positive improvements in women’s football across the world since Infantino took office in 2016. The past decade has included long overdue, albeit still very important and welcome, enhancements to provisions for players and coaches at women’s tournaments, a sizeable growth in financial investment and huge uplift in prize money, albeit from a very low bar. It is also fair to say that there are many key figures in the women’s game, across all continents, who support Infantino and are appreciative of the gradual improvements that are being made, while acknowledging that there is still a very long way to go.View image in fullscreenLucy Bronze has backed a boycott.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PABut everyone associated with women’s football should be concerned that the 25-page sales pitch that was titled Fifa Forward Enterprise Member Materials contained only one token reference to women’s football. It is why the England defender Lucy Bronze was right to use her voice to say she backed a boycott “for the good of the game”.On Friday morning, the latest twist in Infantino’s future delivered both positives and negatives for the under-fire president, as on the one hand, the Oceania Football Confederationdeclared its support for Infantino, while the confederation’s biggest member, New Zealand, withdrew its backing for him. New Zealand, impeccable co-hosts of the most recent Women’s World Cup, will have had plenty of reasons to support Infantino but has chosen to use its platform to call for “stronger governance, accountability and transparency”.Shortly before that news, on Thursday, a feature article was published on Fifa’s website entitled “Europe’s finest hours at the Under-20 Women’s World Cup”, looking back at dazzling performances of young breakthrough stars such as Spain’s Salma Paralluelo’s in 2022 or the Germany striker Alexandra Popp in 2010. Next month six European teams – including the hosts, Poland – are scheduled to show the world what they are capable of, but – whether the timing of that article was purely coincidental, political or ironic – European women’s under-20 teams’ finest hour may still be yet to come.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsWomen's footballcommentShareReuse this content

title: I feel guilt talking to those left behind in Afghanistan. While I enjoy freedom, they are prisoners | Nelufar Hedayat | The Guardian
description: Five years since the Taliban returned to power, life – especially for women – is merciless and suffocating, says Afghan-British journalist Nelufar Hedayat
Author: Nelufar Hedayat
Headline: Five years since the Taliban returned to power, life – especially for women – is merciless and suffocating, says Afghan-British journalist Nelufar Hedayat
