Content: A Taliban soldier stands guard as women arrive to receive food supplies in Kabul, 25 March 2025.Photograph: Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Taliban soldier stands guard as women arrive to receive food supplies in Kabul, 25 March 2025.Photograph: Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAfghanistanI feel guilt talking to those left behind in Afghanistan. While I enjoy freedom, they are prisonersNelufar HedayatFive years since the Taliban returned to power, life – especially for women – is awful. We must keep the people’s stories alive and hope they will be free againSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.32 EDTShareThere are fewer and fewer stories coming out of the land of my birth. Before, I would open Instagram and see my cousins, lip-syncing to trending videos, posing with flowers at a rose garden or at a trendy cafe in their coolest outfits, keeping a record of their lives. I would hear British-Afghan friends talk about their recent trips to the provinces, towns and cities of their foremothers and the buzz of learning about their heritage. I would eagerly await the latest music video from Afghanistan’s many pop stars, all vying to become the hottest track played at weddings, not just inAfghanistanbut all over the world. Afghanistan, its culture, and people felt closer back then.Five years ago today, the brittle peace of the fragile new democracy was shattered by the withdrawal of western military, diplomatic and charitable groups that had intervened in the country’s fate since 2001. Overnight, on Sunday, 15 August 2021, Afghanistan was undone and abandoned.I spent the rest of the month glued to my phone, monitoring WhatsApp groups sprouting every day or so, with people asking for information and help, begging me to get them out of the country because we all knew what was coming, though the rest of the world seemed to lag behind.I was most focused on evacuating one friend from Kabul. She was a headteacher, and it was always her house I would go to first, whenever I went to Afghanistan. I had to have achingly tough phone conversations with her. “You can’t bring your children or your husband. I can only do this for you,” I said. She would agree. “I think I can get you to Albania or Qatar, but you might be in a refugee camp for months or years.” She would agree.The closest we came to getting her out her came six months later, in February 2022. I finally managed to get her a passport when it was virtually impossible to do so, but by then it was too late. TheTalibanwere running the airport and had cracked down on Afghans leaving the country.The last conversation we had on the phone was one of the hardest of my life. I had to tell the woman who had inspired me for so long, a feminist and someone who had advocated for education and self-fulfilment her whole life, that I was going to stop trying to rescue her. “I’ve tried everything I can think of and pushed everyone I know, but I can’t get you on a flight out.” I felt her spirit break as her uncertain fate collapsed into one reality – a life under Taliban rule.In a higher register than I had ever heard her voice before, she told me that this was going to wreak havoc on her already unmanageable diabetes; that she would never work or be self-sufficient again, and then she asked me a terrible question: surely to end her life now was better than carrying on?After all, this was the second time in my friend’s life that she would have to live under a Taliban regime. Neither of us spoke in a protracted, painful silence as we both felt the crushing weight of a learned helplessness that she and millions of Afghans would become intimately familiar with. The line went dead.Since then, our lives have diverged so much we cannot have a proper conversation. We try to speak but it feels as if the phone line is connecting parallel universes. Mine is full of work, family gatherings, gigs and holiday plans and hers of bombs, “morality police” and hand-to-mouth living. We both hesitate to share stories about our lives for fear it will upset the other. We have been rendered speechless.With the birth of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan ruled de facto by the Taliban regime, life changed immediately for my family and friends. The systemic assault on the female sex has resulted in the UN calling for gender apartheid to be recognised as adistinct crime against humanity.“During the previous government, my mother forced me to go to school, attend taekwondo classes, and visit the library,” says a friend who was 14 at the time of the western desertion of Afghanistan. “She wanted me to learn and have opportunities. My father agrees with the Taliban’s rules. He believes I should get money from my future husband instead. For me, this feels like being sold, and it is something I cannot accept.”It’s not just a gender war that has been raging in Afghanistan. In February 2026,Pakistan declared“open war” with its neighbour, unleashing airstrikes that killed hundreds, displacing many thousands more and devastating lives.A cousin tells me of the unadulterated fear these airstrikes brought on the citizens of Kabul. “It was truly frightening. Pakistani drones were launching rocket attacks, and we could only see the flames and hear the explosions in despair. I kept thinking that perhaps this time a rocket might strike our house.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAdd this to the 6 million refugeesforced back to Afghanistanby Iran and Pakistan, the EU meeting with the Taliban in Brussels forclosed-door talks, and half the population facingsevere food insecurity, and you’d be forgiven for thinking, like me, that even God is merciless when it comes to the land of my birth.It’s not that similar things hadn’t happened in Afghanistan before August 2021; it’s that I would also hear of other stories. Stories of heroism, a fight for democracy, a burgeoning arts scene, or event skating teenagers rocking the streets of Kabul. Now, there’s so little to do, such little movement possible, that almost everyone I speak to in Afghanistan sounds as though they’re suffocating. There is no distraction nor relief from the abject suffering of everyday Afghan people.The question now is what does resistance and resilience look like? The Taliban are not an inevitability. In their entire history, they have been in power half as long as UK and US forces were in Afghanistan: 10 years.Afghan people must keep their stories alive, of who and what we are, to help us rebuild an identity of our own making outside occupation and brutal theocracy for when the day arrives that the Taliban are no more. For me, that will mean calling my friend to learn about her life – to have, for the first time in five years, the impossible conversation.Nelufar Hedayat is an Afghan-British journalist, and the presenter and co-director of the documentary In Real Life: the God ThievesDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsAfghanistanOpinionViolence against women and girlsTalibanWomenSouth and central AsiacommentShareReuse this content

title: Sure, ‘Woke 1’ had its issues – but we have far bigger problems on our hands | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: AOC’s remarks about past excesses have been ripped out of context. Progressives shouldn’t get roped into this sideshow
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: AOC’s remarks about past excesses have been ripped out of context. Progressives shouldn’t get roped into this sideshow
Content: ‘Progressives also shouldn’t play into their hands by talking about Woke 1.0 instead of focusing on the dire state of the country right now.’Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Progressives also shouldn’t play into their hands by talking about Woke 1.0 instead of focusing on the dire state of the country right now.’Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesThe Week in PatriarchyUS politicsSure, ‘Woke 1’ had its issues – but we have far bigger problems on our handsArwa MahdawiAOC’s remarks about past excesses have been ripped out of context. Progressives shouldn’t get roped into this sideshowSat 15 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTShareThere is probably no word that has been more used and abused in the last decade than “woke”. It has been rendered completely meaningless, but it refuses to die. Indeed, it has now taken on new life: in the past week, there’s been a flurry of headlines about “Woke 1.0” or “Woke One”. If you haven’t seen the phrase pop up in your newsfeed yet, it will soon.So what is this cursed phrase? There’s no official definition, but the term is largely being used to refer to the period between 2018 and 2021 when social justice language was at its peak in mainstream culture. Certain progressives, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have started to use “Woke 1” disparagingly, as a way todistancethemselves from that period and signal that they stand for a new form of left-leaning politics that is more palatable to centrist Democrats. “Woke 2”, I suppose.We can blame the New York City councilmember Chi Ossé for coining the phrase. Back in May, hewrote on X: “Woke 1 was crazyyyy.” This was in response to someone reminding him that, in 2021, he’d said: “A cis white man should not be the next speaker of the Council.”Not that many people paid attention to the May post. But then Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez quoted it on arecent appearanceon ABC News’s This Week when she was asked about some statements the Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong had made. In 2020, Hong, who lost this week’s gubernatorial primary, tweeted that Thanksgiving should be cancelled. She also posted about defunding the police. AOC responded to a question about these “controversial” tweets by saying Hong had moved away from these positions.The congresswoman then noted: “I have a local city councilman that has this saying: ‘Woke 1.0 was crazy.’” After laughing at the phrase, Ocasio-Cortez went on to add: “During the pandemic, the doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place. And I actually think that the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful … I think that, you know, during lockdown, of course, rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today.”When you look at AOC’s full quote about Woke 1.0, it’s pretty reasonable. However, it has been ripped out of context and is being willfully misinterpreted by some people to suggest that Ocasio-Cortez thinks the excesses of that period were funny.Stephen Miller, for example, almost exploded on air after Fox News’s Will Cain played a clip of AOC talking about Woke 1 to him on air. Millerrantedfor almost five minutes about how woke policies resulted in a “historic increase in murders”. (Gun violencesurged in the US during Covid, but that wasn’t because of protests orbecausesome people wanted you to say “folx” instead of “guys”. It was for myriad reasons that we are still trying to understand but include school closures in low-income areas.)Miller added: “We’re all going to have a good laugh about that? ‘Sorry your husband was murdered.’ ‘Sorry your mom was killed.’ ‘Sorry your loved ones are six feet under the ground now.’ We’re going to have a good laugh about that? It’s sickening, it’s disgusting and the thing is, [Woke 1.0] never stopped.”The Atlantic, meanwhile, published a pieceheadlined“The Democrats Can’t Just Laugh Off ‘Woke 1’”, which argued: “Republicans have no incentive to let them forget past excesses.”Maybe not, but progressives also shouldn’t play into their hands by talking about Woke 1.0 instead of focusing on the dire state of the country right now. This isn’t to say we can’t learn from past mistakes. I think we can all agree that there were some embarrassing excesses between 2018-2020. There was the time, for example, when a Mexican American San Diego Gas and Electric employee got fired because someone thought he was doing the White Power symbol with his hand. All he was doing was hanging his arm out of his truck andcracking his knuckle. There was no evidence to prove he held white supremacist views, there was just a baying mob on Twitter.Was that incident bad? Yes, of course! Was some of the earnest discourse from the time cringe? Absolutely! But just take a minute and look around, why don’t you? The president of the US is monetizing his position in anunprecedented way. Pregnant women are dying preventable deaths because they can’t get access to safe abortions, and immigrants are being snatched off the street by masked thugs. Freedom of speech is under attack, and you can get deported for talking about the ongoing genocide in Gaza. Getting upset right now about Woke 1 is crazyyyy.ICE is locking people up for things their grandmother didDo take the time to read this shocking piecein the Nationby Maryam Tahmasebi, who is currently in ICE detention with her family because her mother-in-law was a translator for the Iranian hostage takers back in 1979. Tahmasebi and her husband are both professors and legal residents without so much as a traffic ticket on their records. They’re now locked up in separate facilities. Their son, who has been a legal resident of California for 12 years and wasn’t even born during the hostage crisis, was also taken from his school in handcuffs. He’s in a facility with his mother with no end to their detention in sight. “This is bloodline punishment,” Tahmasebi writes.Half of Afghan women rarely leave home because of Taliban restrictionsThat’s according to a UN Women analysis that found more than half of the women surveyed leave their houseno more than twice monthly. There’s also nowhere for them to go: Afghanistan is the only country in the world where girls are banned from secondary education and university. Meanwhile, Saif-ul-Islam Khyber, spokesperson for the dystopian-sounding Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, told Reuters that women have access to all their rights. Depends on how you define “rights”, I suppose.Can antihistamines help with PMDD and menopause?The latest viral health claim is that a combination of over-the-counter antihistamines Pepcid AC and Allegra does wonders when it comes to treating debilitating symptoms connected to premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) and menopause. The Guardian looked into whether the science backs this up, and ultimately it seems that we just don’t have enough information to know. Another reminder that there needs to be a lot more researchinto women’s health.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsraeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homesTwo Palestinian familieshave been trappedin their homes as Israeli militants wage a campaign of terror on them to try and drive them out. When the al Tubasi family’s two-year-old daughter fell ill, the “settlers” blocked an ambulance from getting to the house. This is part of a wider campaign of state-sanctioned ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.Tesla paid Elon Musk 2.5m times more as CEO than its average workerAccording to anew report, Musk received the median Tesla worker’s pay every 4.23 seconds in 2025. While Musk is an extreme case, theratio of CEO to worker payin the US continues to grow. Last year the majority of S&P 500 CEOs made more in a day than the average worker made in a year.Jon Hamm becomes a first time dad at 55Very funny how all the conservative menup in armsabout Alexandria Ocasio-Cortezfreezing her eggshave nothing to say aboutthis.The week in pawtriarchyTwo pygmy goats got loose in Portland this week and decided to try out paw-blictransit. They boarded an FX 2 bus without paying but were promptlyshooed off. Now they are nowhere to be seen; they seem to have goat away. Kids these days, eh?Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUS politicsThe Week in PatriarchyAlexandria Ocasio-CortezIsraelDemocratsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)PalestineTeslacommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump shows off article on lower drug prices that says Biden deserves credit, not him | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president credits himself with lowest drug prices in 60 years, when article says drop is more likely due to Biden
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: US president credits himself with lowest drug prices in 60 years, when article says drop is more likely due to Biden
Content: Donald Trump holds a print-out of an article crediting Joe Biden with lowering drug prices, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Saturday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump holds a print-out of an article crediting Joe Biden with lowering drug prices, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Saturday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump shows off article on lower drug prices that says Biden deserves credit, not himUS president credits himself with lowest drug prices in 60 years, when article says drop is more likely due to BidenRobert MackeySat 15 Aug 2026 18.02 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe White House flooded social media on Saturday with an image of Donald Trump showing off the recentWashington Postheadline “Prescription drug prices record sharpest drop in more than 60 years”, but failed to mention that experts cited in the article actually attributed the price drop to Joe Biden, not Trump.On its official accounts, the White House triumphantlycaptioned the photographof Trump: “POV: you bring the receipts.” Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, also shared it.The image was one of several taken during a staged photo-op on Friday, when Trump approached reporters with a copy of the headline he wanted them to see. Holding up a print-out of the headline, and the first five lines of the article, the presidentwaved the page aroundand encouraged the press pool to record and photograph it.“The headline today is exactly that,” he said proudly. “Did you see it?”He then read the good news aloud and held up the print-out again for the cameras. “OK, got it? Everybody have it?” he asked. “I told you that was going to happen.”Before stepping away from the press, Trump repeated the line that he wanted them to relay the news to the public, and held his hands wide apart as if he had just performed a magic trick. “Prescription drug prices down more than at any time over 60 years,” he said. “What else do I have to say?View image in fullscreenDonald Trump at the staged photo-op.Photograph: Samuel Corum/Getty ImagesWhat the president did not say is thatthe text of the article, published by the Post on Thursday, reported that while the Trump White House “took credit for” the biggest year-over-year drop in drug prices in more than 60 years in July, independent experts “said a Biden-era policy that requires Medicare to negotiate prices for some popular prescription drugs is more likely to be driving down costs”.“The Inflation Reduction Act was a signature accomplishment of former president Joe Biden, a sprawling measure enacted in 2022 that aimed to lower prescription drug prices by requiring Medicare, the federal health program for the elderly, to begin negotiating the prices it pays drugmakers for an array of popular and costly prescription drugs,” the Post’s report noted. “Thefirst price reductionstook effect at the beginning of this year.”The price of prescription drugs fell by 3.1% in July, according toConsumer Price Index datareleased by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, whose former head was fired by Trump last year over weaker-than-expected job numbers he called “fake”.The Post quoted Richard Frank, a professor emeritus of health economics at Harvard University, expressing doubt Trump’s policies were behind the drop in drug prices.“If I was a betting guy on what mattered most, it would be probably stuff around the Inflation Reduction Act,” Frank said, adding that Trump’s efforts “wouldn’t be where I’d place my money”.Another expert, Stacie Dusetzina, a health policy professor at Vanderbilt University, told the Post the law signed by Biden was a more likely explanation for the decline in prices than any of Trump’s initiatives.While just 10 drugs have had their prices negotiated in line with the Inflation Reduction Act, Dusetzina said, they are commonly used ones “and their prices would likely be reflected in the prescription drug index”.Steven Cheung, the White House communications director,posteda screenshot of the Post’s headline on his X account on Thursday with no link to the article. “All thanks to President Trump!” Cheung wrote.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpJoe BidenPharmaceuticals industryWashington PostTrump administrationUS healthcareBiden administrationShareReuse this content

title: Powerful earthquake kills dozens in eastern Indonesia | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Quake struck Flores region early on Saturday, prompting thousands to seek higher ground for fear of a tsunami
Author: William Christou
Headline: Quake struck Flores region early on Saturday, prompting thousands to seek higher ground for fear of a tsunami
Content: Strong earthquake hits IndonesiaIndonesiaPowerful earthquake kills dozens in eastern IndonesiaQuake struck Flores region early on Saturday, prompting thousands to seek higher ground for fear of a tsunamiWilliam Christouand agenciesSat 15 Aug 2026 11.34 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 19.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 7.7-magnitude earthquake that struck easternIndonesiahas killed at least 47people, causing widespread panic and collapsing buildings and homes in a region prone to deadly seismic events.Rescuers have yet to reach Nagekeo, the area closest to the epicentre, because roads were blocked by landslides and communications disrupted.Authorities issued a tsunami warning, which has since been lifted, but there were at least 235aftershocks, including one of magnitude 6.1. Indonesian authorities said monitoring showed no significant sea level changes that could indicate a tsunami.View image in fullscreenA motorcyclist rides past a crack in a road in East Nusa Tenggara province.Photograph: Ignasius Kunda/EPATsunami waves of ⁠ 1.5 metres(3ft) were recorded in several areas.The Indonesian geophysics agency, BMKG, recorded the first quake at 4.58am on Saturday local time at a depth of 9 miles (15km) in the country’s Flores region.A second earthquake of magnitude 6.1struck off northern Sumatra, Indonesia, hours after the initial quake, with no casualties yet reported.Rescuers around the port town of Maumere found 20 people dead, six severelyinjured and two trapped under the rubble, said Fathur Rahman, the head of the city’s rescue agency. Eight of those dead had been killed in a landslide. Maumere is the main town in Sikka regency on Flores Island in the east of Indonesia’s vast archipelago.View image in fullscreenPatients are treated in the hallway of a hospital in Labuan Bajo, East Nusa Tenggara province.Photograph: Firdia Lisnawati/APA video on Facebook, verified by Reuters as being at a port in Maumere, shows parts of a building collapsing as people scream and run in the street. Another video showed a coastal village covered in mud and debris after a 1.61-metre tsunami wave hit Ngada village in east Manggarai.Indonesia earthquake map graphicPreliminary data showed that 346 homes, 87 schools and more than a dozen health facilities had been damaged.Indonesian authorities said residents were trapped in several buildings in the affected area.“I have never felt an earthquake this big,” said Yulian Juita Ekalia, a university professor who lives more than 60 miles from the epicentre. “It felt like we were on a trampoline, it was really scary.”The epicentre was located off the north coast of Flores, about 42 miles north-west of the coastal town of Ende, US and Indonesian authorities said.View image in fullscreenPeople are forced to leave their homes in Talibura village, Sikka, East Nusa Tenggara.Photograph: Arnold Welianto/AFP/GettyTeams had not been able to reach Nagekeo, the region closest to the epicentre, and ​communications signals there had been affected, Fathur said. Road access was blocked ‌by landslides, and a team was attempting to reach the area by ferry, he said.The police chief of East Nusa Tenggara province, Rudi Darmoko, said the earthquake caused power cuts that made communication difficult between cities and villages, complicating rescue efforts.“We are continuing to collect reports of damage and casualties, but there are communication disruptions,” he said. He said landslides in Ende regency had cut off the Trans-Flores highway, a 435-mile mountain road.View image in fullscreenPatients receive treatment inside a makeshift tent outside a hospital in Labuan Bajo, East Nusa Tenggara province.Photograph: Firdia Lisnawati/APResidents in Nagekeo regency raced for higher ground immediately after the earthquake.“Suddenly it started to shake and I panicked,” Lukas Lotar, a hospital customer service official, said. “Patients also fled the hospital, the jolt was big. I saw some walls were cracked.”Yohanes Babo, 56, a Nagekeo resident, said he was at a market when the quake hit. “The shaking was strong. Thankfully, we were already outside the house,” he said. “People were panicking, running here and there. We’re evacuating for the time being … and trying to get to the hills. My family is safe. No one was harmed.”View image in fullscreenDamaged homes in Ruteng, East Nusa Tenggara.Photograph: Selo/AFP/GettyAbout 2,000 people in Nagekeo evacuated, and damage to ‌a number of houses, warehouses and government facilities was reported, the national disaster mitigation agency, the BNPB, said. Authorities also reported traffic congestion and power cuts affecting parts of the regency, it said.Local television showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution after the quake. Healthcare workers set up temporary treatment facilities outdoors, moving beds, IV stands and oxygen on to the streets.The BNPB, which put the quake’s toll at one dead and four injured, said it was still gathering data.Images broadcast on Indonesian television showed hundreds of people in nearby Nagekeo regency evacuating the area, surrounded by the rubble of damaged buildings.Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency in East Nusa Tenggara province, said a number of buildings had been damaged by the strong shaking and panicked people ran to higher ground. “Many buildings here were damaged … I saw that the waiting room at the port terminal in Maumere had collapsed,” she said.Indonesia, consisting of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the “ring of fire”, an arc of geophysical activity in the Pacific basin.In 2004, a 9.1-magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of western Indonesia, causing a tsunami that killed 220,000 people in theAsia Pacificarea.With Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsIndonesiaEarthquakesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Multiple people injured in shooting at Virginia State University | Virginia | The Guardian
description: School said shooting involved ‘multiple suspects’ as campus was locked down and police responded to scene
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: School said shooting involved ‘multiple suspects’ as campus was locked down and police responded to scene
Content: Police investigate the scene of a shooting on the campus of Virginia State University on 15 August 2026.Photograph: WWBT/APView image in fullscreenPolice investigate the scene of a shooting on the campus of Virginia State University on 15 August 2026.Photograph: WWBT/APVirginiaMultiple people injured in shooting at Virginia State UniversitySchool said shooting involved ‘multiple suspects’ as campus was locked down and police responded to sceneAdam GabbattSat 15 Aug 2026 09.20 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 14.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMultiple people were injured in a shooting atVirginiaState University (VSU), police said on Saturday morning, with several suspects still at large.The campus, about 20 miles (32km) south of Richmond, was temporarily put on lockdown as police released initial details about the shooting.“A shooting occurred in the area of the Quad Annexes involving multiple victims, who were transported to area hospitals,” the VSU police department said ina statement.VSU saidthe shooting involved “multiple suspects”. Chesterfield county police, whose jurisdiction includes VSU, said officers discovered five people suffering from gunshot wounds outside campus dormitories when they arrived.The five victims were transported to hospitals, and one initially listed as having life-threatening injuries was later upgraded to critical condition, county police said. The other victims sustained non-life-threatening injuries, police said.At least one of the wounded people was confirmed to be a student, according to a VSU statement.Police told WTVR that police were called to university dormitories at 1.30am.The campus had a large law enforcement presence on Saturday morning. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the sheriff’s office of adjacent Hanover county were assisting, police said.After the campus lockdown was lifted, VSU said in a statement that authorities did not believe there was an immediate threat to the school community.“We recognize the concern this incident has caused among our students, parents, alumni, friends, and the broader VSU community,” the statement said. “The safety and well-being of our students remain our highest priority.”As of Saturday morning, there had been nearly 300 mass shootings reported across the US so far for the year, according to theGun Violence Archive.The nonpartisan resources defines mass shootings as cases in which at least four victims are wounded or killed.The US has perennially registered high numbers of mass shootings, with a considerable portion of those occurring at school and university campuses or activities. Those numbers have prompted calls for more substantial federal gun control, though Congress over the years has not implemented such restrictions.The shootings happened just before the start of the academic year at Virginia State. According to the university’s website, residence halls opened for students a week ago, and classes are set to begin on Monday.Many students had just completed the university’s “New Trojans Experience” for incoming students, an event alluding to the nickname for the school’s athletic teams.The public university has about 5,700 students, most of whom are undergraduates.VSU has grown in recent years while attempting to improve safety and retain its historic charm, according to Arthur Fridrich, the university’s former director of distance education, who lives near the campus and visits regularly.For VSU’s community, a shooting just as students return for classes is heartbreaking, he said.“To start a new year with this event is very tragic. It casts a shadow in the minds of all students,” he said.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsVirginiaGun crimeUS universitiesUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Dangerously hostile’: heatwaves leave hospital wards unsafe, data reveals | NHS | The Guardian
description: Figures disclosed by 33 NHS trusts show temperatures on wards during July rose above 28C limit set by NHS England
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Figures disclosed by 33 NHS trusts show temperatures on wards during July rose above 28C limit set by NHS England
Content: Some NHS hospitals have been forced to cancel operations because operating theatres have become too hot during the heatwaves.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSome NHS hospitals have been forced to cancel operations because operating theatres have become too hot during the heatwaves.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesNHS‘Dangerously hostile’: heatwaves leave hospital wards unsafe, data revealsFigures disclosed by 33 NHS trusts show temperatures on wards during July rose above 28C limit set by NHS EnglandDenis CampbellHealth policy editorSat 15 Aug 2026 04.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 04.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHospitals in England have recorded temperatures of almost 42C this summer, with surgeries being cancelled because operating theatres’ cooling unitsstopped workingin the intense heat.The Northern Care AllianceNHSfoundation trust, which runs four hospitals in Greater Manchester, recorded a temperature of 41.8C during last month’s heatwave – 14C above the recommended safe maximum.Figures disclosed by 33 NHS trusts under freedom of information laws show that temperatures on wards during July averaged 31.9C – above the 28C which NHS England advises is the limit hospitals should maintain in order toprotect the safety of staff and patients.The Liberal Democrats, who obtained the data, said hospitals are being affected so badly by record-breaking temperatures that ministers must set up a new “NHS rapid adaptation unit” to heatproof hospitals and care homes by installing ways to keep them cool, such as air conditioning.It would “heatproof vulnerable facilities, make air conditioning mandatory in all care homes and urgently upgrade NHS buildings to withstand future heatwaves. We need to make our hospitals fit for the future,”said Helen Morgan, the party’s health spokesperson.Hospitals are getting so hot that they become “dangerously hostile environments for patients and healthcare workers”, she added.This summer’s relentless heat has meant that some have been forced to cancel surgeries because operating theatres have become dangerously hot. In some hospitals this is because cooling units which regulate the temperature in operating theatres, which are often sited on the roof of hospital buildings, have failed as a result of exposure to the heat.Affected trusts have been forced to reschedule planned surgeries. The NHS Alliance, which revealed the intense heat’s latest impact on the NHS, could not say how many of England’s 205 NHS trusts have had to scrap operating lists for that reason.But a survey it ran of how trusts are coping with the heat also showed that:Some patients are also cancelling their own surgery because it is too hot for them to travel.Hospitals and GP surgeries are offering frail elderly patients appointments at the start and end of the day, when it is less hot, to make it easier for them to attend.Ambulance services are struggling to keep some medications at the right temperature because it gets so hot in the back of their vehicles.NHS ambulance trusts have relaxed their usual dress code rules to help crews stay cooler, for example by wearing shorts rather than trousersSome NHS services have been hiring air conditioning units to try to keep staff and patients cool, with one trust renting at least 600 units.There is mounting alarm that hospitals are getting so hot thatnurses have been fainting. NHS staff organisations say that much of the health service’s estate is so old that many buildings cannot cope with heatwaves – a concern underlined by the evidence collected by the Liberal Democrats and NHS Alliance.“Overheating NHS hospitals are affecting the health and wellbeing of patients and staff and the temperatures we have seen repeatedly this summer show what an urgent issue this has become,” said David Williams, the body’s deputy director of policy.“A lack of investment in the NHS estate over many years has left crumbling buildings and dilapidated equipment in need of urgent repair.”Explore more on these topicsNHSEnglandExtreme heatHealthExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds arrested on suspicion of arson in France as wildfires rage across Europe | France | The Guardian
description: One person killed and hundreds evacuated in Croatia as blazes also hit Germany, Greece and Spain
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: One person killed and hundreds evacuated in Croatia as blazes also hit Germany, Greece and Spain
Content: A wildfire burns near Omiš, Croatia.Photograph: Jakov Prkic/CROPIX/SIPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA wildfire burns near Omiš, Croatia.Photograph: Jakov Prkic/CROPIX/SIPA/ShutterstockFranceHundreds arrested on suspicion of arson in France as wildfires rage across EuropeOne person killed and hundreds evacuated in Croatia as blazes also hit Germany, Greece and SpainJon Henleyin ParisSat 15 Aug 2026 11.32 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost 500 people have been arrested on suspicion of starting wildfires in France since the start of the summer, authorities have said, as firefighters in half a dozen European countries tackle ferocious blazes amid a record-breaking heatwave.A fire engulfed ⁠homes in a Croatian holiday resort on Friday, killing one person, injuring 40 and forcing 1,200 to evacuate, officials said, as the EU warned that pockets of “very extreme” wildfire conditions stretched across the continent.Hundreds more people were evacuated from villages in westernGermanyand south-west France, while stranded holidaymakers were picked up from beaches threatened by flames in Greece, and the army rescued historic relics in Spain.Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame?Read moreResidents in Belgium’s Liège province were also asked to evacuate their homes on Saturday afternoon, as the biggest fire on the country’s record burned through the High Fens, Belgium’s largest nature reserve.With three in five Europeans facing temperatures of at least 30C on Friday and about 150 million enduring 35C or more, France’s interior ministry said 474 people, including 183 minors, had been detained over wildfires in the country since 1 July.View image in fullscreenA helicopter prepares to drop water over a wildfire in the High Fens, Belgium’s largest nature reservePhotograph: Nicolas Lambert/Belga/AFP/GettyAbout 70% of those arrested were suspected of deliberately starting fires and the rest of doing so accidentally. French media said a 15-year-old boy had been detained in connection with a fire near Bordeaux airport that killed two firefighters in July.French authorities on Friday evacuated more than 525 people from the village of Luglon in the south-west region of Landes after a new wildfire tore through almost 1,100 hectares (2,700 acres) of tinder-dry pine forest in less than 24 hours.“The situation is unfavourable and the fire remains raging,” Gilles Clavreul, a regional official, told reporters, ​adding that 500 firefighters were tackling ‌the flames and six water-dumping aircraft ‌had been sent to assist. Roads to the village were closed.View image in fullscreenA firefighter with the French air force looks on as a wildfire burns through the Landes forest in Luglon, south-west France.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/GettyLuglon is about 62 miles (100km) south-east of the popular holiday destinations of Arcachon Bay and the Lège-Cap-Ferret peninsula wheretwo huge wildfiresdestroyed more than 50,000 hectares in late July,forcing the evacuation of as many as 220,000 people.Scientists say climate breakdown is causing more frequent and more extreme weather events,evaporating soilsand waterways, fuelling wildfires and leading tothousands of excess deathsin France. Europe isheating at about twice the globalaverage rate.The EU’s Copernicus climate change service warned in its weekly outlook of “very extreme” conditions across a ​large area of central and eastern Europe, with other pockets over southern Britain, Ireland, northern France and southern Sweden.The average high across western Europe on ‌Friday was forecast to be 31.2C, which is 8C above what was typical from 1961 to 1990, data from the Reuters Climate Monitor showed. The temperature for Europe as a whole was 1.6C above the 1961-1990 norm.In western Germany, more than 2,000 people fled their homes early on Friday morning to take shelter in a nearby primary school after a ⁠wildfire in the nearby Hürtgen forest spread to within a few hundred metres of the village of Gey.“This forest fire threatens to hit the local ‌community hard,” Mona Neubaur, the deputy premier of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, posted on social media. Unexploded second world war ordnance was also hampering firefighting efforts.View image in fullscreenA police helicopter carries water to be dumped on ⁠wildfire in the Hürtgen forest in western Germany.Photograph: Roberto Pfeil/AFP/GettyThe news agency dpa reported explosions could be heard as munitions detonated in the flames, forcing firefighters to stay out of the area, not far from the Belgian border, for safety. German army tanks and helicopters were providing support.In Croatia, a wildfire driven by strong winds descended on the tourist town of Lokva Rogoznica on the Dalmatian coast overnight. Police said they had located the body of one person while searching burned areas on Friday afternoon.Emergency ​shelters opened in several nearby towns. Of 36 people treated by ambulance services in the city of Split, about 15.5 miles to the north, 14 were admitted to hospital and seven had life-threatening injuries, local health officials said.View image in fullscreenCroatia’s prime minister described the blaze that spread to Omiš as ‘one of the worst fires in recent years’.Photograph: Tom Dubravec/AP“It was a strong fire, it swept everything on ‌its way … there has been huge material damage,” Slavko Tucaković, the regional chief fire commander, said on Friday, adding that the blaze appeared to have calmed by Friday morning.The country’s prime minister, Andrej ‌Plenković, said on a visit to nearby Omiš, where the evacuees were sheltering in a sports hall, that the blaze was “one of the worst fires in recent years” but “most importantly” there were no confirmed fatalities so far.View image in fullscreenA painting is removed as a wildfire nears the San Juan de la Peña monastery in Aragón, north-east Spain.Photograph: UME/AFP/GettyIn north-eastSpain, an army unit removed the remains of three 11th-century Aragonese kings from the San Juan de la Peña monastery after it was threatened by a wildfire and took them to a ​museum in nearby Huesca.The fire, which began on Monday, intensified on ⁠Thursday, authorities said, driven by higher temperatures and strong winds that have enabled it to burn through more ​than 9,000 hectares, forcing ​the evacuation of 16 towns and villages.View image in fullscreenLocal residents and tourists are evacuated from Siviri as a forest fire threatens the resort on Halkidiki peninsula, Greece.Photograph: Alexandros Avramidis/ReutersA ​much larger wildfire in southern Spain also worsened on Thursday. It has so far burned 31,000 hectares in the province of Huelva and forced the evacuation of about 700 people.In northern Greece, a fleet ofsmall boats evacuated about 500 holidaymakersfrom beaches on Thursday as a forest fire threatened Siviri and Fourka, two popular resorts on the Halkidiki peninsula, south of the city of Thessaloniki.The 2-mile-long fire front, with flames up to 30 metres (98ft) high, was brought under control later in the day, the regional civil protection chief said, though crews remained on alert for flare-ups. Two injured firefighters were taken to hospital, the fire service added.View image in fullscreenThe remains of homes in Stoke-on-Trent smoulder on Friday as wildfire raced across the West Midlands.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesA maximum level-five alert for fires was issued for much of the Greek mainland and officials in Halkidiki have banned access to the region’s dense pine forests. Winds of up to 62mph were forecast for Friday.In the UK,wildfires raced across the West Midlands, burning several houses to the ground in “one of the most significant” incidents the region’s fire service has ever had to deal with, the regional fire chief, Simon Tuhill, said.Reuters and Agence-France Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsFranceWildfiresGermanySpainCroatiaGreeceEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: The 20-year search for a vanishing custard-and-chocolate coloured moth | Insects | The Guardian
description: Yorkshire common was thought to be the only known site of dark bordered beauty moths in England – until now
Author: Safeerah Ahmed
Headline: Yorkshire common was thought to be the only known site of dark bordered beauty moths in England – until now
Content: After finding no dark bordered beauty moths at Wallington in Northumberland in 2024, Dr David Wainwright made a remarkable discovery while revisiting.Photograph: Henrik_L/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAfter finding no dark bordered beauty moths at Wallington in Northumberland in 2024, Dr David Wainwright made a remarkable discovery while revisiting.Photograph: Henrik_L/Getty ImagesInvertebrate of the year 2026InsectsThe 20-year search for a vanishing custard-and-chocolate coloured mothYorkshire common was thought to be the only known site of dark bordered beauty moths in England – until nowVote here for your favourite invertebrate of the yearSafeerah AhmedSat 15 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDave Wainwright first surveyed Wallington inNorthumberlandfor a rare custard-and-chocolate coloured moth in 2004. He parked two miles from the site, hauled a moth trap across, and was bitten by a million flies.He did not find a single dark bordered beauty that night. The ground was heavily grazed by sheep, and the creeping willow the caterpillars depend on was “quite well plucked”.But he was determined not to give up.Twenty years later, walking the same Northumberland estate with project officer Charlotte Rankin and National Trust rangers, Wainwright finally found what he had been looking for since he started the job: a population of dark bordered beauty moths, the first recorded at the site since 1952.“It was a pretty amazing feeling,” he says. “That particular site had been recorded before, but 74 years ago. I surveyed the site about 20 years ago and couldn’t find it … actually finding it after that much effort was really fulfilling.”The dark bordered beauty is a moth with lemon-yellow wings and a deep chestnut border, sometimes described as custard-and-chocolate coloured. It is also one of the rarest moths in England.Until this summer, Strensall Common in Yorkshire was the only known site where it survived in the country, and even that population has been collapsing. Hundreds of moths were recorded 20 years ago. The numbers record last barely reached double figures, hit by climate breakdown and a wildfire that tore through much of the reserve.Wainwright, who is head of conservation in England at ButterflyConservation, has spent years chasing that narrow margin across some of the country’s landscapes.“I’ve been to a lot of remote places, particularly in Northumberland, Yorkshire and Cumbria,” he says. “I always felt the dark bordered beauty would be there. I had a sneaking suspicion, but whether or not I’d actually find it, I didn’t know.”View image in fullscreenDr David Wainwright finds a dark bordered beauty moth at the Wallington site. He says the discovery is the highlight of this career.Photograph: Charlotte RankinLooking back at that fruitless night in 2004, he now thinks the moth may have been there all along, hidden in plain sight in willow scrub too battered by grazing to support it. “It must have been there,” Wainwright says, “which makes it all the more rewarding.”The site looks very different now to how it did back then. Where the willow was once cropped bare, there is now lush vegetation and wildflowers. This is the result of years of work between the National Trust and Fiona Goodfellow, a tenant farmer who manages the land as part of a nature recovery project spanning the estate’s 20 sq miles (5,200 hectares).The discovery came out of a £300,000 grant awarded to Butterfly Conservation last year by the Elgol Fund for Nature to study how rare species across the north of England were coping with climate and human pressures.For Wainwright, what makes the find matter is not just the science. It is what it means for a species he had feared was running out of time.“Because I thought we were going to lose [dark bordered beauties] as a species,” he says, when asked why he calls this a highlight of his career.“You don’t want a species to go extinct on your watch … you feel really powerless. It’s gratifying just knowing that the species isn’t as far down the road to extinction as we feared.”One of the main challenges in conserving the species is that its caterpillar only eats two plants: aspen and creeping willow.View image in fullscreenWainwright  now thinks the moth may have been there all along, hidden in plain sight in willow scrub too battered by grazing to support it.Photograph: Charlotte RankinHowever, Wainwright still remains wary of moving too fast. The moth has survived at Wallington for more than 70 years without anyone intervening on its behalf, and he would rather understand exactly why the habitat works before anyone starts changing it.“We wouldn’t want to rush into major changes,” he says. “You could do more harm than good by modifying it without knowing what you’re doing.”Wainwright explains that as of right now, the work is mostly watching.Butterfly Conservation is also in the early stages of a captive breeding programme, already planned in partnership with YorkshireWildlifeTrust at Strensall Common. There is a longer-term hope of introducing the moth to new sites once the right conditions can be created.Wainwright has spent his career doing the work of finding out what is actually out there and “putting dots on maps”, often in places barely anyone visits. He argues that this is important so that conservation money goes where it is needed most.It is slow, forensic work, chasing eggs and caterpillars to work out what a moth needs to survive. But every so often, it pays off.It’s invertebrate of the year!Vote here for your favouritebefore midnight on Sunday 16 August.Explore more on these topicsInsectsInvertebrate of the year 2026AnimalsWildlifeConservationNorthumberlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cheap travel is not a defence’: the parents facing court for school absences in England | School attendance and absence | The Guardian
description: In one court in Kent, most cases relate to term-time holidays, but non-attendance is a complex issue and post-pandemic rates remain high
Author: Amelia Gentleman
Headline: In one court in Kent, most cases relate to term-time holidays, but non-attendance is a complex issue and post-pandemic rates remain high
Content: Researchers have previously warned of a ‘seismic shift’ in attitudes to school attendance since Covid. Picture posed by model.Photograph: Manuel Arias Duran/GettyView image in fullscreenResearchers have previously warned of a ‘seismic shift’ in attitudes to school attendance since Covid. Picture posed by model.Photograph: Manuel Arias Duran/GettySchool attendance and absence‘Cheap travel is not a defence’: the parents facing court for school absences in EnglandIn one court in Kent, most cases relate to term-time holidays, but non-attendance is a complex issue and post-pandemic rates remain highAmelia GentlemanSat 15 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 09.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the long school summer break approached its mid-point recently, Margate beach was crowded with families enjoying the brief reprieve between the year’s fourth and fifth heatwaves. For most, thoughts of the classroom were probably not at the forefront of their minds.But for the seven mothers and two fathers who were summoned at 10am to a stuffy room in the town’s magistrates court, set just behind the beachfront strip of arcades, the subject was unavoidable. They were among hundreds of parents due in courts acrossEnglandthis month for failing to ensure their children had regularly attended school over the course of the last academic year.They faced fines, or in extreme cases the theoretical possibility of three months in prison, depending on the reasons provided for the absences.The first defendant to be called in admitted that he had travelled abroad with his partner and daughter for 10 days at the start of the summer term. Taking her out of school to go on holiday for the third time in three consecutive years had pushed her annual attendance rate below 75%.But the family had needed a break, he told the court, because two close friends had recently died, and the child’s mother had been unwell. The timing of the trip – immediately after rather than during the Easter holidays – was, he said, prompted by the strain the family had been under, rather than because travel was cheaper during term time.“There’s a lot going on at home,” he told the court, in weary explanation.The three magistrates presiding over court two represented the sharp end of an ongoing drive to try to improve school attendance rates in England, which have never fully recovered after the closure of schools during Covid. Parents can be taken to court as a last resort if gentler attempts by the local authority to help them improve persistently poor attendance have failed, or if they have received multiple penalty notices for their child’s non-attendance within three years.View image in fullscreenThe beach in Margate, Kent.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAIt is a drive that is faltering. In the same week in London, the Department for Education released data showing the overall absence rate for the academic year 2025-26 for pupils in England was running at 6.93%, a slight rise on the previous year, and still significantly above the 2018-19 pre-Covid levels when the national overall absence rate in England was just 4.7%. Persistent absence rates have doubled since the pandemic, with nearly one in five children now missing at least 10% of school.In Margate, the magistrates listened as a representative forKentcounty council told the court that a girl’s parents had been fined a year earlier, for taking her with them while they made a time-term trip abroad for dental treatment, and also the year before that when they had taken an unauthorised holiday during school time.“Unfortunately the availability of cheap travel is not a defence,” the local authority official said.The father countered that his daughter had done some work on his iPad while they were away and showed no sign of having fallen behind; he was annoyed, he added, that staff from the primary school appeared to be monitoring his social media posts to track his movements, which he felt was a breach of his privacy. After some discussion with the magistrates, he accepted he was guilty, and was issued with a £166 fine.“You have a duty to send your daughter to school, and the council has a duty to prosecute you if you don’t,” the lead magistrate told him, warning that the fine needed to be paid at a rate of £20 a month, to avoid bailiffs being sent to his home.A record 492,825 penalty notices for unauthorised absences were issued to parents in England in 2024-25 (the most recent year for which records are available), a slight increase on the year before and a sharp rise from the pre-Covid level of 333,388 penalties in 2018-19. Researchers have previouslywarnedof a “seismic shift” in attitudes to attendance since the pandemic, with concern that some parents no longer automatically subscribe to the view that children must be in school full-time.View image in fullscreenFridays are a particular weak spot for non-attendance, while some parents say they are keeping their child off school because of bullying.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAThe new education minister Paul Waugh acknowledged that progress on pulling attendance back to pre-pandemic levels had slowed, noting that data showed that absences due to illness were now 25% higher on Fridays than the rest of week. “It’s possible that where pupils are less engaged with school overall, Friday is becoming a particular weak spot for attendance,” he wrote in response to the new figures.The next parent in the Margate court was charged with the more serious offence –section 444(1A)of the Education Act 1996 – of “knowingly” allowing her child to miss school without a valid reason, a charge that can attract a fine of £2,500 or up to three months in prison, although custodial sentences are rarely handed down. This case was not a matter of a slightly lax approach to attendance on Fridays, but involved a 14-year-old boy whose annual attendance rate was just 19%.A duty solicitor requested some time to talk to the mother, who appeared exhausted as the representative for the county council set out the charges against her. The case was subsequently adjourned because the solicitor needed time to collate evidence that her son had been seriously bullied at the school and was frightened of being attacked.“I’m keeping him home. It’s a sad world where you need to keep a child home for their safety,” the mother said after the hearing, adding that her son had been diagnosed with ADHD and autism and that problems had begun when he switched to secondary school, when mild bullying from his peers progressed to violent abuse. The police had been called on several occasions. “My son’s had his ribs broken by bullies. He was threatened with a Stanley blade.”She had been alarmed at being summoned to court. “I didn’t sleep last night,” she said, adding that she felt she had been doing her best in challenging circumstances, trying to teach her son at home, showing him how to bake, telling him about castles and how to manage money, although her capacity to teach a full curriculum was hampered by her own dyslexia. “I’m concerned he is becoming lonely. He struggles with friends, with going out.”She has had extensive support from Kent’s children’s services team and in September her son is due to start a specialist college for children who display complex barriers to education; he would like in time to become a mechanic, and she was hopeful that the switch to the new school could still make that a realisable goal. A new court date was set for the autumn.By late morning, the non-attendance hearings paused briefly because the seven remaining summonsed parents had not turned up to court. Staff seemed unsurprised that parents who struggled to get their children to school found it challenging to attend court on time, and decided to hear their cases in absentia.Third of disadvantaged white pupils in England leave primary school without being able to read properlyRead moreWhile a couple of the Margate cases involved chronic, unexplained failures to get children to school, most concerned term-time holidays. More than 90% of fines nationally (459,288 penalties in 20245-25) are issued for this reason. One mother, charged with taking her seven-year-old daughter out of school for a third unauthorised holiday in three years, had emailed to say that she was unable to attend court, but wanted the magistrates to know that she was not planning to repeat the offence. She had chosen to break the law because she would not otherwise have been able to afford to go away. She was issued with a £140 fine, and ordered to pay £252 (once surcharge and court costs were added) at a rate of £20 reduction a month from benefits.Waugh noted that in addition to unauthorised holidays there were a range of reasons behind the absences – from the effect of screens on sleep, bullying associated with social media use, a rising number of children with special educational needs, the summer’s heatwaves, winter flu.Prosecutions remain controversial, with campaigners arguing that penalties are usually issued against mothers, and that fines have an impact on already-tight family budgets. But the Department for Education is committed to using them as a final resort, pointing out that secondary school pupils who are persistently absent are three times more likely to join the rising numbers of young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet).A spokesperson for Kent county council said staff were working on understanding the triggers for school avoidance and had improved attendance in Kent schools to bring it “broadly in line with the national average”, adding that taking parents to court was “not a decision that is taken lightly and only where all other routes have failed”.Explore more on these topicsSchool attendance and absenceSchoolsSocial exclusionChildrenYoung peopleEnglandMental healthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Met apologises for exposing 143 email addresses of Mohamed Al Fayed victims | Mohamed Al Fayed | The Guardian
description: London police force tells Telegraph incident was result of ‘human error’ and it is conducting an investigation
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: London police force tells Telegraph incident was result of ‘human error’ and it is conducting an investigation
Content: Mohamed Al Fayed pictured in 2013. The Metropolitan police said that victims’ email addresses had been made visible to others on a distribution list.Photograph: Daniel Hambury/PAView image in fullscreenMohamed Al Fayed pictured in 2013. The Metropolitan police said that victims’ email addresses had been made visible to others on a distribution list.Photograph: Daniel Hambury/PAMohamed Al FayedMet apologises for exposing 143 email addresses of Mohamed Al Fayed victimsLondon police force tells Telegraph incident was result of ‘human error’ and it is conducting an investigationSammy GecsoylerSat 15 Aug 2026 08.22 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheMetropolitan policehave apologised for accidentally exposing the email addresses of more than 140 victims of Mohamed Al Fayed.In a group update about its investigation into the formerHarrodsowner, the force copied the email addresses of 143 victims of Fayed in a message that included about 12 other recipients, the Telegraph reported.The force said it understood the “impact this may have on victims” and blamed “human error” for the incident. It has referred itself to the information commissioner.The Met said the update was informing victims who had signed up to its email distribution list that three more suspects, one in their 70s and two in their 80s, had been interviewed under caution. In total, seven people have been interviewed under caution.A Met spokesperson told the Telegraph: “On Tuesday, 11 August, officers issued a monthly update to victims regarding progress in our investigation into those who may have facilitated Mohamed Fayed’s offending.“Due to human error, recipients’ email addresses were visible to others on the distribution list. The issue was identified quickly and immediate action was taken.At least five Mohamed Al Fayed abuse survivors confirmed as human-trafficking victimsRead more“We understand the impact this may have on victims and sincerely apologise. Everyone affected was contacted directly on the day of the incident.”They said the incident was being investigated as a matter of “priority”, and that the force was reviewing its processes in order to help prevent a similar breach from happening again.More than 400 allegations of sexual misconduct have been made against Fayed for the period between 1977 and 2014, including claims of rape, sexual assault, human trafficking, false imprisonment, drugging, physical violence and forced abortions.The Egyptian businessman died in 2023aged 94, without facing any charges.The Met’s approach to the case has been criticised by Fayed’s victims. In June, three survivors complained to theIndependent Office for Police Conductabout the force’s handling of allegations between 2018 and 2024. That same month, the Met sent the handwritten accounts of survivor Joanna Brittan to another victim in Australia.In May, the IOPC launched an investigation into a servingMetofficer and four former officers over their handling of allegations against the late businessman.The Met is investigating allegations made by at least 155 victims, at least 21 of whom are understood to have come forward before Fayed’s death.Operation Cornpoppy, launched 21 months ago, is looking at potential suspects who may have facilitated or enabled Fayed’s crimes. As of last weekit had interviewedjust four people under caution.Victims of the former Harrods owner havecalled for a wider investigationinto trafficking, arguing that without it the “true scale” of the billionaire’s alleged network would remain hidden.No One Above, a collective founded by victims of abuse at the hands of Fayed, has urged the National Crime Agency to set up a joint investigation team with the Met and have oversight of the inquiry.Lawyers representing the Justice for Fayed andHarrodsSurvivors group said 421 people had come forward about abuse that allegedly took place at the luxury department store in central London, as well as at the Ritz hotel in Paris, Fulham FC, and other places owned by Fayed.Explore more on these topicsMohamed Al FayedMetropolitan policeLondonPoliceHarrodsData protectionEmailnewsShareReuse this content

title: Heathrow airport roads reopen after flooding from burst water main | Heathrow airport | The Guardian
description: Heathrow says airport operating as normal after passengers told not to travel by road and use rail and tube instead
Author: Daniel Lavelle
Headline: Heathrow says airport operating as normal after passengers told not to travel by road and use rail and tube instead
Content: Access to Heathrow carparks was also impeded, leaving people unable to access vehicles.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyView image in fullscreenAccess to Heathrow carparks was also impeded, leaving people unable to access vehicles.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyHeathrow airportHeathrow airport roads reopen after flooding from burst water mainHeathrow says airport operating as normal after passengers told not to travel by road and use rail and tube insteadDaniel Lavelleand agenciesSat 15 Aug 2026 10.58 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDisruptions caused by flooding from a burst water main on a ring road atHeathrow airportrestricted access to Terminals 2 and 3 on Saturday morning. The leak has been contained and the affected areas are operating as normal.Water in the central terminal area prevented anyone trying to travel by road to or from Terminals 2 and 3. Passengers had to travel by rail and tube instead. Access to the carparks was also impeded, leaving people with parked cars unable to access them.A spokesperson for Heathrow said: “Following earlier flooding in the central terminal area impacting access to Terminals 2 and 3, all roads have now reopened and the airport continues to operate as normal.“We apologise for any inconvenience caused and we thank passengers for following the advisories we had put in place while our teams worked to resolve the situation.”The disruption occurred during the school holidays, one of the airport’s busiest periods. Heathrow said 19 July had been its busiest day of the year so far with more than 267,000 passengers passing through the airport as many schools broke up for summer.The airport was recently affected by disruption to rail services after a water leak prompted the closure of a tunnel.The airport is one of the busiest in the world, with as many as 1,300 flight movements – takeoffs and landings – every day.Julie Hamilton, 54, had been staying in the Isle of Sheppey and was due to fly from Heathrow to her home in New Jersey in the US.Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airportRead moreAsked how the flooding had affected her, she said: “Well I wasn’t notified so I just had to go via Terminal 5 and get a train over here because I obviously can’t get dropped to Terminal 2.”Hamilton said the airline with whom she was flying had not informed her about the disruption and she only realised there were issues when her father read about it on the news.Hamilton, who runs a non-profit bookstore in New Jersey, told the Press Association: “It’s really frustrating. Luckily, I got my brother to drop me to Terminal 5 and I just had to navigate how to get from Terminal 5 to Terminal 2.“I have to be here three hours early and now I’m half an hour late.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrish Macfarlane, 59, and Cindy Hastie, 65, arrived at Terminal 2 without any issues. Macfarlane, an accoutant, who was due to fly to Singapore, said: “We got a cab from Kensington and it was fine. He just drove us straight here.“We booked a taxi yesterday and we came in that. There’s been no flooding we have seen.” She said she saw news about the flooding on Facebook on the way to the airport.Earlier, the consumer rights group Which? urged passengers to check airline policies on booked flights and advised against unnecessary travel.The editor of Which? Travel, Rory Boland, said: “Passengers heading to Heathrow today will understandably be worried, so it’s important to follow the airport’s advice and avoid travelling by road to Terminals 2 and 3, instead allowing extra time and using public transport where possible.“If you’re worried you may miss your flight because of the disruption, contact your airline as soon as possible. Airlines have different policies on missed flights, so it’s worth finding out if you are entitled to a free rebooking or refund if your flight has operated.“If you’ve paid for airport parking but can no longer use it because of the road closures, contact the parking provider as soon as possible to see if you can amend your booking or get a refund. You should also check your travel insurance to see whether you’re covered for any costs you incur because of the disruption, such as a missed flight or additional travel expenses.”Explore more on these topicsHeathrow airportAir transportTransportRoad transportLondonAirline industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon kill 11 in worst toll since June truce | Lebanon | The Guardian
description: Rescue services search for survivors and bodies after airstrikes hit homes in Ansar and Deir al-Zahrani
Author: William Christou
Headline: Rescue services search for survivors and bodies after airstrikes hit homes in Ansar and Deir al-Zahrani
Content: A man inspects the damage after an Israeli airstrike on homes in the village of Ansar in southern Lebanon.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA man inspects the damage after an Israeli airstrike on homes in the village of Ansar in southern Lebanon.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockLebanonIsraeli strikes on southern Lebanon kill 11 in worst toll since June truceRescue services search for survivors and bodies after airstrikes hit homes in Ansar and Deir al-ZahraniWilliam ChristouSat 15 Aug 2026 09.55 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 02.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEleven people have been killed, including three children, and 19injured in two Israeli airstrikes on southern Lebanon, the worst toll since deals in June brought a lull in hostilities between Israel andHezbollah.Israeli warplanes bombed a home on the outskirts of the village of Ansar, killing seven people and flattening the building early on Saturday morning. Rescue services were working at the site to try to find survivors and locate bodies.Another airstrike hours later on a home in the town of Deir al-Zahrani killed two, wounded nine and covered the streets in rubble and smoke. An Israeli drone also targeted a motorcycle in the nearby city of Nabatieh, but it was unclear if the driver was killed.Israel deliberately starting wildfires in southern Lebanon, firefighters sayRead moreThe escalation came despite a June ceasefire in which most fighting between Israel and Hezbollah ended.Residents of southernLebanonwondered if the attacks signalled further escalation to come or if it was safe to stay in their homes. Neither village was in Israel’s self-declared “security zone” – a 231-square-mile area occupied by its forces.The roads out of Nabatieh and the surrounding villages were choked with traffic after the strikes as people fled north in search of safety.The Israeli military spokesperson, Ella Waweya, said Israel had attacked “Hezbollah infrastructure” in the Ansar and Nabatieh area in response to the group’s fighters attacking soldiers in the Ali Taher area.View image in fullscreenRescue workers and residents search for survivors after an Israeli airstrike on Deir al-Zahrani in southern Lebanon.Photograph: Abdul Kader Al Bay/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockAli Taher is a hill where the Israeli military says large underground Hezbollah command and control centres are located, and it has been shelling the area for months.The Lebanese prime minister, Nawaf Salam, condemned the Israeli attacks, calling them “extremely dangerous” and said they undermined efforts to establish stability in the south.He called on Israel to stop the escalation. “The seven martyrs of the Israeli strike on the town of Ansar were not ‘military infrastructure’ and the children and women killed were not military targets,” he said.Hezbollah condemned the attacks in a statement and said they would be met with a response. The group also accused the Lebanese government of serving Israel’s interests by negotiating with it.“The Israeli enemy must clearly understand that its attacks, violations and attempts to impose a fait accompli cannot continue, and will be met with an appropriate response in defence of Lebanon,” Hezbollah’s media relations department said.The latest round of fighting in Lebanon started after Hezbollah struck Israel with rockets on 2 March in retaliation for the killing of Iran’s supreme leader. Israel responded with an aerial campaign and invasion that killed more than 4,300 people and occupied about 6% of the country’s territory.Violence has significantly decreased since the signing of a US-Iran memorandum of understanding in June on the broader Middle East war, and a US-sponsored framework deal between Lebanon and Israel agreed later that month.But Lebanon still reports intermittent Israeli strikes occasionally causing casualties, and the broad demolitions of civilian buildings in southern villages and towns.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the damage in Deir al-Zahrani after an Israeli warplane carried out an airstrike in southern Lebanon.Photograph: Abdul Kader Al Bay/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe news agency NNA said “the valley between Ansar and Zarariyeh was also subjected to a strike, the first at this geographical depth since the ceasefire two months ago”.It also said “Israeli warplanes carried out a series of airstrikes targeting the Ali al-Taher ridge”. The news agency said Israeli forces detonated homes in the town of Bint Jbeil near the border.The Israel-Lebanon framework deal includes the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from south Lebanon, and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in “pilot zones”.On Friday, Hezbollah’s chief, Naim Qassem, accused Lebanese authorities of subjecting the country’s armed forces to undue pressure by implementing the deal. “How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?” he said.This week, Human Rights Watch urged the UN to keep an international force in Lebanon after its peacekeepers’ mandate ends this year, saying “peacekeepers are a crucial deterrent against attacks on civilians and human rights abuses”.Explore more on these topicsLebanonIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaIranHezbollahnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zimbabwe boat accident death toll hits 68 as 22 more bodies recovered | Zimbabwe | The Guardian
description: Eighteen children among the people killed after ferry capsized on Lake Kariba
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Eighteen children among the people killed after ferry capsized on Lake Kariba
Content: A coffin with the body of a victim of the capsized passenger ferry, leaves the Kariba hospital mortuary after his body was identified for burial in Kariba, on 14 August 2026.Photograph: Jekesai Njikizana/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA coffin with the body of a victim of the capsized passenger ferry, leaves the Kariba hospital mortuary after his body was identified for burial in Kariba, on 14 August 2026.Photograph: Jekesai Njikizana/AFP/Getty ImagesZimbabweZimbabwe boat accident death toll hits 68 as 22 more bodies recoveredEighteen children among the people killed after ferry capsized on Lake KaribaNadeem BadshahSat 15 Aug 2026 15.39 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 17.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty-two more bodies have been recovered after a boat accident inZimbabwe, taking the death toll to 68, police said on Saturday.The ferrycapsized on Tuesday on Lake Kariba, on the border with Zambia. An investigation has suggested it was overloaded when it turned over during heavy winds.Eighteen children were among the people killed, Zimbabwe’s police said, in what is believed to be the country’s deadliest such disaster.Most of the passengers are believed to be villagers and fish traders who lived around the lake.Officials said the vessel was authorised to carry 90 people but was packed with 114 adults, five crew members and an unspecified number of children.Lt Col Joseph Muchechesi, commander of the boat regiment involved in the search operation, said: “So far today we have managed to take 22 bodies. We are confident that we will manage to retrieve all the bodies.”The civil protection unit said on Wednesday that 77 people had been rescued.Hundreds of people gathered at the district hospital in the lakeside town of Kariba to identify the bodies of their relatives and loved ones.View image in fullscreenFamily members walk past caskets carrying their loved ones during a memorial service for the victims of the boat accident in Kariba, Zimbabwe, 13 August 2026.Photograph: Mkhululi Thobela/APA public memorial service was held in Kariba, nearly 280km (175 miles) north-west of the capital Harare, on Thursday before the burials started.Survivors said they pleaded with the ferry driver to turn back as the vessel had begun taking on water soon after departing.Chance Siyamavhu, 45, told Agence France-Presse: “Thank God that a wave pushed the sinking vessel and we managed to climb on top.“When the boat capsized, most of the people scrambled to get the lifejackets but most of them did not even know how to use them.“Most people could not make it.”Lake Kariba is the world’s largest manmade lake by volume.
