It stretches more than 200km (124 miles) and is up to 40km (25 miles) wide in places.It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people.In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.On the Zimbabwean side, five passengers drowned in a 2021 incident.Explore more on these topicsZimbabweAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Secondhand booksellers in UK and Ireland suspect AI firms behind ‘strange’ bulk orders | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Development comes after Anthropic was found to have spent millions on books to scan for ‘data acquisition’
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Development comes after Anthropic was found to have spent millions on books to scan for ‘data acquisition’
Content: ‘My theory is that it’s masses and masses of AI money’: Stuart and Mary Manley, the co-owners of Barter Books in Alnwick, Northumberland.Photograph: suppliedView image in fullscreen‘My theory is that it’s masses and masses of AI money’: Stuart and Mary Manley, the co-owners of Barter Books in Alnwick, Northumberland.Photograph: suppliedAI (artificial intelligence)Secondhand booksellers in UK and Ireland suspect AI firms behind ‘strange’ bulk ordersDevelopment comes after Anthropic was found to have spent millions on books to scan for ‘data acquisition’Dan MilmoGlobal technology editorSat 15 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSecondhand booksellers in the UK and Ireland are reporting a flurry of bulk orders from mystery buyers, amid speculation AI companies are acquiring the tomes for their data.Bookshops contacted by the Guardian say they have been receiving orders from buyers in the US, Canada, continental Europe and the UK. The increase has been replicated around the world, with booksellers in the US, Australia and Europe also reporting unusual orders.Stuart Manley, the co-owner of Barter Books in Alnwick, Northumberland, said the orders, which began arriving three months ago, were unusual because they did not follow the typical pattern of being grouped into themes such as sport or motoring.“It’s definitely a strange combination of books,” said Manley. “Normally a book order is on a theme but this is all over the place.”A recent order included requests for an Estonian translation of John le Carré’s The Mission Song, a copy of Anne Brontë’s Agnes Grey from a specific imprint and the October 1983 edition of Warship, a monthly magazine. Manley said he had sold “hundreds” of random books to three buyers for a total of about £4,000.Jim Shaughnessy, the owner of MW Books in Claregalway, Ireland, said his business had been receiving large, varied orders since May.“They are sporadic, presumably machine-driven and have little in terms of thematic currency; books on agricultural implements in 18th century Africa through to biographies of 1950s racing car drivers,” he said. “Personally, I don’t see we have the right to dictate what any customer does with their purchases but it is more than curious to see what’s being selected.”David Gower-Spence, the owner of BookLovers of Bath, said he had received a rush of orders between May and July for about 200 books from buyers who have also been cited by other sellers contacted by the Guardian for this article.One, the Canada-based Zoom Books, which has featured in other media reports, describes itself as “North America’s leading book recycling company”. Zoom has been contacted for comment by the Guardian.“It was overwhelming for a while and I’m relatively well organised,” said Gower-Spence.One UK-based secondhand bookseller, speaking on condition of anonymity, said some random orders could come from different buyers but be delivered to the same address. “The aliases behind these orders are very opaque even to experienced booksellers,” the source said.One delivery postcode seen by the Guardian and used by different buyers points to a group of freight warehouses near Heathrow airport.The bookseller, who has received orders for 6,000 books from similar buyers since January worth thousands of pounds, said the buyers were paying “top whack” and were not seeking a discount despite requesting titles in bulk.“It’s disrupting the secondhand bookselling business because this isn’t typical for the trade,” the bookseller said. “It appears to be either a human or a machine dipping into the sandbox of secondhand books and what they are buying makes no sense in terms of the wider trends in the market.”The Guardian reported this month thatAustralian booksellers had also received a burst of orders, with one saying the sudden scale of demand was “driving me nuts”.The spate of orders has fuelled speculation among booksellers that AI companies are acquiring the books to scan their contents before pulping them.Manley said: “My theory is that it’s masses and masses of AI money being squandered.”Massachusetts teen accused of killing mother and brother used ChatGPTRead moreThe Washington Post revealed this year thatAnthropic, a leading AI company and developer of the Claude chatbot, had spent tens of millions of dollars acquiring books and slicing off their spines so their contents could be scanned before the books were sent for recycling.Anthropic said: “Claude is trained on a mix of publicly available web data, commercially acquired datasets, and data we generate ourselves. Sourcing books is a widely used approach for training large language models across the AI industry. None of our data acquisition programs buy and destroy rare or antiquarian books.”Last month, the tech news site 404 Media reported that a books database was telling booksellers “the world’s best AI training data is sitting on a shelf”, adding that books published before 2022 were ideal material for AI companies because their text was unpolluted by material that could have been generated by chatbots. The database in question, ISBNdb, said the report wasbased on a webpagethat was a “test of market interest” and had since been taken down.AI tools such as chatbots are “trained” on vast amounts of data to help them generate responses, a requirement that has set tech companies searching for fresh sources of material to build new models. Secondhand books, some of them published decades before ChatGPT exploded on to the scene and not available online, could be a source of fresh data.One post on an online forum for booksellers, seen by the Guardian, said: “Shame these are all destined for AI training, and will therefore get the covers stripped and ultimately end up being pulped.”Other posts expressed puzzlement at the erratic orders, while some questioned whether they could be intended for AI training when requests included books available for nothing in the public online domain such as Gulliver’s Travels, published in 1726.Orders are typically placed through book marketplaces including Biblio and the Amazon-owned AbeBooks. Biblio and AbeBooks have been contacted by the Guardian for comment.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingAmazonAnthropicInternetE-commerceRetail industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Science or fiction? Shadowy ‘paper mills’ let you pay to be a published author – of fraudulent research | Science | The Guardian
description: Paper mill activity has exploded in recent years, polluting the scientific ecosystem with falsified data and compromising medical research
Author: Jackson Ryan
Headline: Paper mill activity has exploded in recent years, polluting the scientific ecosystem with falsified data and compromising medical research
Content: Scientists are under constant pressure to publish new research papers. Paper mills offer a fraudulent shortcut.Composite: Getty Images/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenScientists are under constant pressure to publish new research papers. Paper mills offer a fraudulent shortcut.Composite: Getty Images/Guardian DesignScienceScience or fiction? Shadowy ‘paper mills’ let you pay to be a published author – of fraudulent researchPaper mill activity has exploded in recent years, polluting the scientific ecosystem with falsified data and compromising medical researchJackson RyanSat 15 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 21.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDr Reese Richardson’s phone constantly buzzes with notifications. The scientific research integrity specialist has been tracking shadowy organisations known as “paper mills”, which turn a profit by offering fraudulent academic authorship of scientific papers, IP registrations and other scholarly outputs.For a fee, paper mills offer to list people as authors of scientific journal articles, often of falsified research that bypasses the peer review process.Richardson has joined dozens of groups across apps such as Telegram, WhatsApp and Facebook where a buffet of fraudulent and fabricated research is advertised to hundreds of members. “I can just look through my notifications and I can see that I’ve gotten, like, 20 WhatsApp messages from paper mills in the last 24 hours,” he says.Scientists are under constant pressure to publish new research papers which, in many parts of the world, remain the currency of academia. They beget more grant funding and accolades, and enhance academic profiles. But robust, high-quality science takes time, and papers can take years to get published.Paper mills offer a fraudulent shortcut, using instant messaging and social media platforms to find prospective buyers looking for papers and patents to stack their CVs. According to an analysis Richardson conducted with Anna Abalkina and Spencer Hong, the median price to buy authorship is around US$800 (A$1,150).In arecent paper,which has not yet been peer reviewed, the trio of scientists led by Richardson, formerly at Northwestern University in the US, detailed more than 18,000 advertisements from seven paper mills across seven countries between 2020 and 2026.Is the staggeringly profitable business of scientific publishing bad for science?Read more“We wanted to get an idea, across a wide range of paper mills, countries, topics and product types how much these things actually go for,” he says. “What we put together is the largest ever dataset of paper mill advertisements.”They found many groups advertising authorship of scientific manuscripts across Telegram, Facebook and various websites for as little as US$30.In the last 15 years, paper mill activity hasexploded, with one estimate produced by Richardson in 2025 suggesting their products have been doubling approximately every 18 months. The journal articles produced by these paper mills typically bypass the accepted scientific editorial process of peer review, either because the journals do not institute those processes or because editors are themselves part of paper mill activities.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsThis amounts to an industrialised injection of falsified data, polluting the scientific ecosystem and compromising medical research, drug discovery and clinical trials. The scale is massive: in 2023, Hindawi, a now defunct journal brand owned by major publisher Wiley,retracted more than 8,000 articles. A further 3,000 retractions came by the end of 2024.Richardson says his research is a useful starting point for trying to grapple with how and where paper mills operate, and who they target. The advertisements are like fingerprints at a crime scene, potential evidence of malicious activity. “You can get a lot of information from the advertisements,” he says. He has directly tracked some of these to fraudulent papers in the scientific literature.Designs and IP for saleOther advertisements relate to copyrights and design registrations, another area ripe for fraud, which may provide buyers with legitimate intellectual property rights. Richardson notes one of the reasons to do this is to bolster resumes in service of academic advancement.Richardson haspreviously identifiedexploitation of IP systems in the UK, finding thousands of design registrations. His new work identifies 12 instances where design registrations were advertised by a paper mill operating in India and catering to Indian academics.Richardson’s data shows these design registrations are being advertised as “Australian design patents”. The paper mills sell positions as “owners” of design registrations, charging between $95 and $150 per owner, for up to eight people to be registered on any given design. A design registration application through IP Australia costs $200 in total.Guardian Australia identified cases where the registrations were listed as patents on CVs.“They’re using the services of the Australian government to defraud others,” Richardson says. He points to several unusual instances of design registrations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne Australian design registration, for an “AI based membrane bioreactor for treatment of wastewater”, belongs to six people whom Guardian Australiahas traced to research institutes in India. Five of the six were contacted; none responded to requests for comment.A “GS Collison” is listed under the address for service on the registration, as well as for 11 other design registrations. However, there is no trace online of GS Collison as an entity, and the address listed for it – level 11 in one of Sydney’s Darling Park towers – corresponds to the offices of IAG, an insurance firm. In response to questions from Guardian Australia,an IAG spokesperson noted level 11 is occupied by a series of meeting rooms.Doing your own research isn’t a bad thing, I tell my patients. But just how will they spot the fraudulent papers? | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreAnotherexample, a “Smart humanoid robot for industrial applications”, includes Dr Nilesh Torwane, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Queensland as a design owner. When contacted by Guardian Australia,Torwane says he “did no design work on the product” but was invited to be named on the design by others listed on the registration. He also noted the registration “never formed part of any claim I have made for professional or academic advancement”.“I have disclosed the matter proactively to the University and am taking steps to correct the record, including seeking removal of my name from the registration,” Torwane says. Guardian Australia is not suggesting that the registration is not for a legitimate product, only that Torwane was not involved in its design.When contacted by Guardian Australia,a spokesperson for IP Australia suggested it was not aware of the research paper by Richardson and colleagues.“IP Australia welcomes any information that may indicate that the designs registration system is not being used for its intended purposes, and we will consider the implications raised by the research paper. However, we have no data to suggest that there is widespread misuse of the Australian designs registration system in the manner suggested.”Though Richardson’s paper goes some way to exploring how paper mills are operating, the mills remain “shadowy organisations”, according to Prof Adrian Barnett, a metascience researcher at the Queensland University of Technology who has previously published with Richardson.“It could be some techie kid in their bedroom, or some of them might be larger organisations that even have morning teas and employees of the month,” he says. “Who knows? But we can see they’re making a decent amount of money.”While Richardson is being interviewed, his phone buzzes again: another advertisement in a WhatsApp group. The organisations are operating at such a scale and speed it’s hard to keep up.“We’ve still barely scratched the surface,” he says.Explore more on these topicsScienceAustralian universitiesAustralian educationAcademic expertsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK’s biggest EV battery gigafactory shelves expansion as Jaguar Land Rover talks stall | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Chinese-owned AESC has pushed back plans in sign of slowing transition from petrol and diesel to electric cars
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Chinese-owned AESC has pushed back plans in sign of slowing transition from petrol and diesel to electric cars
Content: AESC’s battery gigafactory in Sunderland is situated next door to a Nissan car plant.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAESC’s battery gigafactory in Sunderland is situated next door to a Nissan car plant.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianAutomotive industryUK’s biggest EV battery gigafactory shelves expansion as Jaguar Land Rover talks stallChinese-owned AESC has pushed back plans in sign of slowing transition from petrol and diesel to electric carsAndy Burnham moves to cut new EV sales targetsJasper JollySat 15 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s biggest gigafactory has shelved plans to expand production in Sunderland because of stalled talks on a deal to supply electric car batteries toJaguar Land Rover.Chinese-owned AESC produces batteries for Nissan at its gigafactory next door to the Japanese carmaker’sSunderlandplant. However, AESC has had to push back its ramp-up plans because of lower-than-expected demand from Nissan and the lack of a deal with JLR, according to people with knowledge of the situation.The delays are another sign of the slowing transition from petrol and diesel to electric cars. Andy Burnham’s Labour government on Friday revealed that itcould cut the UK’s electric car sales targets further, in a potential blow to the electric vehicle supply chain.Andy Burnham moves to cut new EV sales targetsRead moreBattery manufacturers in the UK and Europe have had a difficult few years as carmakers have retreated from previous ambitious targets to switch from internal combustion engines to electric vehicles. Several big European battery projects have gone bankrupt, while others have been forced to scale back plans in an industry dominated byChinese players such as CATLandBYD, the world’s biggest maker of electric cars.JLR’s sister company, Agratas, is building its own gigafactory in Somerset, England. That plant is not scheduled to start production until 2027. The Guardian in Junereported that Agratas has faced construction difficultiesthat could delay the start of production further.View image in fullscreenA model of a battery factory that Jaguar Land Rover’s sister company Agratas plans to build in Somerset.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/PAJLR, Britain’s largest automotive employer, wasclose to a supply dealwith AESC last year as part of its efforts to secure cells until the Agratas factory is up and running. It is understood JLR has reached agreements with other battery suppliers in the meantime.The failure to secure JLR as a customer has had a knock-on impact on AESC. The Sunderland gigafactory has two manufacturing lines operating, but has so far held off installing a third line to supply JLR.One person familiar with the situation said talks had stalled between JLR and AESC because the carmaker was unwilling to make formal financial commitments. Another person suggested that disputes over the cost and timing of the supply of batteries were the issue.AESC also has plans for two more lines to supplyNissan. That is still understood to be the long-term plan, but the carmaker has slowed down its shift to electric as it goes through a painful process of shutting factories and laying off thousands of workers.Some people who spoke to the Guardian said they had concerns over the scale of demand for Nissan in the next few years. Nissan has stopped production of its own cars on one of its two assembly lines in Sunderland inpreparation for making cars for China’s Chery. Chery could theoretically also source batteries for its cars from AESC, but it has not yet finalised the deal with Nissan.The uncertainty over the plans reflects the changing mood in the electric car industry in recent years. Carmakers’ commitments to rapid electrification of their products have been scaled back as demand did not rise as quickly as expected and some governments – notably the US under Donald Trump – have turned against electric cars.The slowdown in the transition plus higher interest rates caused problems – often terminal – for Europe’s battery makers. The most high-profile collapses wereSweden’s NorthvoltandUK imitator Britishvolt, while Automotive Cells Company, co-owned by carmakers Stellantis and Mercedes-Benz and oil company TotalEnergies, has cancelled two gigafactory plans and China’s SVolt ended efforts to build a German plant.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSome people have expressed concerns over the scale of demand for Nissan cars in the next few years.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesSpeaking at an industry conference in June, an Agratas executive underlined the complexity of building and expanding gigafactories. Karthik Selvan, the Agratas chief procurement officer, said 1,000 shipping containers are needed to transport the equipment for a single assembly line, with half a kilometre of machines from end to end. Agratas’s gigafactory in Somerset will have 500km of pipes and 600km of wiring, he said.Much of the factory must be operated as a clean room to prevent contamination of cells, while robots must be able to cut and seal cells to an accuracy of about two microns. A human hair can be about 40 or 50 microns thick.The business that became AESC was first started within Nissan, producing batteries for the carmaker’s pioneering Leaf electric car with 1.8 gigawatt hours (GWh) of total capacity each year. In 2021, amid the coronavirus pandemic boom in spending on green technologies, AESC said it wastargeting a huge 38GWhof annual capacity. In recent years the company has said that was more an aspirational goal rather than a firm target. AESC is now aiming for annual output of 15.8GWh, enough for about 300,000 electric cars.AESC has other European plants. Its French factory is understood to be performing well thanks to strongdemand for the Renault 5, a hit electric car. However, construction of another gigafactory in Spain has been delayed.A person familiar with the situation said that AESC is still confident in the prospects for long-term battery demand, including the possibility of making to store energy from intermittent solar and wind power. Last year AESC was able to secure a£1bn refinancing, including money from the UK government, to fund the Sunderland gigafactory.The slower-than-expected ramp-up has also cast doubt on plans to build a “microgrid” to include power generation beside the factory for AESC and Nissan. The microgrid would have offered cheaper energy, making the energy-intensive factories more competitive against European or Chinese peers who pay less for electricity.AESC, Chery and JLR declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryJaguar Land RoverNissanElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsSunderlandEnergy storagenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A tax on being thin’: only high earners make overall savings on food bills from weight-loss drugs  | Weight-loss drugs | The Guardian
description: Users need discretionary income of nearly £100,000 a year to make savings on their grocery spend after paying £1,200 for GLP-1s, analysis finds
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: Users need discretionary income of nearly £100,000 a year to make savings on their grocery spend after paying £1,200 for GLP-1s, analysis finds
Content: It is estimated that nearly 3m people in Britain are on weight-loss medication. Most users buy the drugs privately with a prescription.Photograph: Jon Challicom/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt is estimated that nearly 3m people in Britain are on weight-loss medication. Most users buy the drugs privately with a prescription.Photograph: Jon Challicom/Getty ImagesWeight-loss drugs‘A tax on being thin’: only high earners make overall savings on food bills from weight-loss drugsUsers need discretionary income of nearly £100,000 a year to make savings on their grocery spend after paying £1,200 for GLP-1s, analysis findsZoe WoodSat 15 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe high cost of weight-loss medication is a “regressive tax on being thin” because the outlay outweighs any saving on food costs for all but the highest earners.Someone needs to have discretionary income of nearly £100,000 a year to actually save money after covering the £1,200 annual cost of GLP-1 medication, according to an analysis by the consultancy Baringa.“Our analysis shows that GLP-1s risk becoming a driver of inequality,” said Paddy Winters, a partner at Baringa. “Only very high earners will benefit from savings to their groceries whilst taking the GLP-1 pill.”A regressive tax is one that takes a larger percentage from lower-wage earners’ income compared with those who are more wealthy. Most users buy the drugs with a private prescription.A GLP-1 user with £39,000 left over after tax and essentials will spend £481 less a year on food. But it is not until someone has £97,500 left to spend after tax and other outgoings that their grocery spend is reduced by £1,200, according to Baringa. The cost is an average for the pill form of the medication.For “everyone else” the annual cost of the drug outweighs any reduction in spending on groceries, Winters said. “On top of that, users are spending more on vitamin supplements and personal care products like hair care, to manage side effects. In effect, GLP-1s become a regressive tax on being thin.”“We’re already seeing early signs that some people cancel their prescription after a few months because the cost adds up – but the weight comes back once you stop,” he added. “So the pattern is likely to be start, stop, regain and return, and to fund that cycle, we may well see people turn to debt.”There are 14.3 million adults living with obesity in England, according to theKing’s Fund. In a recent report, the charity said the government “needs to ensure that the people who benefit from [weight-loss medication] most are not priced out of accessing them, and that we don’t end up with wider health inequalities caused by obesity due to affordability and access”.View image in fullscreenThe launch of the Wegovy pill could lead to cost reductions for weight-loss medication.Photograph: David Parry/PAIt is estimated that 5% of adults, or nearly 3 million people, in Britain are on weight-loss medication, while 9% have taken it at some point, according to separateresearch by accountancy firm PwC.It expects this number to rise to 13% by the end of next year.About 60% of GLP-1 users are women, according to PwC. Among current users 6% come from households with income of less than £20,000, whereas 20% are from the wealthiest, earning above £100,000.Dr Leyla Hannbeck, the executive chair of the Independent Pharmacies Association, said that access to GLP-1s on theNHSis “limited only to a small eligible cohort and many people who might benefit are unable to access treatment at all unless they can afford private care”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The NHS commissioning currently protects against some of the financial inequity, but access is limited,” Hannbeck said.The price of weight-loss drugs varies significantly depending on the retailer, drug, dose and whether any discounts or subscription is being used.Hannbeck said there had been some price volatility – notably in summer 2025 the cost of Mounjaromore than doubled– but the market was becoming more competitive.“We are seeing a growing pipeline of GLP-1 products, including oral formulations and next-generation therapies,” she said, pointing to the recent launch of theWegovy pill.Those working in the industry regularly see a pattern where a patient is losing weight but ends up discontinuing treatment due to cost pressures and so regains it, said Hannbeck said. “This … reinforces the message that weight-loss is a journey and it must go hand in hand with lifestyle changes, such as diet and exercise, to maintain a healthy weight rather than a short-term quick fix.”Explore more on these topicsWeight-loss drugsInequalityPharmaceuticals industryHealthObesityNHSPrivate healthcarenewsShareReuse this content

title: Borges and Me review – a sweetly imagined literary odyssey through the Highlands | Movies | The Guardian
description: Luis Gnecco brings warmth, wit and quiet melancholy to Jorge Luis Borges in this gently enchanting adaptation of Jay Parini’s semi-fictional memoir
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Luis Gnecco brings warmth, wit and quiet melancholy to Jorge Luis Borges in this gently enchanting adaptation of Jay Parini’s semi-fictional memoir
Content: Like Sancho Panza and Don Quixote … Luis Gnecco and Fionn Whitehead in Borges and Me.Photograph: Courtesy EIFF 2026View image in fullscreenLike Sancho Panza and Don Quixote … Luis Gnecco and Fionn Whitehead in Borges and Me.Photograph: Courtesy EIFF 2026MoviesReviewBorges and Me review – a sweetly imagined literary odyssey through the HighlandsEdinburgh film festivalLuis Gnecco brings warmth, wit and quiet melancholy to Jorge Luis Borges in this gently enchanting adaptation of Jay Parini’s semi-fictional memoirPeter BradshawSat 15 Aug 2026 16.36 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 16.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is great sweetness and high-minded, unworldly charm in this adaptation ofAmerican author Jay Parini’s embellished memoir, a romantic account of his road trip through the Scottish Highlands that, as a young doctoral student at St Andrews in 1971, he really did take withJorge Luis Borges, the great writer whose blindness had become part of his mystique. Author of poetry, enigmatic short stories and metaphysical vignettes untranslatably known as the “ficciones”, Borges is described here as “the father of magical realism” – although he is surely more unique and interesting than that.Parini drives Borges around, describes everything to the maestro (who is rapt and beaming), and shields him when he uninhibitedly urinates in public; all the while he is almost entirely unaware of Borges’ reputation and the enormous honour that this therefore was. Fionn Whitehead plays the callow young Parini, in specs and duffle coat resembling a young Tom Courtenay, wretched that he may have inadvertently persuaded his brother Billy back home to volunteer for military service in Vietnam. He is ungratefully grumpy that he has to spend time away from his PhD for this babysitting task, assigned to him by his supervisor, poet and Borges translator Alastair Reid, played byAlan Cumming.Borges himself is entertainingly played by the Chilean actor Luis Gnecco; priestly, childlike, mischievous and sly, a performance executed with theatrical panache – I can imagine him doing it on stage – but without hammily overdoing the milky-eyed upward gaze. His Borges is a man who like all charming people has cultivated a dependency on others, and we can see how he has had a lifetime to deploy the combination of his huge reputation and the poignant helplessness of the blind. He has come to Scotland without a nurse or amanuensis and has to rely on the (cowed) kindness of strangers.Parini and Borges are like Sancho Panza and Don Quixote, whose presence is duly hallucinated at one stage, though it is odd that Borges, that profound Scotophile, does not specifically invokeBoswell and Johnson in the Outer Hebrides. It may be that screenwriter Oren Moverman, or Parini himself, is influenced by Gore Vidal’s memories of guiding around his blind grandfather, US senator Thomas Pryor Gore, whom he described as a “passionate sightseer”. Borges himself, in this film, on being introduced to the hesitant Parini, whimsically says: “Speak up – I am blind!” Borges is a huge Bob Dylan fan – and, apropos Vietnam, anti-war – although the script does not specifically anticipateBorges’ description of the Falklands war: two bald men fighting over a comb.The source material is avowedly fictionalised and unreliable, and this is never more obvious here than in the fanciful scene in which Borges demands to be rowed by Parini out into the middle of Loch Ness so he can commune with the monster’s presence – and actually falls in the water, supposedly gets rescued by Parini and the film cuts sharply to Borges cordially drying off later in the local pub. Try clambering into a rowboat from the water and you’ll know how plausible this is. But maybe Parini and Borges swam to shore. And yet in many ways, the story does have the ring of truth – particularly in the section in which Parini has to talk to a second and entirely different twinkle-eyed literary legend, the poet George Mackay Brown, on whom Parini is supposed to be writing his PhD, played with opaque geniality byPeter Mullan. If this story was simply fictional, introducing a second figure of this sort would be struck out by any script editor as being an unnecessary duplication. But this is the messy wrongness of real life.The title alludes to Borges’ storyBorges and I, which reflects on the difference between the writer’s public persona and his private identity. For almost the entire film, the indefatigable Borges seems to be putting on an act and yet, while quizzing Parini on his amorous adventures with a local woman (Freya Mavor), he reveals something of his own loneliness and regret. The effect is genuinely affecting and sad, and it is a lovely performance from Gnecco.Borges and Me screened at theEdinburgh film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmBiopicsJorge Luis BorgesFilm adaptationsScotlandAlan CummingPeter MullanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Thirty years after Tupac Shakur’s killing, can a murder trial offer justice? | Tupac Shakur | The Guardian
description: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis faces trial on Monday over rap star’s death that marked notorious chapter in hip-hop’s history
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis faces trial on Monday over rap star’s death that marked notorious chapter in hip-hop’s history
Content: Duane Davis speaks with his attorney during jury selection in his murder trial, related to Tupac Shakur’s killing, in Las Vegas on Thursday.Photograph: Bizuayeha Tesfaye/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDuane Davis speaks with his attorney during jury selection in his murder trial, related to Tupac Shakur’s killing, in Las Vegas on Thursday.Photograph: Bizuayeha Tesfaye/AFP/Getty ImagesTupac ShakurThirty years after Tupac Shakur’s killing, can a murder trial offer justice?Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis faces trial on Monday over rap star’s death that marked notorious chapter in hip-hop’s historyUwa Ede-OsifoSat 15 Aug 2026 10.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn September 1996, rap starTupac Shakurwas gunned down in a drive-by shooting near the Las Vegas strip, succumbing days later to his injuries. His killing, which remained unsolved for decades, gave rise to fervent conspiracy theories and conjecture.Thirty years later, one man is facing trial for the ambush: Duane “Keffe D” Davis.Authorities do not accuse Davis, a former gang leader, of firing the shots that killed Tupac. Rather,prosecutors allege he orchestrated the attack and provided the murder weapon.Opening statements in the trial of Davis, 63, are set to begin on Monday, a long-awaited moment in the case.Tupac Shakur’s family files wrongful death lawsuit against suspectRead moreThe trial, expected to last four weeks, may not resolve the question of who killed Shakur, butmembersof his family have described it as the culmination of years of grief and trauma.Davis has pleaded not guilty to the murder charge. If convicted, he could face life in prison without parole.Prosecutors havehingedtheir case on Davis’s 2019 memoir, in which he touted his status as one of the last surviving eyewitnesses to the deadly shooting.During a trip to Las Vegas to watch a Mike Tyson boxing match, Davis’s nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, got into an altercation with Shakur and his entourage, according to the memoir, titled Compton Street Legend.Davis hatched a plan to find Shakur, his label head, Marion “Suge” Knight, and other Death Row Records affiliates, he wrote. He brought a 0.40 Glock into a car they were traveling in.“The next few seconds all happened so quickly,” Davis wrote of the moment when his posse encountered Shakur’s crew.“No words were exchanged, the time for talking had passed, the shit was on! Tupac made an erratic move and began to reach down beneath his seat. It was the first and only time in my life that I could relate to the police command to, ‘Keep your hands where I can see them.’ Instead, Pac pulled out a strap, and that’s when the fireworks started. One of my guys from the back seat grabbed the Glock and started bustin’ back,” he continued.Davis did not specify who reached for the weapon. Authorities suspect his nephew, whodiedin a 1998 unrelated shootout, or another passenger, Deandre “Big Dre” Smith, who died in 2004, pulled the trigger, according to court documents.In his memoir, Davis wrote he felt “a deep sense of remorse for what happened to Tupac”, but maintained, “them jumping on my nephew gave us the green light to want to do something to their ass. Pac chose the wrong game to play …”Davis’s defense attorneys have sought to rule the book as inadmissible, arguing that he and his co-author exaggerated and embellished details.“Think of it this way: Shakur’s murder was essentially the entertainment world’s JFK assassination – endlessly dissected, mythologized, monetized – so it’s not hard to see why someone in Davis’s position might falsely place himself at the center of it all for personal gain,” his lawyers wrote in an earlier court filing.View image in fullscreenTupac Shakur and Marion ‘Suge’ Knight attend a Mike Tyson fight in Las Vegas in March 1996, six months before the fatal shooting.Photograph: Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagicThe Nevada judge Carli Kierny denied their request, saying at a Junehearing, Davis “promotes this book as his book. He encourages people to buy it to get the real truth.”Prosecutors are expected to also present evidence from interviews Davis gave to law enforcement officials in 2008 and 2009. In the book, he characterized it as an “exceptional deal”, in which he shed light on the murder of Shakur in exchange for immunity on possible drug charges.The state argued Davis’s previous media appearances and memoir publicizing details of the shooting opened the door for the police interviews to be considered in court.During his life, Shakur was a polarizing figure. Fans saw him as a frank chronicler of inner-city life, while his detractors regarded his music as a glorification of drug use and gang violence. Despite his east coast roots, Shakur was an emblem of west coast hip-hop, joining Knight’s Death Row Records in their bitter and gang-intertwined rivalry with Sean “Puffy” Combs’s New York City-based Bad Boy Records.“Tupac’s a great hero to a lot of people – part of his appeal was his sense of having a different kind of manhood,” said writer William Shaw, who interviewed Shakur in the mid-90s. The events preceding his death, though, played into the “over-macho” posturing and paranoia of the time.That notorious chapter could be revisited during the trial.Knight, who drove the vehicle Shakur was in and was shot, is on a list of witnesses. He is serving a 28-year sentence for a fatal hit-and-run in California. When asked by ABC News if he would testify at the trial, Knightsaid: “I don’t get paid to solve homicides.”Tupac’s sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, and his stepbrother, Maurice Shakur, who recently brought a wrongful death civil lawsuit against Davis, could also potentially be called to the stand.Jury selection wrapped last week, with fans sporting Tupacparaphernaliaand some of Shakur’s relatives present at the Las Vegas courthouse.Kendrick Lesane, Shakur’s cousin, called for justice, telling the Associated Press: “Whoever had anything to do with it, whoever set it up, whoever had any hand in it should be locked up in prison.”Another cousin, William Lesane, espoused Tupac’s enduring legacy, saying toFox 5he has been surprised by the rapper’s loyal fan base over the years. “He is dead in the physical form but spiritually Tupac is still alive.”The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTupac ShakurNevadaUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Snapshot review – fun found-footage scarer follows amateur Ripper hunters in the 1880s | Movies | The Guardian
description: A women’s spiritualist investigation team go after the serial killer, braving evil forces conjured into being by fear, misogyny and political rage
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: A women’s spiritualist investigation team go after the serial killer, braving evil forces conjured into being by fear, misogyny and political rage
Content: Eerie and intriguingly jittery … Snapshot.Photograph: Courtesy EIFF 2026View image in fullscreenEerie and intriguingly jittery … Snapshot.Photograph: Courtesy EIFF 2026MoviesReviewSnapshot review – fun found-footage scarer follows amateur Ripper hunters in the 1880sEdinburgh film festivalA women’s spiritualist investigation team go after the serial killer, braving evil forces conjured into being by fear, misogyny and political ragePeter BradshawSat 15 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a cheerfully ingenious lo-fi movie experiment from first-time feature director Joseph Archer and writer-performer Cathy Wippel; it’s a found-footage horror with hints of Blair Witch and Peeping Tom, set in the Victorian London ofJack the Ripper. The footage that’s been found, incidentally, is composed of unearthed reels of monochrome film from the 1880s, which we see entirely in a kinetoscope-style circular screen, flickering and glitching and buzzing with eerie accidental jump cuts from one weird scene to the next.It was supposedly shot by an enterprising pioneer called Tamworth (we hear his voice from behind the camera, but never see his face), who, it becomes clear, is a sensational and until now unacknowledged genius of early cinema – in that he manages to record lip-sync sound on to wax cylinders so we can actually hear what everyone is saying. With a cheeky touch of implied black comedy, the film is suggesting that Tamworth was somehow able to carry his camera and recording equipment to these places of Victorian horror and underclass shame as easily as an iPhone.And what he was filming was a fly-on-the-wall record of an attempt by an ad hoc women’s spiritualist investigation team to discover the truth about the Ripper murders. These women hang out with his potential victims in pubs, brothels and opium dens, believing that these crimes are not attributable to a single cloaked and top-hatted individual slipping creepily in and out of the fog, as per traditional portrayals, but the work of ghosts, uncanny and evil forces conjured into being by fear, misogyny, poverty, press misinformation and political rage. The music-hall songTwo Lovely Black Eyesleads to a ghastly finale.It is an amusing, unnerving film, and yet I felt it could also be something you would see performed by a young cast on stage at the Edinburgh fringe. It is a film that’s in the business of taking risks and having ideas, but the performances are perhaps rather one-note and the pace a little unvarying as well. Well, it’s an intriguingly jittery, paranoid sliver of anxiety from the Victorian age.Snapshot screened at theEdinburgh film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmEdinburgh film festivalThrillersHorror filmsPeriod and historical filmsCrime filmsJack the RipperreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Little Bird: this beautiful, moving Canadian drama will fill you with visceral anger | Television | The Guardian
description: There is dignity and tenderness to this drama based on the real story of the Sixties Scoop – the scandal of First Nations children who were forcibly taken from their parents and adopted by white families
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: There is dignity and tenderness to this drama based on the real story of the Sixties Scoop – the scandal of First Nations children who were forcibly taken from their parents and adopted by white families
Content: Kidnapped … Bezhig Little Bird and her sister and brother are ripped away from their home in Saskatchewan.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.View image in fullscreenKidnapped … Bezhig Little Bird and her sister and brother are ripped away from their home in Saskatchewan.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.The watcherTelevisionLittle Bird: this beautiful, moving Canadian drama will fill you with visceral angerThere is dignity and tenderness to this drama based on the real story of the Sixties Scoop – the scandal of First Nations children who were forcibly taken from their parents and adopted by white familiesRhik SamadderSat 15 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere’s one you’ll like: a man comes home to find his wife handcuffed to the wall and his young children missing. They have been taken by child protection services due to the lack of a fridge in the house, which is treated as a sign of neglect. When he confronts law enforcement officials outside, they beat him to death. Decades later, one of the children, now adopted into a Jewish home in Montreal, goes looking for the family she lost, risking the collapse of her new life to do so. I never said it was a joke. Although it turns out there was a fridge, behind the house.Watching Little Bird (18 August, 9pm, Sky Atlantic), I was reminded that TV is capable of more than mere entertainment, something we lose sight of when we think of it as a purely profit-or loss-making enterprise. I felt the visceral anger and sadness of this story of a First Nations woman caught between cultures, robbed by forces beyond her control and stonewalled by the authorities. Set in Canada, the attitude, if not the events, feel shamefully familiar.Although fiction, the story is real. Canada’s colonial history includes the Sixties Scoop – the mass abduction of First Nations children, forcibly taken by welfare services and rehomed with white families. Their adoption papers were sealed, effectively giving them no contact with parents or clue as to their heritage. Little Bird’s six episodes examine the long shadow of this cultural genocide through one family. At the end of each episode we are reminded that there are more Indigenous children in the care system than ever before.Our self-elected detective is Esther Rosenblum, now in her 20s. Her only clue is a clipping of the newspaper advertisement placing her up for adoption. This is how she knows her real name: Bezhig Little Bird. Bezhig is Ojibwe for one – a fact with a cruel flipside, revealed later in her search. As for Little Bird, it’s a name that could signify rootlessness, fragility or the possibility of transcendence.View image in fullscreenNew life … Bezhig/Esther (Darla Contois) goes in search for her real family in Little Bird.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.Esther/Little Bird is punishingly self-reliant, being barely accepted by her Jewish in-laws, despite converting at a young age. She tracks down family living on reserves, who are surrounded by poverty but have each other. She is isolated by her relative privilege. Another family member abducted at the same time was taken in by a family who needed an indentured servant, and made to sleep in an outhouse.The show brilliantly dissects racism, from the sweeping and systemic to the petty and everyday. The Ojibwe men know any emotionalism or frustration with authority will be interpreted as aggression and brutally punished. Little Bird, a trained lawyer, is repeatedly told to calm down, act with decorum, while officials fob her off, oozing contempt. Any person of colour will wince with recognition when a case worker remarks: “You look so put together,” or her fiance’s mother tells her: “You’re one of the good ones.” (Unless they aren’t put together or one of the good ones, I suppose.)The show is, ironically, at its best when restrained, training a cool eye on the banality of injustice. We are not given access to the architects of brutal welfare policy but we do meet the staff who enact it. “You’re not going to be able to do this job if you can’t get past being nice,” an experienced child protection services officer tells Adele Halpern, a greenhorn struggling to suppress her own humanity. Adele’s attempt to be more of a bureaucratic bastard is heartbreaking – and hopefully temporary. I’ve not seen all the episodes yet, but there’s a chance she may be one of the good ones.Barrel of laughs? No. But Little Bird has dignity, tenderness and beauty. Filmed on location at Treaty 1 Territory in Manitoba, Esther’s suppressed memories of her stolen life are shot through with lushness as they return, though they aren’t all happy. The Indigenous Cree-Saulteaux actor Darla Contois gives a graceful, very moving performance as Little Bird, and the show cleaned up at the Canadian Screen Awards, winning 13 trophies. It would be easy for it to be lost in a crowded marketplace amid flashier, more commercial offerings. That would be further injustice. Watching it, you’ll be angry. And that’s OK.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a gripping new thriller about the fall of Kabul | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: How the US abandonment of the Afghan capital destroyed lives. Plus: celebrating Paul Simon’s legendary Graceland album at the Proms. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: How the US abandonment of the Afghan capital destroyed lives. Plus: celebrating Paul Simon’s legendary Graceland album at the Proms. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: A tragic and shameful train of events … Kabul on BBC Four.Photograph: BBC/© Cinétévé - 24 25 Films - France Télévisions/Domniki MitropoulouView image in fullscreenA tragic and shameful train of events … Kabul on BBC Four.Photograph: BBC/© Cinétévé - 24 25 Films - France Télévisions/Domniki MitropoulouTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a gripping new thriller about the fall of KabulHow the US abandonment of the Afghan capital destroyed lives. Plus: celebrating Paul Simon’s legendary Graceland album at the Proms. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Priya ElanandSimon WardellSat 15 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKabul9pm, BBC FourWhen Joe Biden decided it was “time to end America’s longest war”, he set in motion a tragic and shameful train of events, dramatised in this gripping thriller. As Americans withdrew from Kabul the Taliban moved in, which meant hell for women, dissidents and anyone who had collaborated with the occupiers. Through the eyes of the Nazany family – trying to decide whether to stay or flee – Kabul illuminates the human dilemmas behind the geopolitics.Phil HarrisonCelebrating Graceland at the Proms7.30pm, BBC TwoA barely believable 40 years have passed since the release of Paul Simon’s remarkable album Graceland. As befitting their prominence on the original record, South African choral group Ladysmith Black Mambazo will be at the heart of the action at this Royal Albert Hall concert. They’re joined by Laura Mvula and James Bay.PHBettany Hughes’ Lost Worlds: Dawn of Civilisations8pm, Channel 4Historian Hughes concludes her journey across ancient Anatolia with a whistlestop tour of Neolithic sites. Amid the ruins of Karahantepe, she marvels at life-size human statues dating back 12,000 years, before travelling to Gordion to untangle some knotty myths about King Midas.Graeme VirtueGhosts US8.40pm, BBC ThreeView image in fullscreenThrilling scares … Ghosts US on BBC Three.Photograph: Bertrand Calmeau/BBC/CBS ©2024 CBS Broadcasting Inc. All Rights Reserved.Four back-to-back episodes open the fifth series of this American reimagining of the hit comedy – including a Halloween special involving an Egyptian ghost who is accidentally summoned. It’s zippy enough, with the spoilt Hetty, camp Issac and ditzy Flower being as watchable as their UK counterparts – even if the main couple are no match for Charlotte Ritchie and Kiell Smith-Bynoe.Priya ElanConcorde Crash: Days That Shocked the World10pm, Channel 4The 2000 Concorde crash in Paris wasn’t just a tragedy for the 113 people who lost their lives. It also marked the end of an era in terms of supersonic passenger flight. This fascinating one-off documentary explores the circumstances around the crash and asks if it could have been prevented.PHThe Staircase11pm, ITV1If you didn’t know it was based on a celebrated true-crime documentary, the revelations in this tense family drama might seem implausible. But after a lengthy trial, novelist Michael Peterson (Colin Firth) has finally been jailed for the death of his wife Kathleen. Will it give his shattered clan closure? (Short answer: no.)Graeme VirtueFilm choiceSignal One (Jonathan Sobol, 2026), 3.05pm, 10.20pm, Sky Cinema PremiereOne for fans of Denis Villeneuve’s film Arrival and the Netflix thriller 3 Body Problem, Jonathan Sobol’s science-fiction puzzler also digs into the complexities of first contact with extraterrestrials. Dennis Quaid’s tech billionaire Sam lures computer genius Annika (Isabelle Fuhrman) to his Caribbean island, where David Thewlis’s physicist Perry is on the verge of communicating with aliens. But how do you talk to them? And are they friendly or hostile? A sharp mystery in which scientific hubris vies with humanity.Simon WardellThe Batman (Matt Reeves, 2022), 9pm, ITV2View image in fullscreenBrooding … Zoe Kravitz and Robert Pattinson in The Batman on ITV2.Photograph: Jonathan Olley/APProbably the most brooding Batman on record, Robert Pattinson’s masked vigilante barely raises his voice above a whisper or his hopes above the despairing in Matt Reeves’s wonderfully dark take on the urban hero. In a crime-sodden Gotham, the murder of the mayor by a killer with a penchant for riddles plunges Bruce Wayne and his alter ego into a reckoning with widespread corruption and his own legacy. Zoë Kravitz, as the cat-like Selina Kyle, and Colin Farrell, unrecognisable as the Penguin, provide the zing as our implacable do-gooder battles chaos.SWLive sportAthletics: European Championships, 10am, BBC OneThe penultimate day sees Georgia Hunter Bell and Laura Muir in the 1500m heats from the Alexander Stadium, Birmingham.Championship Football: Sheffield Utd v Birmingham, 5.15pm, Sky Sports Main EventOn Sun, Watford v Southampton is at 12.30pm, followed by Burnley v West Ham at 3.45pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightPaul SimonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Their Strength Through Joy conversation is killing me’: Samuel Beckett’s German diaries | Samuel Beckett | The Guardian
description: Published for the first time this month, the Irish writer’s record of his months in pre-war Germany is a fascinating insight into his understanding of, and unease with, Nazism
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Published for the first time this month, the Irish writer’s record of his months in pre-war Germany is a fascinating insight into his understanding of, and unease with, Nazism
Content: ‘They’ll need to fight soon (or burst)‘ … crowds at Pariser Platz, Berlin, on the city’s 700th anniversary in 1937.Photograph: ullstein bild Dtl./Ullstein bild/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘They’ll need to fight soon (or burst)‘ … crowds at Pariser Platz, Berlin, on the city’s 700th anniversary in 1937.Photograph: ullstein bild Dtl./Ullstein bild/Getty ImagesSamuel Beckett‘Their Strength Through Joy conversation is killing me’: Samuel Beckett’s German diariesPublished for the first time this month, the Irish writer’s record of his months in pre-war Germany is a fascinating insight into his understanding of, and unease with, NazismKate ConnollySat 15 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWar was not yet on the immediate horizon whenSamuel Beckettvisited the German city of Hamburg in October 1936, but after watching the apoplexy that Adolf Hitler’s braying induced in ordinary Germans, the Irish playwright was certain that peace could not last. “They’ll need to fight soon (or burst),” he noted in his diary on 6 October.View image in fullscreenSamuel Beckett as a young man.Photograph: Estate of Samuel Beckett c/o Rosica Colin Limited, LondonThe six notebooks that Beckett compiled during his six-month journey across Germany between late September 1936 and April 1937, published for the first time by German publisherSuhrkamp on 20 Augustthis year, put paid to a commonly held view of the author of Waiting for Godot as a poet of pure pessimism, interested in despair and stasis but unconcerned by real-life politics.On the basis of letters and diary extracts, critics of the past concluded that the 1969 Nobel Prize winner travelled acrossGermanyin a state of self-absorption, without paying attention to the rise of totalitarianism. But the notebooks in their entirety show that Beckett was studying National Socialist resentment in close detail.He noticed changes in fashion, such as the predominance of the “Hitler coat”, and collected the “holy phrases” of the Nazi movement in lists:Führer(“leader”),Bewegung(“movement”),Blut und Boden(“blood and soil”), andFreiheit und Ehre(“freedom and honour”), even if they repulsed him.Ihre Kraft durch Freude Unterhaltung macht mich fertig, he noted in German on1 November 1936: “Their Strength Through Joy conversation is killing me.”For now Beckett, who would join the French resistance in 1940, kept his disgust mostly private, merely taking pleasure in subtle parodies of totalitarian behaviour, by “(sticking) the wrong arm out” when invited to give the Nazi salute.View image in fullscreen‘Very dubious at the moment’ … Samuel Beckett’s 1936 notebook.Photograph: Laura Bennetto“He was aware that his diaries could have been confiscated,” said the notebooks’ co-editor Mark Nixon, a professor of modern literature and Beckett studies at the University of Reading. “He has to be careful as he has to get out of Germany with them. Maybe he could have been more explicit had this danger not hung over him. But they do clearly form a rebellion against Nazi rationalising discourse.”Beckett’s tour of some 30 German towns and cities, including Hamburg, Berlin, Dresden and Munich, was motivated by a desire to view works of art and to improve his language skills. An interest in German – his third language after English and French – was probably influenced by lengthy visits between 1928 and 1932 to his cousin and sweetheart Peggy Sinclair and her family, who lived in Kassel.The curiosity about German language and culture was reminiscent of the American English writer Christopher Isherwood, who, asked how he documented Germany between 1929 and 1933, said: “I am a camera with its shutter open, quite passive, recording not thinking.”Beckett’s observed the country’s descent into totalitarianism in an already depressed state of mind. Peggy had died in Germany of tuberculosis in May 1933, his father of a heart attack the following month. The remaining Sinclairs, of Jewish descent, had been forced to flee Germany in 1936.By the time he set out for Cuxhaven, Beckett had two years of psychoanalysis behind him, and his diaries reflect deep anguish, psychosomatic complaints, medical ailments, bodily functions, financial woes and angst over his writer’s block. At times, it is hard to separate his own problems from the darkening political situation around him.Bald fange ich wirklich an zu kotzen. Oder fahr heim(“soon I’ll really start to puke. Or I’ll go home”)he writes on 15 January, 1937.View image in fullscreenThis 1931 portrait by Karl Leyhausen depicts Peggy Sinclair, Samuel Beckett’s cousin, who died in 1933.Photograph: piemags/Alamy“Beckett writes what he sees, that’s the value of him,” Nixon said. “At the same time the diaries are an important part of the journey of Beckett becoming Beckett. In the diaries he keeps telling himself to be more minimal, which is the Beckett we know, who strips everything away that doesn’t matter.”The writer’s subsequent move to France and involvement with the French resistance can be seen as a reaction to what he witnessed in Nazi Germany, Nixon believes. “He was an eye witness to totalitarianism,” he said. “His literature is very clearly based on this experience.”Filled with tiny, hard-to-decipher right-leaning handwriting, the 545 pages of the German diaries were found in the cellar of his Paris flat after his death in 1989 by his nephew Edward Beckett, who has worked with the editors Nixon and Oliver Lubrich to bring the 120,000 words to publication.They are, Nixon says, Beckett’s own personal witness statement, and were not meant for publication. Some entries reveal an unsavoury side to the revered modernist master, including misogynistic remarks and accounts of brothel visits.“Their value as a historical document is in large part due to the fact that he never edited them. The reason it’s ethically OK to be publishing them is that he didn’t destroy them like he did other things.”While Suhrkamp’s bilingual edition, translated by Gaby Hartel, is tailored to political historical interest, an English-language edition, expected to be published next April, will concentrate more on the place of the diaries in Beckett’s literary development. Rights have been acquired by China, France and Italy among other countries.Samuel Beckett: German Diaries (German and English version) is published bySuhrkamp on 20 AugustExplore more on these topicsSamuel BeckettAutobiography and memoirGermanyNazismEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Art Spiegelman: ‘The US needs a counter-revolution’ | Art Spiegelman | The Guardian
description: More than four decades after his Holocaust story Maus transformed the graphic novel genre, Art Spiegelman discusses Trump, the shadow of 9/11 and the rise of fascism in America
Author: Sophie McBain
Headline: More than four decades after his Holocaust story Maus transformed the graphic novel genre, Art Spiegelman discusses Trump, the shadow of 9/11 and the rise of fascism in America
Content: Art Spiegelman.Photograph: Hannah Assouline/Hannah ASSOULINE / opale.photo / eyevineView image in fullscreenArt Spiegelman.Photograph: Hannah Assouline/Hannah ASSOULINE / opale.photo / eyevineArt SpiegelmanArt Spiegelman: ‘The US needs a counter-revolution’More than four decades after his Holocaust story Maus transformed the graphic novel genre, Art Spiegelman discusses Trump, the shadow of 9/11 and the rise of fascism in AmericaSophie McBainSat 15 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTShareWhen the cartoonistArt Spiegelmanbegan dating his future wife, Françoise Mouly, in the mid 70s, she would tell him not to worry about walking her home, because even the New York muggers didn’t bother venturing to where she lived in Soho. He moved in with her quite suddenly not long after, when his apartment in Greenwich Village burned down. His landlord, who lived on the ground floor, was a hoarder – once, when he came to collect Spiegelman’s rent, a cockroach crawled up from under his shirt collar – and eventually his accumulated junk caught alight.This feels like a quintessential New York story, but then much of Spiegelman’s life does, or at least fits with the kind of stories we like to tell ourselves about the city. The Soho apartment Spiegelman and Mouly have lived in for five decades is worth millions now and is surrounded by high-end designers; his studio, down the road, is above a branch of Tiffany’s. “It’s just kind of an embarrassment, I mean Tiffany’s is not my class,” says Spiegelman, who refers to these flash new arrivals, dismissively, as “very fancy airport mall stores”.The couple used to print their own “oddball” comics from a printing press that Mouly, who had dropped out of architecture school in France, installed in their house. Today, they are a New York art establishment power couple. Mouly is the art editor of the New Yorker, having been recruited by Tina Brown in the 90s, when she was looking to make the highbrow magazine “hot”. Spiegelman, who in 1992 became the first cartoonist to win a Pulitzer prize for Maus, a graphic novel about his father’s memories of the Holocaust, has done more than anyone to establish comics as a serious art form, capable of tackling difficult political and personal subjects. The couple’s trajectory had “its own weird logic, although it wouldn’t be anyone else’s. It’s not a ‘recipe for success’,” Spiegelman jokes. “We were wilfully just doing what we wanted to do.”He is 78 years old, slight and scruffy-looking, with a grizzled goatee and wispy grey hair, and he can still talk faster than most people can think. He offers me a coffee when I arrive at his home on a sweltering June day, but then keeps getting distracted from making it by his own anecdotes. He takes me on an impromptu tour, showing me the living room that held Mouly’s huge, 1,000lb Multilith printing press, until they had a toddler and it became too dangerous to keep. There is a mural painted by the cartoonist Gary Panter on the living room wall, and another just above their bed, painted to replace a set of bookshelves that collapsed on to the couple when they were asleep, breaking Mouly’s nose and prompting a big book clear out. “Is this book worth dying for?” Spiegelman says they asked of themselves, a more hardcore alternative to Swedish death cleaning, but even so there are full bookshelves in every room, and pieces of art and curios everywhere.As a young man, Spiegelman earned a living designing collectible parody cards for Topps bubblegum, while cutting his teeth in San Francisco’s underground comics scene. After moving to New York, he started Raw magazine with Mouly. Raw published experimental work by comic artists from all over the world, and “it created its own Potemkin village of, yes, all these artists have one thing in common, which is they ain’t like each other,” he recalls. Maus was initially serialised as an insert in Raw – new issues came out sporadically, whenever Spiegelman had finished a chapter.View image in fullscreenArt Spiegelman and his wife, Françoise Mouly, in San Francisco.Photograph: Corbis/VCG/Getty ImagesHe struggled to find a publisher for the book, because no one knew what to do with such an unusual work, an autobiographical history of the Holocaust that depicted Jews as mice and Nazis as cats. The responses were “pretty universal that whatever this is, is interesting. But it’s not publishable,” he says. Eventually, Pantheon published it, and Maus became a bestseller. Spiegelman has said he struggled to emerge from the shadow of his best-known creation, but when I ask if he still feels ambivalent about Maus’s success he replies, “I’m ambivalent about absolutely everything … I knew that I wanted it to be read, but it just didn’t occur to me that it would become a phenomenon, it was such an outlier.”Maus took 13 years to make. For Spiegelman, making comics is often a tortuous process. If many artists complain of creative blocks, then what he experiences is more like a “blockade: there’s no way in or out. I think it’s like a version of impostor syndrome,” he says. “I know I’ve done comics before and they work, but I have no idea how to do it when I start a new one … I have to rethink what it might be to make a comic.” He feels acutely aware of his limitations – “I always understood that I wasn’t the best drawer on the block” – and every square must be painstakingly reworked, dozens of times. “It seems like I don’t function well. I mean, I don’t go: ‘OK, I finished this graphic novel, I’ll do another one – by God!’ – and then off to the races. Something has to make me go through what is such a difficult process for me,” he says.double quotation markWhatever our democratic ideals were, at least we had them – now it’s all so cynicalSpiegelman had virtually stopped making comics and was focused on writing essays and designing covers for the New Yorker when the 9/11 attacks took place. The ground shook, and from his Soho apartment he could see the north tower burning. His first thought was to run to collect his daughter Nadja, who had just started high school at the foot of the towers. Then, fearing that the United Nations might be targeted next, they rushed uptown to collect his son Dash, who was at the UN School. This was the kind of catastrophe his parents, both Auschwitz survivors, had always warned him about, when world history and personal history collide. “I’m not going to get past this unless I start drawing about it,” he realised afterwards, and he vowed to make comics again.View image in fullscreenArt Spiegelman’s studio in New York.Photograph: Tim Knox/eyevineHe produced a series about 9/11 for the German magazine Die Zeit, which was later run by other European magazines and American Jewish weekly the Forward. On one page he describes himself as “equally terrorised by al-Qaida and by my own government”. He felt that other American publications were too quiescent in the aftermath of the attacks, and not yet receptive to his fear that the US government was using 9/11 as cover for a massive crackdown on civil liberties and to launch xenophobic wars. “Sigh! It’s hard to be an artist who is consistently Seconds Ahead of His Time,” he writes in the foreword to In the Shadow of No Towers, a book that compiled these comics and is being reissued to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11. (Although, he says, it may come out late – a shipment has been held up in the strait of Hormuz.)Why was he so alert to the implications for US civil liberties? “Well, my tendency is not to trust the government, so that came easily,” he says. “But it also seems so obvious, like all of a sudden there were police cars and military trucks on Canal Street. We were being told where we could walk, where we couldn’t walk, what we could say, what we couldn’t say. It’s visceral. It’s not like: ‘OK, I’ve read this book on propaganda and here’s how it works.’” Spiegelman notes the direct link between the post-9/11 security crackdowns and some of the excesses of the Trump administration: Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Ice, was created in the aftermath of the terror attacks.A theme running through Spiegelman’s work is trauma, and its long and toxic aftermath. His parents were Polish Jews who survived the camps but lost most of their family, including their first-born son, Richieu, during the Holocaust. They resettled in Rego Park, Queens, where Spiegelman was born in 1948. In 1968, his mother, Anja, killed herself. Spiegelman was living with his parents at the time, having been hospitalised after suffering a psychotic episode while studying at Harpur College, New York, where he had been experimenting with every drug he could find. Maus is partly about Spiegelman’s fraught relationship with his father Vladek, who is depicted as mean, difficult and racist – a man who complicates the comforting lie we tell ourselves that suffering must make a person kinder or nobler. In one comic, published in Breakdowns (2008), Spiegelman hands a treasure chest to his young son, a family heirloom that was given to him by his own father. Excited, Dash opens the box, only to reveal a terrifying monster. “It’s magical! It makes you feel so worthless you don’t believe you even have the right to breathe,” Spiegelman tells his son, a cigarette hanging from his mouth.When it comes to 9/11, however, Spiegelman’s perspective has shifted. He no longer views the day as an “end of the world moment”. “It was a big deal. But it was a small big deal compared to the big deals that are going on now,” he tells me. “I’d much rather be in New York than in Iran, for example.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Art SpiegelmanAround 50 minutes after Spiegelman fires up his Nespresso machine, he finishes making two coffees, and we carry them up to his sunny roof terrace, which as he promised has beautiful views of downtown Manhattan. Spiegelman muses that the US’s volatile politics might reflect humankind’s natural tendency to self-destruction. “I guess, after a while, you get restless, so if you get too comfortable you create problems for yourself, even in more mundane, small-time life, never mind as a nation. At this point, we just had the bad luck of having a megalomaniac walking on to the scene,” he says, of the Trump presidency. American politics is, after all, “entertaining if you don’t give a shit, if you’re nihilistic”.Spiegelman’s mood is sombre as he discusses how Trump has “very effectively dismantled” the country’s democratic ideals: “Whatever the ideals were, we never lived up to them, but at least we had them. Now it’s all so cynical and sordid and stupid.” The president “is cutting off civil liberties and using his powers to squelch dissent and enrich himself in such thoroughly illegal ways, it’s kind of mindblowing”, Spiegelman says, and he finds himself watching in alarm as the “plutocrat in chief” and his “few dozen toadies” get ever richer while ordinary Americans struggle and suffer a “new indignity every day”. He has no hesitation in describing the Trump administration as fascist. “It’s fascism,” he says. “It’s not nazism, per se, but it has a template that it’s following. And it does have to do with othering, which is the basis of what Maus is about, it’s: ‘OK, you guys are mice, we’re cats.’” Maus is among the many books to be banned by various Republican school boards in recent years, but Spiegelman says he has a “predilection” for producing the kind of art people will seek to ban. Sales of Maus spiked in response to the bans.“I tend to be pessimistic, but this is worse than most things I know,” he says of American politics. “I just don’t see how we get out of this.” The media are struggling with how to convey the stakes in this post-truth era, he explains, the courts are packed with Trump appointees, democratic norms have been destroyed, and there is no effective opposition. The Republicans are “at this point the equivalent of made men in the mafia,” Spiegelman says, “they’ve committed a murder, they’re complicit in something and they have to keep moving as a complicit unit, so it’s very hard to get someone to blow the whistle and say ‘This is crazy.’” The US needs a “counter-revolution”, Spiegelman says. “But I don’t know where to look for it because the Democrats are so timid.”An alert sounds on Spiegelman’s phone, and for a moment he is flustered, trying to figure out why on Earth this thing is producing noise. “In some ways I’m slowing down, in other ways I’m still doing what interests me, and sometimes I’m capable of being interested in something more challenging, sometimes less,” he says. He plans, after this interview, to work on a lithograph, his friend having dropped off some stone for him to carve. He hopes to keep living and working in Soho for the rest of his life – but his apartment is a walk-up, and he concedes fate might have other ideas for him. “Anyone can be a genius at 25; at 50 it takes some doing,” Spiegelman writes in one comic. What about at 78, I ask? “I feel like an idiot at this point!” he jokes. “I can’t think the way I thought when I was 25,” he says. He has become more forgetful, for instance, but takes consolation in knowing he can still produce challenging, original art. “There’s still enough wiring that makes it somewhat unorthodox, but I don’t think I’m as far off the grid as I had been.”A new edition of In the Shadow of No Towers by Art Spiegelman will be published by Penguin in September. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com

title: Charlene Kaye: Diversity Shredder review – killer riffs slay toxic music industry | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: This is a fun and feverish journey, with well-crafted comedy and screaming guitar, through the star’s career so far
Author: Arusa Qureshi
Headline: This is a fun and feverish journey, with well-crafted comedy and screaming guitar, through the star’s career so far
Content: Magnetic … Charlene Kaye.Photograph: Luci StansfieldView image in fullscreenMagnetic … Charlene Kaye.Photograph: Luci StansfieldEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewCharlene Kaye: Diversity Shredder review – killer riffs slay toxic music industryGilded Balloon Teviot, EdinburghThis is a fun and feverish journey, with well-crafted comedy and screaming guitar, through the star’s career so farArusa QureshiSat 15 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn an industry that claims to be inclusive, it’s so easy to feel tokenised. For musician and comedian Charlene Kaye, it has been an uphill battle feeling like the token queer Asian female guitar player, in demand to cater to people’s otherwise superficial concern around diversity, as well as their attempts at being perceived as politically conscious. But if you’re booked and busy, and genuinely skilled at what you do, does it matter if the requests come in through slightly nefarious means?Diversity Shredder is a fun and feverish romp through Kaye’s journey of finding her artistic voice, and what it means to be an Asian American musician in the context of a very broken and unbalanced capitalist system. Using well-crafted, multi-genre musical comedy along with her masterful guitar skills, Kaye reflects on the mental gymnastics at play when you’re a person of colour trying to navigate a career in music, when all people really seem to want is Cassandra from Wayne’s World.Flamenc Oh!! review – frills, flirting and fierce footwork in breezy Spanish comedyRead moreKaye has built a global following via Instagram and TikTok with videos in which she parodies popular music trends and genres such as K-pop, and chart-topping stars from Taylor Swift to Ed Sheeran. Going viral on social media doesn’t automatically translate to physical stage presence but as a musician who has consistently toured, playing solo and with multiple bands, her aura is magnetic and only amplified by her natural, conversational humour and unbridled sass.A large screen on stage displays obnoxiously written emails from prospective collaborators – from a fresh-faced Soundcloud rapper, to a monotonous folk singer-songwriter – as well as clips of the few examples of “Asian music” that exist in the western pop canon. Think the Vapors’ Turning Japanese, David Bowie’s China Girl, and the massively problematic Asian Girlz by LA band Day Above Ground.There’s a lot of material packed into this hour, largely because Kaye has such a hefty and high-quality bank of content. At times, it could do with some breathing room to allow for Kaye’s witty lyricism and uncompromising punchlines to land.
