title: Ayo Adenekan: Homeland Insecurity review – SNL UK writer woos the room with summer romance | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A fringe fling is the backbone for a mischievous set with deft jokes and a fresh perspective but some of this material needs another draft
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: A fringe fling is the backbone for a mischievous set with deft jokes and a fresh perspective but some of this material needs another draft
Content: ‘Stop the trains!’ … Ayo Adenekan.Photograph: Matthew StrongeView image in fullscreen‘Stop the trains!’ … Ayo Adenekan.Photograph: Matthew StrongeEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewAyo Adenekan: Homeland Insecurity review – SNL UK writer woos the room with summer romanceCabVol @ Monkey Barrel, EdinburghA fringe fling is the backbone for a mischievous set with deft jokes and a fresh perspective but some of this material needs another draftBrian LoganSat 15 Aug 2026 06.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAyo Adenekan’s ascent has been swift. Last year, the rookie comic cracked a joke on stage about Doctor Who’s Ncuti Gatwa. This year, he scripted jokesforGatwa, as a writer on Sky’sSaturday Night Live UK. In this second fringe set, the Edinburgh man shows why TV producers spirited him away after last year’s debut: his perspective is fresh, he writes a deft joke, and he has the warmth to win over a room. But he’s not the finished article. He could vary the pace, which tends to the sonorous. Several of his ideas go underdeveloped. And the story Homeland Insecurity tells is unremarkable.It’s a love story, Adenekan tells us at the start, about a summer romance splashed across the canvas of the Edinburgh fringe. A meaningful but fly-by-night fling, it provides the backbone for an hour in which the 24-year-old ranges across his relationship with his dad, his “straight white man friends”, and his outrage when a namesake comedian comes up from London to steal his thunder at last year’s festival. “I’m not concerned about the boats, man. Stop the trains!” There’s a running visual gag too about product placement, which could be something, but Adenekan never really commits to the bit.That’s not the only instance where the material might benefit from one more draft: see the routine about his discomfort with dating black men. Elsewhere, I wanted Adenekan to give the delivery a bit more welly. Instead, he repeats and circles back on himself: the more times he tells us (and there were several) that he’s delighted to be back in this venue after last year’s success, the more I found my own delight diminishing.Jordan Brookes: The Part of You That’s Always Screaming review – former fringe champ’s chewy croissant taleRead moreBut no doubt Adenekan has the raw materials to fashion something distinctive, with his under-exposed angle on life (Gatwa notwithstanding) as a queer Scottish-African, his smooth and mischievous manner, and the ability to drop choice lines including (of his Nigerian diaspora family) “we’re Muslim like Meghan Markle is black”. Even if his summer romance story finally feels generic, there’s enough here to suggest others will soon be queueing up to give Adenekan the love.AtCabVol @ Monkey Barrel, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The bar here is low’: the best (and worst) supermarket brioche burger buns, tasted and rated | Bread | The Guardian
description: Brioche buns make an indulgent, rich home for a burger – but which have the perfect fluffy texture and which come with a chemical-like plastic aroma?
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Brioche buns make an indulgent, rich home for a burger – but which have the perfect fluffy texture and which come with a chemical-like plastic aroma?
Content: Our resident tester analysed everything from the packet to the egg wash.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonView image in fullscreenOur resident tester analysed everything from the packet to the egg wash.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterBreadReview‘The bar here is low’: the best (and worst) supermarket brioche burger buns, tasted and ratedBrioche buns make an indulgent, rich home for a burger, but which have the perfect fluffy texture and which come with a chemical-like plastic aroma?The best supermarket veggie burgersTom HuntSat 15 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrioche is a fabulously luxurious dough enriched with eggs and copious amounts of butter (often 25% or more of the total dough). Supermarket brioche buns, however, are a little different: the best products contain about 6-11% butter at most and some, surprisingly, contained none at all, using replacements such as palm fat and rapeseed oil instead.But all is not lost: even the most processed products were passable, and the best were quite delicious. I tested these straight from the packet, analysing the egg wash, type of crumb and texture. I scored on flavour, value, processing, sustainability (though most products lack standards and certifications) and animal welfare.The bar here is pretty low, though, with most buns sitting firmly in UPF territory. Squishy, carotene-coloured and stored in plastic, they’re fabricated from a cocktail of fats, emulsifiers and preservatives, creating remarkable shelf life but unremarkable buns with little authenticity.The best supermarket brioche burger bunsBest overall:Waitrose No 1 brioche rollsView image in fullscreen£1.60 for two at Waitrose (80p each)★★★★☆An extra-large bun with a light, fluffy texture and open crumb, with a distinguishable nutty flavour from the brown butter. A notably simple ingredients list, including a good ratio of free-range egg and butter. Emulsifier- and preservative-free.Best bargain:Co-op Irresistible four brioche bunsView image in fullscreen£1.75 for four at Co-op (44p each)★★★☆☆A large, round, dark-golden bun with a turmeric-yellow crumb and a really nice, buttery flavour. Contains eggs, emulsifiers and flavouring.And the rest …M&S Collection brioche buns made with sourdoughView image in fullscreen£2.20 for two at Ocado (£1.10 each)★★★★☆An extra-large bun with a dark-brown glaze and an open, cakey crumb. Made with a simple ingredients list, including sourdough, which gives it a sour twang. Enriched with butter from Brittany, free-range egg and clotted cream. No emulsifiers, preservatives or acidity regulators.Aldi Specially Selected brioche burger bunsView image in fullscreen99p for four at Aldi (25p each), in store only★★★☆☆Four French-made, small, shiny golden buns with a closed crumb and springy texture. A great burger bun with good flavour, rich, sweet, and without the sourness found in some other products. Contains emulsifiers, eggs, and no artificial flavourings or preservatives.Asda Exceptional brioche burger bunsView image in fullscreen£1.42 for four at Asda (36p each)★★★☆☆A medium-sized classic, airy brioche bun with a nice, golden carotene-coloured closed crumb and sour twang. Rich, sweet and soft. Made with free-range eggs. Contains emulsifiers, palm fat, preservatives and maltodextrin.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSainsbury’s Taste the Difference brioche burger bunsView image in fullscreen£1.50 for four at Sainsbury’s (38p each)★★★☆☆A medium-sized bun with a classic texture, light and fluffy, with a closed crumb. Rich and buttery and quite sweet, with a sourness from the vinegar. Contains eggs and palm oil. No artificial flavourings or preservatives.Morrisons the Best brioche burger bunsView image in fullscreen£1.50 for four at Morrisons (38p each)★★☆☆☆A small, soft and buttery roll with an open crumb and sweet finish. A long ingredients list including eggs, palm fat, emulsifiers, preservative, maltodextrin and flavouring.Tesco Fire Pit brioche burger bunsView image in fullscreen£1.95 for eight at Tesco (24p each)★★☆☆☆A party pack of eight egg-glazed brioche buns. Sweet with a sour twang from the fermented wheat flour. Soft but a little bready, with a light but open crumb; holds together well, though. Contains eggs, palm oil and emulsifiers.St Pierre brioche bunsView image in fullscreen£2.90 for six at Sainsbury’s (48p each)£2.90 for six at Tesco (48p each)★★☆☆☆A sweet, small, sliced French brioche, with a uniform glaze. Soft in texture with a closed crumb and a chemical-like plastic aroma (probably from the packaging). Contains eggs, invert sugar syrup, flavouring and emulsifier.La Boulangère brioche burger bunsView image in fullscreen£1.60 for four at Ocado (40p each)★☆☆☆☆A long-life French import made with barn eggs and no butter (just rapeseed oil) so arguably not brioche at all. A classic, golden egg glaze, a white bready texture, with good bounce and an open crumb. It contains preservatives and has a chemical aroma, but it is emulsifier-free.For more, read the bestsupermarket salad bagsandbest supermarket veggie burgersExplore more on these topicsBreadThe FilterBarbecueFoodBurgersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From food to tech to travel: the best student deals and discounts | Student finance | The Guardian
description: You can save money at university, especially using schemes such as UNiDAYS, Student Beans or TOTUM
Author: Joe Pinner
Headline: You can save money at university, especially using schemes such as UNiDAYS, Student Beans or TOTUM
Content: Many food retailers offer money off with a UNiDAYS, Student Beans or TOTUM account.Photograph: Maureen McLean/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMany food retailers offer money off with a UNiDAYS, Student Beans or TOTUM account.Photograph: Maureen McLean/REX/ShutterstockThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Student financeFrom food to tech to travel: the best student deals and discountsYou can save money at university, especially using schemes such as UNiDAYS, Student Beans or TOTUM‘Watch your spending, use free perks’: an insider’s tips on student moneyJoe PinnerSat 15 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith rents on the up and food costing more, maintenance loans are stretched thinner than ever. Knowing how, and where, to get a discount can make a real difference.A golden rule is to register with the big discount websites and apps – UNiDAYS, Student Beans and TOTUM – using your university email address as soon as you have one. Each has a slightly different roster of retailers, so it is worth signing up to all three.Many of the deals below are only unlocked once you have verified your student status. The sites explain how to do this. If you are unable to verify using email, you may be able to upload, for example, an acceptance letter from your university.Food and essentialsView image in fullscreenSandwiches in a Marks & Spencer store.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBoots: anAdvantage Card gets you 10%off thousands of products instore and online – handy for weekly toiletries and the odd emergency paracetamol run. You need to apply for a card then go into a shop with a valid student ID to activate your membership and qualify for the discounts.Marks & Spencer: 25% off in store’s “food on the move” range through UNiDAYS. This range includes sandwiches, wraps, poké bowls and salads, plus a variety of snacks.Uber One: after a four-week free trial, students get half-price membership (£2.49 a month), for discounted delivery and takeaways – useful on the days when a big supermarket shop feels like one task too many.The Co-op: 10% off your shop in-store – but now only for some students, such as those with a Young Scot card. Central Co-op and Southern Co-op give Student Beans members 10% off at their participating stores.Going outMany pub and restaurant chains – including Greene King, Pizza Express and Zizzi – offer money off. Greene King offers 20% off all food and drinks (show your student ID at the bar to get one of its 20% off student cards).Tech and subscriptionsView image in fullscreenHave you checked out ways to make savings on your technology and subscriptions?Illustration: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesAmazon Prime for Students: new sign-ups get six months of Prime free, after which it drops to half price (£4.49 a month).Link your Amazon and Deliveroo accounts through a site such as UNiDAYS and you will also get a year’s worth of Deliveroo Plus – which gets you free delivery on orders above £15 from restaurants, or above £25 from shops – at no extra cost instead of the usual £3.49 a month.Kindle Unlimited: claim 30 days free through UNiDAYS – useful for clearing a reading list without buying every set text.Microsoft365: many universities give students free access to the full Office suite – Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook – via their institution’s IT department, so check before you pay for anything.Spotify Premium: one month free, then £5.99 a month – roughly half the standard price.Apple: offers “education pricing” – a variety of reductions on MacBooks and other items – to students who have a UNiDAYS account.Microsoft: up to 15% off items such as laptops and accessories bought directly.Adobe Creative Cloud:If you are on a creative course or just want to develop your skills, Adobe offers a 75% saving on its Pro subscription for students, reducing the cost from £66.49 a month to £16.24.Gyms and fitnessThe Gym Group: up to 25% off via the student discount sites.Fitness First: up to 25% off via the student discount sites.Strava: 30 days of its premium plan for free, then 50% off the subscription (taking it down to £27.49 a year).University gyms are almost always cheaper than commercial ones, andBUCS (BritishUniversitiesand Colleges Sport) UNIversal Gym schememeans if your own university’s gym is signed up, you can use any other participating gym for free. That’s great if you are visiting friends or family at or near another campus and don’t want to break your routine.TravelView image in fullscreenStudents can get National Express discounts via various websites.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesFlixBus: 20% off fares via UNiDAYS and Student Beans.National Express: up to 20% off coach tickets via UNiDAYS, Student Beans and TOTUM.16-25 Railcard: one-third off most rail fares (you can get one for free for four years if you open a Santander Edge student current account). Alternatively, students get 15% off the cost of the card via Student Beans and UNiDAYS – typically it’s £35 a year.FashionAsos and Nikeoffer 10% off via UNiDAYS, Student Beans and TOTUM, with JD Sports offering 20%.Urban Outfittershas 10% off all year-round for students.Always carry proof of student status – a university ID card, or a UNiDAYS, Student Beans or TOTUM card or login.Also, don’t be afraid to ask if a student discount isn’t advertised. Many independent shops and cafes offer one but don’t always put up a sign.Explore more on these topicsStudent financeSaving moneyStudentsConsumer affairsUniversitiesHigher educationUK cost of living crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meera Sodha’s vegan black rice salad with tomatoes, tamarind and green beans – recipe | Salad | The Guardian
description: Change up your seasonal salads with an easy-to-prep dish that centres on slow-cooked rice and a lively Asian dressing
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: Change up your seasonal salads with an easy-to-prep dish that centres on slow-cooked rice and a lively Asian dressing
Content: Meera Sodha’s black rice salad with tomatoes, tamarind and green beans.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence. Photo assistant: Sophie Bronze.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha’s black rice salad with tomatoes, tamarind and green beans.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence. Photo assistant: Sophie Bronze.The new veganSaladMeera Sodha’s vegan black rice salad with tomatoes, tamarind and green beans – recipeChange up your seasonal salads with an easy-to-prep dish that centres on slow-cooked rice and a lively Asian dressingMeera SodhaSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere’s a recipe straight out of the low-effort, high-reward school of cooking, in which you chop the vegetables and nuts, boil the rice and beans, throw over a dressing … and it’s done! It was written in the middle of a heatwave, when cooking felt impossible, but I couldn’t look at another watermelon and feta salad. The trade-off is that this dish relies heavily on a couple of key ingredients: sambal oelek (which gives the salad its sparkle) and black rice, which, unlike other types of rice in a salad, never tastes worthy.Black rice salad with tomatoes, tamarind and green beansWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appBlack rice is sometimes sold as “venus black rice” or “black pearl rice”, and cooking times vary from 20-40 minutes, depending on whether the rice has been par-cooked (you’ll know only by checking the cooking time listed on the packet). Sambal oelek can be bought from Asian supermarkets or online, while tamarind paste can vary, though branded ones available from supermarkets tend to be good – if yours is from an Asian supermarket, however, I’d suggest adding it half a tablespoon at a time only at the end, until the mix tastes right to you.Prep15 minCookUp to 1 hr(depending on the rice)Serves45 tbsp neutral oil(eg, groundnut, sunflower or rapeseed)2 garlic cloves, peeled and minced4½ tbsp light soy sauce1½ tbsp tamarind paste1 tbsp dark brown sugar½ tbsp sambal oelek– I like Lucullus200g fine green beans, topped350g black venus rice(AKA black pearl rice)350g cherry tomatoes, halved100g frozen shelled edamame beans, defrosted60g roasted unsalted cashews, roughly chopped40g fresh coriander, choppedBring a large pan of water to a boil, then cock a lid over the top. Meanwhile, make the dressing: in a large bowl, mix the oil, garlic, soy, tamarind paste, sugar and sambal oelek.Once the water is boiling, drop in the beans and cook for six to eight minutes, until tender. Scoop out with a slotted spoon or tongs, shake off the excess water, then tip into the dressing bowl.Gently pour the rice into the still boiling water, then cook according to the packet instructions, until tender. Drain, rinse under cold water and drain again well.Tip the rice into the bean bowl, add the tomatoes, edamame, cashews and coriander, toss to combine, then serve.Explore more on these topicsSaladThe new veganMain courseVegetablesFoodRicerecipesShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘I got the impression he liked me well enough, but who knows?’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Andrew, 75, is a retired graphic designer / cartographer and meets Gilli, 64, is a training consultant, group facilitator and counsellor
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Andrew, 75, is a retired graphic designer / cartographer and meets Gilli, 64, is a training consultant, group facilitator and counsellor
Content:
Photograph: Joel Goodman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joel Goodman/The GuardianBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘I got the impression he liked me well enough, but who knows?’Andrew, 75, a retired graphic designer, meets Gilli, 64, a counsellorSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 04.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenAndrew on GilliWhat were you hoping for?An exciting evening in a great restaurant with a lovely lady I might be able to start a relationship with.First impressions?Gilli looked absolutely fantastic, with lovely curly hair.What did you talk about?The usual … Life history and relationships. The difference between acquaintances and friends. Where we are in life. Music. Hobbies. U3A groups. No politics.Most awkward moment?Perhaps me choosing oysters for my starter.Good table manners?Excellent. And we both chose healthy meals – no grills for us. And no alcohol as we were both driving.Best thing about Gilli?Her beauty, and her enthusiastic and confident conversation.Would you introduce Gilli to your friends?Definitely.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Gilli in three wordsVivacious, loquacious and beautiful.What do you think Gilli made of you?I really don’t know, though I hope she found me smiley, chatty, confident and humorous. But perhaps she thought I was too old?Did you go on somewhere?She said she was tired and didn’t want to go to another venue. Manchester was buzzing, so that was a shame.And ... did you kiss?Two pecks on the lips!If you could change one thing about the evening, what would it be?An earlier start so we could have had more time – it flew by.Marks out of 10?9.Would you meet again?We discussed meeting again (and swapped numbers), but the age gap and different desires for the future make another date pointless.View image in fullscreenAndew and Gilli on their date.View image in fullscreenGilli on AndrewWhat were you hoping for?A warm, interesting connection with friendship or relationship potential.First impressions?A confident, happy and lively person. Andrew didn’t seem at all nervous, so it was relaxed from the get-go.What did you talk about?Our careers. Life paths. Travel and where we’ve both lived. Food.Most awkward moment?I was shattered, so really could not stay out late. I sensed Andrew was a bit disappointed that I needed to get home.Good table manners?I didn’t notice anything untoward.Best thing about Andrew?He is an interesting and engaging person who likes to live life to the full. He has interesting ideas for his life going forwards.Would you introduce Andrew to your friends?He likes to go dancing, as do my friends and I, so he’d go well with them.Describe Andrew inthree wordsEngaging, lively and happy.Blind date: ‘We were chatting as soon as we sat down’Read moreWhat do you think Andrew made of you?I got the impression he liked me well enough, but who knows?Did you go on somewhere?Andrew walked me to my car.And … did you kiss?We had a goodbye peck.If you could change one thing about the evening what would it be?I would have preferred a lunchtime meet-up as we could have gone on to a gallery or somewhere and made a day of it.Marks out of 10?9.Would you meet again?We may meet up to do arty things but we both knew there wasn’t any relationship potential due to the age gap and different life stages.Andrew and Gilli ate atGrand Pacificin Manchester. Fancy a blind date? Emailblind.date@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsDatingBlind dateRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: No 10’s ads for a TikTok team show why social media is a smart career move | Social media | The Guardian
description: The Guardian’s deputy editor of social platforms on the demand from high-profile people and brands for help in harnessing the power of TikTok
Author: Augusta Anthony
Headline: The Guardian’s deputy editor of social platforms on the demand from high-profile people and brands for help in harnessing the power of TikTok
Content: Andy Burnham during a video call published on TikTok. No 10 has created five new roles for social media professionals.Photograph: ScreengrabView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham during a video call published on TikTok. No 10 has created five new roles for social media professionals.Photograph: ScreengrabSocial mediaNo 10’s ads for a TikTok team show why social media is a smart career moveThe Guardian’s deputy editor of social platforms on the demand from high-profile people and brands for help in harnessing the power of TikTokAugusta AnthonySat 15 Aug 2026 04.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdidn’t want to work in social media. If you’d asked 15-year-old me my dream job, I might have said foreign correspondent, or maybe travel writer. So you can imagine my surprise to now find myself giving these very colleagues advice on how to get the best selfie angle or write the sharpestTikTok‘hook’.But taking a job as the Guardian’s deputy editor of social platforms, may prove to be one of my smartest career moves if the current job market is to be believed.You don’t need to be a digital native to have noticed the way that celebrities, brands and, yes, the prime minister, are taking their social media game seriously these days.Westminster watchers keeping an eye on the government jobs board to get an idea of the type of people Burnham’s operation wants to recruit, noticed no less than five newly created roles for social media professionals – the most senior of them earning a touch under £70,000 per year.Burnham’s wholesale commitment to feeding the algorithm may feel like a relative novelty on this side of the pond, but social media has been a political battleground in the US for much longer.Early in Trump’s presidency, outgoing press secretary Karoline Leavitt could regularly be seen recapping the administration’s “successes” with the catchy“Maga minute”, and New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s masterful use of social comms is the envy of politicians the world over.But while it’s true that the internet game requires a charismatic personality, backstage there is a squad of editors, producers and strategists making the whole thing sing. That’s where we come in.View image in fullscreenBurnham running alongside Mo Farah also made the cut on his TikTok.Photograph: Andy Burnham/TikTokMy journey into social media began when my team at CNN took over producing for the TikTok channel in 2023. I realised that’s where audiences, including myself, really were.If you hear the word TikTok and think it’s just dance trends and memes, think again. My job involved getting phone calls from war zones asking if I had what I needed and being sentselfies from craters. When I left earlier this year we had grown the account to almost 12 million followers.Now mainstream media is trying to beat content creators at their own game. Oxford’s Reuters Institutethis year reportedthat social and video networks have overtaken news websites and apps by audience share. The BBC has even hired agen z whisperer.As with most things in the world of social media, this change has happened rapidly, one of the consequences of that change is that there is really no such thing as a “traditional route” into the industry.View image in fullscreenBurnham talking about homelessness on TikTok.Photograph: Andy Burnham/TikTokLauren Spearman is an accidental influencer who found a TikTok following, now at 62,000, while documenting her own frustrations finding a full-time role in marketing. She now enjoys a successful freelance career consulting with the benefit of two decades of experience in social. She says she’s seen a recent shift in businesses hiring for content creators.“Social is often infantilised but it is business critical,” Spearman said. And she’s right, the trope for years has been thatinterns are running the accountsof your favourite businesses, but you’re much more likely to find a savvy millennial with a marketing degree behind a brand’s X feed.What remains to be seen is if C-suites and business leaders really understand the needs of their audiences, or those they’re hiring to cater to them. “The biggest challenge has always been educating up,” said Spearman, noting that she often sees junior roles with small salaries but large scopes and unclear remits.“A lot of times I’ll go into businesses and there is no strategy that ladders back into what the business is doing,” she said. Let’s not forget that your social producers are often on the frontline of customer interactions and what most consumers see but often still misunderstood and sidelined.Social media can, of course, be a place for slop; for fearmongering, for misinformation. But the vast majority of good actors are on it as a place to be entertained, informed and even exercise their civic duties.In many ways it’s still the closest to a global town square we’ve got, fraught with algorithmic problems and regulatory loopholes as it might be. It’s time to start taking the people behind these accounts seriously.Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaAndy BurnhamEnglandTikTokfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Watch your spending, use free perks’: an insider’s tips on student money | Student finance | The Guardian
description: Avoid getting into debt at university with tricks to save cash, earn extra funds and have a good time
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Avoid getting into debt at university with tricks to save cash, earn extra funds and have a good time
Content: While at university Erin has made money from selling secondhand clothes and has found ways to attend events for free.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWhile at university Erin has made money from selling secondhand clothes and has found ways to attend events for free.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianStudent finance‘Watch your spending, use free perks’: an insider’s tips on student moneyAvoid getting into debt at university with tricks to save cash, earn extra funds and have a good timeThe best student deals and discountsRupert JonesSat 15 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the past two years university student Erin has been giving Martin Lewis a run for his money when it comes to hunting down the best hacks, tips and tricks to save cash and earn money.The 21-year-old has seen Oasis for free; earned tickets to race days; made money from selling secondhand clothes (£200 in one weekend alone); and enjoyed cut-price treats with friends.On Thursday, tens of thousands of young people found out if they had achieved the grades for the course of their choice. Now, as they celebrate, or hurriedly activate, their plan B, the day-to-day costs of student life probably aren’t uppermost in their mind. But perhaps they should be: research from Nationwide Building Society reveals that money mistakes dominate students’ list of regrets.From failing to budget and track spending properly, overspending on nights out and relying too heavily on their overdraft, to blowing their entire student loan payment in the first few weeks, six of the top seven mistakes students have made are related to money.“Our research shows just how much more financial pressure today’s students feel compared with previous generations,” says Tom Riley, Nationwide’s director of retail products.Erin, who is about to start the third year of a psychology and cognitive neuroscience degree at the University of Nottingham, says going to university has “taught me loads” about managing money.“Before I started, I’d worked and saved, but when that student loan lands in your account, it can feel a bit like free money,” she says. “It’s easy to fall into ‘girl math’ logic and justify little extras that quickly add up.”She says that working before university and during the holidays “definitely gave me a better sense of what things actually cost”.Erin sets herself a budget and has a rule that if she needs to go over it, she has to dip into the savings earned from her job, which, she says, focuses the mind on whether she needs to spend that money.Her view is that wherever possible, the money she is saving “is not money I can spend [as] that is undoing all the good work I’ve done”.To cut spending, she makes the most of discounts and deals, and joins with friends to maximise the benefits. She, and some of her friends, have Nationwide FlexStudent bank accounts, which offers a £10 Just Eat voucher every month for the first 12 months.In her first year, she says, they pooled their vouchers and had “floor picnics” in their halls of residence, where they would all sit and share their takeaways.It was, she says, “a life-saver because we didn’t have great cooking facilities and were on really limited budgets … It was a nice way to treat ourselves”.View image in fullscreenErin has worked as a volunteer at events.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianSaving money has not meant missing out on a social life, as she has found ways to get into gigs and events that do not involve spending.As a brand rep for a company that organises days out at racecourses around the UK, she gets a free ticket and transport to any events she has promoted. Tickets can be pricey for these “race day” outings, which are popular with students. She had to post a promotional message on her social media and send a link to three group chats, and she earned commission on any ticket bought via her link.Signing up with an agency for voluntary work at events has also got her into gigs and festivals for nothing. “I got to see Oasis last year for free,” she says. “I think I did an eight-hour shift scanning tickets.” Her shift finished just as the support act ended, so she was able to watch the band’s entire set. “I was front row – that would have cost a lot of money,” she says. Her stint included a staff meal voucher.Last year, she volunteered at Truck festival in Oxfordshire. Typically, she says, with volunteering at a festival, you may have to do two or three shifts over the weekend, but still get plenty of free time to enjoy the event.Her savings pay for things she cannot get for free: this year the big thing she was saving for was the college ski trip. “Every bit I saved I put towards that.”View image in fullscreenErin says working before university and during the holidays ‘definitely gave me a better sense of what things actually cost’.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianHere are her money-saving tips:Think in hours, not poundsBefore buying something, work out how many hours you would need to work to pay for it. “A couple of cocktails on a night out can easily be the equivalent of more than an hour’s wages from a summer job. It’s a good reality check and makes me think twice about the impulse purchases.”Volunteer for freebies and perksThere are lots of firms that recruit volunteers for festivals and one-day events – Erin signed up with Festaff and Wicked Events.Turn fashion into a side hustleErin snaps up quality pieces from charity shops and similar, some of which she upcycles before selling them on platforms such as Vinted, along with her own items that she no longer wants.Look out foropportunitiesA lot of universities have brand ambassador programmes.Studentsoften act as brand reps for nightclubs, as well as other events and venues.Pool rewards with friendsYou could combine discounts and deals with housemates or friends to get better value and reduce everyday spending.Treat a student loan like income, not free moneyErin advises setting a budget early and keeping track of spending in order to avoid overspending on the little extras.Explore more on these topicsStudent financeSaving moneyStudentsConsumer affairsUniversitiesHigher educationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carry on collecting: why old British shopping bags are suddenly in demand | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Vintage classics from WH Smith, M&S and Tesco are being bought online, perhaps as part of a nostalgic return to owning tangible items
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Vintage classics from WH Smith, M&S and Tesco are being bought online, perhaps as part of a nostalgic return to owning tangible items
Content: Vintage plastic bags are being sold on sites such as eBay.Photograph: EbayView image in fullscreenVintage plastic bags are being sold on sites such as eBay.Photograph: EbayLife and styleCarry on collecting: why old British shopping bags are suddenly in demandVintage classics from WH Smith, M&S and Tesco are being bought online, perhaps as part of a nostalgic return to owning tangible itemsLauren CochraneSat 15 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen it comes to everyday objects, a supermarket carrier bag could be the ultimate one – a thing we’re more accustomed to squeezing into a drawer or using until it falls apart than giving any special treatment.But these most mundane items are now enjoying something of a new life.On secondhand sites including eBay, Vinted and Depop, old Marks & Spencer carrier bags and those for other supermarkets such as Tesco, Netto and Waitrose are being sold for about £10 – a big mark-up considering they were originally given away for free. Vinted reports that searches in 2026 have risen by 35% since last year.Once a deeply unremarkable receptacle for the weekly shop, the humble carrier bag has become a bona fide collectors’ item. There’s even an Instagram account dedicated to them -Carry a Bag Manhas more than 15,000 followers.Jeremy Leslie, the founder of MagCulture, a magazine shop in London, sees this as part of a wider trend toward the tangible. “We see it with magazines,” he says, “people want real things in their lives. These are nostalgic items that take people back to when they were growing up, as a reassuring totem.”If some might balk at the idea of collecting old plastic bags, Tim Sumner is not one of them. He set up thePaper Bag Archivein 2020, and now has more than 3,500 old paper bags plus some plastic ones. Sumner describes these bags as “great symbols of social history, they track the tastes and flavours of our time across each decade … It’s important to celebrate these insignificant objects; they often create memories that last a lifetime.”The M&S St Michael bag, ubiquitous on high streets throughout the 80s and 90s, is a particularly popular choice now. The label is nostalgic across generations because it was seen on items at the store from 1928 until 2000, but it is also sought by those too young to remember it.It is now central to the store’s latest collaboration – a collection by the cult London streetwear label Aries arriving on 20 August. It includes a £90 leather tote bag styled to look remarkably like an old St Michael carrier.Lisa Illis, the head of womenswear design at M&S, said: “Turning an everyday carrier bag into a collectable leather accessory perfectly captures what this partnership is about – celebrating the cultural relevance of St Michael while introducing it to a new audience. It takes something deeply familiar and reimagines it through a completely contemporary lens.”View image in fullscreenAries’s M&S leather tote bag ‘celebrates the cultural relevance of St Michael’.Photograph: M&SNostalgia is central across the Aries collaboration. Sofia Prantera, the designer and founder of Aries, says she drew on formative experiences. “Growing up, M&S was part of family life. [It] is a true British institution that has played a role in so many people’s lives and memories.”Vintage St Michael clothing is sought after on secondhand sites. “St Michael occupies a unique place in British culture,” says Illis. “For many people, it represents memories of a trusted brand that was part of everyday life, while for younger consumers it has become a coveted piece of fashion history.”Old carrier bags also contain this sense of fashion history – and they contrast against the bags that are now available for 20p at most supermarkets. “They seem much sturdier than what you get today,” says Sumner, “although any after 2000 turn to dust if you touch them as they were made to biodegrade faster.”Of course, it is now frowned upon to use plastic bags at supermarkets, following anti-plastic campaigns in the 2000s and items such as Anya Hindmarch’s “I am not a plastic bag” tote, whichsaw 80,000 queue to purchase one in 2007. Single-use plastic bags were phased out at supermarkets in 2015 when a mandatory charge was put in place by the government. By 2023 sales of plastic bags in supermarkets had beenreduced by 98%.This shift is also reflected in the secondhand market. The canvas bags given away for free by brands including APC, Octobre Editions and Alo with a purchase are popular, selling for upwards of £10. This week, Vogue named the Alo bag“this summer’s trending beach bag”while the canvas bag from the American grocery store Trader Joes – bought for $4 in store – has a new life on the streets of London assomething of a status symbol.If some think old carrier bags are appreciated because design in the past was more considered, Leslie says the opposite might be true. “Part of the joy of the old stuff is that it is so basic and so thrown together rather than carefully mediated through an in-house design studio poring over different colour possibilities,” he says. “This was ‘our colour is green, that green is good enough, we’ll go with that’.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleMarks & SpencerCollectingRetail industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 20 of the best cabins, campsites and hotels in Europe’s mountains, lakes and forests | Europe holidays | The Guardian
description: From a 500-year-old inn in the Italian Dolomites to a log cabin in Finland’s lake district, these boltholes offer a tranquil getaway
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From a 500-year-old inn in the Italian Dolomites to a log cabin in Finland’s lake district, these boltholes offer a tranquil getaway
Content: Rifugio Val di Togno in northern Italy.View image in fullscreenRifugio Val di Togno in northern Italy.Top 20sEurope holidays20 of the best cabins, campsites and hotels in Europe’s mountains, lakes and forestsFrom a 500-year-old inn in the Italian Dolomites to a log cabin in Finland’s lake district, these boltholes offer a tranquil and restorative getawayFiona KerrSat 15 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the mountains …A remote refuge in northern ItalyIt’s not easy to get toRifugio Val di Togno,at 1,317 meters (4,320ft). The dirt road from the nearest town winds for 4 miles through 27 hairpins and is best done in a four-wheel drive, or it’s a solid two-hour hike from the tiny hamlet of Carnale. But as managers Luna Lybeer and Wout Allegaert say: “We offer guests nothing so they can get away from everything.” Although you can hardly describe this beautifully renovated mountain hideout as “nothing”. Every room looks down the valley, whether through a porthole-like round window or huge floor-to-ceiling sliding doors. Breakfast, lunch (or a picnic to take on a hike), afternoon snack,aperitivoand a two-course dinner are included too – delicious vegetarian meals made using produce from the couple’s garden, or foraged nearby, along with homemade kombucha, sourdough and gnocchi.Doubles from£298 all-inclusive(three-night minimum),rifugiovalditogno.comAn Austrian train station turned B&BBuilt in 1910, the old station at Lermoos in Austria’s Tirol had stood empty for years before Johann Ehmann and his wife Cleo Weber bought it in 2019. “We were fascinated by it and contacted Austrian Railways regularly for more than five years asking if it was for sale,” says Ehmann. Now the couple have converted the classic Alpine building at the foot of Zugspitze (Germany’s highest peak) intoLermooser, a design B&B. The eight rooms range from a cosy bunk bed “cabin” to the “team XL” with three single beds and a double in a row. There’s a communal kitchen and a kiosk downstairs for coffee, pastries and homemade soups. The train still stops right outside, and hikes up to the Tuftl Alm viewpoint, and to Seebensee and Drachensee, start right from the door.Doubles from £106 B&B,lermooser.comA historic wilderness hotel in NorwayView image in fullscreen‘Røisheim, a time capsule of a turf-roofed hotel.’In summer, the sun doesn’t set until 11pm atRøisheim, which sits on the fringes of Jotunheimen national park in southern Norway. That means all the more time to go on blue ice glacier walks and swim in mountain lakes, cycle over the Sognefjellet pass or tackle Galdhøpiggen, Norway’s tallest mountain at 2,469 metres (8,100ft). The first recorded ascent of Galdhøpiggen in 1850 started from Røisheim and the trail still leads from the courtyard of the hotel, although most hikers now choose quicker routes starting from nearby Spiterstulen. Røisheim, a time capsule of a turf-roofed hotel, has been welcoming mountain-lovers since 1858 and many of the rooms are faithfully preserved with timber-clad walls, carved wooden beds and barrel-like tubs.Doubles from £243 B&B,roisheim.noAlpine apartments in BavariaView image in fullscreenAn apartment at Karls Mittenwald.Photograph: Jessica Lerchenmüller“We didn’t choose Mittenwald because we wanted to open a hotel, we chose it because we wanted to live somewhere that summer still feels like summer,” says Anne-Sophie Trinkgeld, who recently openedKarls Mittenwaldin this pretty small town near the Austrian border with her husband Dario. Mittenwald came out top in their search for the best combination of climate, outdoor activities and accessibility in the Alps – it’s surrounded by mountains but just 40 minutes from Innsbruck. The couple turned the former bakery into 11 thoughtfully designed one- and two-bedroom apartments with a cafe downstairs serving breakfast spreads and homemade cakes. Just the fuel for days spent swimming in the clear waters of Lautersee, cycling to the source of the Isar River through theKarwendel nature parkor hiking to Germany’s highest brewery, Karwendelbräu.Apartments from £145 a night,karls-mittenwald.deAn eco-campsite in the Austrian TirolView image in fullscreenGerhardhof on the Mieming Sun PlateauNearly 1,000 metres (3,280 ft) above sea level, the wide Mieming Sun Plateau is known for its mild microclimate and looping hikes through pine forests and Alpine meadows. Josef Volgger grew up on a farm here,Gerhardhof, which his parents also ran as a small guesthouse. Now Volgger, along with two business partners, has transformed Gerhardhof into a sustainability-minded campsite with grey water recycling, wood-chip heating and solar energy, as well as a naturally filtered swimming pond. You’ll still see Josef’s mother Edith in the bakery, turning out apple strudel, and there is a restaurant for dinners of wiener schnitzel andKäsespätzle(an Alpine mac and cheese).Pitches from £38 a night,gerhardhof.comA 500-year-old inn in the Italian DolomitesView image in fullscreenOver its five centuries in the South Tirolean town of Lana, the building that now houses1477 Reichhalterhas had many incarnations, including a butcher, bakery, sawmill, stable and tavern. Since 2018 it has been a restaurant with eight bedrooms dressed in mid-century furniture. Room number 4, Helmsdorf, has a balcony with views of the Vigiljoch mountain and Braunsberg Castle (you can borrow a bike to explore further), while Schönmüller is another favourite for its raw plaster walls and tiledstubestove. Downstairs, tables spill on to the pedestrianised street from the restaurant, which dishes up a delicious beef tartare and house salad made with homemade pickled vegetables and whatever’s in season from the kitchen garden at sister hotel Villa Arnica.Doubles from £170 B&B,1477reichhalter.comA Bauhaus guesthouse in Italy’s South TirolFor 40 years, Johanna Fink ran her family’s Alpine hotelBriolwith simple efficiency: sheets air-drying on the line, guests summoned to dinner by cowbell at precisely 7pm. Recently, her children Victoria and Valentin von Klebelsberg have taken over, but Briol remains charmingly the same. The main house was renovated in 1928 by artist Hubert Lanzinger inmodernist Bauhaus style– the bedrooms have no heating (there is a hot-water bottle service), guests share a bathroom and there are no TVs, wifi or pictures on the walls. But with views like this, from a mountain meadow high above Barbiano and the Eisack valley, the lack of distraction is very welcome, and hiking trails fan out from the doorstep.Doubles from £255 half-board,briol.itBy the lake …A houseboat on a Swedish lakeView image in fullscreen‘It’s all about the lake’ at Stugbaat and its five houseboats on Lake Lelång.Photograph: Beyond Oceans MediaStugbaatis a collection of five houseboats that bob around the huge Lake Lelång in Dalsland. Each floats on an aluminium or stainless steel pontoon, and comes with a little motorboat for towing the tiny house to a quiet corner or pootling ashore to explore. On dry land, there are mountains to climb (Egersknatten), berries and chanterelles to forage in the forest, a straw museum in Bengtsfors and a microbrewery in Torrskog. But, really, it’s all about the lake: fish from or dive off the wooden deck that surrounds the cabin or take out the paddleboard included with each booking. You can hire a kayak, check out the floating sauna, or simply drop anchor and do nothing.From £233 a night (two-night minimum), sleeps 4,stugbaat.seBack-to-nature cabins in SwedenView image in fullscreenLife is off-grid at Naturbyn on Lake Eldan.Thomas Peterson started with just one log cabin, which he handbuilt on a section of pine and spruce forest on the shores of Lake Eldan in Värmland. Then he built another, and one up in the treetops, and one floating on the water. There are now seven atNaturbyn, all off-grid (no wifi or electricity, just wood-burning stoves and paraffin lamps), all with views of the lake and some with grass roofs dotted with tiny wild strawberries. This being Sweden, there’s a sauna on the lakeshore. Beyond that, borrow a canoe, forage in the forest, watch for elk among the trees, catch a pike for supper or count shooting stars across the inky sky.Cabins from £160 a night, sleeps 2,naturbyn.seA waterfront hotel in JutlandView image in fullscreenNy Hattenæs on the shores of Brassø Lake.In the heart of the Danish Lake District on the Jutland peninsula, the 19th-century mill town of Silkeborg is known as Denmark’s outdoor capital. Just south of Silkeborg, the waterfront hotelNy Hattenæshas sat on the forested shore of Brassø Lake since 1896 when it opened as a summer boarding house. It is now open year-round, but summer is still the loveliest time to stay, when days are long, the lake is filled with people swimming, paddleboarding and canoeing, and the terrace at Ny Hattenæs is the perfect place to catch the lingering twilight. Revamped in 2022 by the trio of siblings behind Danish design houseSociety of Lifestyle, the 14 bedrooms are filled with House Doctor furniture and the bathrooms stocked with Meraki natural products. Room number 7 is the plum pick, with a large balcony overlooking the water.Doubles from £205 B&B,nyhattenaes.comA new-gen hotel in BavariaLess than an hour’s drive south of Munich, Tegernsee is where city folk flock in the summer to drink in leafy beer gardens, tuck intoknödeldumplings in farmhouse restaurants and boat on the lake. Lederhosen and dirndls are still a regular sight in some parts here, but the recently opened hotelBlyb, in the quiet village of Gmund am Tegernsee, is as far from the usual Bavarian cliches as you can get. The villa dates back to 1892, and while it still has original stucco paintings and ornate wooden balconies, they’ve been updated with crisp monochrome decor, a restaurant from the team behind the hip Munich spotMural, an outdoor yoga deck and events that might include a doner kebab and DJ pop-up or intimate unplugged gigs in the library.Doubles from £112 room-only,blyb.coLakeside cabins in a German biosphere reserveBerlin school friends Julian Trautwein, Johann Ahlers and Christopher Eilers founded Raus in 2021 with the simple idea of getting city-dwellers like themselves out into nature. They started with a handful of sustainably built cabins near German cities and this year have added their 100th.Lodge am Seetakes the Raus concept and turns it into a little cabin resort, with 17 huts by a lake in the Unesco Elbe River Landscape Biosphere Reserve, between Berlin and Hamburg. The area is known for its quiet cycle paths, but the water is just as attractive, and there are free paddleboards to borrow, canoe hire nearby and sea eagles, storks and cranes to spot above the wetlands.Cabins from £126a night, sleep 2,raus.lifeskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLog cabins in Finland’s vast LakelandView image in fullscreenThe Sahanlahti Resort ‘has sleek modern villas that come with wraparound terraces’Finnish Lakelandis Europe’s largest lake district, a watery labyrinth of thousands of lakes, rivers and channels. Its biggest body of water, Lake Saimaa, is like an inland archipelago of nearly 14,000 forest-covered islands. In summer, Finns flock here to lakeside log cabins (known as amökki), which are an essential part of Finnish culture. On the site of a historic sawmill on Saimaa’s rippling shoreline,SahanlahtiResortembodiesmökkitradition old and new, with timeless red-painted wooden cabins (some with their own saunas) and sleek modern villas that come with wraparound terraces. You may even spot a Saimaa ringed seal, one of the world’s rarest.Cabins from £93 a night, sleep 4,sahanlahtiresort.fiAn adults-only hideout in the Austrian AlpsView image in fullscreenJust outside the medieval town of Kitzbühel, Schwarzsee is known for its mineral-rich peat waters (its name means black lake), which are some of the warmest in the Alps, reaching 27C in summer. On a hillside above the lake,Seebichlis another black beauty, its darkly painted wooden balconies spilling over with flowers. Brothers Max and Sebastian Witzmann, whose grandfather bought Seebichl in the 1950s, have created an artsy take on a traditional Alpine hotel, with bright orange Eames chairs rather than classic carved-wood Tirolean ones and contemporary art on the walls instead of antlers. And if Schwarzsee or the heated pool in the garden at Seebichl get too balmy, hike up to the nearbySintersbach Waterfallfor a chillier dip.Doubles from £170 B&B,hotel-seebichl.atIn the forest …A-frame cabins in the Slovenian AlpsView image in fullscreen‘A peaceful base for exploring the surrounding Savinja valley.’Photograph: Mamoot/Andrej LamutFamed for its emerald green water, theSavinja riverruns from the Rinka Falls at the head of the pristine Logar valley in northern Slovenia down through forested gorges in the Slovenian Alps. Along its banks,Forest Camping Mozirjeis a peaceful base for exploring the surrounding Savinja valley. Tents and campervans pitch up in meadows among the trees. For those allergic to pegging in a ground sheet, there are bell tents and A-frame-shaped wooden “forest beds” built from local timber. Campers swap hiking tips and debate rafting versus canyoning over dinner at communal tables in the well-stocked covered kitchen. Afterwards, gather around one of the campfires or kick back in a hammock next to the little outdoor library.Pitches from £15plus £14per adult. Forest Beds from £84,campingmozirje.comA design hotel in the Black ForestView image in fullscreenArtbau Designhotel and its treetop views.Photograph: Maris MezulisGermany’s Black Forest (Schwarzwald) is named for the canopy of conifers so dense it blocks out much of the sunlight. It’s a mysterious place, often linked to the dark fairytales of the Brothers Grimm, although the siblings actually collected and wrote their folktales farther north around the city of Kassel. It is easy to imagine Hansel and Gretel or Little Red Riding Hood trotting down the trails, although you’re more likely to encounter German families or a hilltop castle. In the Black Forest town of Waldkirch, famous for the production of church and fairground organs,Artbau Designhotelis a sharply modern riposte to all that fairytale tweeness, with concrete walls and steel tables softened by Moroccan textiles and balconies that look out to the treetops.Doubles from £115 room-only,artbau-designhotel.deA forest sauna in LatviaView image in fullscreen‘The glass cabin bedrooms … looking out across wildflower meadows by day and up to star-filled skies after dark.’Photograph: Stikla istabaDeep in a pine forest near theGauja national park,Ziedlejasis dedicated to the Latvian tradition ofpirts– steamy wood-fired bathhouses heated to about 65C. There are three here: the glass pirts beside the swimming pond, the smoke pirts under the grey fir trees and the wool pirts with walls made from sheep’s wool (which releases skin-soothing lanolin). Sessions last around four hours, guided by a pirts master (pirtnieks),who takes guests through the ritual, which includes “whisking” (tapping and brushing) bodies with bundled sticks, herbal scrubs, massage and alternating hot and cold water. The glass cabin bedrooms are just as restorative, looking out across wildflower meadows by day and up to star-filled skies after dark.Cabins from £110 a night, sleeps 2,ziedlejas.lvFamily-friendly huts and camping in the French AlpsView image in fullscreenThe Huttopia Bozel en Vanois campsite.Photograph: Manu ReybozHuttopia has dozens of nature-immersed campsites all over France (and a handful farther afield). There’s a formula – tree-shaded spots often beside lakes and rivers, pre-pitched safari tents if you don’t fancy BYO, a wood-fired pizza restaurant for the evening – and it works, with families returning year after year. Set among pine and fir trees on the banks of the Doron de Bozel river,Huttopia Bozel en Vanoiseis at the gateway to the Vanoise national park near the Italian border, which is criss-crossed with hiking trails and home to ibex, marmots and chamois. Closer still is the lake beach – a five-minute walk – or canyoning on the Doron de Bozel; while back at camp kids can join the forest-school-like Petits Trappeurs or hang with new friends at after-dinner magic shows and open-air film screenings.Nature pitch from £20, Trappeurwood and canvas tent from £146 a night,huttopia.comTiny houses in a Swedish forest full of wildlifeView image in fullscreenAn off-grid cabin at InforestThe only alarm clock at the four off-grid cabins that make upInforest,2½ hours north-east of Gothenburg, is the sound of robins, blackbirds and chaffinches, perhaps joined in their dawn chorus by the odd woodpecker or cuckoo. Each solar-powered tiny house here is a kilometre apart, so your only neighbours will be the roe deer, hares and the odd moose roaming among the hectares of pine, spruce and birch trees. Almost 70% of Sweden is covered in forest and the right of public access, orallemansrätten, means you can walk or bike in every direction. For a little more action, head to the perfectly preserved wooden town of Hjo on the edge of Lake Vättern, just 4 miles away, for a sauna on the harbour or to sail on the steamship Trafik before scurrying back into the woods.Cabins from £155 a night, sleep 2-4,inforest.seModernist treehouses on a farm in SwedenView image in fullscreenSuites on stilts at Trakt Forest Hotel.Photograph: James Silverman PhotographyIn the summer of 2022, this family farm in Småland opened five striking suites on stilts among the treetops of the surrounding pine forest. This spring,Trakt Forest Hoteladded seven bedrooms in its historic Erik’s House farmstead, the design more rattan headboards, crocheted cushions and views of cows grazing than the angular minimalism and secluded stillness of the treehouses. There is a restaurant, Traktköket, in a nearby log cabin and much of the food is grown on the farm or sourced locally. Outside, there’s a little sauna hut beside the farm pond, with a wood-fired bath squirrelled away deeper in the forest. The team can prepare afika(coffee break) backpack with coffee, cake and a sandwich to take out on a hike further into the wilderness.Doubles from £184 B&B,traktforesthotel.comSome of the areas mentioned above have been affected by wildfires this summer. Please check before booking.Explore more on these topicsEurope holidaysTop 20sHotelsBed and breakfastsCamping holidaysCottagesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gen Z flocks to BirdTok as birding takes flight: ‘It’s a craving for something real’ | Birds | The Guardian
description: Social media and Shazam-like birdsong apps drawing young people to hobby as they seek a gentler connection to the outside world
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Social media and Shazam-like birdsong apps drawing young people to hobby as they seek a gentler connection to the outside world
Content: Jack Baddams is one of several social media birding stars.Photograph: Jack Baddams/TikTokView image in fullscreenJack Baddams is one of several social media birding stars.Photograph: Jack Baddams/TikTokBirdsGen Z flocks to BirdTok as birding takes flight: ‘It’s a craving for something real’Social media and Shazam-like birdsong apps drawing young people to hobby as they seek a gentler connection to the outside worldDan MilmoGlobal technology editorSat 15 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 08.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSorry Elon, but they’re not your kind of tweets. Social media users are flocking toTikTokto join a burgeoning trend for birding videos as the hobby attracts a younger demographic.With the internet ever more cluttered with polarising, shouty and AI content, evidence is emerging of Britons preferring a gentler, more melodic window on the world in the shape of footage of the nation’s feathered friends.TikTok says UK posts of #birdwatching and #birdtok videos have risen by a third over the past three months as users flock to feathered friend content. The number of #birding posts has risen by 40% in the UK and the global number of posts carrying one of those three hashtags now stands at 1m. A video of Steven,a relatively tame seagull, being fed raw Tesco salmon fillet has more than 52m views.Posts by the Royal Society for the Protection ofBirdshave received nearly 9m views over the past year, with a third of those coming from under-24s. Dedicated birders say the boom is down to the popularity of apps such as Merlin – a kind of Shazam for birdsong – a resurgence in curiosity about the natural world, a desire for analogue hobbies and the power of social media.BirdTokkers Tim Jones and Jack Baddams – loop“It’s a craving for something ‘real’ and birding is a really nice gateway to that,” saysJack Baddams, 33, a Derbyshire-based bird enthusiast whose videos about tagging birds have had millions of views.“Anyone can walk outside or look out of their window and see a bird. And there are communities that build off the back of that.”Baddams, who has 300,000 followers, is a TV researcher and one of 3,000 bird “ringers” for the British Trust for Ornithology, who places identification rings around birds to help monitor phenomena such as population changes or migratory patterns. A video on his account explaining the craft of bird ringing has had 7.5m viewsBaddams admits he has been “shocked” by the scale of interest.“I’m not tagging rare birds. A lot of them are very common birds. It seems like the more common and recognisable the bird, the more interest it gets. People have a relationship to them,” he says.Birds tagged by Baddams include blackbirds, blue tits and meadow pipits, the latter dubbed a “classic little brown job” – birding jargon for the small, sparrow-like brown birds that tend to be indistinguishable from each other at first glance.Tim Jones, 35, a professional ornithologist from York, says social media has helped spread the word about a hobby that is not normally associated with younger age groups. As well as48,000 followers on TikTokfor videos such as “learn one birdsong this week”, Jones has 210,00 on Instagram under his Begin Birding handle. Other birding stars on Instagram include Jacob Cobb, who is attempting to find “every bird in the world”, and US birder-singer Bonner Black.View image in fullscreenJack Baddams posts videos about tagging birds that have had millions of views.Photograph: Jack Baddams/TikTok“If you saw a birder under the age of 40 a few decades ago it would be notable. That’s really changing now because you’re seeing twentysomethings and teenagers all the time,” says Jones.Nomenclature is also shifting, with the catch-all term of “birding” preferable to “birdwatching” for younger people, while “twitcher” refers to the devotees who will drop everything to attend a rare bird sighting and does not reflect the majority of bird hobbyists, says Jones.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Social media has shown people that it’s interesting and cool to do these hobbies and that there are other young people out there doing them,” he says.‘They do look majestic’: tears and pride as first white storks set free in CornwallRead moreThis avenue is due to be cut off, however, as the government prepares a social media ban for under-16s coming in next year. Jones describes “10 to 13” as the age when people typically get into birding, although he believes the dominant demographic among social media followers is thirtysomethings.The British Trust for Ornithology told the Guardian there has been a surge in interest in events tailored for young birders, including bird camps, walks and talks for 11-25-year-olds.“It was a struggle getting young people to events but now are seeing huge demand for everything we do,” said Samuel Levy, a member of the BTO’s youth engagement team. “It’s the first time in my life I can call myself trendy.”Young wildlife and bird photographers are also proving popular on TikTok, under accounts such as @TomSkylark and @TommyMcewan. The RSPB said it was “brilliant” to see interest in birdwatching growing among a younger demographic.“It’s hugely encouraging to see more young people engaging with birds and wildlife. That interest can be an important first step towards building a lasting connection with the natural world,” said Joshua Edwards, the RSPB’s social media manager.Explore more on these topicsBirdsBirdwatchingTikTokInstagramAnimalsMetaWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: who is the secret admirer leaving gifts for the dog? | Family | The Guardian
description: Soft toys and furry things keep appearing in the garden. I wouldn’t rule out the fox at this point
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: Soft toys and furry things keep appearing in the garden. I wouldn’t rule out the fox at this point
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: who is the secret admirer leaving gifts for the dog?Soft toys and furry things keep appearing in the garden. I wouldn’t rule out the fox at this pointTim DowlingSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter weeks without rain, the garden has turned a uniform beige. Whole shrubs have perished in the unrelenting heat, their crisp brown leaves disintegrating in the breeze. In the middle of the scorched lawn lies the prone body of a large dead bird.On closer inspection, it appears to be a stuffed toy fashioned into the form of a limp duck carcass. When I open the back door for a closer look, the dog steps out between my legs, picks up the bird and carries it inside. It was clearly made with dogs in mind.“What is that?” my wife says as she walks into the room with a shoe in each hand.“I think it’s a duck,” I say.“I’ve never seen it before,” she says, sitting on the sofa. The dog climbs up and sits next to her, duck in mouth.“Me neither,” I say. “But it’s clearly not new.”The dog begins to pull one of the wings off the duck with a sharp tearing sound.“Not in here!” my wife says. “Take your duck outside.” The dog climbs down, walks out of the door, and sits down on the grass to dismember the duck.“I’ll be back in an hour,” my wife says. “Don’t forget it’s haircuts.”double quotation markOn the lawn, where the disemboweled duck lay the day before, sits a pair of furry headphonesMy wife means that today is our standing appointment with Kelly, the hairdresser who is coming to the house to do three haircuts: me, my wife and the middle one. The oldest one stayed the night and is somewhere upstairs asleep, but he’s too out of sync with the haircut cycle to join in.When Kelly arrives it is determined that I will go first. I wash my hair, as instructed, with washing-up liquid, standing at the kitchen sink with my head bent under the running tap.I put a towel around my shoulders and sit down. While Kelly cuts we chat about the heat, the drought, the scorched, unsalvageable garden.“What’s all that white stuff out there?” Kelly says, looking out the window at the lawn.“That,” I say, “is the inside of a duck.” Further down the lawn, the dog is methodically eviscerating the toy, throwing bits of the stuffing into the air with a flick of her head and watching them float off on the breeze.“I still have no idea where that duck came from,” my wife says.“Dog toy, is it?” says Kelly.“It was in the garden this morning,” I say. “Maybe someone threw it over the wall.”“Or maybe the fox left it,” she says. “Do they do that sort of thing?”I think back to two nights before, when I switched on the garden light to find the fox standing at the back door, looking in.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markThe dog wakes me at 6am with a heavy paw on my chest to let me know she has pressing business in the gardenIt’s time to admit it: my dog has a bigger social network than meRead more“Do foxes give stuffed toys as gifts?” I say. “Is that your question?”Later I have trouble sleeping, preoccupied as I am by the idea of strangers leaving presents for my dog in the night. I’m much more at ease with the idea of foxes bearing gifts.The next morning, the dog wakes me at six with a heavy paw on my chest to let me know she has pressing business in the garden. With the dog crowding me on the stairs, I stagger down to unlock the back door. There on the lawn, where the disembowelled duck lay the day before, sits a pair of outsized headphones made entirely of shaggy brown fur.I open the door. The dog runs out, grabs the headphones and brings them inside.“Where did she find those?” my wife asks later that morning, while the dog gnaws on the headphones in the middle of the kitchen floor.“They were just there when I woke up,” I say. “Meanwhile, all the duck toy stuffing had mysteriously disappeared.”“It didn’t disappear,” she says. “I cleaned it up.”“Did you leave giant furry headphones in its place?”“No,” she says. “What kind of stupid toy is that for a dog?”“They’re not for dogs,” I say.“What do you mean?” she says.“I looked up the company on the tag,” I say. “They’re actual headphones, for people. Bluetooth.”“In that case, should she be chewing them up?”“I don’t want them,” I say. “Do you?”“I meant because of the wires, or whatever else is inside,” she says. “Hello? Are you even listening?”I am not listening. I am imagining a fox in its cosy den, surrounded by plush toys of every size and description, stolen from bedrooms with windows open to the hot night air, and carefully deciding which one to bestow next.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Berry-Dee is the UK’s all-time bestselling true crime author. Is he also a violent abuser of women and children? | Books | The Guardian
description: The British writer is known for his unique ability to get inside the heads of serial killers. But a Guardian investigation reveals multiple accusations of assault and child sexual abuse. What is the truth about the man described by his own daughter as ‘absolute evil’?
Author: Lucy Osborne
Headline: The British writer is known for his unique ability to get inside the heads of serial killers. But a Guardian investigation reveals multiple accusations of assault and child sexual abuse. What is the truth about the man described by his own daughter as ‘absolute evil’?
Content: Christopher Berry-Dee.Composite: Ian Tuttle/Shutterstock/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenChristopher Berry-Dee.Composite: Ian Tuttle/Shutterstock/Guardian DesignBooksChristopher Berry-Dee is the UK’s all-time bestselling true crime author. Is he also a violent abuser of women and children?The British writer is known for his unique ability to get inside the heads of serial killers. But a Guardian investigation reveals multiple accusations of assault and child sexual abuse. What is the truth about the man described by his own daughter as ‘absolute evil’?Warning: this article contains descriptions of sexual abuse and violenceLucy OsborneandSirin KaleSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTShareFrom the outside, it looked like the sort of happy family home a child might draw. Red brick, surrounded by rolling countryside, in Curdridge, near Winchester. Here lived the true crime writer Christopher Berry-Dee, with his second wife, Tracey Dee, and their two young daughters, Zoe and Sasha, in the early 1990s. Inside, it was a house of horrors, full of murder memorabilia. In a wardrobe were the clothes a nine-year-old girl had been murdered in. One afternoon, Zoe was playing when she found them. The now 38-year-old council worker from Romsey says she remembers “putting it all on … going downstairs and everyone being absolutely traumatised”. Later, another gruesome memento was added to the collection: the Austin Metro that convicted murderer Michael Sams had used to transport a body in 1991. Bloodied sections of the seatbelts had been cut out for forensic tests.Berry-Dee was the serial killer man. He wrote to convicted murderers in jail and befriended them. They told him everything. Through them he saw the terror in their victims’ eyes, watched their anguished death throes, heard their final screams. He listened to tapes of their confessions in his study. Zoe grew used to hearing them echo through the house. “It would always be on,” she says. “At the time, it felt normal.”The writer would go on to channel his unique insights into the psyches of these murderous criminals into a three decade-long career. With total sales of nearly 1m, Berry-Dee is the UK’s bestselling true crime author since records began, according to NielsenIQ BookData; a self-styled “investigative criminologist” who routinely appears on TV documentaries and podcasts, and at true crime conferences.His fascination with serial killers is underpinned, he says, by a profound sympathy with their victims. “I speak,” Berry-Dee wrote in 2002, “for the victims who have suffered at the hands of the monsters with two faces … for the next of kin who have lost loved ones.”double quotation markI’ve always thought he gets off over it. There’s something about hurting women and children. That’s why he’s in the job that he does – it’s his thingView image in fullscreenSasha, one of Berry-Dee’s daughters.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianBut to his friends, family, former associates and the families of the murder victims he writes about, Berry-Dee’s intentions are not noble. They say he is a violent abuser of women and children, a man with criminal convictions, who has been reported to the police multiple times for child sexual abuse. They allege that he takes perverse satisfaction in restaging the violent rapes and murders of women and children through his writing. Over the course of a six-month investigation, the Guardian spoke with multiple alleged victims and witnesses to Berry-Dee’s abuse, some of whom, despite the incidents being described taking place decades ago, remain too frightened of the author to speak publicly.Get in touchContact Lucy Osborne and Sirin Kale about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Lucy and Sirin using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.To send a message to Lucy and Sirin, please select 'Investigations (UK and Global)' as the recipient.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emaillucy.osborne@theguardian.comandsirin.kale@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.For other options, see our guide attheguardian.com/tips.Show more“I’ve always thought he gets off over it,” says Sasha, 35, a physically slight woman with tattoos, who lives on the south-west coast. When Sasha talks about her father, whom she calls Chris rather than Dad, she shakes uncontrollably. “There’s something about hurting women, hurting children and violent crimes.
