That’s why he’s in the job that he does, because it’s histhing.”Berry-Dee, who is 78, declined to be interviewed for this article, citing a recent near-death stroke and medical advice to avoid heavy stress, but insists, “I have not once committed any of the crimes you accuse me of.”Friends and acquaintances alike all agree on one thing: Berry-Dee is a highly memorable person. “Once met,” says the writer and editor Paul Woods, who knew Berry-Dee in the 90s when Woods ran a small true crime press, “never forgotten.”Berry-Dee’s former agent, Derek Block, recalls visiting the writer at his home in Shedfield, Hampshire, in the mid-90s. He says his house “was absolutely pitch black, then he opened the front door and the light came out through the door” – he was in silhouette – “and it was like Psycho or something”.Born Christopher Dee in Winchester in 1948, Berry-Dee proudly traces his lineage to John Dee, the Elizabethan occultist and alchemist. He is a tall, physically imposing presence, who wears a masonic ring, favours a cravat and has been known to seal his letters with a wax stamp. Before he became a true crime writer, Berry-Dee was an artist, known for painting naval scenes around his home town of Portsmouth. He was also a convicted fraudster, having served a one-year sentence in Ford open prison, West Sussex, after a 1982 conviction for forgery, in addition to a separate 1988 conviction for obtaining credit and evading liability while an undischarged bankrupt.double quotation markHe slammed down on the table photos of the girls’ dead bodies. It was a real gut feeling: you’re not doing this because you care about themView image in fullscreenInvestigative journalist Eileen Fairweather.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianBy the time the journalist Eileen Fairweather met Berry-Dee in 1990, he had reinvented himself as a true crime writer. Both were investigating the then unsolved murders of two schoolgirls, Karen Hadaway and Nicola Fellows, in Brighton’s Wild Park in 1986. The Babes in the Wood murders, as they came to be known, convulsed Brighton throughout the late 80s, particularly after the man long believed to be the killer, Russell Bishop, was acquitted following a botched prosecution in 1987.Fairweather recalls her first meeting with Berry-Dee, in a cafe. “He suddenly slammed on the table photos of the girls’ dead bodies,” she says. “It was a real gut feeling as a woman: you’re not doing this because you care about little girls.” She felt that he got a “kick” out of showing her the photographs. A true crime writer who met Berry-Dee in the 2000s likewise recalls Berry-Dee showing him a photograph of a dead child. “It was a horrible picture,” he shudders.Tracey Dee is an elegant, softly spoken woman with thick, dark hair and candy-pink lipstick. She also has a small scar on her face. Tracey, who works in healthcare and lives in West End, near Southampton, says that once, during an argument when she was pregnant, Berry-Dee put out a cigar on her face.Tracey and her daughters allege that the author beat Tracey often. Once, she says, Berry-Dee knocked her unconscious. She woke up in the bath, covered in her own blood. Another time he stood over her, holding a butcher’s knife. “He was shaking so much that I could actually see he was struggling to control himself.”On another occasion, during an argument, Tracey says he pointed a loaded shotgun at her. Her fear was so intense, “I wet myself.” She alleges that Berry-Dee threatened to send his friends round to rape her, to teach her how to have sex “properly”. “I was terrified,” Tracey says, “because I actually believed they would do that.”Tracey would send the children out of the house when she felt a beating was imminent. But there was a limit to what she could do. Sasha says she remembers coming downstairs one morning to find her mother with two black eyes. Zoe alleges that she washed blood from her mother after Berry-Dee ripped out her earrings, and watched him punch her in the leg when she stalled the car. Friends and relatives of Tracey likewise recall seeing her with injuries around the time of her marriage to Berry-Dee, including black eyes. “I saw domestic violence so many times,” Zoe says. “He was just absolute evil.”View image in fullscreenTracey Dee, Berry-Dee’s ex-wife, with their daughters Sasha and Zoe.Photograph: courtesy of the familyIn a lengthy, discursive email responding to the allegations in this article, punctuated by anecdotes about his many interactions with grateful police officers and notorious serial killers, Berry-Dee denies abusing his former wife. He claims the small scar on her face predated their marriage, and that he never heard her complain of waking up in a pool of blood. He doesn’t recall the family even owning a butcher’s knife. “Never once during our marriage did I threaten her,” he says.Tracey fled Berry-Dee while he was on a work trip to the US in 1994, interviewing murderers for the pioneering documentary series The Serial Killers. She obtained a court order preventing Berry-Dee from removing their children from her care. He had only sporadic contact with his daughters as they grew up. Zoe last saw her father around 2008, when she was 20. Walking past a bookshop in Winchester, she saw he was doing a book signing and joined the queue. At the front, Zoe gave her first name, wondering if it would spark any recognition, but, she says, “He didn’t recognise me.”Berry-Dee is open about how he secures his interviews with murderers. “Tell them straight off that you think they are innocent,” he writes in his 2023 book Talking With Psychopaths and Savages: Letters from Serial Killers. “Tell them you intend to write a book about the miscarriage of justice they are suffering; go as far as saying that a major UK TV broadcaster is interested, with maybe even some cash in it for them at the end of the day, and they cannot fail to rise to the surface and take your literary bait as fast as a mousetrap snaps shut. Of course, you are telling them a bucketful of lies.”Berry-Dee claims to have “interviewed and interrogated over 30 of the world’s most notorious killers”, including Ted Bundy, one of the most famous serial killers of all time. In 2019’s Talking With Psychopaths and Savages: Beyond Evil, Berry-Dee quotes Bundy saying, “We serial killers are your sons, we are your husbands … we are everywhere. And there will be more of your children dead tomorrow. What’s one less person on the face of the Earth anyways?”Bundy experts dispute these quotes. “They seem to be kind of a mash-up,” observes Margaret Vandiver, a retired professor of criminal justice at the University of Memphis, who was with Bundy in his final weeks. Some “sound like Ted”, she says, but others “don’t sound like him at all. It sounds like someone’s imagination of what he would have said.”“My quotes are drawn from open sources and most carefully checked,” Berry-Dee says. He was not able to provide a link to any verifiable Bundy interview in which these quotes appeared.double quotation markIf I need to get inside a serial killer’s head, I use any tools I canView image in fullscreenBerry-Dee, who has a three decade-long career as a true crime writer.Photograph: Ian Tuttle/ShutterstockLiving serial killers also allege that Berry-Dee invents quotes, which he attributes to them in his books. “They are complete fabrications by CBD,” says Kenneth Bianchi, now Anthony D’Amato, the convicted US serial killer widely known as the Hillside Strangler. “He is one very twisted pathological liar. I never, on paper, in email or tape, ‘confessed’ those things to him.”The Bafta-winning documentary film-maker David Monaghan, who has been investigating Bianchi’s claims of wrongful conviction since 2016, argues that one either believes facts are important for everyone, or no one at all. “Some may say they would play the world’s smallest violin for lying to serial killers,” he says. “But this is a man being published as a ‘world-renowned investigative criminologist’, whose ethics start with deception and continue into outright fraud by inventing quotes.”Lucian Randall, Berry-Dee’s former commissioning editor at his publisher John Blake in the 2000s, says it would not be normal practice in a publishing house to ask authors to provide their source materials, such as interview transcripts or tapes, if the author was already a successful writer, as Berry-Dee was when they started working together. “There’s a certain amount of checking that goes on,” Randall says. “But I think if someone comes and they’ve already done a book, I wouldn’t normally ask to see source material.” For an established, bestselling author, “I’m not sure anyone else would be saying at that point, where is your information for all of this? That feels like you’re doubting the book.”Berry-Dee does not deny he lies to secure interviews. “So what?” he writes in his response to the Guardian. “If I need to get inside a serial killer’s head, I use any tools I can. These murderous people are not angels, you know.”By 2000, Berry-Dee had become an established crime writer, who taught art on the side. It was this reputation that reassured Sally, when she dropped off her 13-year-old daughter, Helen (both pseudonyms), at his Castle School of Art in Portsmouth’s Venture Tower, she was in safe hands. “The fact that he was investigating criminals gave me confidence,” Sally says. “He seemed on the side of the good guys.”An academically gifted child with a talent for art, Helen had a sheltered upbringing: she’d never even held hands with a boy. Berry-Dee, she would later write in a submission to the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority (CICA), presented as “intensely charismatic”, with “an amiable rogue personality”.Within a month of her starting at the school in August 2000, Helen says Berry-Dee, then 52, kissed her. She did not tell her parents. He then began “slowly turning up the pressure gauge”, says Helen, now a 39-year-old artist.She documented what she says happened next in her diary, which she handed over to Hampshire constabulary in 2006. A formal statement drawn up by police investigators quoted its contents: on 2 October 2000, she wrote that Berry-Dee had asked her to perform oral sex. She did not know what this meant, so he explained it to her. By December, he was making her do it. “It was always aggressive and he was constantly reiterating that I was leading him on,” she says.Berry-Dee was insistent, she says, that they should have sex before she turned 14. “He would say he would leave me if I wouldn’t have sex with him,” she says. The day before her 14th birthday, in February 2001, he got what he wanted. “After that,” she says, “there was a pattern of him having sex with me about five times a week for the next 10 months.” (Helen refers to these incidents as “sex” to differentiate them from a later time when she says Berry-Dee raped her, but under UK law any sex with a child is defined as statutory rape.)double quotation markIt’s shocking to see my abuse mirrored in his books, his sick perversions hidden under the guise of ‘serious research’View image in fullscreenHelen, a former art student of Berry-Dee, who she says raped her when she was 13, pictured now …… and on her 13th birthday. Photographs: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The Guardian; courtesy of the familyOn weekdays, it would happen during class. Berry-Dee would look up at the ceiling, or down at the floor, to signal whether he wanted Helen to meet him in the upstairs or downstairs toilets. On Saturday afternoons, when her mother dropped her off for private art classes with Berry-Dee, she says the abuse happened multiple times. In between, they’d talk about his crime writing. “When he spoke about the things he was writing about,” Helen says, “he didn’t speak about them with horror. He spoke about them with admiring fascination.”She says Berry-Dee was a “sadist” who appeared to enjoy causing her pain: “The sex was very violent and I was still a developing girl, so it was incredibly painful.” As the abuse went on, she developed vaginal infections and began self-harming. She says when she told him about her self-harm, he said it was “kinky”.Helen was not the only student Berry-Dee targeted. Gina Hutton, 41, a family support worker from Portsmouth, began attending the school at 15 – the only other teenager in the class. In 2001, when she was 16, she says, Berry-Dee kissed her on the lips. “I remember the bristles because he had a moustache and a beard,” Hutton says. She made an excuse and quickly left.Helen says her relationship with Berry-Dee ended in 2001. But in January 2002, at his request, she reluctantly agreed to meet with him one last time. At this meeting, when she was still only 14, she says he violently raped her against a wall. According to medical records, in October that year, when Helen was 15, she visited a sexual health clinic, where she was tested for HIV and prescribed a pessary for cervical thrush.In 2002, Berry-Dee also published his breakout hit, Talking With Serial Killers: The Most Evil Men in the World Tell Their Own Stories, which he researched and wrote during the period Helen says he abused her. She read it as an adult and realised, to her horror, that some of the extreme sexual practices Berry-Dee had inflicted upon her as a child were included in the book. Like the US serial killer Harvey Carignan, Helen says, Berry-Dee inserted foreign objects into her body. She says he would often accuse her of playing mind games with him, a term also favoured by Carignan. She says Berry-Dee liked to have violent oral sex, a practice favoured by another US serial killer, Kenneth McDuff, whom Berry-Dee writes about in the book. “It’s shocking,” Helen says, “to see elements of my abuse mirrored in his books, for the inspiration for his sick perversions to be hidden under the guise of ‘serious research’.”Helen is not the first woman to report Berry-Dee to the police for child sexual abuse. In 1983, Tracy Hurdle, his stepdaughter from his first marriage, went to the police, alleging Berry-Dee raped her when she was 12. In 1984, Berry-Dee was arrested and charged with having unlawful sexual intercourse with a girl under 13, but the case was dropped when the prosecution offered no evidence. Berry-Dee says Hurdle had in fact been raped by somebody else, but declined to say who.Hurdle was a popular girl who loved horse riding. In photos from the time, she peeks out from behind a sweeping blond fringe, her smile revealing her dimples. She died in a car crash at the age of 16. A family member who was at her funeral remembers, “The whole of her school year went. It was absolutely packed with young people in dark clothing, sobbing.” Also in attendance, they recall, was Berry-Dee.View image in fullscreenTracy, Berry-Dee’s stepdaughter from his first marriage, accused him of raping her when she was 12, which he denies.Photograph: courtesy of the familyIt was reading an article about Berry-Dee appearing in court over Hurdle’s allegations that made Helen realise she wasn’t alone and finally, on 11 September 2006, prompted her to go to the police. On 26 September, she was interviewed by Hampshire officers. As well as her diaries, which documented the alleged abuse in real time, she brought them the physical evidence she had: a tissue that she spat Berry-Dee’s semen into, and a sanitary towel stained with his semen and her blood.Berry-Dee was arrested in January 2007 and denied having had a sexual relationship with her. In June 2007, an officer called Helen with bad news. According to the law at the time, Section 6 of the Sexual Offences Act 1956, allegations of unlawful sex involving children aged 13 to 16 had to be reported within a year. “Spoke to [Helen] and updated her that [Berry-Dee] would NOT be charged as there are no offences,” reads a police report from 6 June 2007. “She was crying.”Helen’s parents hired a lawyer to write to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and ask them to reconsider their decision, including whether they could pursue alternative charges, such as rape, that are not time-barred. Helen had extensive contemporaneous evidence, in the form of diaries and the people she told about the abuse soon afterwards, in addition to the forensic material. But in an October 2008 letter, the CPS said there was still “insufficient evidence to have a realistic prospect of conviction”.Since 2007, Helen has tried to get Hampshire police to reopen the case, give her a copy of the forensic report and return her potential evidence, to no avail. When Helen asked one detective whether she could have her forensic evidence back, she says she was told, “What do you want with that? It’s a dirty old piece of tissue.”Although she did not get to see Berry-Dee appear in court, in 2009 the CICA found that, on the balance of probabilities, she was a victim of violent crime, awarding Helen £18,480.When contacted for comment, Berry-Dee did not admit to a sexual relationship with Helen and denied taking inspiration for his conduct from the serial killers he interviewed: “Quite how and why Helen has transposed this on to me regarding her is total fiction … Indeed I was arrested and questioned, and the matter was apparently dropped,” he says. He claims to have met Helen several times since, even bumping into her in a supermarket where they “chatted amicably”, a claim Helen vehemently denies.Over the last 20 years, Helen has tried to move on from Berry-Dee’s crimes, but she cannot escape the nightmares about those months in the art school. “I’m in a strange, dilapidated version of the Venture Tower,” Helen says, “and he’s in there somewhere, trying to get me, and I’m trying to get out, and can’t.”‘As my loyal readers will know,” Berry-Dee wrote in 2023, “I always treat the relatives, close friends and work colleagues of the deceased … with the deepest respect, for they are victims too.”But throughout his career, Berry-Dee has been repeatedly accused of mistreating the families of the victims of crimes.In November 1995, Diana Lamplugh, mother of the missing estate agent Suzy Lamplugh, told the Guardianshe was appalled to see her daughter’s photo on the cover of Berry-Dee’s book Unmasking Mr Kipper: Who Really Killed Suzy Lamplugh, without her permission. “I looked at it and said, ‘How could this be allowed?’ But you have no rights when someone goes missing. Your daughter doesn’t belong to you.”Berry-Dee’s entanglement with the families of the Babes in the Wood murder victims led to a two-decade feud that ended up in court. The family of Nicola Fellows, one of the nine-year-old girls killed, agreed to provide Berry-Dee with police files and crime scene photographs for a book. But Berry-Dee did not try to help bring Russell Bishop, the prime suspect who was eventually convicted of the murders, to justice. Instead, he enthusiastically championed Bishop’s innocence. And Berry-Dee had his own theory about who might have murdered the schoolgirls: Nicola’s father, Barrie Fellows.In 2007, Ian Heffron, Barrie’s brother and Nicola’s uncle (who changed his surname from Fellows at 18), sued Berry-Dee for libel, after complaining that the author, writing on his blog, had accused Nicola’s family of being involved in a cover-up in relation to the then still unsolved murders. “He said,” Heffron says, “that he will expose and name the killers of the girls, and said it was a close family member.” Two years later Heffron recovered his legal costs from Berry-Dee’s book royalties, directly through his publisher, John Blake, through a third-party debt order.However, John Blake, founder of the eponymous publishing house, said he had no recollection of Berry-Dee being required to pay court-ordered damages out of his royalties. He stated he “looked into it and I was satisfied obviously with the explanations [from Berry-Dee].” Before ringing off, Blake added, “Don’t be too hard on him; he’s not a bad man.”Police arrived to arrest her father for sexual abuse. But he was making it all upRead moreIn 2019, Heffron was interviewed by the former Evening Standard courts correspondent Paul Cheston for his book on the Babes in the Wood murders. It was to be published by John Blake, by then an imprint of the larger Bonnier Books. Heffron told Cheston about Berry-Dee’s mistreatment of Nicola’s family, and Cheston included these allegations in a draft of his book, though they were later cut. The Bonnier editor explained why in an email to Cheston, sent on 3 April 2019: “As for the Chris Berry-Dee stuff – that may have to come out even if the claims can be substantiated, purely due to the obvious conflict of interest. He is our author and, as dreadful an author as he is, we can’t really be seen to be dragging him through the mud, even in this case.” (A spokesperson for Bonnier said the firm was not currently working with Berry-Dee and that “publishing decisions made at the time were based on legal advice”.)Berry-Dee has a further curious tie to the Babes in the Wood case. In 1991, the BBC journalist Martin Bashir obtained the clothes that Karen Hadaway was wearing when she was murdered, only for the clothes to subsequently go missing. Prior to Bashir, however, at least one other person seems to have had the clothes: Berry-Dee, who wrote in one of his books about the Hadaways giving him the clothes “with tears in their eyes”, apparently for the purposes of securing DNA testing. The clothes seem to have been returned shortly before Bashir began investigating.More strangely, however, four sources recall Berry-Dee boasting about having the clothes, or saw what they believed were the clothes, after Bashir and the BBC had apparently misplaced them. His daughter Zoe even believes they were the bloodied clothes she discovered and put on as a child. Her mother agrees, recalling Zoe wearing them when she was four or five. Berry-Dee says it is “100% correct” that he obtained the clothes, but denied Zoe ever wore them. He declined to elaborate on whether, or how, he had obtained them a second time. He claims to have since burned them.Besides Helen and Hurdle, at least one other woman is known to have reported Berry-Dee to Hampshire police for child sexual abuse: his own daughter, Sasha. Sasha says she has memories of her father touching her inappropriately in the shower when she was three or four years old. These recollectionsresurfaced in 2024, prompting a mental health crisis. She confided in her mother and sister at the time, and went to the police the following year.Whether children so young can recall traumatic events is highly controversial. Two academics who specialise in childhood memory formation, consulted for this piece, said that Sasha not having received therapy makes her a more credible source, as therapists have been known to implant false memories. But they also said children seldom recall incidents in as much detail as Sasha, and her awareness of the sexual abuse allegations involving Hurdle could have influenced her memories. Berry-Dee denounced the suggestion that he molested Sasha as “unfounded” and a “very spiteful allegation, probably engineered by her mother”.View image in fullscreenSasha and Zoe, whose mother fled Berry-Dee while he was away interviewing serial killers in 1994.Photograph: courtesy of the familyWith no corroborating evidence, only a police investigation could assess the credibility of Sasha’s allegations. But almost a year after contacting the police, Sasha was still having to chase them even to take her statement. The case by then had been referred to Devon & Cornwall Police (DC), so Sasha could be interviewed closer to where she lives, but it did not progress further for months, with interviews cancelled at short notice due to paperwork issues.“DC are still claiming they haven’t received the information for the interview?” Sasha texted her police contact on 12 January 2026, nearly nine months after she first contacted them. On 29 January, she followed up: “Still nothing?” On 10 February: “Is this happening?”In February 2026, Devon & Cornwall police attempted to arrange a video-recorded interview, but Sasha says she was told she would not be allowed to speak with a therapist for support as she prepared, because it could undermine her credibility. “I could not sit in that room for three and a half hours with cameras on me without having any sort of coping mechanism,” she says. Disheartened, Sasha requested to pause her interview.In 2024, Bonnier rebranded Berry-Dee for a younger,TikToking and true crime podcast-loving audience. His books are reviewed often on BookTok, TikTok’s literary subcommunity. But not all his reviews are positive. He “berate[s] female victims for not taking his advice, implying their stupidity was to blame for their murders”, writes one Goodreads reviewer. A second points to the way he describes “the rape of young girls as ‘sex’ or ‘three-ways’”.Even when not lascivious, Berry-Dee’s prose can be mercilessly cruel. One murder victim is described as a “nagging bag of wind” whose “good looks and figure had long abandoned her”. The convicted US murderer Carol Bundy is “a common slut” who “would have cheap sex with any man who looked just the once at her”. An 11-year-old rape victim is a “sexually advanced youngster”; another 11-year-old sexual abuse victim is “physically well-developed”. The mentally ill are residents of the “nuthouse”; women are “into lesbianism”; and a gay murder victim is a “deviant”.But Berry-Dee’s books remain most shocking for their orgiastic depiction of violence. In 2011’s Talking With Serial Killers: Dead Men Talking, Berry-Dee writes, “I started to play a little death game with her, use her like a toy, an amusement,” quoting the serial killer Keith Hunter Jesperson. “I choked her, let her wake up, choked her again, let her wake up again ... finally she caught on and just accepted the game.” In 2019’s Talking With Psychopaths and Savages: Beyond Evil, he directs readers “with more than a particular fascination for the macabre” to online photos of a 20-year-old murder victim’s decapitated head, which Berry-Dee jocularly describes as resembling “an ugly Barbie doll”.“What are people getting out of reading this voyeuristic, sensationalist stuff?” Helen asks. “Who is it helping? For sure, not the victims, nor the victim’s families. I can only think that it feeds some people’s basest desires.”Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: ‘In the heatwaves, it’s crucial’: the fight to save France’s rural swimming pools | France | The Guardian
description: Ageing facilities offering daily refuge face funding threat as record temperatures parch the countryside
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Ageing facilities offering daily refuge face funding threat as record temperatures parch the countryside
Content: Suzy Bernard, left, is part of the campaign to save the Hauts-d'Anjou pool in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, France, which costs €100,000 a year to runView image in fullscreenSuzy Bernard, left, is part of the campaign to save the Hauts-d'Anjou pool in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, France, which costs €100,000 a year to runFrance‘In the heatwaves, it’s crucial’: the fight to save France’s rural swimming poolsAgeing facilities offering daily refuge face funding threat as record temperatures parch the countrysideAngelique Chrisafisin Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe and Rochefort-sur-Loire; photographs by Thomas LouapreSat 15 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuzy Bernard took a breath and jumped into the deep end of her village swimming pool with a splash.“There’s a wonderful feeling of wellbeing in the water,” said the former hospital healthcare assistant, who recently learned to swim aged 75 and was now gliding along with her daughter and grandson.View image in fullscreenSuzy Bernard: ‘We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives’The municipal swimming pool, bordered by shady oak trees in the village of Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, in westernFrance, has been the Bernard family’s daily refuge from the sweltering heatwaves this summer. Bernard is a member of the village collective, Touche Pas à Ma Piscine (Hands Off My Pool), campaigning to defend the Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe facility and calling for more government support for rural swimming pools. “We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives and stays open,” she said.As a summer ofrecord temperaturesparched much of the French countryside, local village swimming pools, with cheap entry tickets, have often been the only shelter from the heatwaves for rural families on low incomes who cannot afford to go on holiday or who live inheat-trap homes. The pools are also crucial for teaching rural communities to swim. A total of 274 people died fromdrowningin France between 1 May and 15 July this year, with most deaths occurring when people jumped into rivers and waterways to cool down.Families enjoy local swimming pools in western FranceBut France’s ageing rural swimming pools, many of which were built in 1970s, are in crisis as village mayors with shrinking budgets struggle to pay the high running costs and some pools are forced to close owing to lack of funds.In Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, a village of 3,200 people in Les Hauts-d’Anjou, a farming area of the Pays de la Loire, the new mayor, Véronique Langlais, said she was determined to keep running the village pool that opened in 1973, despite an annual cost of at least €100,000 (£85,000) to the town hall’s modest budget. Three other rural pools had closed in the surrounding countryside, making this the only pool in a radius of about 20 miles.View image in fullscreenVéronique Langlais, mayor of Hauts-d’Anjou, in the changing rooms of the Hauts-d’Anjou swimming pool“This pool is a treasure that we have to protect,” Langlais said. But any sudden need for a costly new part or major repair could force the pool’s closure owing to lack of funds. “There’s a sword of Damocles hanging over our head.”In 1969, after France’s poor swimming performance at the 1968 Mexico CityOlympics, and a series of tragic drownings across the country, the government under Georges Pompidou launched a plan to build 1,000 pools in mainly rural areas to encourage swimming. Over 600 were built, but those still in use – as well as later 1980s pools – are in urgent need of costly renovation.View image in fullscreenSwimming lessons for children at the Hauts-d’Anjou outdoor swimming pool in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, FranceView image in fullscreenThe outdoor swimming pool, which opened in 1973François Gernigon, a centre-right lawmaker for the Maine-et-Loire, has petitioned the government for a funding plan. He recently surveyed rural mayors, finding more than 75% feared their village pools risked closure in the short-term. He said the heatwaves made it essential to protect pools as “the only place of leisure to relax in rural areas”. He said village pool closures “make residents feel abandoned”.View image in fullscreenEmma-Özlen Kaya: ‘We didn’t go on holiday because my parents didn’t have the budget’Emma-Özlem Kaya, 45, is a printmaker whose Turkish father moved to Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe in 1972 when the local tannery recruited artisan leather-workers from Istanbul. “We didn’t go on holiday because my parents didn’t have the budget,” she said. “So every day in summer, I’d grab my swimming bag and walk to the pool with my siblings and friends and we’d spend the afternoons there with our towels laid out.” She now attends water aerobics classes there and campaigns to protect the pool.View image in fullscreenThe Hauts-d’Anjou outdoor swimming poolNadine Lemonnier, a local teacher who is also part of the collective, remembered childhood summers at another local village pool: “whole days spent diving for objects and having deep teenage conversations at the edge”. For her, protecting rural pools that offered children swimming lessons was crucial because her three-year-old cousin died from drowning in a private pool.Across France, there are dozens of rural village collectives mobilising to protect local pools: campaigning, volunteering to help run them and even painting and carrying out maintenance work.View image in fullscreenGuillaume, a swimming instructor, leads an aqua aerobics class at the Louet municipal swimming pool in Rochefort-sur-LoireView image in fullscreenChris is teaching his daughter Seren how to dive at the Louet municipal swimming poolIn Rochefort-sur-Loire, a village of 2,400 people near Angers, members of the local pool support group gathered at the water’s edge. In recent years, they had decorated the village with flippers and rubber rings to convince a visiting government minister to secure funds for reopening the indoor teaching pool. They hosted a poet in residence at the pool and run theatre performances there.“It’s about making our village pool the focus of life in the community,” said Nicolas Robin, a sociologist.On 18 July 1969, at nearby Juigné-sur-Loire, 19 children drowned in the River Loire on an outing from a school holiday club – one of many tragedies that led the government to improve swimming teaching facilities.Swimminglessons remain key. There are three rivers in the area and the village is often hit by flooding in winter.View image in fullscreenThe Louet River, now dry, right next to the Louet municipal swimming pool in Rochefort-sur-LoirePhotograph: Thomas Louapre/The Guardian“People need to know how to swim to protect themselves in the flooding season too,” said Guillaume Lusteau, the pool’s lifeguard and swim coach.The pool sits beside the River Louet, a branch of the Loire that is usually a paddling spot. But the summer heatwaves have left the river level too low for a dip, increasing the number of swimmers at the pool.View image in fullscreenDidier Le Gall, mayor of Rochefort-sur-Loire: ‘The pool is part of our village’s identity’The mayor, Didier Le Gall, said that in this area, with a large proportion of organic farming, health was a priority and the pool was essential, particularly for families on low incomes. “It’s important for children learning to swim, but also for the social lives of people who don’t go away on holiday,” he said. “The pool is part of our village’s identity, and in the heatwaves it has become a crucial place to cool down. The pool’s impact on mental health and physical health is considerable.”Le Gall said the town hall wanted to keep the pool open, despite the €100,000 basic running cost. “But we need help in the long-term,” he said.View image in fullscreenLouet municipal swimming pool, in Rochefort-sur-LoireView image in fullscreenLouet Municipal swimming pool, in Rochefort-sur-LoireBruno Cheminat, 73, a former special educational needs teacher and one-time competitive swimmer, clocks up 2,000 metres every day, and has also helped with painting and maintenance work as a volunteer. “It’s beautiful to be the first in the water in the morning,” he said.Estelle, a former flight attendant who works on the pool reception, said it boosted her mood to be in the water, looking out at trees towards the church: “It’s like swimming in a picture postcard.”Explore more on these topicsFranceSwimmingClimate crisisExtreme heatEuropeEurope weatherfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Let’s see what he can do’: will Burnham bring voters back in Labour heartlands? | Labour | The Guardian
description: With questions over Farage’s finances and a new face in No 10, could Barnsley council be a bellwether for changing Labour fortunes?
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: With questions over Farage’s finances and a new face in No 10, could Barnsley council be a bellwether for changing Labour fortunes?
Content: Jill Hibbert, pictured with her husband, Keith, voted Reform in May but says she will probably return to Labour.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJill Hibbert, pictured with her husband, Keith, voted Reform in May but says she will probably return to Labour.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianLabour‘Let’s see what he can do’: will Burnham bring voters back in Labour heartlands?With questions over Farage’s finances and a new face in No 10, could Barnsley council be a bellwether for changing Labour fortunes?Hannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentSat 15 Aug 2026 05.55 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour marked its worst performance in more than 50 years when voters went to the polls inBarnsleyin May, but 100 days on from those seismic local elections, the political landscape has shifted drastically.Could theSouth Yorkshiretown, where Reform UK reaped the benefits of dissatisfaction with Labour, prove to be a test case for whether the governing party has turned the tide?Labour had run Barnsley’s council since its inception in 1974, but was left with just 11 councillors after Reform triumphed with 42 seats.“I knew that it would be the most challenging set of elections that we’ve ever faced in Barnsley’s history,” said the councillor James Higginbottom, the new Labour group opposition leader. “What I didn’t necessarily expect was the scale of the Reform victory.”View image in fullscreenBarnsley’s Labour council group leader, James Higginbottom.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianCatastrophic results in places such as Barnsley were a catalyst for Keir Starmer’s resignation. He has been replaced as prime minister by the former mayor of Greater ManchesterAndy Burnham, who won the Labour leadership uncontested after a landslide byelection victory.Meanwhile, the Reform leader, Nigel Farage, is facing scrutiny over his financial affairs. While he was decisively re-elected in Clacton on Thursday, after he called a byelection in protest over a parliamentary standards investigation into his financial gifts, the contestwas largely viewed as a sideshowafter other major parties declined to stand. The parliamentary standards investigationhas now resumed.Labour is now ahead in the polls for the first time since March 2025, with a YouGov poll on Monday giving Labour a two-point lead, at 24 points to Reform’s 22.Many in Barnsley used their vote in May to punish Starmer’s government, and while almost everyone the Guardian spoke to there this week said it was too early to judge the Reform council on their record, the new national political picture appears to be enticing at least some back to Labour.In the town of Penistone, Richard Riding, 71, a retired HGV driver, said he was normally a Labour voter but had backed Reform in May “just for a change”.“The current government were in a total mess,” he said, “and we’ve had a lot of problems.”But he is no fan of Farage. “If you think the country’s in a mess now with Europe, it’s going to be totally destroyed if he takes over.” he said. “[Burnham] did a very good job in Manchester so let’s see what he can do now,” he added, saying he would vote Labour next time.View image in fullscreenRichard Riding backed Reform in May but is no fan of Nigel Farage.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianLabour’s Barnsley council was not your usual local administration. It had won both the Local Government Chronicle and the Municipal Journal (MJ) council of the year awards in 2023, becoming the first local authority to win both titles in the same year. In February, Barnsley was named in the top 10 most productive councils in the country, coming in seventh in the Impower Index, published by the MJ.View image in fullscreenBarnsley council under Labour brought in several initiatives, including hospital services in the town centre.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianWhile in many towns people felt as dissatisfied with local administrations as they did with national government,Barnsley had launched a number of pioneering initiatives,including“health on the high street”, making it the first local authority to bring hospital services into the town centre, and free bus travel for under-18s, a version of which Burnham has since adopted nationally.Barnsley parents also received free school uniforms for their children in a scheme that saved families about £2.5m in a year. It has already been scaled back by Reform. (Reform’s council leader and local party chair did not respond to interview requests.)Despite this innovative work, voters still punished Labour at the ballot box. “By and large, people were saying to us: ‘I like what the council’s doing’,” Higginbottom said, “but that national stuff, we just couldn’t overcome that.”View image in fullscreenMartin Harvey said he voted Reform UK at the local elections as he is worried about immigration.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianMartin Harvey, 75, who worked in engineering, said he “has been Labour all my life”, but concerns about immigration meant he turned to Reform in May, and plans to stick with them.“I’ve just been watching on TV, GB News, and I don’t know, locally everything around here seems to be fine,” he said, but added: “Politics in general, I’m frightened, I am frightened of what’s happening. It’s just frightening how many boats are coming across.”Jessica Morgan, 31, a retail worker, was always a Labour voter, but she voted Reform for the first time in May. “I’m still happy with that decision,” she said.“I just want the roads to be fixed, the potholes to be filled,” she added. “Labour were just cushty, because Barnsley has always been Labour. Even my grandad, he used to be a pit miner and he’s always voted for Labour, but this time … no. He also voted Reform.”But there are early signs that some voters are thinking of returning to Labour. In the Penistone East ward of Barnsley, a council byelection has been triggered by the resignation of a Reform councillor. In May, Labour won two of the seats that were up for grabs, and Reform won the third. But a Labour source said they were “confident we will win” the third seat on Thursday.Higginbottom said: “I think that will be a good barometer as to where we are; are we reconnecting with voters who in May didn’t feel able to put their trust in us?”View image in fullscreenJessica Morgan would not change her vote for Reform UK in May.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianLabour has spoken to more than 1,000 voters in the ward so far and aims to double that by polling day.“I’m not saying they’re rushing out to suddenly say: ‘Yeah, we love Labour and we’re going to be voting for you en masse’,” Higginbottom said, “[but] some are willing to give us a fair hearing, and to listen to what we’ve got to say.”Marie Tidball, the Labour MP for Penistone and Stocksbridge, said she had “definitely” noticed a shift in voter attitudes while campaigning for the byelection, in comparison to May.“It really does feel like it’s cut through in terms of Andy being boldly and confidently and authentically Labour once again, and I think people do seem to really identify with him as a person in a very powerful way,” she said.Keith Hibbert, 67, a retired project manager in engineering, voted Labour in May, as he “wasn’t convinced yet” by Reform. His wife, Jill, a former nurse, also 67, switched to Farage’s party based on “just the manifesto”, having always voted Labour in the past. Both are cautiously optimistic about Burnham’s leadership.“I think they’ve given Labour a new leaf, because there’s a new face, a new personality,” Keith said. Jill added she would probably vote Labour again.Dan Jarvis, the MP for Barnsley North, said: “Reform did well when people could only judge their promises. Unfortunately for them, their actions will now be judged too.”Stephanie Peacock, the MP for Barnsley South, said: “It’s still in early days, but I’ve seen already that residents across Barnsley are more open and willing to give the Labour party a hearing.”She said one woman who had previously been “pretty anti-government, and pro-Reform” had told her she would vote Labour with Burnham as prime minister. “It’s not just the PM’s focus on tacking the cost of living,” she said, “it’s the government’s more hopeful and positive tone that is cutting through.”Explore more on these topicsLabourReform UKBarnsleyLocal governmentAndy BurnhamNorth of EnglandYorkshirefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Zimbabwe boat accident death toll hits 68 as 22 more bodies recovered | Zimbabwe | The Guardian
description: Eighteen children among the people killed after ferry capsized on Lake Kariba
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Eighteen children among the people killed after ferry capsized on Lake Kariba
Content: A coffin with the body of a victim of the capsized passenger ferry, leaves the Kariba hospital mortuary after his body was identified for burial in Kariba, on 14 August 2026.Photograph: Jekesai Njikizana/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA coffin with the body of a victim of the capsized passenger ferry, leaves the Kariba hospital mortuary after his body was identified for burial in Kariba, on 14 August 2026.Photograph: Jekesai Njikizana/AFP/Getty ImagesZimbabweZimbabwe boat accident death toll hits 68 as 22 more bodies recoveredEighteen children among the people killed after ferry capsized on Lake KaribaNadeem BadshahSat 15 Aug 2026 15.39 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 17.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty-two more bodies have been recovered after a boat accident inZimbabwe, taking the death toll to 68, police said on Saturday.The ferrycapsized on Tuesday on Lake Kariba, on the border with Zambia. An investigation has suggested it was overloaded when it turned over during heavy winds.Eighteen children were among the people killed, Zimbabwe’s police said, in what is believed to be the country’s deadliest such disaster.Most of the passengers are believed to be villagers and fish traders who lived around the lake.Officials said the vessel was authorised to carry 90 people but was packed with 114 adults, five crew members and an unspecified number of children.Lt Col Joseph Muchechesi, commander of the boat regiment involved in the search operation, said: “So far today we have managed to take 22 bodies. We are confident that we will manage to retrieve all the bodies.”The civil protection unit said on Wednesday that 77 people had been rescued.Hundreds of people gathered at the district hospital in the lakeside town of Kariba to identify the bodies of their relatives and loved ones.View image in fullscreenFamily members walk past caskets carrying their loved ones during a memorial service for the victims of the boat accident in Kariba, Zimbabwe, 13 August 2026.Photograph: Mkhululi Thobela/APA public memorial service was held in Kariba, nearly 280km (175 miles) north-west of the capital Harare, on Thursday before the burials started.Survivors said they pleaded with the ferry driver to turn back as the vessel had begun taking on water soon after departing.Chance Siyamavhu, 45, told Agence France-Presse: “Thank God that a wave pushed the sinking vessel and we managed to climb on top.“When the boat capsized, most of the people scrambled to get the lifejackets but most of them did not even know how to use them.“Most people could not make it.”Lake Kariba is the world’s largest manmade lake by volume. It stretches more than 200km (124 miles) and is up to 40km (25 miles) wide in places.It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people.In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.On the Zimbabwean side, five passengers drowned in a 2021 incident.Explore more on these topicsZimbabweAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Moroccan police arrest more than 100 people as they attempt to enter Ceuta | Morocco | The Guardian
description: Border security tightened after social media posts call for another mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Border security tightened after social media posts call for another mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory
Content: Moroccan police were seen monitoring dozens of migrants on the outskirts of the border town of Fnideq on Saturday.Photograph: Mohamed Siali/EPAView image in fullscreenMoroccan police were seen monitoring dozens of migrants on the outskirts of the border town of Fnideq on Saturday.Photograph: Mohamed Siali/EPAMoroccoMoroccan police arrest more than 100 people as they attempt to enter CeutaBorder security tightened after social media posts call for another mass crossing into Spain’s north African territoryReutersSat 15 Aug 2026 14.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMoroccan police have arrested 111 people as they tried to enter Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, amid ⁠tightened security on both sides after social media posts ​called for another mass crossing.The attempted crossing on Saturday came two weeks after more than72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta, causingtensions within the EUand prompting anti-immigration rhetoric among far-right parties worldwide. At least 96 people died trying to ⁠reach European soil.A source in Morocco’s interior ministry told news agency Reuters that those detained included 109 migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and two Moroccan citizens arrested in or around Fnideq, the Moroccan city near Ceuta.Moroccan police used teargas to disperse groups of migrants ⁠gathered on hills about 1.9 miles (3km) from the border, according to Spanish news agency EFE. Reuters later saw hundreds of police officers, some in riot gear and others in plainclothes, returning from the hills outside ​Fnideq.EFE and Spanish state broadcaster TVE said Morocco’s interior ministry ordered their journalists ‌to leave Fnideq immediately, without providing an explanation.View image in fullscreenWitnesses said they saw teargas being fired at migrants on hills near the border.Photograph: Jalal Morchidi/EPAIn Ceuta, ‌Spanish soldiers guarded supermarkets while police patrolled the main streets. The city was calmer than in the days after thedeadly crossing attempton 30 July.Madrid has ‌since installed a maritime barrier and deployed more than 500 additional police officers from mainlandSpain, raising the total in Ceuta to more than 1,600. The interior ministry said the reinforcements would remain for as long as needed.“We’ll continue to deploy whatever personnel are necessary to restore normality as soon as possible and prevent events like those of 30 July from happening again,” Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said on Thursday.About 5,000 migrantsremained in Ceuta, the minister added. Reuters saw hundreds sheltering from scorching heat under makeshift bamboo shelters on the urban beach of El Trampolin.View image in fullscreenMigrants seen sheltering from the sun on El Trampolin beach in Ceuta.Photograph: Jorge Guerrero/AFP/Getty ImagesGrande-Marlaska said migrants who entered irregularly would not be allowed to stay in the territory, travel to mainland Spain or ‌obtain legal status, except in rare cases involving extreme vulnerability. Those without a right to remain would be returned to Morocco, he added.Earlier this week, Rabat said it was monitoring “the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin” calling for a mass crossing ​on 15 August, warning it would prosecute organisers and participants.A Reuters witness saw reinforced security near the border, including police vans with wire shields and road checkpoints. Local media reported similar measures near Melilla, another Spanish territory in north Africa.Authorities prevented several groups from boarding trains and buses to northern Morocco in cities such as Casablanca, Fez and Kenitra. However, witnesses told Reuters that some migrants from sub-Saharan Africa were bypassing security checkpoints by taking mountain routes towards Fnideq.One witness said the schools in Fnideq had been turned into accommodation for security forces deployed near the ⁠border.Explore more on these topicsMoroccoSpainAfricaMigrationRefugeesEuropeMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Powerful earthquake kills dozens in eastern Indonesia | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Quake struck Flores region early on Saturday, prompting thousands to seek higher ground for fear of a tsunami
Author: William Christou
Headline: Quake struck Flores region early on Saturday, prompting thousands to seek higher ground for fear of a tsunami
Content: Strong earthquake hits IndonesiaIndonesiaPowerful earthquake kills dozens in eastern IndonesiaQuake struck Flores region early on Saturday, prompting thousands to seek higher ground for fear of a tsunamiWilliam Christouand agenciesSat 15 Aug 2026 11.34 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 19.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 7.7-magnitude earthquake that struck easternIndonesiahas killed at least 47people, causing widespread panic and collapsing buildings and homes in a region prone to deadly seismic events.Rescuers have yet to reach Nagekeo, the area closest to the epicentre, because roads were blocked by landslides and communications disrupted.Authorities issued a tsunami warning, which has since been lifted, but there were at least 235aftershocks, including one of magnitude 6.1. Indonesian authorities said monitoring showed no significant sea level changes that could indicate a tsunami.View image in fullscreenA motorcyclist rides past a crack in a road in East Nusa Tenggara province.Photograph: Ignasius Kunda/EPATsunami waves of ⁠ 1.5 metres(3ft) were recorded in several areas.The Indonesian geophysics agency, BMKG, recorded the first quake at 4.58am on Saturday local time at a depth of 9 miles (15km) in the country’s Flores region.A second earthquake of magnitude 6.1struck off northern Sumatra, Indonesia, hours after the initial quake, with no casualties yet reported.Rescuers around the port town of Maumere found 20 people dead, six severelyinjured and two trapped under the rubble, said Fathur Rahman, the head of the city’s rescue agency. Eight of those dead had been killed in a landslide. Maumere is the main town in Sikka regency on Flores Island in the east of Indonesia’s vast archipelago.View image in fullscreenPatients are treated in the hallway of a hospital in Labuan Bajo, East Nusa Tenggara province.Photograph: Firdia Lisnawati/APA video on Facebook, verified by Reuters as being at a port in Maumere, shows parts of a building collapsing as people scream and run in the street. Another video showed a coastal village covered in mud and debris after a 1.61-metre tsunami wave hit Ngada village in east Manggarai.Indonesia earthquake map graphicPreliminary data showed that 346 homes, 87 schools and more than a dozen health facilities had been damaged.Indonesian authorities said residents were trapped in several buildings in the affected area.“I have never felt an earthquake this big,” said Yulian Juita Ekalia, a university professor who lives more than 60 miles from the epicentre. “It felt like we were on a trampoline, it was really scary.”The epicentre was located off the north coast of Flores, about 42 miles north-west of the coastal town of Ende, US and Indonesian authorities said.View image in fullscreenPeople are forced to leave their homes in Talibura village, Sikka, East Nusa Tenggara.Photograph: Arnold Welianto/AFP/GettyTeams had not been able to reach Nagekeo, the region closest to the epicentre, and ​communications signals there had been affected, Fathur said. Road access was blocked ‌by landslides, and a team was attempting to reach the area by ferry, he said.The police chief of East Nusa Tenggara province, Rudi Darmoko, said the earthquake caused power cuts that made communication difficult between cities and villages, complicating rescue efforts.“We are continuing to collect reports of damage and casualties, but there are communication disruptions,” he said. He said landslides in Ende regency had cut off the Trans-Flores highway, a 435-mile mountain road.View image in fullscreenPatients receive treatment inside a makeshift tent outside a hospital in Labuan Bajo, East Nusa Tenggara province.Photograph: Firdia Lisnawati/APResidents in Nagekeo regency raced for higher ground immediately after the earthquake.“Suddenly it started to shake and I panicked,” Lukas Lotar, a hospital customer service official, said. “Patients also fled the hospital, the jolt was big. I saw some walls were cracked.”Yohanes Babo, 56, a Nagekeo resident, said he was at a market when the quake hit. “The shaking was strong. Thankfully, we were already outside the house,” he said. “People were panicking, running here and there. We’re evacuating for the time being … and trying to get to the hills. My family is safe. No one was harmed.”View image in fullscreenDamaged homes in Ruteng, East Nusa Tenggara.Photograph: Selo/AFP/GettyAbout 2,000 people in Nagekeo evacuated, and damage to ‌a number of houses, warehouses and government facilities was reported, the national disaster mitigation agency, the BNPB, said. Authorities also reported traffic congestion and power cuts affecting parts of the regency, it said.Local television showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution after the quake. Healthcare workers set up temporary treatment facilities outdoors, moving beds, IV stands and oxygen on to the streets.The BNPB, which put the quake’s toll at one dead and four injured, said it was still gathering data.Images broadcast on Indonesian television showed hundreds of people in nearby Nagekeo regency evacuating the area, surrounded by the rubble of damaged buildings.Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency in East Nusa Tenggara province, said a number of buildings had been damaged by the strong shaking and panicked people ran to higher ground. “Many buildings here were damaged … I saw that the waiting room at the port terminal in Maumere had collapsed,” she said.Indonesia, consisting of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the “ring of fire”, an arc of geophysical activity in the Pacific basin.In 2004, a 9.1-magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of western Indonesia, causing a tsunami that killed 220,000 people in theAsia Pacificarea.With Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsIndonesiaEarthquakesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: One Nation senator says parents who support their trans children are engaging in ‘child abuse’ | One Nation | The Guardian
description: ‘There’s male, there’s female, and then there’s mental illness,’ Tyron Whitten says on YouTube show
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: ‘There’s male, there’s female, and then there’s mental illness,’ Tyron Whitten says on YouTube show
Content: Tyron Whitten (centre) campaigning with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson (right).Photograph: Pauline Hanson/XView image in fullscreenTyron Whitten (centre) campaigning with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson (right).Photograph: Pauline Hanson/XOne NationOne Nation senator says parents who support their trans children are engaging in ‘child abuse’‘There’s male, there’s female, and then there’s mental illness,’ Tyron Whitten says on YouTube showFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerSat 15 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne Nation senator Tyron Whitten has claimed parents supporting their children who identify as transgender are engaging in “child abuse”, telling a fringe YouTube show: “there’s male, there’s female, and then there’s mental illness”.Guardian Australia has unearthed several incendiary comments from Whitten and fellow One Nation senatorsPauline Hansonand her longtime lieutenant Malcolm Roberts, about transgender Australians.“They’re saying you can cut your dick off and become a woman … That’s a complete distortion of science,” Roberts told a podcast in June.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailWhitten filmed an interview at Parliament House in August 2025 with a YouTube page called “Billboard Battalion”. The host recounts overhearing a Parliament House attendant escorting a group of schoolchildren.“She turned around and said to me ‘thanks very much for your patience’, and I said, ‘thanks very much for calling them boys and girls’… when I was a young bloke, I never ever thought that would be a thing,” the host said.Whitten responded: “Neither did I. Look, there’s male, there’s female, and then there’s mental illness.”One Nation staffer accused of posing as leftwing content creator in ‘undercover’ videosRead more“If you want to wear a dress, that’s fine. I don’t care. But they can’t keep saying ‘hey kids, that’s normal’. Well, no, it’s not.“You’re going to be a boy or you’re going to be a girl. And parents that are promoting this, I think that’s child abuse.”The Australian Human Rights Commissioncitesstatistics that “around 2-3% of young Australians aged 11 to 18 years identify as transgender or gender diverse.”Referencing research from youth advocacy group Minus18, the AHRC said “9 in 10 LGBTQIA+ young people said they had faced bullying or violence because of who they are, leaving many feeling isolated and unsupported.”The offices of Whitten, Hanson and One Nation’s head office were contacted for response but did not respond to inquiries.Roberts, whose previouscomments on fringe podcasts about immigrationandconspiracy theories have drawn controversy, in June was dismissive of transgender Australians in a YouTube interview.Discussing problems he saw in Australia, Roberts said: “If you cut off your dick … you’re not a woman. [But] that’s now ingrained in law in Australia that you are.“Not as crudely as that, but it just says that if you want to identify as a male, if you want to identify as a female and you’re a male, that’s your choice.”In a March 2024 interview with former television host and AFL identity Sam Newman, Hanson – listing a number of her political concerns – mentioned “this transgender crap that’s going on, it frustrates me”.“We’re allowing children under the age of 18 to have life-changing operations that destroy their lives, ending up like vegetables, just destroyed, locked away in their bedrooms.”However, the AHRCadvises: “It is not legal in Australia to perform most gender-affirming surgeries on people under 18 years in the public health system.“The only surgery allowed is breast reduction surgery for trans men, and only in very extreme circumstances,” it said in a fact sheet on transgender issues.Parental consent and professional assessment is generally required for children to receive gender-affirming care, including hormone treatment or “puberty blockers”. Otherwise, a court order is required.Equality Australia CEO, Anna Brown, said Australian law had “recognised trans people and their rights for decades”.“Targeting one of Australia’s smallest and most marginalised communities isn’t just unfair, it fuels division, creates confusion and causes real harm. Trans people make up less than 1% of the population, yet they are being forced to carry the weight of a divisive and incredibly cruel culture war,” she said.“This is a community that already experiences disproportionately high rates of discrimination, violence and exclusion. It’s clear some politicians are taking advantage of a lack of familiarity with trans people to manufacture fear and division, because turning minorities into political targets is an easy way to generate attention and relevance.”The ABC reported on Wednesdaythe comments of Parminder Singh, who was third on One Nation’s ticket for the legislative council at the 2025 WA state election. Asked in a YouTube interview whether he thought people were born gay, Singh replied: “No, it’s a mental illness”.Hanson on Thursday distanced herself from his comments, saying: “He’s not standing for One Nation … they’re not my views.”Barnaby Joyce said on Wednesday, speaking to the ABC: “I don’t concur with [Singh’s] views.” He also defended One Nation’s record on LGBTQ+ issues, saying: “I think you should get [One Nation party director] James Ashby on the show and ask him, he’s gay.”“I think we’reone of the gayest parties in Australia,”he added.Explore more on these topicsOne NationPauline HansonAustralian politicsLGBTQ+ rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Naidoc awards honour ‘fearless, brilliant’ promoter of First Nations culture Rhoda Roberts | Indigenous Australians | The Guardian
description: Proud Widjabul Wiyebal woman of the Bundjalung nation recognised posthumously with the lifetime achievement award
Author: Douglas Smith
Headline: Proud Widjabul Wiyebal woman of the Bundjalung nation recognised posthumously with the lifetime achievement award
Content: Rhoda Roberts outside the Koori Mail in Lismore, 2024. ‘Her legacy will continue to inspire generations to come,’ Naidoc awards organisers say.Photograph: Natalie Grono/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRhoda Roberts outside the Koori Mail in Lismore, 2024. ‘Her legacy will continue to inspire generations to come,’ Naidoc awards organisers say.Photograph: Natalie Grono/The GuardianIndigenous AustraliansNaidoc awards honour ‘fearless, brilliant’ promoter of First Nations culture Rhoda RobertsProud Widjabul Wiyebal woman of the Bundjalung nation recognised posthumously with the lifetime achievement awardFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastDouglas SmithIndigenous affairs reporterSat 15 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Australia’s greatest cultural ambassadors has been recognised posthumously for dedicating her life to sharing, preserving and promoting First Nations culture through language, dance and ceremony.A proud Widjabul Wiyebal woman of the Bundjalung nation,Rhoda Roberts died in Marchaged 66. On Saturday night in Alice Springs, she was posthumously awarded the lifetime achievement award at the Naidoc awards.The Naidoc (National Aborigines and Islanders Day Observance Committee) awards recognise the outstanding contributions, achievements and excellence of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples across Australia.Rhoda Roberts, Indigenous broadcaster and cultural powerhouseRead moreThe co-chair of the National Naidoc Committee, Lynette Riley, paid tribute to Roberts, saying she “was a force” and her legacy would continue to inspire future generations.“(She was)fearless, brilliant and deeply committedto community and culture,” she said. “Rhoda had been selected for this honour, and we felt strongly that it was important to continue recognising her extraordinary contribution.“Her legacy will continue to inspire generations to come.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe minister forIndigenous Australians, Malarndirri McCarthy, said this year’s winners “embody the spirit of Naidoc”, with the annual event celebrating 50 years.“They are leaders, advocates, artists, educators, innovators and community champions whose work is creating positive change and inspires others,” she said.“As we celebrate 50 Years of Deadly, we also celebrate the generations of First Nations people who have strengthened our communities and helped shape a better future for all Australians.”At the Sydney Olympics in 2000, Roberts worked as a creative director and choreographed the Awakening segment of the opening ceremony, which was watched by millions of people around the globe.She was also recognised as the first Aboriginal person to host a prime-time current affairs program, SBS’s Vox Populi in 1991, and then working in radio in 1992 she co-founded Deadly Sounds, which ran for 21 years, giving Indigenous people a voice across Australia and the Pacific.Roberts also became the inaugural head of Indigenous programming at the Sydney Opera House in 2012. While there, she initiated Dance Rites, a First Nations dance competition, and advocated for the inclusion of Bangarra Dance Theatre and the Deadly awards.She also became creative director of the Parrtjima festival of light in Alice Springs/Mparntwe in 2017.Other winners recognised on the night include:Person of the year:Aunty Pat TurnerFemale Elder of the year:Christine CorbyMale Elder of the year:Dr Stephen HaganSportsperson of the year:Caitlyn CostelloYouth of the year:Tyson Neal-EdwardsCreative talent award:Kaylene WhiskeyCaring for country and culture award:Southern Aboriginal CorporationEducation award:The Aboriginal & Islander Independent Community School (The Murri School)Innovation award:Young Indigenous Women’s STEM AcademyExplore more on these topicsIndigenous AustraliansnewsShareReuse this content

title: First Australian death of little penguin with H5 bird flu confirmed on Phillip Island | Bird flu | The Guardian
description: Authorities confirm first Australian death of species found with virus near where it attracts crowds to a ‘penguin parade’
Author: Lisa Cox
Headline: Authorities confirm first Australian death of species found with virus near where it attracts crowds to a ‘penguin parade’
Content: Authorities had been racing to vaccinate 40,000 little penguins on Phillip Island before the first confirmed case of H5 bird flu in the colony.Photograph: ozflash/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenAuthorities had been racing to vaccinate 40,000 little penguins on Phillip Island before the first confirmed case of H5 bird flu in the colony.Photograph: ozflash/Getty Images/iStockphotoBird fluFirst Australian death of little penguin with H5 bird flu confirmed on Phillip IslandAuthorities confirm first Australian death of species found with virus near where it attracts crowds to a ‘penguin parade’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLisa CoxEnvironment and climate correspondentSat 15 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 01.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s first case of the deadly H5 bird flu in a little penguin has been confirmed on Victoria’s Phillip Island, only days after the state government announced it would begin vaccinating the species.Confirmation of the virus in the little penguin will spark a race to vaccinate thousands of birds, with the government announcing on Saturday it would begin the rollout on Monday.The government did not provide the exact location where the bird was found, but said it was not inside the island’s famouspenguin paradearea.A spokesperson confirmed the little penguin had died.There are about 40,000 little penguins on Phillip Island, making it the world’s biggest colony of the species and a major tourist attraction.Bird flu has been evolving and migrating for 30 years. It is a far more deadly virus that has now arrived in AustraliaRead moreEnvironment advocates have been concerned about the potential for mass deaths of little penguins if the virus reached the island.Euan Ritchie, a professor in wildlife ecology and conservation at Deakin university, said the detection of H5 bird flu in the much-loved little penguin population was “devastating”.“Phillip Island is home to a diverse array and significant populations of native wildlife, including Australian fur seals, eastern barred bandicoots, and recently reintroduced bush stone curlews,” he said.“Governments must provide whatever resources are needed to help wildlife survive through and recover from this bird flu outbreak.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailOn Wednesday, the Victorian government announced plans for the world’s largest H5 bird flu vaccination program of wild birds.The government said it would vaccinate up to 5,000 little penguins across populations at Phillip Island and at Melbourne’s St Kilda beach. While vaccinating wild birds is challenging, it was considered possible in Victoria’s wild little penguins because they generally return to the same burrows at Phillip Island and St Kilda each night.But vaccination requires the delivery of two doses with a gap of a few weeks between each dose.The detection on Phillip Island will spark concern that it may be too late for some little penguins to develop immunity.Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said he understood Victorians would be worried about the detection of the deadly virus in a little penguin.“We know that the detection in a little penguin on Phillip Island is of concern,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But we are proceeding with vaccination of the little penguin colony on Phillip Island and at St Kilda as a meaningful way in which it can help mitigate the impact of H5 on those populations.“We know that little penguins are iconic and highly valued by Victorians, and for that reason, we are working as a priority to protect those colonies.”The state’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said Agriculture Victoria and Phillip Island Nature Parks “activated plans” to vaccinate little penguins as soon as the federal government authorised the vaccines for priority native bird species.“Agriculture Victoria is working closely with Phillip Island Nature Parks to support vaccination of little penguins from Monday,” he said.“While the first detection in a little penguin is a concern, vaccination of little penguins on Phillip Island remains a meaningful way to help protect this important colony.”The Victorian government said there had been two further detections of H5 in greater crested terns, one at Lakes Entrance and the other at Dromana on the Mornington peninsula.Todd said the Lakes Entrance detection was significant because it showed the virus was continuing to move through wild bird populations across Victoria.On Saturday, the NSW government also confirmed the fifth detected case in the state, in a tern found at Eden on the far south coast.The government said it would increase surveillance in the area as a result.There have been two other confirmed cases in local birds in the state, one at Narooma on the state’s south coast and one at Wentworth in the far south-west. All of the confirmed cases in local birds have been in greater crested terns.Explore more on these topicsBird fluVictoriaBirdsConservationWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My heart breaks into a million pieces’: emotional tributes to Kumanjayi Little Baby at Alice Springs funeral | Alice Springs | The Guardian
description: Hundreds gathered with flashes of pink to farewell the five-year-old girl, who was allegedly murdered in April
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hundreds gathered with flashes of pink to farewell the five-year-old girl, who was allegedly murdered in April
Content: Hundreds attended the funeral of the five-year-old girl known as Kumanjayi Little Baby in Alice Springs on Saturday. Her disappearance in April sparked one of the largest searches in NT history.Photograph: Rhett Hammerton/EPAView image in fullscreenHundreds attended the funeral of the five-year-old girl known as Kumanjayi Little Baby in Alice Springs on Saturday. Her disappearance in April sparked one of the largest searches in NT history.Photograph: Rhett Hammerton/EPAAlice Springs‘My heart breaks into a million pieces’: emotional tributes to Kumanjayi Little Baby at Alice Springs funeralHundreds gathered with flashes of pink to farewell the five-year-old girl, who was allegedly murdered in AprilWarning:This story contains references to Indigenous Australians who have diedGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressSat 15 Aug 2026 00.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA sombre funeral service for Kumanjayi Little Baby has been attended by hundreds of people from theAlice Springscommunity and surrounds.Wearing pink and some dressed in T-shirts bearing the face of the five-year-old girl, the crowd gathered under grey skies in the red centre capital on Saturday.Family members surrounded a small coffin adorned with flowers and cried together.The girl’s grandfather, Robin Japanangka Granites, opened the funeral to the public to allow the community to grieve as one.“You come because you are one of our family,” he told them.“You are from here and we need you because we both cried at that same time.”View image in fullscreenMourners attend the funeral service for Kumanjayi Little Baby in Alice Springs on Saturday.Photograph: Rhett Hammerton/AAPIn a eulogy read on her behalf, Kumanjayi Little Baby’s mother, Jacinta Roy, urged that her daughter be remembered for who she was.She was a girl who loved watching shows like Masha and the Bear and Bluey, as well as playing games on her mum’s phone, Roy said.The young girl also loved cuddling puppies and the colour pink.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“As a mother, my heart breaks into a million pieces,” she said. “I miss her.“As a Christian, I would like to thank Father, Son and Holy Spirit for gifting me with a beautiful, precious little baby girl for the precious time that I was her mother here on Earth.”The family of the allegedly murdered girl invited the desert community to farewell her on Saturday while embracing her favourite colour, pink.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKumanjayi Little Baby went missing on the outskirts of Alice Springs in late April.Photograph: Rhett Hammerton/AAPThe service comes months after her disappearance sparked one of the largest searches inNorthern Territoryhistory.Kumanjayi Little Baby – as she is known for cultural reasons after her death – went missing on the outskirts of Alice Springs in late April.It prompted an intensive five-day search by emergency services and local volunteers in grassy bushland.The discovery of her body prompted a nationwide outpouring of grief, with vigils held across the country.A 47-year-old man is awaiting trial after being charged with her murder.Japanangka Granites, a Warlpiri elder, thanked locals for their efforts to locate Kumanjayi Little Baby and for their support of his family.Kumanjayi Little Baby would be with our “father in heaven”, he said at the time.Indigenous Australians can call13YARNon 13 92 76 for information and crisis support; or call Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Mensline on 1300 789 978Explore more on these title: Body found in Romania believed to be missing British hiker George Smyth | Romania | The Guardian
description: Family paid tribute to Bristol University geology student, 18, after being notified by Avon and Somerset police
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Family paid tribute to Bristol University geology student, 18, after being notified by Avon and Somerset police
Content: His family said Smyth ‘was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends’,Photograph: Family handout via Salvamont BrașovHis family said Smyth ‘was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends’,Photograph: Family handout via Salvamont BrașovRomaniaBody found in Romania believed to be missing British hiker George
