But Evans, who turns 18 on Friday, went on from the bench and sealed the points for Steve Cotterill’s side.Veteran striker Ched Evans scored the only goal of the game, finding the net against one of his former clubs to giveFleetwoodan opening day 1-0 victory atChesterfield.Josh March headed the winner in the fifth minute of stoppage time as 10-manCrewegot the better of nine-manCrawleyat the Broadfield Stadium.Late goals from Isaac Moore, James Connolly and Aaron Pressley did the damage asWalsallsecured a fine 3-0 away win overGillingham.Grimsbygot off to a winning start at the expense of newly-relegatedExeterwith a tightly-contested 1-0 triumph at Blundell Park.Harvey Rodgers gave the hosts the lead 36 minutes in as he got on the end of a corner from Charles Vernam, with the linesman calling it over the line before it was cleared.Tranmerecompleted a 2-0 victory overShrewsbury.Jordan Davies’ first league goal for the club and a Charlie Whitaker wonder strike secured the points in an entertaining opening-day clash at Prenton Park.NorthamptonandSwindonplayed out a goalless draw at Sixfields.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Charlton’s manager, Nathan Jones, said later that he was hoping to secure Campbell on a new contract. His current deal expires next summer. “TC gets in those positions all the time and one-v-one he is a threat. We just want the outcomes from him. We are in really advanced negotiations with him. We’re hoping we can get that done.”Adam Idah snatched the winner with his first touch asSwanseabattled back from a goal down to beatStoke2-1. The Republic of Ireland international had been on the pitch for barely 60 seconds when he scored in the 66th minute as the Swans claimed their first win at Stoke for more than five years. Eric Bocat had fired Stoke into a 10th-minute lead and Joseph Opoku hit a 23rd-minute equaliser for the Swans, powering in with a sweet right-foot shot after some poor defending.Sheffield UnitedandBirminghammade an underwhelming start to the season in a goalless draw at Bramall Lane. Both sides have ambitions of mounting promotion challenges but there was not too much to get excited about.The only action of note in the opening half came just before the half-hour. The Blades went first as Patrick Bamford hooked Femi Seriki’s deflected cross just wide. Birmingham responded straight away and Alex Cochrane’s cross was perfect for Paik Seung-ho but the South Korean could not get enough on his header.Birmingham had a big moment in the 58th minute when Carlos Vicente was played through on goal but his attempted pass was cut out by Japhet Tanganga when the better option was to shoot. The visitors produced the first shot on target in the 62nd minute when Jay Stansfield’s low show was kept out by Michael Cooper.Explore more on these topicsFootballChampionshipMiddlesbroughLincoln CityNorwich CityWest Bromwich AlbionMillwallShareReuse this content

title: Scotland hope to name 39-year-old Pocognoli as successor to Clarke in fresh approach | Scotland | The Guardian
description: The Belgian, sacked by Monaco in June, would become Scotland’s first foreign manager since Berti Vogts from 2002-04
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The Belgian, sacked by Monaco in June, would become Scotland’s first foreign manager since Berti Vogts from 2002-04
Content: Former Monaco manager Sébastien Pocognoli led Union Saint-Gilloise to their first title in 90 years in 2025.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAView image in fullscreenFormer Monaco manager Sébastien Pocognoli led Union Saint-Gilloise to their first title in 90 years in 2025.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAScotlandScotland hope to name 39-year-old Pocognoli as successor to Clarke in fresh approachBelgian would be first non-Scot in role since Berti VogtsScotland face Slovenia on 26 September in Nations LeagueEwan MurraySat 15 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Scottish Football Association hopes to name the Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke as manager early next week. The 39-year-old, who was sacked by Monaco in June, will become the country’s first non-Scottish manager since Berti Vogts, who was in charge from 2002-04.Clarke’s abrupt departurecame asScotland exited the World Cupat the group stage. He had signed a four-year contract extension immediately before the tournament. It quickly became clear the SFA would turn towards a foreign manager; Jon Dahl Tomasson and Kasper Hjulmand were linked with the position.Pocognoli will probably be welcomed byScotlandfans in respect of a fresh approach. Clarke was in position for a generally successful seven years, but was often criticised for a pragmatic style.After a period in youth coaching, Pocognoli enjoyed a successful time in charge of Union Saint-Gilloise in his homeland. Under Pocognoli, Union won their first title in 90 years in 2025. A move to Monaco followed, but Pocognoli lasted eight months and 38 games in France.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland begin their Nations League campaign with the visit to Slovenia on 26 September. Pocognoli’s first home game in charge will be Switzerland’s visit to Glasgow three days later.Explore more on these topicsScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s U20 World Cup boycott may hurt in short term but can send Fifa a vital message | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Women’s football has much to gain from the kind of reforms that threats to snub upcoming tournaments might prompt. Infantino should be taken on
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Women’s football has much to gain from the kind of reforms that threats to snub upcoming tournaments might prompt. Infantino should be taken on
Content: Gianni Infantino congratulates Spain’s players after their 2023 Women’s World Cup win. Some progress has been made under Fifa’s president but it remains heavily male-dominated.Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino congratulates Spain’s players after their 2023 Women’s World Cup win. Some progress has been made under Fifa’s president but it remains heavily male-dominated.Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty ImagesFifaWomen’s U20 World Cup boycott may hurt in short term but can send Fifa a vital messageTom GarryWomen’s football has much to gain from the kind of reforms that threats to snub upcoming tournaments might prompt. Infantino should be taken onSat 15 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTShare“And I say to all the women … Pick the right battles. Pick the right fights. You have the power to change. You have the power to convince us men what we have to do and what we don’t have to do. You do it. Just do it. With men, withFifa, you will find open doors. Just push the doors. They are open.”Those werethe condescending words of Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, three years ago during a tone-deaf speech in Sydney, which left his audience, including some of the most senior women in the game, exasperated. It is a damning indictment of Infantino’s tenure that his patronising monologue on the eve of the Women’s World Cup final now barely even creeps into the top 10 of the most controversial moments since his latest re-election, in March 2023.Europe’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsedRead moreYet, with the Swiss administrator’s future hanging finely in the balance, the power to enforce once-in-a-generation change at Fifa may well be in the hands of women’s teams after all, as the threat of a boycott lingers over September’s Women’s Under-20 World Cup, the Women’s Under-17 World Cup, which gets under way in October, and that month’s senior World Cup playoff ties for next summer’s major showpiece, the Women’s World Cup in Brazil.This week Lisa Nandy told the BBC that Infantino “should go” and, overall, the culture secretary spoke well on the matter, but she added that she would not support a boycott of the U20 World Cup and said she was “not generally in favour of sporting boycotts full stop – because they unfairly penalise athletes and competitors who are not responsible for the reason that these boycotts take place”. On that specific element, it is important to respectfully disagree with Nandy and the many others who share that view.Yes, it would feel deeply unjust for football’s political turmoil to have an adverse impact on the development of the world’s best young women footballers through no fault of their own, but that is why any participating countries being prepared to boycott the upcoming under-20 tournament would send such a powerful message.It is tempting to follow the stance that many working within the women’s game are taking privately, which is that it would be a travesty if women’s football, having been neglected and let down by the authorities for generations, was harmed again by disruption to such a significant tournament, but the painful reality is that the young generation of women’s stars stand to be most affected by the decisions that are made by governing bodies in the days, weeks and months ahead.View image in fullscreenNorth Korea celebrate winning the most recent Women’s U20 World Cup, in 2024.Photograph: Julian Medina/SPP/ShutterstockAnd yes, is it unfair for women’s teams, and young women’s teams in particular, to shoulder the responsibility of taking a stance against the now-scrapped vision of selling off a stake in Fifa tournaments – which, we should remember, would include all Fifa’s women’s tournaments too – through the murky concept of the Fifa Forward Enterprise subsidiary, but it is their futures, and the organisation of the World Cups finals that will come to define their careers, which are at stake.And the future of the governance of the sport, and decisions about who runs the game, is a debate that women’s football players, coaches and fans all deserve a much more vocal say in, on far more deep-rooted injustices than those that have dominated the news in recent weeks.Is it fair that, for example, there are only two women – Paola López of Mexico and Vietnam’s Thi My Dung Nguyen – among the 18 members of Fifa’s disciplinary committee, which hit the headlines amid the farcical Folarin Balogun scandal this summer? Or that all 10 of the members of Fifa’s Future of Football committee are men?Is it fair that, of the 37 members of Fifa’s council, the organisation’s strategic and oversight body, 29 are men and only eight are women? Or that seven of the eight vice-presidents are men?Is it fair that the 2023 Women’s World Cup prize money totalled $110m and this summer’s men’s World Cup’s prize pot was around eight times larger, at a record-breaking $871m?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt would be wrong to say that there have not been positive improvements in women’s football across the world since Infantino took office in 2016. The past decade has included long overdue, albeit still very important and welcome, enhancements to provisions for players and coaches at women’s tournaments, a sizeable growth in financial investment and huge uplift in prize money, albeit from a very low bar. It is also fair to say that there are many key figures in the women’s game, across all continents, who support Infantino and are appreciative of the gradual improvements that are being made, while acknowledging that there is still a very long way to go.View image in fullscreenLucy Bronze has backed a boycott.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PABut everyone associated with women’s football should be concerned that the 25-page sales pitch that was titled Fifa Forward Enterprise Member Materials contained only one token reference to women’s football. It is why the England defender Lucy Bronze was right to use her voice to say she backed a boycott “for the good of the game”.On Friday morning, the latest twist in Infantino’s future delivered both positives and negatives for the under-fire president, as on the one hand, the Oceania Football Confederationdeclared its support for Infantino, while the confederation’s biggest member, New Zealand, withdrew its backing for him. New Zealand, impeccable co-hosts of the most recent Women’s World Cup, will have had plenty of reasons to support Infantino but has chosen to use its platform to call for “stronger governance, accountability and transparency”.Shortly before that news, on Thursday, a feature article was published on Fifa’s website entitled “Europe’s finest hours at the Under-20 Women’s World Cup”, looking back at dazzling performances of young breakthrough stars such as Spain’s Salma Paralluelo’s in 2022 or the Germany striker Alexandra Popp in 2010. Next month six European teams – including the hosts, Poland – are scheduled to show the world what they are capable of, but – whether the timing of that article was purely coincidental, political or ironic – European women’s under-20 teams’ finest hour may still be yet to come.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsWomen's footballcommentShareReuse this content

title: London City Lionesses’ Mapi León: ‘It is a club created for women. It is beautiful and exciting’ | London City Lionesses | The Guardian
description: Spain defender talks to Tom Garry about swapping Barcelona for Bromley, embracing the contrasting style of the WSL – and her newfound love for beans and crumpets
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Spain defender talks to Tom Garry about swapping Barcelona for Bromley, embracing the contrasting style of the WSL – and her newfound love for beans and crumpets
Content: Mapi León says she ‘would like to bring a bit of calm to the game’ amid the hustle and bustle of the WSL.Photograph: Kate Green/WSL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMapi León says she ‘would like to bring a bit of calm to the game’ amid the hustle and bustle of the WSL.Photograph: Kate Green/WSL/Getty ImagesLondon City LionessesInterviewLondon City Lionesses’ Mapi León: ‘It is a club created for women. It is beautiful and exciting’Tom GarrySpain defender on swapping Barcelona for Bromley, embracing the contrasting style of the WSL – and her newfound love for beans and crumpetsSat 15 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘No, I can’t, I’m sorry, it’s a secret!” Mapi León roars with laughter, in response to being asked what persuaded her to joinLondon City Lionesses. Does this bode badly for our interview? Fear not, the Spain centre-back is in as banterous and jovial a mood as you could imagine any new signing to be, as she embarks on her first major interview since signing for the Women’s Super League club.Across the course of our conversation, in bright sunshine outside a quiet hotel near Maidstone, it is evident that the 31-year-old could scarcely be happier about her decision to swap Barcelona for south-east England. She is sorely missing her cat, Bagheera (“Here, you ask for so many things for pets, you can’t [really] fly with them, it’s so many documents, so many things”) but, that aside, she is buoyant, relaxed and clearly embracing English life. She says she likes the “little bread” in the morning, and we eventually establish she is referring to crumpets, and reveals: “I like the beans in the morning. It’s really interesting. My Spanish teammates like Alexia [Putellas] and Jana [Fernández] are like: ‘What are you doing eating beans in the morning? You need to train.’ I go: ‘No, it’s fine I like it.’”‘It was horrendous’: Durham captain relieved WSL2 club survived after fears of foldingRead moreHowever, English breakfasts were surely not what attracted her to Kent to play for London City Lionesses so, returning to that first question, she explains thoughtfully: “My body was craving something different. I spent many years in a comfortable position, because playing at Barça has been absolutely wonderful and very nice; it is a style of game that suits me a lot and coming to England, the football is very different from the Spanish one, at first glance. So, I think [the reason was] being able to challenge myself and see if I am capable. I am going to make an effort to adapt to this league and also to show myself that I’m able to compete in another style of play that is not the one that makes me stand out the most.”An undisputed club legend at Barcelona, León certainly stood out in Spain as the best ball-playing centre-back of her generation, and won seven league titles, seven Copa de la Reina’s and – most impressively – four Champions League titles, during a nine-year period of relentless dominance with Barcelona, whom she joined from Atlético Madrid in 2017.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThis summer she was one of four members of the Spain starting XI thatbeat England 4-0in June in Mallorca to leave Barcelona, together with Arsenal’s new signing Ona Batlle, OL Lyonnes’ new winger Salma Paralluelo and, most notably, her London City Lionesses teammate Alexia Putellas. Together, León and Putellas drew raised eyebrows across the women’s game by swapping the reigning European champions for a lesser-known team that finished sixth in the WSL last term, but they have been joined by a series of other world-renowned names including the former England goalkeeper Mary Earps and the France winger Kadidiatou Diani.The club’s new signings meet the vision of their ambitious owner, the American businesswoman Michele Kang, of whom León says: “The impression I get is of an empowered woman, with a winning mindset, driven by a desire to see things improve and a drive to win. And that is a competitive and winning mentality. And if in the end, I want to be part of it because it is a club created for women and that is not common, I think it is beautiful and exciting.“Everything counts when you make this kind of a decision, and of course, [Kang] was an important part because seeing another woman doing so much to help women’s sports, and women’s football grow, I think it’s impossible not to value that. I think it’s something very powerful.”View image in fullscreenMapi León hugs the Champions League trophy after Barcelona’s victory over Wolfsburg in 2023, the second of four WCL titles the defender had won with the club.Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty ImagesThe club’s signings of Putellas and León were announced five days apart in July, which prompts the question: did they discuss their decision with one another and was it a case of “If you go, I’ll go too”?“No, not really, no. I think we take the issue of personal matters very seriously,” León says. “It’s a very different challenge. You come from a league where you win every year. Where you have achieved great things internationally and you come to a club that finished mid-table with some different challenges. And I think it is a very personal decision for each individual to make, choosing what is best for you personally.“[You ask yourself] what do you really need right now? What is your body telling you? What do you think is best for you to keep improving, to keep pushing yourself, and to maintain that ambition? And I think each person needs different things. So, there wasn’t much communication between us. And that the decision wasn’t planned.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe more she reflects on her move, the tactical differences between Liga F and the WSL become clear as a key factor, as the Zaragoza-born defender continues: “The English league can give me a lot. You can learn a lot. The transitions, the style of play, playing with more space. The pressing is different too because I’m used to teams often sitting back in a mid-to-low block, whereas here, it’s probably more of a high press. I’d like to bring a bit of calm to the game.“I don’t know if that really fits with English football, but no, of course, I don’t want to change the system, but simply the timings as a centre-back. I am a centre-back so I see everything. And I like to control a little bit of the timings so maybe we can try to have a little bit more of the ball. Or there are many spaces, so we can go. So I like to have a bit of control.View image in fullscreenMapi León is one of several big summer signings made by London City Lionesses and was attracted by the competitive nature of the WSL.Photograph: Sally Rawlins/London City Lionesses“The league is so competitive, the commitment the league is making, the clubs, I mean, I think everything makes it very attractive to come because I have been following the English league over these years and it feels like it can’t let you relax even for a second, not in any match, not during the match. Not a single second can relax you, because the English league is much more competitive.”Her new side open the season at home to Manchester United on 4 September. Until then, she is embracing a comparatively quiet life and enjoying not being recognised in public, adding: “It’s so different [here]. It’s not a bad thing but, I can just walk to buy food, and no one recognises me! And sometimes it’s nice, because in Barcelona we are not ‘famous’ but people know us. It’s one of the many amazing things. But also sometimes you miss this freedom. Like, just go and shop.”How long that newfound anonymity will continue is hard to tell, as it will surely not take long for León to become one of the most recognisable faces in the WSL if she can bring her form for Spain and Barcelona straight to London City Lionesses. For now, she can enjoy her beans and her crumpets in peace.Explore more on these topicsLondon City LionessesWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballBarcelona WomeninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Farewell Cristian Romero, you actually always were ‘that type of player’ | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: You can’t help but feel the Argentinian with a penchant for red cards has arrived at his spiritual home with his move to Diego Simeone’s Atlético Madrid
Author: Max Rushden
Headline: You can’t help but feel the Argentinian with a penchant for red cards has arrived at his spiritual home with his move to Diego Simeone’s Atlético Madrid
Content: Cristian Romero has won plenty of silverware, but picked up a lot more red and yellow cards.Illustration: Matthew GreenView image in fullscreenCristian Romero has won plenty of silverware, but picked up a lot more red and yellow cards.Illustration: Matthew GreenTottenham HotspurFarewell Cristian Romero, you actually always were ‘that type of player’Max RushdenYou can’t help but feel the Argentinian with a penchant for red cards has arrived at his spiritual home with his move to Diego Simeone’s Atlético MadridSat 15 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 04.29 EDTShare“He’s not that kind of player” is perhaps the greatest of the co-commentators’ meaningless banalities. Used shortly after a “nice guy” has scythed someone in half about a day after the ball has gone, it is by definition nonsense because if you have scythed someone in half about a day after the ball has gone, then you are indeed that kind of player.But I don’t recall ever hearing anyone saying “the thing is Clive/Brian, heisthat kind of player”. I haven’t analysed every foul in Premier League history to tell if you those kinds of challenges are carried out by players all of us would consider to be “that kind of player” as opposed to the opposite – but the list of players with the most red cards suggests a pattern – Richard Dunne, Duncan Ferguson, Patrick Vieira with eight reds, Lee Cattermole and Roy Keane on seven, Vinnie Jones, Joey Barton and Alan Smith (obviously not that one) among those on six.How will the three promoted teams fare in the Premier League?Read moreThis article is about Cristian Romero – who I would have in tier A of “that kind of player” if I had any idea how to do one of those Instagram reels where you rank things (posh hotels you can’t afford, non weight-bearing exercises for middle-aged people, biscuits of the 80s etc). There is not a debate about the category in which he belongs.A player with a permanent look of mild confusion about the situation he finds himself in – am I really playing for Spurs? Consistently inconsistent. And always just a moment away from just giving the whole game a Falling-Down-full-Michael-Douglas-ing.Six red cards in his Spurs career. It feels like so many more. The one that sticks in my mind isin the Champions League last-16 exit to Milan in 2023. Hopefully you don’t remember the game, it was awful. 1-0 going into the second leg, it’s goalless in the 77th minute at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Spurs aren’t doing much. Romero’s already on a booking for lunging into Rafael Leão. And then for no apparent reason he flies into Théo Hernandez on the touchline.It’s peak Romero. That sense that he was just a bit annoyed he wasn’t playing for someone better and so he needed a release. And in this case Hernandez was that release.His four Premier League red cards feature all your favourites. Two yellows against Manchester City featuring a wild late tackle on Erling Haaland deep in the City half – really letting him know he was there.There are a couple of straight red get-the-ball-really-get-the-man challenges that he probably would have got away with in 1986.One against Chelseawhen Spurs were top of the league and 1-0 up early in the Ange Postecoglou tenure earned a “oh nooooo Romero, you … you … you …” from Gary Neville. The otheron Casemiro last seasoncame shortly after hecriticised the club on social mediaprompting calls for Thomas Frank to strip him of the captaincy. It was his second red of the season after getting two yellows for dissent and kicking Ibrahima Konaté on the floor against Liverpool last December. “What’s he doing?” Neville again.View image in fullscreenCristian Romero is sent off at Old Trafford last season with his international defensive teammate Lisandro Martínez celebrating in the background for good measure.Photograph: James Gill/Danehouse/Getty ImagesIt’s often said the great defenders don’t go to ground – but it feels like that is exactly where Romero spent his entire Spurs career.And yet. And yet – he spent most of theEuropa League final win against Manchester Unitedon the floor – hurling himself at shots, and United players, in a man-of-the-match performance. People rightly remember the Micky van de Ven goalline clearance, but Romero was unbeatable in that game. He can’t not be good. Gasperini, Scaloni, Conte, Postecoglou, Frank, Simeone all like him. He has played in two World Cup Finals (if you accept any Argentinians actually played in the last one).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll fans like a player who flies into challenges – we like to think we’re subtle, but we evolved from primates – one of your own putting in a reducer, an oof into the turf perhaps it takes us back somewhere deep into our past. And he scored vital goals too.Atlético Madrid feels so perfect. The people I talk to who watch Spanish football (ie Sid Lowe once he’s actually replied to a WhatsApp) tell me Atléti aren’t the Atleti we want them to be anymore. It’s not all Godín Giménez and Juanfran. Perhaps Simeone is taking them back there. But we should all be thankful that he has arrived in his spiritual home.As soon as the Atleti rumours began it felt perfect – it is rare for a player to feel like they fit at a club before they’ve even worn the colours. But in the same way James Maddison always looked like he should be in a Spurs shirt, perhaps Romero never did, even when he was wearing it – even when he was playing brilliantly in a gritty backs-to-the-wall job in a Europa League final. Is that really emblematic of what a Spurs centre-back should be? At their best Spurs centre-backs are Gary Mabbutt or Ledley King, Jan Vertonghen or Toby Alderweireld – solid, reliable, measured. At their worst – well there have been lots of them, but not many as rash as Romero.It is perhaps a fault of mine, or a fault of how we watch and consume football, that I’ve already made my mind up. Watching Romero I was either annoyed by something he’d done, or annoyed that I was going to be annoyed about something he was going to do later. This permanent pre-annoyance rendered an objective judgment impossible.So when people talk about his leadership and especially his ability on the ball, I was never totally convinced. But good luck Cristian, I get the feeling it will be much less stressful watching you play for a team I am less invested in. He might leave Spurs a club legend, it’s hard to say for sure; but if he does, he leaves as an incredibly infuriating one.Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurAtlético MadridLa LigaEuropean club footballcommentShareReuse this content

title: Amy Hunt claims third European Championships gold in relay triumph for ‘fantastic four’ | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Amy Hunt sealed a hat-trick of golds at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham as the women’s and men’s British teams won the 4x100 relays
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Amy Hunt sealed a hat-trick of golds at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham as the women’s and men’s British teams won the 4x100 relays
Content: The victorious British teams: back row (from left): Success Eduan, Zharnel Hughes, Dina Asher-Smith  and Louie Hinchliffe. Front row (from left) Romell Glave, Imani Lansiquot, Jeremiah Azu and Amy Hunt.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe victorious British teams: back row (from left): Success Eduan, Zharnel Hughes, Dina Asher-Smith  and Louie Hinchliffe. Front row (from left) Romell Glave, Imani Lansiquot, Jeremiah Azu and Amy Hunt.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAmy Hunt claims third European Championships gold in relay triumph for ‘fantastic four’Men’s and women’s 4x100 teams complete wins in styleHunt will aim for fourth gold in mixed relay on SundaySean Ingleat the Alexander Stadium, BirminghamSat 15 Aug 2026 18.36 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 19.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo sooner had Amy Hunt won a staggering third European gold medal in five days than she pointed at the superwomen guiding her closer to history. “We’re the fantastic four,” she said.It was hard to argue with that, especially after watching Britain’s 4x100m women power to glory in 42.05secs, more than 10 metres clear of Switzerland and Poland.“It’s such a privilege to be able to step on the track with these ladies, and the individual superpowers that we bring,” said Hunt. “It’s no joke. We’re all superwomen together out there.”European Athletics Championships: Double gold for Great Britain in 4x100m relays – live reactionRead moreFirst she addressed Dina Asher-Smith, who ran the first leg and whose gold equalled the Polish sprinter Irena Szewinska’s overall record tally of 10 medals at the championships. “I’m stood next to Dina, she’s the most decorated European athlete in history,” she said. “She has got thousands of medals.”Then Hunt turned to the emerging 21-year-old star Success Eduan, who is three weeks from completing a degree in midwifery. “This girl, Success, is a midwife,” said Hunt. “She brings new babies into the world.”Finally, Hunt pointed to Imani-Lara Lansiquot, who had brilliantly carried the baton home. In 2021 she had also written a play, Armour of Gaza, about growing up in Peckham. “Imani, that girl wrote a play,” said Hunt, clearly deeply impressed.The overall message was clear. On Sunday, Hunt will attempt to become the first athlete to win four gold medals at a single edition of a European championships in the mixed 4x100m relay. But she wanted this night to be about her teammates most of all.And that included praise for Britain’s new relay coach, Richard Kilty, who told the women a simple message before they stepped out on to the track: “Go out and break their hearts.”The British team certainly did that. Everyone played their parts, including the newcomer Eduan, who is now intending to become a full-time sprinter. “I finish in three weeks and I graduate in November, hopefully,” she said.Is it harder to deliver a baby or a baton, she was asked. “A baby! Someone’s life is in my hands,” she said smiling.It was a great night overall for Britain’s relay teams given that 15 minutes earlier the men’s quartet of Jeremiah Azu, Louie Hinchliffe, Zharnel Hughes and Romell Glave also took gold, in 38.45secs, ahead of Germany and Belgium.Before the drama of the relays there were a series of extraordinary performances across the night. The best of them? That surely came in the triple jump, where Italy’s Andy Díaz’s stunning leap of 18.15m – the fourth furthest in history – brought him gold by 39cm from Portugal’s Pedro Pichardo.View image in fullscreenAndy Díaz won triple jump gold with the fourth longest jump of all time.Photograph: Maja Hitij/Getty Images for European AthleticsBut not far behind was Sweden’s Andreas Almgren’s destructive display in the men’s 10,000m. After a dawdling first kilometre, Almgren gradually broke the resistance of all his rivals and lapped most of the field, to win by nearly 20 seconds in a championship record 27mins 23.44secs.“If someone is going to beat me, they are going to have to suffer for it,” said Almgren. “I’m in the best 10k shape of my life.”The Swiss athlete Dominic Lobalu took silver, while the world champion Jimmy Gressier won bronze in a sprint finish from Italy’s Yeman Crippa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSoon afterwards, Germany’s Julian Weber broke Steve Backley’s javelin championship record with a monster 90.40m final round throw to beat his compatriot Nick Thumm.“I’m delighted for him,” said Backley. “Julian Weber is my favourite thrower. A brilliant athlete. He has thrown ridiculously far tonight. Records are there to be broken and it is why we love Championships. Medals are for keeps, records are to borrow.”In the women’s 400m, Norway’s Henriette Jaeger was just as impressive as she took gold in 49.04, a second clear of Natalia Bukowiecka of Poland with Lieke Klaver of the Netherlands winning bronze.It was also a great night for Ireland as Kate O’Connor took gold in the women’s heptathlon with a score of 6751. Behind her were two Dutch athletes, Emma Oosterwegel and Sofie Dokter, who scored 6712 and 6664 points respectively.Afterwards, O’Connor dedicated her gold medal to her father and coach, Michael. “He still turns up to training, day in, day out, because this is my dream – but it is also his dream too,” she said.However, Katarina Johnson-Thompson vowed to fight on despite finishing 23rd. “I’ve had a really difficult season behind the scenes, and I didn’t know what form I was going to come here in,” she said. She is reported to have been battling a calf injury. “I obviously trusted myself to perform in major championships. I just didn’t have the preparation that I truly needed to be competitive.”The biggest surprise of the night, meanwhile, came in the men’s 1500m. Most had expected the world champion and silver medallist from 2025, Isaac Nader and Jake Wightman, to be battling it out for gold. But Nader faded to tenth, and Wightman found nothing when leading with 100m to go.And that left Stefan Nillessen, a 6ft 4in 23-year-old, to weave his way through for a shock success in 3:35.70. “The smile won’t go off my face for a long time,” said Nillesen, who runs a bit like Forrest Gump.Finally, in the women’s high jump, Yaroslava Mahuchikh cleared 1.97m to take gold from Poland’s Maria Zodzik and Montenegro’s Marija Vukovic.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Finlay Tarling’s NSN team withdraw from Volta a Portugal day after his death | Cycling | The Guardian
description: NSN Development has said: ‘We will continue to hold Fin in our hearts,’ as they announced their withdrawal from the Volta a Portugal
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: NSN Development has said: ‘We will continue to hold Fin in our hearts,’ as they announced their withdrawal from the Volta a Portugal
Content: Finlay Tarling was reportedly involved in a head-on collision.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPAView image in fullscreenFinlay Tarling was reportedly involved in a head-on collision.Photograph: Nuno Veiga/EPACyclingFinlay Tarling’s NSN team withdraw from Volta a Portugal day after his death19-year-old killed on Friday by collision with van‘We will continue to hold Fin in our hearts’Agence France-PresseSat 15 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTFirst published on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinlay Tarling’s NSN Development team withdrew from the Volta a Portugal on Saturday, the day afterthe death of the 19-year-old British riderin an accident during the race.Tarling, the younger brother of the Ineos rider Josh, was reportedly involved in a head-on collision with a vehicle unconnected with the event that was travelling in the opposite direction.“Following Fin Tarling’s tragic passing, the NSN Development Team has withdrawn from the remaining Volta a Portugal stages,” NSN said. “With the full support of Fin’s parents, the World Tour team will race on at Czech Tour and the Arctic Race of Norway.“We will continue to hold Fin in our hearts as we race in his honour, doing what he loved most.”Friday’s eighth stage was suspended with about 20km remaining and the podium ceremony was cancelled.A spokesperson for Portugal’s national republican guard said there had been a collision between a cyclist and a light vehicle towards the back of the peloton. “We do not yet know exactly the circumstances in which it unfolded. We will investigate.”The race resumed on Saturday with the leader, Alex Guerin, wearing a black jersey and riders wearing black armbands on the penultimate stage.“The ninth stage of the Volta a Portugal set off in an atmosphere of mourning,” said organisers on social media. “Before the symbolic start, a minute of silence was observed in memory of Finlay Tarling.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOrganisers said sponsors had cancelled planned activities this weekend out of respect. “The race continues. There will be a sporting competition but not a party,” they said in a statement. “This Saturday, the Tour cycles for Finlay.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lani Pallister dethrones Katie Ledecky to claim Pan Pacs 400m freestyle crown | Swimming | The Guardian
description: Australian claims gold in 3:58.42 with American great second, while Sam Short wins men’s 400 free with Pan Pacific Championships record time
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Australian claims gold in 3:58.42 with American great second, while Sam Short wins men’s 400 free with Pan Pacific Championships record time
Content: Australia’s Lani Pallister celebrates winning the 400m freestyle alongside Katie Ledecky and Erika Fairweather on day three of the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships.Photograph: Sean M Haffey/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia’s Lani Pallister celebrates winning the 400m freestyle alongside Katie Ledecky and Erika Fairweather on day three of the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships.Photograph: Sean M Haffey/Getty ImagesSwimmingLani Pallister dethrones Katie Ledecky to claim Pan Pacs 400m freestyle crownAustralian claims gold with American great secondSam Short wins men’s 400 free with Pan Pacs recordUS end Aussies’ nine-year run in women’s 4x100m freeAustralian Associated PressSat 15 Aug 2026 05.05 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLani Pallister and Sam Short have showcased Australia’s glittering 2028 Olympic middle-distance swimming prospects by claiming multiple gold medals at the Pan Pacific championships in California.The 24-year-oldPallister continued her stunning meetwhen she downed American legend Katie Ledecky to win the 400m freestyle title on Saturday (AEST), following her 200m freestyle victory over Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh and silver behind Ledecky in the 1500m free, as well as gold in the 200m free relay.Australia golden girl Meg Harris reels in Gretchen Walsh to snatch Pan Pacs crownRead more“It’s been an incredible week,” Pallister said. “Chasing my goals, chasing dreams and having fun doing it.”Short backed up his 800m freestyle gold when he clocked a career-best time of three minutes 40.52 seconds to win the men’s 400 freestyle, eclipsing the great Ian Thorpe’s Pan Pacs meet record of 3:41.83 set in Sydney in 1999, four years before Short was born.He won from China’s Zhang Zhanshuo (3:42.42) and American Aaron Shackell (3:43.44) at the William Woollett Aquatics Center in Irvine.“I thought I was going 3:39. I had so much ​left for the end, but personal best – can’t complain, and to beat Thorpe’s record … it’s about time it went,” Short said.“He was one of my heroes growing up. I’ve watched every single one of his races.”View image in fullscreenSam Short has claimed 400m freestyle gold at the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, California.Photograph: Sean M Haffey/Getty ImagesBoth Pallister (800m) and Short (1500m) have the chance to add more gold to their carry-on luggage on the final day of competition.Pallister was under world-record pace in her 400m final through 150 metres, before touching in 3:58.42. Ledecky had over a second to make up on the final lap and took silver in 4:00.15.“I could see Katie catching me on the last 150 and that’s a very nerve-racking feeling,” said Pallister, who also won four gold medals and a silver at the recent Commonwealth Games.“The back end got me. Gosh, it hurt a lot. But it’s so much fun standing up in an international final and racing the best in the world and trying to challenge for top times.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toAustralia SportGet a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports deskEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 29-year-old Ledecky was philosophical about her loss to Pallister.“I never like being over four minutes in an international final, but I put together the best race I could,” she said. “I thought I had a good back half, just wasn’t out quick enough.“I’ve never taken my competition for granted, even when I was winning by big margins. I just have a lot of great competition from all over the world right now.”Australia’s Sam Williamson won the men’s 50m breaststroke in a championship-record time of 26.36 seconds. American Van Mathias and Michael Houlie of South Africa tied for silver in 26.42.And Aussies also went 1-2 in the men’s 100 butterfly, with Matthew Temple winning gold and teammate Ben Armbruster earning silver.The US swept the 4x100m freestyle relays, beating Australia in both the men’s and women’s races. The women hadn’t defeated the Aussies in the event since 2017.Explore more on these topicsSwimmingAustralia sportKatie LedeckySummer McIntoshnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Here we are 30 years later’: the Olympic team that transformed US basketball | USA women's basketball team | The Guardian
description: The 1996 US women’s Olympic team enter the Hall of Fame on Saturday after giving momentum to the WNBA and re-launching an era of American dominance
Author: Nina Mandell
Headline: The 1996 US women’s Olympic team enter the Hall of Fame on Saturday after giving momentum to the WNBA and re-launching an era of American dominance
Content: Jennifer Azzi (8), Dawn Staley (5) and the rest of the US women’s basketball team celebrate after winning the gold medal against Brazil.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJennifer Azzi (8), Dawn Staley (5) and the rest of the US women’s basketball team celebrate after winning the gold medal against Brazil.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesUSA women's basketball team‘Here we are 30 years later’: the Olympic team that transformed US basketballThe 1996 US women’s Olympic team enter the Hall of Fame on Saturday after giving momentum to the WNBA and re-launching an era of American dominanceNina Mandellin Uncasville, ConnecticutSat 15 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the US women’s basketball team, the 1996 Olympics weren’t just about winning gold in front of their home crowd.It was about the future of women’s basketball in America. The US women were knocked out of the 1992 Olympics in the semi-finals by the Commonwealth of Independent States – a stunning and embarrassing defeat. Heading into the 1996 Games, which were held in Atlanta, turning around the program was a top priority not just for USABasketball, but the NBA as well, which was looking to start a women’s league that would become the WNBA.With the support of the NBA, USA Basketball selected a national team to travel around on a year-long international tour, led by Stanford coach Tara VanDerveer, who took a sabbatical from the Cardinal to coach the team.“Our group was a really tight-knit group, really tight,” Olympic guard Dawn Staley said Friday. “We had been through so much together that yes, we often talked about what it meant [to be competing for the US at the time]. We had the perfect, in retrospect, the perfect coach in Tara that allowed us to handle any type of pressure that we would face because of the pressure she put on us to perform at a high level daily. She didn’t let her foot off the gas.View image in fullscreenDawn Staley smiles during Friday’s media availability ahead of the Hall of Fame enshrinement ceremony at the Mohegan Sun in Uncasville, Connecticut.Photograph: Nathaniel S Butler/NBAE/Getty Images“And because of that, we knew we could handle anything physically, because the physical part of what we were doing strengthened us mentally and it never really broke our spirit. So we felt like if this team was going to be the team that pushes women’s basketball, professional women’s basketball over the line, it was [the team] that we could handle the pressure.”By the time the Olympics came around, the gamble paid off: Staley, Lisa Leslie, Teresa Edwards, Carla McGhee, Ruthie Bolton, Nikki McCray, Sheryl Swoopes, Venus Lacey, Katy Steding, Jennifer Azzi, Rebecca Lobo and Katrina Felicia McClain had become unstoppable – and the excitement domestically was palpable.When the US team brought home gold, it helped boost the launch for not only theWNBA, but the league that directly preceded and briefly overlapped with it – the ABL – as well.The WNBAcelebrated its 30th seasonthis year.“It was pressure enough to play in the Olympic games in our home country after losing in Barcelona,” said Staley. “And then you’re adding another big ticket item of a women’s professional league starting in the States. And we felt somewhat responsible for the league starting and growing. And I mean, here we are 30 years later. It’s incredible.”For USA Basketball, it also was the start of what has beena winning streak of eight gold medals.View image in fullscreenSheryl Swoopes, Jennifer Azzi, Lisa Leslie, Carla McGhee, Katy Steding, Katrina McClain, Rebecca Lobo and Venus Lacey (left to right) look on from the podium.Photograph: Rick Stewart/Getty ImagesOn Saturday, the 1996 US women’s basketball team will be inducted in the Hall of Fame along with three players who followed in the league they helped create: Chamique Holdsclaw, the first overall WNBA draft pick in 1999; Candace Parker, drafted first overall in 2008 and Elena Delle Donne, the second overall pick in 2013.The inductee group also includes NBA coach Doc Rivers, NBA referee Joey Crawford, and retired NBA player A’mare Stoudemire.More than 15 years before she was drafted, Parker remembered watching the Olympic team on her couch, idolizing the game of Leslie, Swoopes and Edwards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“[The 1996 team is] a catalyst for the reason why women’s professional sports, not just basketball and sports, exists,” she said.For Staley, who went on to play in the ABL and WNBAbefore a decorated coaching career, that gold medal was the biggest achievement of her lifetime.“It was the tangible thing that I wanted and I worked really hard for because I only saw women play in the national championship game and the Olympics,” she said. “So those were my two goals that drove me. And when I left college in ‘92, I knew I wasn’t going to get a national championship, right? Because I had not thought about coaching.“But then when I got the gold medal, it was the only one that I thought I had left to check off as a childhood dream.”Parker and Holdsclaw join their late coach, Pat Summitt, in the Hall of Fame.“I think Coach definitely wrote this in the stars for us to go in, in the same class,” Parker said. “I think she’d definitely be super proud. I know she would be on stage with both of us 100%.”Explore more on these topicsUSA women's basketball teamOlympic GamesBasketballUS sportsWNBAfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Secondhand booksellers in UK and Ireland suspect AI firms behind ‘strange’ bulk orders | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Development comes after Anthropic was found to have spent millions on books to scan for ‘data acquisition’
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Development comes after Anthropic was found to have spent millions on books to scan for ‘data acquisition’
Content: ‘My theory is that it’s masses and masses of AI money’: Stuart and Mary Manley, the co-owners of Barter Books in Alnwick, Northumberland.Photograph: suppliedView image in fullscreen‘My theory is that it’s masses and masses of AI money’: Stuart and Mary Manley, the co-owners of Barter Books in Alnwick, Northumberland.Photograph: suppliedAI (artificial intelligence)Secondhand booksellers in UK and Ireland suspect AI firms behind ‘strange’ bulk ordersDevelopment comes after Anthropic was found to have spent millions on books to scan for ‘data acquisition’Dan MilmoGlobal technology editorSat 15 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSecondhand booksellers in the UK and Ireland are reporting a flurry of bulk orders from mystery buyers, amid speculation AI companies are acquiring the tomes for their data.Bookshops contacted by the Guardian say they have been receiving orders from buyers in the US, Canada, continental Europe and the UK. The increase has been replicated around the world, with booksellers in the US, Australia and Europe also reporting unusual orders.Stuart Manley, the co-owner of Barter Books in Alnwick, Northumberland, said the orders, which began arriving three months ago, were unusual because they did not follow the typical pattern of being grouped into themes such as sport or motoring.“It’s definitely a strange combination of books,” said Manley. “Normally a book order is on a theme but this is all over the place.”A recent order included requests for an Estonian translation of John le Carré’s The Mission Song, a copy of Anne Brontë’s Agnes Grey from a specific imprint and the October 1983 edition of Warship, a monthly magazine. Manley said he had sold “hundreds” of random books to three buyers for a total of about £4,000.Jim Shaughnessy, the owner of MW Books in Claregalway, Ireland, said his business had been receiving large, varied orders since May.“They are sporadic, presumably machine-driven and have little in terms of thematic currency; books on agricultural implements in 18th century Africa through to biographies of 1950s racing car drivers,” he said. “Personally, I don’t see we have the right to dictate what any customer does with their purchases but it is more than curious to see what’s being selected.”David Gower-Spence, the owner of BookLovers of Bath, said he had received a rush of orders between May and July for about 200 books from buyers who have also been cited by other sellers contacted by the Guardian for this article.One, the Canada-based Zoom Books, which has featured in other media reports, describes itself as “North America’s leading book recycling company”. Zoom has been contacted for comment by the Guardian.“It was overwhelming for a while and I’m relatively well organised,” said Gower-Spence.One UK-based secondhand bookseller, speaking on condition of anonymity, said some random orders could come from different buyers but be delivered to the same address. “The aliases behind these orders are very opaque even to experienced booksellers,” the source said.One delivery postcode seen by the Guardian and used by different buyers points to a group of freight warehouses near Heathrow airport.The bookseller, who has received orders for 6,000 books from similar buyers since January worth thousands of pounds, said the buyers were paying “top whack” and were not seeking a discount despite requesting titles in bulk.“It’s disrupting the secondhand bookselling business because this isn’t typical for the trade,” the bookseller said. “It appears to be either a human or a machine dipping into the sandbox of secondhand books and what they are buying makes no sense in terms of the wider trends in the market.”The Guardian reported this month thatAustralian booksellers had also received a burst of orders, with one saying the sudden scale of demand was “driving me nuts”.The spate of orders has fuelled speculation among booksellers that AI companies are acquiring the books to scan their contents before pulping them.Manley said: “My theory is that it’s masses and masses of AI money being squandered.”Massachusetts teen accused of killing mother and brother used ChatGPTRead moreThe Washington Post revealed this year thatAnthropic, a leading AI company and developer of the Claude chatbot, had spent tens of millions of dollars acquiring books and slicing off their spines so their contents could be scanned before the books were sent for recycling.Anthropic said: “Claude is trained on a mix of publicly available web data, commercially acquired datasets, and data we generate ourselves. Sourcing books is a widely used approach for training large language models across the AI industry. None of our data acquisition programs buy and destroy rare or antiquarian books.”Last month, the tech news site 404 Media reported that a books database was telling booksellers “the world’s best AI training data is sitting on a shelf”, adding that books published before 2022 were ideal material for AI companies because their text was unpolluted by material that could have been generated by chatbots. The database in question, ISBNdb, said the report wasbased on a webpagethat was a “test of market interest” and had since been taken down.AI tools such as chatbots are “trained” on vast amounts of data to help them generate responses, a requirement that has set tech companies searching for fresh sources of material to build new models. Secondhand books, some of them published decades before ChatGPT exploded on to the scene and not available online, could be a source of fresh data.One post on an online forum for booksellers, seen by the Guardian, said: “Shame these are all destined for AI training, and will therefore get the covers stripped and ultimately end up being pulped.”Other posts expressed puzzlement at the erratic orders, while some questioned whether they could be intended for AI training when requests included books available for nothing in the public online domain such as Gulliver’s Travels, published in 1726.Orders are typically placed through book marketplaces including Biblio and the Amazon-owned AbeBooks. Biblio and AbeBooks have been contacted by the Guardian for comment.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingAmazonAnthropicInternetE-commerceRetail industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Sure, ‘Woke 1’ had its issues – but we have far bigger problems on our hands | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: AOC’s remarks about past excesses have been ripped out of context. Progressives shouldn’t get roped into this sideshow
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: AOC’s remarks about past excesses have been ripped out of context. Progressives shouldn’t get roped into this sideshow
Content: ‘Progressives also shouldn’t play into their hands by talking about Woke 1.0 instead of focusing on the dire state of the country right now.’Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Progressives also shouldn’t play into their hands by talking about Woke 1.0 instead of focusing on the dire state of the country right now.’Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesThe Week in PatriarchyUS politicsSure, ‘Woke 1’ had its issues – but we have far bigger problems on our handsArwa MahdawiAOC’s remarks about past excesses have been ripped out of context. Progressives shouldn’t get roped into this sideshowSat 15 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTShareThere is probably no word that has been more used and abused in the last decade than “woke”. It has been rendered completely meaningless, but it refuses to die. Indeed, it has now taken on new life: in the past week, there’s been a flurry of headlines about “Woke 1.0” or “Woke One”. If you haven’t seen the phrase pop up in your newsfeed yet, it will soon.So what is this cursed phrase? There’s no official definition, but the term is largely being used to refer to the period between 2018 and 2021 when social justice language was at its peak in mainstream culture. Certain progressives, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have started to use “Woke 1” disparagingly, as a way todistancethemselves from that period and signal that they stand for a new form of left-leaning politics that is more palatable to centrist Democrats. “Woke 2”, I suppose.We can blame the New York City councilmember Chi Ossé for coining the phrase. Back in May, hewrote on X: “Woke 1 was crazyyyy.” This was in response to someone reminding him that, in 2021, he’d said: “A cis white man should not be the next speaker of the Council.”Not that many people paid attention to the May post. But then Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez quoted it on arecent appearanceon ABC News’s This Week when she was asked about some statements the Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong had made. In 2020, Hong, who lost this week’s gubernatorial primary, tweeted that Thanksgiving should be cancelled. She also posted about defunding the police. AOC responded to a question about these “controversial” tweets by saying Hong had moved away from these positions.The congresswoman then noted: “I have a local city councilman that has this saying: ‘Woke 1.0 was crazy.’” After laughing at the phrase, Ocasio-Cortez went on to add: “During the pandemic, the doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place. And I actually think that the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful … I think that, you know, during lockdown, of course, rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today.”When you look at AOC’s full quote about Woke 1.0, it’s pretty reasonable. However, it has been ripped out of context and is being willfully misinterpreted by some people to suggest that Ocasio-Cortez thinks the excesses of that period were funny.Stephen Miller, for example, almost exploded on air after Fox News’s Will Cain played a clip of AOC talking about Woke 1 to him on air. Millerrantedfor almost five minutes about how woke policies resulted in a “historic increase in murders”. (Gun violencesurged in the US during Covid, but that wasn’t because of protests orbecausesome people wanted you to say “folx” instead of “guys”. It was for myriad reasons that we are still trying to understand but include school closures in low-income areas.)Miller added: “We’re all going to have a good laugh about that? ‘Sorry your husband was murdered.’ ‘Sorry your mom was killed.’ ‘Sorry your loved ones are six feet under the ground now.’ We’re going to have a good laugh about that? It’s sickening, it’s disgusting and the thing is, [Woke 1.0] never stopped.”The Atlantic, meanwhile, published a pieceheadlined“The Democrats Can’t Just Laugh Off ‘Woke 1’”, which argued: “Republicans have no incentive to let them forget past excesses.”Maybe not, but progressives also shouldn’t play into their hands by talking about Woke 1.0 instead of focusing on the dire state of the country right now. This isn’t to say we can’t learn from past mistakes. I think we can all agree that there were some embarrassing excesses between 2018-2020. There was the time, for example, when a Mexican American San Diego Gas and Electric employee got fired because someone thought he was doing the White Power symbol with his hand. All he was doing was hanging his arm out of his truck andcracking his knuckle. There was no evidence to prove he held white supremacist views, there was just a baying mob on Twitter.Was that incident bad? Yes, of course! Was some of the earnest discourse from the time cringe? Absolutely! But just take a minute and look around, why don’t you? The president of the US is monetizing his position in anunprecedented way. Pregnant women are dying preventable deaths because they can’t get access to safe abortions, and immigrants are being snatched off the street by masked thugs. Freedom of speech is under attack, and you can get deported for talking about the ongoing genocide in Gaza. Getting upset right now about Woke 1 is crazyyyy.ICE is locking people up for things their grandmother didDo take the time to read this shocking piecein the Nationby Maryam Tahmasebi, who is currently in ICE detention with her family because her mother-in-law was a translator for the Iranian hostage takers back in 1979. Tahmasebi and her husband are both professors and legal residents without so much as a traffic ticket on their records. They’re now locked up in separate facilities. Their son, who has been a legal resident of California for 12 years and wasn’t even born during the hostage crisis, was also taken from his school in handcuffs. He’s in a facility with his mother with no end to their detention in sight. “This is bloodline punishment,” Tahmasebi writes.Half of Afghan women rarely leave home because of Taliban restrictionsThat’s according to a UN Women analysis that found more than half of the women surveyed leave their houseno more than twice monthly. There’s also nowhere for them to go: Afghanistan is the only country in the world where girls are banned from secondary education and university. Meanwhile, Saif-ul-Islam Khyber, spokesperson for the dystopian-sounding Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, told Reuters that women have access to all their rights. Depends on how you define “rights”, I suppose.Can antihistamines help with PMDD and menopause?The latest viral health claim is that a combination of over-the-counter antihistamines Pepcid AC and Allegra does wonders when it comes to treating debilitating symptoms connected to premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) and menopause. The Guardian looked into whether the science backs this up, and ultimately it seems that we just don’t have enough information to know. Another reminder that there needs to be a lot more researchinto women’s health.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsraeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homesTwo Palestinian familieshave been trappedin their homes as Israeli militants wage a campaign of terror on them to try and drive them out. When the al Tubasi family’s two-year-old daughter fell ill, the “settlers” blocked an ambulance from getting to the house. This is part of a wider campaign of state-sanctioned ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.Tesla paid Elon Musk 2.5m times more as CEO than its average workerAccording to anew report, Musk received the median Tesla worker’s pay every 4.23 seconds in 2025. While Musk is an extreme case, theratio of CEO to worker payin the US continues to grow. Last year the majority of S&P 500 CEOs made more in a day than the average worker made in a year.Jon Hamm becomes a first time dad at 55Very funny how all the conservative menup in armsabout Alexandria Ocasio-Cortezfreezing her eggshave nothing to say aboutthis.The week in pawtriarchyTwo pygmy goats got loose in Portland this week and decided to try out paw-blictransit. They boarded an FX 2 bus without paying but were promptlyshooed off. Now they are nowhere to be seen; they seem to have goat away. Kids these days, eh?Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUS politicsThe Week in PatriarchyAlexandria Ocasio-CortezIsraelDemocratsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)PalestineTeslacommentShareReuse this content

title: What AOC gets right – and wrong – about ‘Woke 1.0’ | Francine Prose | The Guardian
description: Recent comments by AOC have reignited a fiery debate about ‘wokeism’. But what are we really talking about?
Author: Francine Prose
Headline: Recent comments by AOC have reignited a fiery debate about ‘wokeism’. But what are we really talking about?
Content: ‘Let’s concentrate on coming together to represent the real needs and interests of our citizens and not on labels like “woke”.’Photograph: Nathan Posner/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Let’s concentrate on coming together to represent the real needs and interests of our citizens and not on labels like “woke”.’Photograph: Nathan Posner/ShutterstockOpinionAlexandria Ocasio-CortezWhat AOC gets right – and wrong – about ‘Woke 1.0’Francine ProseRecent comments by AOC have reignited a fiery debate about ‘wokeism’. But what are we really talking about?Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 18.25 EDTShareFull confession: I am one of those who have come to think thatAlexandria Ocasio-Cortezcan essentially do no wrong. At times when I most fear for the future of our country, I watch her videos and am consoled and cheered by her clarity, her honesty, her intelligence, her simple common sense. So I was a little surprised to hear that on a recent interview on ABC This Week, she quoted a political ally as having remarked: “Woke 1.0 was crazy.”What surprised me was not that she called for some moderation of the radical positions – the call to defund the police and the military, for example – that have, at times, been an aspect of progressive politics. But I was frankly a little unnerved to hear her use the word “woke”.The term has its roots in Black slang. “Stay woke” was originally a warning to keep alert to the dangers posed by prejudice and white supremacy. But its meaning has changed to become a synonym for what used to be referred to, also derogatorily, as “PC” – politically correct.I’ve politely asked my colleagues at the college where I teach to avoid the word because it has so effectively been weaponized by the far right to mock and discredit anyone who supports racial justice, economic equity, universal healthcare, and many of the issues in which I too believe.In the ABC interview, AOC explained the ways in which, during the Covid lockdown, “There was a huge opening. The doors were really open to entertain any and every policy that was trying to get us to a better place. But the rhetoric we used at that time is not the rhetoric we use today.” She went on to explain that her primary goal – improving the life of every American – has remain unchanged.Even though I wish she’d used different language for it, I understand her suggestion that Woke 1.0 was crazy. The strict policing of language, the “cancellation” of anyone who had, at any point in their life, made a mistake that was perceived as injurious to women or people of color, the inflexible and frequently impractical notions of what can be said, taught and legislated raised the specter of a dictatorial left that devalued individual liberties and threatened our freedom of speech almost (though not quite) as much as the extreme right.In the current issue of the Atlantic, there’s aneloquent and terrifying essayby Tyler Austin Harper, explaining why the absurd and damaging policies regarding the need to root our racism in the college curriculum and in the larger society made him decide that he – a Black scholar with a tenure-track appointment to teach interdisciplinary humanities in an environmental-studies program – had no choice but to abandon academia forever.In 2021, it was decided that every department at Bates College, where Harper worked, must offer two courses that would “identify areas where white supremacy, ‘colonial’ frameworks, and other forms of bias might be lurking in curricula and major requirements”. This would include the science classes, taught by faculty who often had no idea how to address these complex topics.Such courses might include a math class aimed to help students understand “the role of mathematics as a gatekeeper and driver of injustice”. A colleague suggested that when a student or teacher made a remark perceived to be insensitive, another student should call out “oops” or “ouch” as a helpful corrective.Though some of the more extreme policies were eventually rescinded, the final effect was to make Harper decide that he no longer felt capable of functioning with any degree of personal freedom and integrity on a college campus.The policies implemented at Bates were, I assume, typical of the Woke 1.0 ideology to which AOC was referring. Policies like those, which were heavy-handed interventions in curricula and teaching norms – and the headlines they generated – made it all too easy for the far right to ridicule the ideals of the more moderate and left-leaning Americans, and to use that ridicule as a tool to make sure that the old-fashioned, constitutionally guaranteed aspects of our democracy – including freedom of speech and assembly – could be characterized as “radical” and even “communist”.The infighting and mutual recrimination that this inspired between progressive and centristDemocratsmade it all too easy for the right to dismiss the worthiest of ideals – freely available healthcare, childcare and education, an end to inflation and to the profiteering that has enabled billionaires to widen the income disparity so harmful to average US families – as the kind of folly that allowed the Bates community to describe an argument between white and Black students as a “lynching”.So once again, I agree with AOC. We need to focus on what’s politically viable, on what is attainable, on what the American people so desperately need. Censorship and repression are not only counterproductive but destructive, regardless of whether those efforts come from the right or the left.The midterms are approaching. Our country stands on the brink of a brighter or a much, much darker future. Let’s concentrate on coming together to represent the real needs and interests of our citizens and not on the labels – “woke” or “ultra-conservative” – that only deepen the problems of a nation in which the average family must so often choose between feeding the children or paying the rent.Francine Prose is a former president of the PEN American Center and a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Her latest book is Five Weeks in the CountryExplore more on these topicsAlexandria Ocasio-CortezOpinionUS politicsDemocratsRepublicansUS universitiescommentShareReuse this content

title: The Fauci hearing was painful to watch. But we need answers on Covid-19’s origins | David Relman | The Guardian
description: Despite the recent hearings in Congress, we seem to be even further from the goal of understanding Covid-19’s origin’s than we have ever been
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Despite the recent hearings in Congress, we seem to be even further from the goal of understanding Covid-19’s origin’s than we have ever been
Content: ‘Much is at stake: trust in science, scientists and government, not to mention our ability to thwart and respond to the next pandemic.’Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Much is at stake: trust in science, scientists and government, not to mention our ability to thwart and respond to the next pandemic.’Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersOpinionCoronavirusThe Fauci hearing was painful to watch. But we need answers on Covid-19’s originsDavid RelmanDespite the recent hearings in Congress, we seem to be even further from the goal of understanding Covid-19’s origin’s than we have ever beenSat 15 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTShareAs a microbiologist and infectious disease clinician, it has been tough to watch the recent devolution of public discourse on Covid-19 origins. It has been especially difficult for me to read the comments ofAnthony Fauciabout the origins debate in hisnow-public diary. And it has been painful to watch the televised spectacle hosted by the US senator Rand Paul on 29 July involving a hostile interrogation of Fauci.Despite many early pleas, includingmy own, for a dispassionate, objective assessment of what we know, don’t know and need to know about Covid-19 origins, we seem to be even further from this goal now than we have ever been – plagued by politicization, polarization and illogical thinking.Much is at stake: trust in science, scientists and government, not to mention our ability to thwart and respond to the next pandemic. How did this happen and how do we dig ourselves out?Dr Fauci made mistakes. But his persecution is a travesty | Margaret SullivanRead moreBy the eve of Covid-19, after 20 years of debate, we had agreed to disagree about whether humans were capable of starting a new pandemic. Most public health scientists believed thatnature was the only important “bioterrorist”, based simply on prior probabilities.Other scientists, who focused on the growing power of biotechnology and studied human behavior, believed thathumans had become more than fully capable. When Covid suddenly blew up in late December 2019 in Wuhan, China, and was quickly attributed to a coronavirus with recent ancestors in bats, two possibilities leaped to the fore: a natural “spillover” at one of the unregulated wildlife markets in the city (as with the original 2002 Sars outbreak), and a lab accident in Wuhan, where there happened to be the world’s largest collection of bat-associated coronaviruses.Six years later, despite much mudslinging, each of these possibilities remains viable, supported by circumstantial, but not dispositive, evidence. The virus has not been found in nature, nor in a lab.At the heart of the dispute, two statements are true but not necessarily related. First, we see in scientific publications that risky work with bat coronaviruses was undertaken in Wuhan, some with US National Institutes of Health (NIH) support.Its goal was prediction of disease emergence.Some of this workresembled a form of Russian roulette, in which pieces of novel bat viruses were shuffled to make chimeric viruses and then test their properties (under inadequate biosafety conditions).Yet, this published work does not reveal a plausible Covid precursor virus. Thus, Rand Paul is correct in that risky work was funded by NIH in Wuhan.Anthony Fauciis correct in that the published work, on the face of it, did not cause Covid. Of course, as with any research program, we can assume that much remains unpublished.My own view, for what it is worth, is that a lab accident in Wuhan is the most plausible explanation for Covid, given the kind of work pursued there, the fact that publications by Chinese researchers indicate knowledge about the Sars-CoV-2 virus before late December 2019, and the thousands of negative tests from suspect animal reservoirs. But I could be wrong.If we are to improve our capacity for anticipating, preventing and responding to the next pandemic, several things must happen. First, everyone who insists that they know how Covid began should back off, accept ongoing uncertainty and display a bit more humility.Second, we need an objective and transparent forensic investigation of Covid origins with broad international engagement and proper authorities and accountability.Third, scientists must fully embrace the responsibilities that come with technical power and knowledge and accept guardrails for some kinds of experiments. Similarly, political representatives must embrace their responsibilities for ensuring an educated, balanced public discussion about the trade-offs between a healthy pursuit of public health science and the attendant risks, as well as for balanced public policy addressing risk oversight.One thing that cannot continue to happen is a collective state of wishful thinking that this issue can be ignored or buried, or that nothing useful will result from addressing it. Continuing down the current path comes at our own peril.David Relman is a professor of medicine and microbiology at Stanford University. He was an inaugural member of the US National Science Advisory Board for Biosecurity and president of the Infectious Diseases Society of AmericaExplore more on these topicsCoronavirusOpinionAnthony FauciInfectious diseasesMedical researchBiosciencesMicrobiologyUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Labor is facing an insurgent One Nation. The path it takes on immigration will define its identity for years to come | Frank Bongiorno | The Guardian
description: Labor has always had a divided soul over immigration. Now it faces a predicament as it looks to hold on to suburban and regional seats
Author: Frank Bongiorno
Headline: Labor has always had a divided soul over immigration. Now it faces a predicament as it looks to hold on to suburban and regional seats
Content: Tony Burke’s decision to pull out of a press club speech on a new immigration policy suggests it is an unusually difficult issue for the government, writes Frank Bongiorno.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenTony Burke’s decision to pull out of a press club speech on a new immigration policy suggests it is an unusually difficult issue for the government, writes Frank Bongiorno.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPOpinionAustralian immigration and asylumLabor is facing an insurgent One Nation.
