The path it takes on immigration will define its identity for years to comeFrank BongiornoLabor has always had a divided soul over immigration. Now it faces a predicament as it looks to hold on to suburban and regional seatsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSat 15 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 20.00 EDTShareThe Albanese government places party unity before most other considerations, so it is notable that there is more than one opinion in cabinet on what to do about immigration policy.The decision of the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, topull out of a National Press Club speech this month, having intended to announce a new policy, suggests that this is an unusually difficult issue for the government. One Nation, attracting three in 10 voters in some polling, makes no bones about blaming immigration levels for most of the country’s ills.To be fair, immigration has almost always been a difficult issue for Labor in government. Labor was historically the low immigration party. From its earliest years, it saw migrant workers as a threat to wages and jobs, building on longstanding working-class attitudes towards unfair competition. Not even British workers passed muster, especially when they arrived under contract to local employers. Fear of labour competition trumped white solidarity or imperial brotherhood.Bragg says lower-income earners should accept substandard housing as colleagues rebuke his migration targetRead moreLabor did not invent the White Australia policy, but it was the most fervent supporter of it. The desire for security in the face of the threat of being “swamped” provided the context for the impulse to “populate or perish” for 70 years after federation in 1901. Labor never had the power to prevent such migration and, in any case, all the Labor party’s early leaders were migrants. In the end, the perceived need for a larger white population for the sake of national security challenged Labor’s traditional suspicion or hostility, although it took the arrival of full employment in 1942, along with the prospective “arrival” of a Japanese invader, to tip the balance decisively away from the party’s traditional stand.But Labor had a problem. Labor leaders knew that their supporters opposed high levels of immigration. That would have created difficulty even if the migrants in view were British, but there were not enough of them interested in coming to provide the numbers needed. The claims of national security necessitated the extension of assistance to non-British Europeans, including refugees living in displaced person camps and southern Europeans often despised as “dagos”.The country’s first immigration minister, Arthur Calwell, pretended the migrants would be overwhelmingly British. Many were, and they received preference. But in the 1950s at least, most were not, and they opened the way for an increasingly diverse intake in the decades that followed.There is a myth that these postwar migrants were welcomed with open arms; some commentators today like to contrast these “good, assimilable” migrants with the “bad unintegrated” migrants they see in the present. There was suspicion and even hostility to European migrants. Yet the process of their settlement was still a largely harmonious one, and it is worth asking ourselves why.The late historian John Hirst suggested that there was a strain in old Australia’s settler culture inclined to the polite overlooking of difference for the sake of social peace. That came into play after the war even as the migrant intake looked nothing like anything seen before, nor what the Labor government had promised “old Australians” when they had begun the process at the end of the war.But Labor has always had a divided soul over immigration. Many of its traditional supporters have seen no reason to welcome migration where newcomers enter into direct competition with them for jobs or housing. After the second world war, the long economic boom, robust demand for unskilled labour and government policies that ensured a satisfactory supply of housing underpinned a successful immigration program. When those conditions gradually disappeared from the mid-1970s, so did whatever consensus that had emerged over immigration. Labor was initially at the forefront of the cuts to overseas arrival numbers, during the period of the Whitlam government.The postwar consensus on immigration has never really been restored, any more than post-1973 governments were able to restore the postwar economic order. The closest we came was probably the middle of the Howard era, the early years of this century, when the government increased migrant numbers significantly during a period of economic buoyancy without provoking a public backlash. Its stringent, even cruel, approach to asylum seekers probably helped protect the larger program from the scrutiny and criticism it might have received in other circumstances.Coalition to back Hanson’s migration policy despite pledging to fight One NationRead moreIt was a precarious balance and could probably only have been managed by a conservative government. Today, the perception that Labor is a party of high immigration and careless border administration, however untrue, aligns with the idea that it is a cosmopolitan party of tertiary-educated, metropolitan progressives out of touch with the hopes and fears of ordinary, patriotic working people.The Albanese government has recognised the danger of reinforcing such an impression against the background of an insurgent One Nation eyeing off seats held by Labor in suburban and regional Australia. Also to Labor’s right is a Coalition desperately seeking to meet the One Nation challenge by aping its anti-immigration rhetoric and policies.There are surely in this moment some parallels with Labor’s change of direction on immigration in the mid-1940s. But the environment today is one of rivals scrambling to make hay from the immigration issue rather than, as in the 1940s, an emerging major party consensus in favour of larger numbers and more diversity. Which path it takes in response will likely define the identity of the Labor party – the character of its soul – for many years to come.Frank Bongiorno is director of the Vice-Chancellor’s Centre of Public Ideas and Donald Horne professor of history and public ideas at the University of CanberraExplore more on these topicsAustralian immigration and asylumOpinionLabor partyAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s ‘pioneer’ colonists profited from slavery. That truth must be acknowledged | Paul Daley | The Guardian
description: The veil is slowly being lifted on the forced or coerced migration – ‘blackbirding’ – of Pacific Islanders for labour
Author: Paul Daley
Headline: The veil is slowly being lifted on the forced or coerced migration – ‘blackbirding’ – of Pacific Islanders for labour
Content: Plantation workers in Townsville in 1870.Photograph: State Library of QueenslandView image in fullscreenPlantation workers in Townsville in 1870.Photograph: State Library of QueenslandOpinionSlaveryAustralia’s ‘pioneer’ colonists profited from slavery. That truth must be acknowledgedPaul DaleyThe veil is slowly being lifted on the forced or coerced migration – ‘blackbirding’ – of Pacific Islanders for labourSat 15 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 19.56 EDTShareWhat’s in a name? If that name happens to be Townsville, the coastal north-eastQueenslandcity, the answer is: slavery.While he scarcely went to the place that still bears his name, Robert Towns, the 19th century British-born Australian colonist, has largely been warmly and sentimentally regarded as a genteel, civic-minded merchant and entrepreneur. Like so many bastards of Australian colonisation, history has coddled him insoft biography, and continues to celebrate him in nomenclature and statuary.Sydney’s sugar rush: how the colony’s most powerful profited from Australia’s slave tradeRead moreBut for some years now the veil hasslowly been liftedon Towns and other “pioneers” of colonial Australia who profited hugely from the forced or coerced migration for labour of “blackbirded” (read enslaved) Pacific Islanders – mostly men and boys.Incidentally the Scot John Mackay, after whom another Queensland city was named, wasalso a blackbirder.It’s worth remembering that the term “blackbirding” is not distinct from other forms of slavery that stain British and American history. It comes directly from the African slave trade, and was applied to the no less heinous trafficking by men such as Towns and Mackay of about62,000 Pacific Islandersto Australia between 1860 and 1906. Many were forced to work in colonial Queensland’s sugar industry in appalling conditions (15,000 died on the plantations whose product was refined at the Colonial Sugar Refining Company’s wharves in today’s Pyrmont, Sydney). Others laboured on Sydney’s docks, in maritime industries and elsewhere.View image in fullscreenSouth Sea Islander labourers loading cut sugar cane into a wagon in Queensland.Photograph: Queensland State LibraryAuthor Ryan Butta, in hisnew bookwhich sheds disturbing new light on upper-class colonial Sydney’s intense mercantile interests in the blackbirding trade (and wealth generation through the profits from CSR sugar production), describes Towns as “the founding father of Australian slavery”.Indeed,read a little about Townsand it seems fair to wonder if Townsville might better be named Townsvillain!I’m not recommending renaming any colonial city or town. Just as I’m opposed to removing most statues celebrating our more villainous colonists like Towns or the widely celebrated governorLachlan Macquarie(who ordered the 1816 massacre of First Nations people at Appin, New South Wales, and the theft of their children).But monuments and nomenclature dedicated to terrible people can and should be used as portals into the discovery of greater historical truths.Much was known about Towns’ involvement in Pacific Islander blackbirding when his statue was unveiled inTownsville in 2005, just as Macquarie’s inhuman crimes were well established when one wasdedicated to himin central Sydney in 2013.Both carry benign inscriptions that make no mention of their misdeeds.The statue of Towns (situated in the city’s Pioneer’s Walk) was vandalised in 2020 – the hands daubed in red paint to symbolise blood. I’d never endorse the vandalisation of public property. I’d far prefer to see an additional plaque placed permanently on or near such a statue dedicated to telling the terrible truth about Towns. Add to that the addition of statues in the same place of, for example, South Sea IslanderBonita Mabo– a lifelong activist for her own and Australian First Nations people.Townsville has, it seems, often gone out if its way toprotect the reputation of Towns, at one time insisting he had not “personally condoned or was involved in blackbirding”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis, of course, is simply unaligned with the facts, as Butta’s book, Blackbirding – A reckoning with the Australian slave trade, forensically documents.But as I’ve pointed out elsewhere, this protection racket is pretty widespread.Towns was notorious for the appalling state of his significant Sydney-berthed fleet of ships, some of which were used for blackbirding. Others were crewed by blackbirded Pacific Islanders. His own wharf, known in the day as Rotten Row, relied on blackbirded labour.An official sign down at Towns Place Wharf (near Sydney’s Miller’s point) still fondly celebrates him today as a man who “imported and exported every commodity imaginable: sugar, rope, salt, sandalwood, horses and skins, sperm and black oil, and later wool”. This clearly demands a rethink.So, too, the old sugar wharves – today a beautiful harbourside park that pays homage to the old CSR refinery, its product reliant on slave labour. It would be the perfect place for a monument to the tens of thousands of South Sea Islanders who were kidnapped and transported to Australia and upon whose forced labour the colonies thrived.Incidentally, Towns died at 78 in his palatial Sydney mansion, Cranbrook – something of a citadel to his blackbirding profits – in Bellevue Hill. Cranbrook school was later established on the site in 1918. The school regards Towns as“a great Australian historical figure”whose “ghost … also remains” and has been “seen wandering the halls over the years” by boarders. A spirit besieged by a certain restlessness, it seems. As well it should be if we believe in such things.Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsSlaveryOpinionTownsvilleQueenslandcommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s the SUV tyranny: where have all the normal family cars gone? | Coco Khan | The Guardian
description: They rule the roads and, in their wake, even old-style saloons have been supersized. It’s an illusion of consumer choice, says writer and podcaster Coco Khan
Author: Coco Khan
Headline: They rule the roads and, in their wake, even old-style saloons have been supersized. It’s an illusion of consumer choice, says writer and podcaster Coco Khan
Content: ‘Traditional car body styles have been modified into taller, wider frames.’Photograph: Crispin/Crispin Hughes/Clean Cities Campaign/Climate VisualsView image in fullscreen‘Traditional car body styles have been modified into taller, wider frames.’Photograph: Crispin/Crispin Hughes/Clean Cities Campaign/Climate VisualsOpinionMotoringIt’s the SUV tyranny: where have all the normal family cars gone?Coco KhanThey rule the roads and, in their wake, even old-style saloons have been supersized. It’s an illusion of consumer choiceSat 15 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.40 EDTShareRecently, while traipsing from showroom to showroom in search of a used car for my growing clan, the iconic line from Christopher Nolan’s seminal Batman movie The Dark Knightcame to mind: “You either die a hero, or live long enough to see yourself become the villain.” And by villain, of course, I mean an SUV driver.Because, if you haven’t shopped for a secondhand family car recently, I’ll save you the shock: wherever you look, it’s SUVs.It’s no surprise when these giant cars now makeup 30% of all carson the road and were50% of all new car salesin rich countries in 2023. The look has been so popular that traditional body styles have been modified into taller, wider frames. Even Volvo, the defining family car brand,now only offers SUVsin the UK. All of which means that if, like me, you want a car under 10 years old, hoping it lasts another five, your options are “tank” and “tank-ette”.Britain’s cars and SUVs are growing bigger – but there is a way to stop this deadly ‘carspreading’  | Christian WolmarRead moreDriving the same small city car for nearly 10 years has felt, overall, like a net good. Cheap to run and clean-air-zone-compliant, the compact car is the sociable motor. The people pleaser of the road, at this size a tight parking spot is rarely a worry. Even its horn, a pipsqueak of a beep, conveys more “toodles” than threat. Yes, fine, on a windy motorway it can feel like it might become airborne. But this precious little donkey is reliable and humble. Unlike the flashy warhorse, the SUV, with its ever-widening size (0.5cm wider each year) intimidating other drivers and pedestrians, causing chaos on narrow roads andreducing parking spaceswhen lines are redrawn to accommodate them. Also, a special mention of the branding: so much military language (the JeepCommanderor Land Rover’sDefender, apparently “built toconquer”)– for a vehicle whose main enemy is the roundabout outside Sainsbury’s.So when it came to buying my first family car I figured I’d find an estate, a saloon or a hatchback: something that was safe, since it would carry the most precious cargo of all, children; fuel efficient; wipe-down seats; and a big boot big enough for strollers and bikes, and all the hopes and dreams for a happy family life. But my dreams would soon be dashed.One thing’s for sure, it has been a memorable month hunting for a “normal” family car. The experience of saying “I’m not interested in an SUV” and still being shown one … then a small one … and then one that justlookslike one, but technically isn’t because it can’t go off-road, is the closest thing I’ve experienced to performance art in some years.How can I forget the forecourt so dominated by these cars that the best on offer was a black “mid-size” SUV, a Lexus RX450H, so huge that I genuinely mistook it for a hearse. Or the gentle, sympathetic nature of the used-car salesman showing me a grey and dowdy people carrier. “But, but … I’m in my 30s. I’m still young, I can’t drive this,” I protested, as he gave me a smile conveying “this is all that’s left for you, my friend”.View image in fullscreenWhen smaller was beautiful … children look out from their family’s hatchback.Photograph: FG Trade Latin/Getty ImagesYet,I’m not sure what it is about this that deflates me. Is it the illusion of consumer choice, and how we are funnelled into the same purchases and lifestyles even when we don’t really want them? Or the corrosive quality of fear: against your neighbour’s SUV, your regular car looks flimsy, so you arm up, too. The car lobby has pushed the message that these vehicles are fortresses to keep your children safe inside, with no care for how unsafe they may be outside. The increased height of these bonnets means a child is three times more likely to be killed if hit by an SUV rather than by a conventional vehicle –and, as transport writer Christian Wolmar observes, more likely to be hit at all, since the driving position is often too high to see a child ahead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut mostly I suspect it’s to do with our modern parenting culture, where everything – buggies, cars, technology for baby socks to monitor their breathing – has scaled up to capitalise on our need for safety in a precarious world. Yet the best thing to keep us safe will always be one another, collectivism over individualism. But here we are, driving around in Batmobiles, thinking ourselves heroes, blithely unaware we just might be the baddies.Needless to say, I still haven’t found the right family car. I do (reluctantly) have an SUV test drive booked, though. Perhaps I should embrace the chaos. It could be my Joker moment.Coco Khan is a freelance writer and co-host of the politics podcast Pod Save the UKExplore more on these topicsMotoringOpinionRoad safetyChildrenAutomotive industryTransport policyTravel and transportTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: I feel guilt talking to those left behind in Afghanistan. While I enjoy freedom, they are prisoners | Nelufar Hedayat | The Guardian
description: Five years since the Taliban returned to power, life – especially for women – is merciless and suffocating, says Afghan-British journalist Nelufar Hedayat
Author: Nelufar Hedayat
Headline: Five years since the Taliban returned to power, life – especially for women – is merciless and suffocating, says Afghan-British journalist Nelufar Hedayat
Content: A Taliban soldier stands guard as women arrive to receive food supplies in Kabul, 25 March 2025.Photograph: Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Taliban soldier stands guard as women arrive to receive food supplies in Kabul, 25 March 2025.Photograph: Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAfghanistanI feel guilt talking to those left behind in Afghanistan. While I enjoy freedom, they are prisonersNelufar HedayatFive years since the Taliban returned to power, life – especially for women – is awful. We must keep the people’s stories alive and hope they will be free againSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.32 EDTShareThere are fewer and fewer stories coming out of the land of my birth. Before, I would open Instagram and see my cousins, lip-syncing to trending videos, posing with flowers at a rose garden or at a trendy cafe in their coolest outfits, keeping a record of their lives. I would hear British-Afghan friends talk about their recent trips to the provinces, towns and cities of their foremothers and the buzz of learning about their heritage. I would eagerly await the latest music video from Afghanistan’s many pop stars, all vying to become the hottest track played at weddings, not just inAfghanistanbut all over the world. Afghanistan, its culture, and people felt closer back then.Five years ago today, the brittle peace of the fragile new democracy was shattered by the withdrawal of western military, diplomatic and charitable groups that had intervened in the country’s fate since 2001. Overnight, on Sunday, 15 August 2021, Afghanistan was undone and abandoned.I spent the rest of the month glued to my phone, monitoring WhatsApp groups sprouting every day or so, with people asking for information and help, begging me to get them out of the country because we all knew what was coming, though the rest of the world seemed to lag behind.I was most focused on evacuating one friend from Kabul. She was a headteacher, and it was always her house I would go to first, whenever I went to Afghanistan. I had to have achingly tough phone conversations with her. “You can’t bring your children or your husband. I can only do this for you,” I said. She would agree. “I think I can get you to Albania or Qatar, but you might be in a refugee camp for months or years.” She would agree.The closest we came to getting her out her came six months later, in February 2022. I finally managed to get her a passport when it was virtually impossible to do so, but by then it was too late. TheTalibanwere running the airport and had cracked down on Afghans leaving the country.The last conversation we had on the phone was one of the hardest of my life. I had to tell the woman who had inspired me for so long, a feminist and someone who had advocated for education and self-fulfilment her whole life, that I was going to stop trying to rescue her. “I’ve tried everything I can think of and pushed everyone I know, but I can’t get you on a flight out.” I felt her spirit break as her uncertain fate collapsed into one reality – a life under Taliban rule.In a higher register than I had ever heard her voice before, she told me that this was going to wreak havoc on her already unmanageable diabetes; that she would never work or be self-sufficient again, and then she asked me a terrible question: surely to end her life now was better than carrying on?After all, this was the second time in my friend’s life that she would have to live under a Taliban regime. Neither of us spoke in a protracted, painful silence as we both felt the crushing weight of a learned helplessness that she and millions of Afghans would become intimately familiar with. The line went dead.Since then, our lives have diverged so much we cannot have a proper conversation. We try to speak but it feels as if the phone line is connecting parallel universes. Mine is full of work, family gatherings, gigs and holiday plans and hers of bombs, “morality police” and hand-to-mouth living. We both hesitate to share stories about our lives for fear it will upset the other. We have been rendered speechless.With the birth of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan ruled de facto by the Taliban regime, life changed immediately for my family and friends. The systemic assault on the female sex has resulted in the UN calling for gender apartheid to be recognised as adistinct crime against humanity.“During the previous government, my mother forced me to go to school, attend taekwondo classes, and visit the library,” says a friend who was 14 at the time of the western desertion of Afghanistan. “She wanted me to learn and have opportunities. My father agrees with the Taliban’s rules. He believes I should get money from my future husband instead. For me, this feels like being sold, and it is something I cannot accept.”It’s not just a gender war that has been raging in Afghanistan. In February 2026,Pakistan declared“open war” with its neighbour, unleashing airstrikes that killed hundreds, displacing many thousands more and devastating lives.A cousin tells me of the unadulterated fear these airstrikes brought on the citizens of Kabul. “It was truly frightening. Pakistani drones were launching rocket attacks, and we could only see the flames and hear the explosions in despair. I kept thinking that perhaps this time a rocket might strike our house.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAdd this to the 6 million refugeesforced back to Afghanistanby Iran and Pakistan, the EU meeting with the Taliban in Brussels forclosed-door talks, and half the population facingsevere food insecurity, and you’d be forgiven for thinking, like me, that even God is merciless when it comes to the land of my birth.It’s not that similar things hadn’t happened in Afghanistan before August 2021; it’s that I would also hear of other stories. Stories of heroism, a fight for democracy, a burgeoning arts scene, or event skating teenagers rocking the streets of Kabul. Now, there’s so little to do, such little movement possible, that almost everyone I speak to in Afghanistan sounds as though they’re suffocating. There is no distraction nor relief from the abject suffering of everyday Afghan people.The question now is what does resistance and resilience look like? The Taliban are not an inevitability. In their entire history, they have been in power half as long as UK and US forces were in Afghanistan: 10 years.Afghan people must keep their stories alive, of who and what we are, to help us rebuild an identity of our own making outside occupation and brutal theocracy for when the day arrives that the Taliban are no more. For me, that will mean calling my friend to learn about her life – to have, for the first time in five years, the impossible conversation.Nelufar Hedayat is an Afghan-British journalist, and the presenter and co-director of the documentary In Real Life: the God ThievesDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsAfghanistanOpinionViolence against women and girlsTalibanWomenSouth and central AsiacommentShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Berry-Dee is the UK’s all-time bestselling true crime author. Is he also a violent abuser of women and children? | Books | The Guardian
description: The British writer is known for his unique ability to get inside the heads of serial killers. But a Guardian investigation reveals multiple accusations of assault and child sexual abuse. What is the truth about the man described by his own daughter as ‘absolute evil’?
Author: Lucy Osborne
Headline: The British writer is known for his unique ability to get inside the heads of serial killers. But a Guardian investigation reveals multiple accusations of assault and child sexual abuse. What is the truth about the man described by his own daughter as ‘absolute evil’?
Content: Christopher Berry-Dee.Composite: Ian Tuttle/Shutterstock/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenChristopher Berry-Dee.Composite: Ian Tuttle/Shutterstock/Guardian DesignBooksChristopher Berry-Dee is the UK’s all-time bestselling true crime author. Is he also a violent abuser of women and children?The British writer is known for his unique ability to get inside the heads of serial killers. But a Guardian investigation reveals multiple accusations of assault and child sexual abuse. What is the truth about the man described by his own daughter as ‘absolute evil’?Warning: this article contains descriptions of sexual abuse and violenceLucy OsborneandSirin KaleSat 15 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTShareFrom the outside, it looked like the sort of happy family home a child might draw. Red brick, surrounded by rolling countryside, in Curdridge, near Winchester. Here lived the true crime writer Christopher Berry-Dee, with his second wife, Tracey Dee, and their two young daughters, Zoe and Sasha, in the early 1990s. Inside, it was a house of horrors, full of murder memorabilia. In a wardrobe were the clothes a nine-year-old girl had been murdered in. One afternoon, Zoe was playing when she found them. The now 38-year-old council worker from Romsey says she remembers “putting it all on … going downstairs and everyone being absolutely traumatised”. Later, another gruesome memento was added to the collection: the Austin Metro that convicted murderer Michael Sams had used to transport a body in 1991. Bloodied sections of the seatbelts had been cut out for forensic tests.Berry-Dee was the serial killer man. He wrote to convicted murderers in jail and befriended them. They told him everything. Through them he saw the terror in their victims’ eyes, watched their anguished death throes, heard their final screams. He listened to tapes of their confessions in his study. Zoe grew used to hearing them echo through the house. “It would always be on,” she says. “At the time, it felt normal.”The writer would go on to channel his unique insights into the psyches of these murderous criminals into a three decade-long career. With total sales of nearly 1m, Berry-Dee is the UK’s bestselling true crime author since records began, according to NielsenIQ BookData; a self-styled “investigative criminologist” who routinely appears on TV documentaries and podcasts, and at true crime conferences.His fascination with serial killers is underpinned, he says, by a profound sympathy with their victims. “I speak,” Berry-Dee wrote in 2002, “for the victims who have suffered at the hands of the monsters with two faces … for the next of kin who have lost loved ones.”double quotation markI’ve always thought he gets off over it. There’s something about hurting women and children. That’s why he’s in the job that he does – it’s his thingView image in fullscreenSasha, one of Berry-Dee’s daughters.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianBut to his friends, family, former associates and the families of the murder victims he writes about, Berry-Dee’s intentions are not noble. They say he is a violent abuser of women and children, a man with criminal convictions, who has been reported to the police multiple times for child sexual abuse. They allege that he takes perverse satisfaction in restaging the violent rapes and murders of women and children through his writing. Over the course of a six-month investigation, the Guardian spoke with multiple alleged victims and witnesses to Berry-Dee’s abuse, some of whom, despite the incidents being described taking place decades ago, remain too frightened of the author to speak publicly.Get in touchContact Lucy Osborne and Sirin Kale about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Lucy and Sirin using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.To send a message to Lucy and Sirin, please select 'Investigations (UK and Global)' as the recipient.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emaillucy.osborne@theguardian.comandsirin.kale@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.For other options, see our guide attheguardian.com/tips.Show more“I’ve always thought he gets off over it,” says Sasha, 35, a physically slight woman with tattoos, who lives on the south-west coast. When Sasha talks about her father, whom she calls Chris rather than Dad, she shakes uncontrollably. “There’s something about hurting women, hurting children and violent crimes. That’s why he’s in the job that he does, because it’s histhing.”Berry-Dee, who is 78, declined to be interviewed for this article, citing a recent near-death stroke and medical advice to avoid heavy stress, but insists, “I have not once committed any of the crimes you accuse me of.”Friends and acquaintances alike all agree on one thing: Berry-Dee is a highly memorable person. “Once met,” says the writer and editor Paul Woods, who knew Berry-Dee in the 90s when Woods ran a small true crime press, “never forgotten.”Berry-Dee’s former agent, Derek Block, recalls visiting the writer at his home in Shedfield, Hampshire, in the mid-90s. He says his house “was absolutely pitch black, then he opened the front door and the light came out through the door” – he was in silhouette – “and it was like Psycho or something”.Born Christopher Dee in Winchester in 1948, Berry-Dee proudly traces his lineage to John Dee, the Elizabethan occultist and alchemist. He is a tall, physically imposing presence, who wears a masonic ring, favours a cravat and has been known to seal his letters with a wax stamp. Before he became a true crime writer, Berry-Dee was an artist, known for painting naval scenes around his home town of Portsmouth. He was also a convicted fraudster, having served a one-year sentence in Ford open prison, West Sussex, after a 1982 conviction for forgery, in addition to a separate 1988 conviction for obtaining credit and evading liability while an undischarged bankrupt.double quotation markHe slammed down on the table photos of the girls’ dead bodies. It was a real gut feeling: you’re not doing this because you care about themView image in fullscreenInvestigative journalist Eileen Fairweather.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianBy the time the journalist Eileen Fairweather met Berry-Dee in 1990, he had reinvented himself as a true crime writer. Both were investigating the then unsolved murders of two schoolgirls, Karen Hadaway and Nicola Fellows, in Brighton’s Wild Park in 1986. The Babes in the Wood murders, as they came to be known, convulsed Brighton throughout the late 80s, particularly after the man long believed to be the killer, Russell Bishop, was acquitted following a botched prosecution in 1987.Fairweather recalls her first meeting with Berry-Dee, in a cafe. “He suddenly slammed on the table photos of the girls’ dead bodies,” she says. “It was a real gut feeling as a woman: you’re not doing this because you care about little girls.” She felt that he got a “kick” out of showing her the photographs. A true crime writer who met Berry-Dee in the 2000s likewise recalls Berry-Dee showing him a photograph of a dead child. “It was a horrible picture,” he shudders.Tracey Dee is an elegant, softly spoken woman with thick, dark hair and candy-pink lipstick. She also has a small scar on her face. Tracey, who works in healthcare and lives in West End, near Southampton, says that once, during an argument when she was pregnant, Berry-Dee put out a cigar on her face.Tracey and her daughters allege that the author beat Tracey often. Once, she says, Berry-Dee knocked her unconscious. She woke up in the bath, covered in her own blood. Another time he stood over her, holding a butcher’s knife. “He was shaking so much that I could actually see he was struggling to control himself.”On another occasion, during an argument, Tracey says he pointed a loaded shotgun at her. Her fear was so intense, “I wet myself.” She alleges that Berry-Dee threatened to send his friends round to rape her, to teach her how to have sex “properly”. “I was terrified,” Tracey says, “because I actually believed they would do that.”Tracey would send the children out of the house when she felt a beating was imminent. But there was a limit to what she could do. Sasha says she remembers coming downstairs one morning to find her mother with two black eyes. Zoe alleges that she washed blood from her mother after Berry-Dee ripped out her earrings, and watched him punch her in the leg when she stalled the car. Friends and relatives of Tracey likewise recall seeing her with injuries around the time of her marriage to Berry-Dee, including black eyes. “I saw domestic violence so many times,” Zoe says. “He was just absolute evil.”View image in fullscreenTracey Dee, Berry-Dee’s ex-wife, with their daughters Sasha and Zoe.Photograph: courtesy of the familyIn a lengthy, discursive email responding to the allegations in this article, punctuated by anecdotes about his many interactions with grateful police officers and notorious serial killers, Berry-Dee denies abusing his former wife. He claims the small scar on her face predated their marriage, and that he never heard her complain of waking up in a pool of blood. He doesn’t recall the family even owning a butcher’s knife. “Never once during our marriage did I threaten her,” he says.Tracey fled Berry-Dee while he was on a work trip to the US in 1994, interviewing murderers for the pioneering documentary series The Serial Killers. She obtained a court order preventing Berry-Dee from removing their children from her care. He had only sporadic contact with his daughters as they grew up. Zoe last saw her father around 2008, when she was 20. Walking past a bookshop in Winchester, she saw he was doing a book signing and joined the queue. At the front, Zoe gave her first name, wondering if it would spark any recognition, but, she says, “He didn’t recognise me.”Berry-Dee is open about how he secures his interviews with murderers. “Tell them straight off that you think they are innocent,” he writes in his 2023 book Talking With Psychopaths and Savages: Letters from Serial Killers. “Tell them you intend to write a book about the miscarriage of justice they are suffering; go as far as saying that a major UK TV broadcaster is interested, with maybe even some cash in it for them at the end of the day, and they cannot fail to rise to the surface and take your literary bait as fast as a mousetrap snaps shut. Of course, you are telling them a bucketful of lies.”Berry-Dee claims to have “interviewed and interrogated over 30 of the world’s most notorious killers”, including Ted Bundy, one of the most famous serial killers of all time. In 2019’s Talking With Psychopaths and Savages: Beyond Evil, Berry-Dee quotes Bundy saying, “We serial killers are your sons, we are your husbands … we are everywhere. And there will be more of your children dead tomorrow. What’s one less person on the face of the Earth anyways?”Bundy experts dispute these quotes. “They seem to be kind of a mash-up,” observes Margaret Vandiver, a retired professor of criminal justice at the University of Memphis, who was with Bundy in his final weeks. Some “sound like Ted”, she says, but others “don’t sound like him at all. It sounds like someone’s imagination of what he would have said.”“My quotes are drawn from open sources and most carefully checked,” Berry-Dee says. He was not able to provide a link to any verifiable Bundy interview in which these quotes appeared.double quotation markIf I need to get inside a serial killer’s head, I use any tools I canView image in fullscreenBerry-Dee, who has a three decade-long career as a true crime writer.Photograph: Ian Tuttle/ShutterstockLiving serial killers also allege that Berry-Dee invents quotes, which he attributes to them in his books. “They are complete fabrications by CBD,” says Kenneth Bianchi, now Anthony D’Amato, the convicted US serial killer widely known as the Hillside Strangler. “He is one very twisted pathological liar. I never, on paper, in email or tape, ‘confessed’ those things to him.”The Bafta-winning documentary film-maker David Monaghan, who has been investigating Bianchi’s claims of wrongful conviction since 2016, argues that one either believes facts are important for everyone, or no one at all. “Some may say they would play the world’s smallest violin for lying to serial killers,” he says. “But this is a man being published as a ‘world-renowned investigative criminologist’, whose ethics start with deception and continue into outright fraud by inventing quotes.”Lucian Randall, Berry-Dee’s former commissioning editor at his publisher John Blake in the 2000s, says it would not be normal practice in a publishing house to ask authors to provide their source materials, such as interview transcripts or tapes, if the author was already a successful writer, as Berry-Dee was when they started working together. “There’s a certain amount of checking that goes on,” Randall says. “But I think if someone comes and they’ve already done a book, I wouldn’t normally ask to see source material.” For an established, bestselling author, “I’m not sure anyone else would be saying at that point, where is your information for all of this? That feels like you’re doubting the book.”Berry-Dee does not deny he lies to secure interviews. “So what?” he writes in his response to the Guardian. “If I need to get inside a serial killer’s head, I use any tools I can. These murderous people are not angels, you know.”By 2000, Berry-Dee had become an established crime writer, who taught art on the side. It was this reputation that reassured Sally, when she dropped off her 13-year-old daughter, Helen (both pseudonyms), at his Castle School of Art in Portsmouth’s Venture Tower, she was in safe hands. “The fact that he was investigating criminals gave me confidence,” Sally says. “He seemed on the side of the good guys.”An academically gifted child with a talent for art, Helen had a sheltered upbringing: she’d never even held hands with a boy. Berry-Dee, she would later write in a submission to the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority (CICA), presented as “intensely charismatic”, with “an amiable rogue personality”.Within a month of her starting at the school in August 2000, Helen says Berry-Dee, then 52, kissed her. She did not tell her parents. He then began “slowly turning up the pressure gauge”, says Helen, now a 39-year-old artist.She documented what she says happened next in her diary, which she handed over to Hampshire constabulary in 2006. A formal statement drawn up by police investigators quoted its contents: on 2 October 2000, she wrote that Berry-Dee had asked her to perform oral sex. She did not know what this meant, so he explained it to her. By December, he was making her do it. “It was always aggressive and he was constantly reiterating that I was leading him on,” she says.Berry-Dee was insistent, she says, that they should have sex before she turned 14. “He would say he would leave me if I wouldn’t have sex with him,” she says. The day before her 14th birthday, in February 2001, he got what he wanted. “After that,” she says, “there was a pattern of him having sex with me about five times a week for the next 10 months.” (Helen refers to these incidents as “sex” to differentiate them from a later time when she says Berry-Dee raped her, but under UK law any sex with a child is defined as statutory rape.)double quotation markIt’s shocking to see my abuse mirrored in his books, his sick perversions hidden under the guise of ‘serious research’View image in fullscreenHelen, a former art student of Berry-Dee, who she says raped her when she was 13, pictured now …… and on her 13th birthday. Photographs: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The Guardian; courtesy of the familyOn weekdays, it would happen during class. Berry-Dee would look up at the ceiling, or down at the floor, to signal whether he wanted Helen to meet him in the upstairs or downstairs toilets. On Saturday afternoons, when her mother dropped her off for private art classes with Berry-Dee, she says the abuse happened multiple times. In between, they’d talk about his crime writing. “When he spoke about the things he was writing about,” Helen says, “he didn’t speak about them with horror. He spoke about them with admiring fascination.”She says Berry-Dee was a “sadist” who appeared to enjoy causing her pain: “The sex was very violent and I was still a developing girl, so it was incredibly painful.” As the abuse went on, she developed vaginal infections and began self-harming. She says when she told him about her self-harm, he said it was “kinky”.Helen was not the only student Berry-Dee targeted. Gina Hutton, 41, a family support worker from Portsmouth, began attending the school at 15 – the only other teenager in the class. In 2001, when she was 16, she says, Berry-Dee kissed her on the lips. “I remember the bristles because he had a moustache and a beard,” Hutton says. She made an excuse and quickly left.Helen says her relationship with Berry-Dee ended in 2001. But in January 2002, at his request, she reluctantly agreed to meet with him one last time. At this meeting, when she was still only 14, she says he violently raped her against a wall. According to medical records, in October that year, when Helen was 15, she visited a sexual health clinic, where she was tested for HIV and prescribed a pessary for cervical thrush.In 2002, Berry-Dee also published his breakout hit, Talking With Serial Killers: The Most Evil Men in the World Tell Their Own Stories, which he researched and wrote during the period Helen says he abused her. She read it as an adult and realised, to her horror, that some of the extreme sexual practices Berry-Dee had inflicted upon her as a child were included in the book. Like the US serial killer Harvey Carignan, Helen says, Berry-Dee inserted foreign objects into her body. She says he would often accuse her of playing mind games with him, a term also favoured by Carignan. She says Berry-Dee liked to have violent oral sex, a practice favoured by another US serial killer, Kenneth McDuff, whom Berry-Dee writes about in the book. “It’s shocking,” Helen says, “to see elements of my abuse mirrored in his books, for the inspiration for his sick perversions to be hidden under the guise of ‘serious research’.”Helen is not the first woman to report Berry-Dee to the police for child sexual abuse. In 1983, Tracy Hurdle, his stepdaughter from his first marriage, went to the police, alleging Berry-Dee raped her when she was 12. In 1984, Berry-Dee was arrested and charged with having unlawful sexual intercourse with a girl under 13, but the case was dropped when the prosecution offered no evidence. Berry-Dee says Hurdle had in fact been raped by somebody else, but declined to say who.Hurdle was a popular girl who loved horse riding. In photos from the time, she peeks out from behind a sweeping blond fringe, her smile revealing her dimples. She died in a car crash at the age of 16. A family member who was at her funeral remembers, “The whole of her school year went. It was absolutely packed with young people in dark clothing, sobbing.” Also in attendance, they recall, was Berry-Dee.View image in fullscreenTracy, Berry-Dee’s stepdaughter from his first marriage, accused him of raping her when she was 12, which he denies.Photograph: courtesy of the familyIt was reading an article about Berry-Dee appearing in court over Hurdle’s allegations that made Helen realise she wasn’t alone and finally, on 11 September 2006, prompted her to go to the police. On 26 September, she was interviewed by Hampshire officers. As well as her diaries, which documented the alleged abuse in real time, she brought them the physical evidence she had: a tissue that she spat Berry-Dee’s semen into, and a sanitary towel stained with his semen and her blood.Berry-Dee was arrested in January 2007 and denied having had a sexual relationship with her. In June 2007, an officer called Helen with bad news. According to the law at the time, Section 6 of the Sexual Offences Act 1956, allegations of unlawful sex involving children aged 13 to 16 had to be reported within a year. “Spoke to [Helen] and updated her that [Berry-Dee] would NOT be charged as there are no offences,” reads a police report from 6 June 2007. “She was crying.”Helen’s parents hired a lawyer to write to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and ask them to reconsider their decision, including whether they could pursue alternative charges, such as rape, that are not time-barred. Helen had extensive contemporaneous evidence, in the form of diaries and the people she told about the abuse soon afterwards, in addition to the forensic material. But in an October 2008 letter, the CPS said there was still “insufficient evidence to have a realistic prospect of conviction”.Since 2007, Helen has tried to get Hampshire police to reopen the case, give her a copy of the forensic report and return her potential evidence, to no avail. When Helen asked one detective whether she could have her forensic evidence back, she says she was told, “What do you want with that? It’s a dirty old piece of tissue.”Although she did not get to see Berry-Dee appear in court, in 2009 the CICA found that, on the balance of probabilities, she was a victim of violent crime, awarding Helen £18,480.When contacted for comment, Berry-Dee did not admit to a sexual relationship with Helen and denied taking inspiration for his conduct from the serial killers he interviewed: “Quite how and why Helen has transposed this on to me regarding her is total fiction … Indeed I was arrested and questioned, and the matter was apparently dropped,” he says. He claims to have met Helen several times since, even bumping into her in a supermarket where they “chatted amicably”, a claim Helen vehemently denies.Over the last 20 years, Helen has tried to move on from Berry-Dee’s crimes, but she cannot escape the nightmares about those months in the art school. “I’m in a strange, dilapidated version of the Venture Tower,” Helen says, “and he’s in there somewhere, trying to get me, and I’m trying to get out, and can’t.”‘As my loyal readers will know,” Berry-Dee wrote in 2023, “I always treat the relatives, close friends and work colleagues of the deceased … with the deepest respect, for they are victims too.”But throughout his career, Berry-Dee has been repeatedly accused of mistreating the families of the victims of crimes.In November 1995, Diana Lamplugh, mother of the missing estate agent Suzy Lamplugh, told the Guardianshe was appalled to see her daughter’s photo on the cover of Berry-Dee’s book Unmasking Mr Kipper: Who Really Killed Suzy Lamplugh, without her permission. “I looked at it and said, ‘How could this be allowed?’ But you have no rights when someone goes missing. Your daughter doesn’t belong to you.”Berry-Dee’s entanglement with the families of the Babes in the Wood murder victims led to a two-decade feud that ended up in court. The family of Nicola Fellows, one of the nine-year-old girls killed, agreed to provide Berry-Dee with police files and crime scene photographs for a book. But Berry-Dee did not try to help bring Russell Bishop, the prime suspect who was eventually convicted of the murders, to justice. Instead, he enthusiastically championed Bishop’s innocence. And Berry-Dee had his own theory about who might have murdered the schoolgirls: Nicola’s father, Barrie Fellows.In 2007, Ian Heffron, Barrie’s brother and Nicola’s uncle (who changed his surname from Fellows at 18), sued Berry-Dee for libel, after complaining that the author, writing on his blog, had accused Nicola’s family of being involved in a cover-up in relation to the then still unsolved murders. “He said,” Heffron says, “that he will expose and name the killers of the girls, and said it was a close family member.” Two years later Heffron recovered his legal costs from Berry-Dee’s book royalties, directly through his publisher, John Blake, through a third-party debt order.However, John Blake, founder of the eponymous publishing house, said he had no recollection of Berry-Dee being required to pay court-ordered damages out of his royalties. He stated he “looked into it and I was satisfied obviously with the explanations [from Berry-Dee].” Before ringing off, Blake added, “Don’t be too hard on him; he’s not a bad man.”Police arrived to arrest her father for sexual abuse. But he was making it all upRead moreIn 2019, Heffron was interviewed by the former Evening Standard courts correspondent Paul Cheston for his book on the Babes in the Wood murders. It was to be published by John Blake, by then an imprint of the larger Bonnier Books. Heffron told Cheston about Berry-Dee’s mistreatment of Nicola’s family, and Cheston included these allegations in a draft of his book, though they were later cut. The Bonnier editor explained why in an email to Cheston, sent on 3 April 2019: “As for the Chris Berry-Dee stuff – that may have to come out even if the claims can be substantiated, purely due to the obvious conflict of interest. He is our author and, as dreadful an author as he is, we can’t really be seen to be dragging him through the mud, even in this case.” (A spokesperson for Bonnier said the firm was not currently working with Berry-Dee and that “publishing decisions made at the time were based on legal advice”.)Berry-Dee has a further curious tie to the Babes in the Wood case. In 1991, the BBC journalist Martin Bashir obtained the clothes that Karen Hadaway was wearing when she was murdered, only for the clothes to subsequently go missing. Prior to Bashir, however, at least one other person seems to have had the clothes: Berry-Dee, who wrote in one of his books about the Hadaways giving him the clothes “with tears in their eyes”, apparently for the purposes of securing DNA testing. The clothes seem to have been returned shortly before Bashir began investigating.More strangely, however, four sources recall Berry-Dee boasting about having the clothes, or saw what they believed were the clothes, after Bashir and the BBC had apparently misplaced them. His daughter Zoe even believes they were the bloodied clothes she discovered and put on as a child. Her mother agrees, recalling Zoe wearing them when she was four or five. Berry-Dee says it is “100% correct” that he obtained the clothes, but denied Zoe ever wore them. He declined to elaborate on whether, or how, he had obtained them a second time. He claims to have since burned them.Besides Helen and Hurdle, at least one other woman is known to have reported Berry-Dee to Hampshire police for child sexual abuse: his own daughter, Sasha. Sasha says she has memories of her father touching her inappropriately in the shower when she was three or four years old. These recollectionsresurfaced in 2024, prompting a mental health crisis. She confided in her mother and sister at the time, and went to the police the following year.Whether children so young can recall traumatic events is highly controversial. Two academics who specialise in childhood memory formation, consulted for this piece, said that Sasha not having received therapy makes her a more credible source, as therapists have been known to implant false memories. But they also said children seldom recall incidents in as much detail as Sasha, and her awareness of the sexual abuse allegations involving Hurdle could have influenced her memories. Berry-Dee denounced the suggestion that he molested Sasha as “unfounded” and a “very spiteful allegation, probably engineered by her mother”.View image in fullscreenSasha and Zoe, whose mother fled Berry-Dee while he was away interviewing serial killers in 1994.Photograph: courtesy of the familyWith no corroborating evidence, only a police investigation could assess the credibility of Sasha’s allegations. But almost a year after contacting the police, Sasha was still having to chase them even to take her statement. The case by then had been referred to Devon & Cornwall Police (DC), so Sasha could be interviewed closer to where she lives, but it did not progress further for months, with interviews cancelled at short notice due to paperwork issues.“DC are still claiming they haven’t received the information for the interview?” Sasha texted her police contact on 12 January 2026, nearly nine months after she first contacted them. On 29 January, she followed up: “Still nothing?” On 10 February: “Is this happening?”In February 2026, Devon & Cornwall police attempted to arrange a video-recorded interview, but Sasha says she was told she would not be allowed to speak with a therapist for support as she prepared, because it could undermine her credibility. “I could not sit in that room for three and a half hours with cameras on me without having any sort of coping mechanism,” she says. Disheartened, Sasha requested to pause her interview.In 2024, Bonnier rebranded Berry-Dee for a younger,TikToking and true crime podcast-loving audience. His books are reviewed often on BookTok, TikTok’s literary subcommunity. But not all his reviews are positive. He “berate[s] female victims for not taking his advice, implying their stupidity was to blame for their murders”, writes one Goodreads reviewer. A second points to the way he describes “the rape of young girls as ‘sex’ or ‘three-ways’”.Even when not lascivious, Berry-Dee’s prose can be mercilessly cruel. One murder victim is described as a “nagging bag of wind” whose “good looks and figure had long abandoned her”. The convicted US murderer Carol Bundy is “a common slut” who “would have cheap sex with any man who looked just the once at her”. An 11-year-old rape victim is a “sexually advanced youngster”; another 11-year-old sexual abuse victim is “physically well-developed”. The mentally ill are residents of the “nuthouse”; women are “into lesbianism”; and a gay murder victim is a “deviant”.But Berry-Dee’s books remain most shocking for their orgiastic depiction of violence. In 2011’s Talking With Serial Killers: Dead Men Talking, Berry-Dee writes, “I started to play a little death game with her, use her like a toy, an amusement,” quoting the serial killer Keith Hunter Jesperson. “I choked her, let her wake up, choked her again, let her wake up again ... finally she caught on and just accepted the game.” In 2019’s Talking With Psychopaths and Savages: Beyond Evil, he directs readers “with more than a particular fascination for the macabre” to online photos of a 20-year-old murder victim’s decapitated head, which Berry-Dee jocularly describes as resembling “an ugly Barbie doll”.“What are people getting out of reading this voyeuristic, sensationalist stuff?” Helen asks. “Who is it helping? For sure, not the victims, nor the victim’s families. I can only think that it feeds some people’s basest desires.”Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: Ayo Adenekan: Homeland Insecurity review – SNL UK writer woos the room with summer romance | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A fringe fling is the backbone for a mischievous set with deft jokes and a fresh perspective but some of this material needs another draft
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: A fringe fling is the backbone for a mischievous set with deft jokes and a fresh perspective but some of this material needs another draft
Content: ‘Stop the trains!’ … Ayo Adenekan.Photograph: Matthew StrongeView image in fullscreen‘Stop the trains!’ … Ayo Adenekan.Photograph: Matthew StrongeEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewAyo Adenekan: Homeland Insecurity review – SNL UK writer woos the room with summer romanceCabVol @ Monkey Barrel, EdinburghA fringe fling is the backbone for a mischievous set with deft jokes and a fresh perspective but some of this material needs another draftBrian LoganSat 15 Aug 2026 06.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAyo Adenekan’s ascent has been swift. Last year, the rookie comic cracked a joke on stage about Doctor Who’s Ncuti Gatwa. This year, he scripted jokesforGatwa, as a writer on Sky’sSaturday Night Live UK. In this second fringe set, the Edinburgh man shows why TV producers spirited him away after last year’s debut: his perspective is fresh, he writes a deft joke, and he has the warmth to win over a room. But he’s not the finished article. He could vary the pace, which tends to the sonorous. Several of his ideas go underdeveloped. And the story Homeland Insecurity tells is unremarkable.It’s a love story, Adenekan tells us at the start, about a summer romance splashed across the canvas of the Edinburgh fringe. A meaningful but fly-by-night fling, it provides the backbone for an hour in which the 24-year-old ranges across his relationship with his dad, his “straight white man friends”, and his outrage when a namesake comedian comes up from London to steal his thunder at last year’s festival. “I’m not concerned about the boats, man. Stop the trains!” There’s a running visual gag too about product placement, which could be something, but Adenekan never really commits to the bit.That’s not the only instance where the material might benefit from one more draft: see the routine about his discomfort with dating black men. Elsewhere, I wanted Adenekan to give the delivery a bit more welly. Instead, he repeats and circles back on himself: the more times he tells us (and there were several) that he’s delighted to be back in this venue after last year’s success, the more I found my own delight diminishing.Jordan Brookes: The Part of You That’s Always Screaming review – former fringe champ’s chewy croissant taleRead moreBut no doubt Adenekan has the raw materials to fashion something distinctive, with his under-exposed angle on life (Gatwa notwithstanding) as a queer Scottish-African, his smooth and mischievous manner, and the ability to drop choice lines including (of his Nigerian diaspora family) “we’re Muslim like Meghan Markle is black”. Even if his summer romance story finally feels generic, there’s enough here to suggest others will soon be queueing up to give Adenekan the love.AtCabVol @ Monkey Barrel, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt convinced me to give up on my fashion industry dreams | Culture | The Guardian
description: I was struggling to make ends meet as an unpaid intern when a sarcastic song from the hit comedy gave me the clarity to walk out
Author: Kitty Drake
Headline: I was struggling to make ends meet as an unpaid intern when a sarcastic song from the hit comedy gave me the clarity to walk out
Content: Illustration: Martin O’Neill/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O’Neill/The GuardianMy cultural awakeningCultureUnbreakable Kimmy Schmidt convinced me to give up on my fashion industry dreamsI was struggling to make ends meet as an unpaid intern when a sarcastic song from the hit comedy gave me the clarity to walk outHeidi Denholm; as told toKitty DrakeSat 15 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was 3am in the summer of 2017, and I was lying in a triple bunk bed in a hostel in London, listening to the sounds of the 14 other people in my dormitory snoring. I had been working unpaid internships in the fashion industry in London for the past 18 months and living in £12-a-night hostels. When I couldn’t sleep, I would watch TV on my beaten-up phone to drown out the snores. I was watchingUnbreakable Kimmy Schmidt, an absurdist comedy about a woman who moves to New York after 15 years imprisoned in a doomsday cult’s underground bunker.Her relentless positivity often inspired me to keep going, but on that particular night, the opposite happened: Kimmy gave me the courage to give up.Growing up in Essex, I dreamed about a future in fashion. I saw myself living in an artist’s warehouse, working at Vogue and being invited to the hottest events. This wasn’t the reality. I was 23 and technically employed by one of the biggest fashion magazines, one I grew up worshipping. But as an intern I was paid nothing. I worked 9am to 5pm, often relegated to the fashion closet for hours on end. Then, from 7pm to 2am I did various actual jobs, from flyering for gyms to manning the door of a strip club, trying to scrape together enough money for my hostel bill. Most hostels provided a free breakfast, which was my only hot meal of the day. At the beginning of the week I would buy a loaf of bread and a jar of peanut butter and ate sandwiches for dinner. My parents supported my dream but it was up to me to make it work financially.I desperately wanted to look put-together to fit in at work but it wasn’t safe to leave anything in the hostel, so I had to carry all my belongings around in a backpack. One day my only pair of shoes, silver glittery New Look ballet pumps, fell apart. I hid in the office’s fashion closet and taped my shoe back together. When I looked up I was surrounded by beautiful designer heels.I tried to keep my situation a secret. One fashion PR firm I had interned at found out I was living in hostels and told my whole office that I was homeless. My boss publicly gave me £100 in cash and said I was “so brave”: the same boss who paid me in “experience” and “exposure”.double quotation markThe sooner you quit something that stinks, the sooner you’ll get something that doesn’tEvery unpaid internship came with the suggestion that it “could lead to a full-time job”, encouraging me to believe that I was on the brink of my big break: that if I was just in the right place at the right time, saying the right things and wearing the right outfit, I might make it. But it had been over a year, and the only interns I ever saw progress seemed to already have connections.In the episode ofUnbreakable Kimmy SchmidtI watched that night in the hostel – Kimmy Gives Up! – her optimistic veneer finally cracks. Her landlord Lillian offers her some well-timed advice: “I know you’re tough and you never give up, but sometimes the hardest thing you can do is just quit and walk away.” Lillian also sings a spoof called Just Go On, a sarcastic parody of Tomorrow from the musical Annie. Somewhere in that minute and 53 seconds, everything shifted into place.I remember being in that triple bunk bed with tears silently streaming down my face. I’d been so positive, just like Kimmy, and bending over backwards for these internships – but I couldn’t pretend any more. The next day, I quit. I told my boss I had run out of money, was living in hostels and I couldn’t work for free any more. She was unbothered. She made it clear I was utterly replaceable. But another well-placed quote from Lillian echoed in my ears: “The sooner you quit something that stinks, the sooner you can find something that doesn’t. Save your hope for that”. So I did.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI have since built a career in film and TV, mainly comedies. Just Go On has become something I listen to often when I’m torn between staying or leaving. If I had never walked out of that office, I wouldn’t have found what was waiting for me all along.Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. They will only be seen by the Guardian.Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information.
