title: Little Bird: this beautiful, moving Canadian drama will fill you with visceral anger | Television | The Guardian
description: There is dignity and tenderness to this drama based on the real story of the Sixties Scoop – the scandal of First Nations children who were forcibly taken from their parents and adopted by white families
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: There is dignity and tenderness to this drama based on the real story of the Sixties Scoop – the scandal of First Nations children who were forcibly taken from their parents and adopted by white families
Content: Kidnapped … Bezhig Little Bird and her sister and brother are ripped away from their home in Saskatchewan.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.View image in fullscreenKidnapped … Bezhig Little Bird and her sister and brother are ripped away from their home in Saskatchewan.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.The watcherTelevisionLittle Bird: this beautiful, moving Canadian drama will fill you with visceral angerThere is dignity and tenderness to this drama based on the real story of the Sixties Scoop – the scandal of First Nations children who were forcibly taken from their parents and adopted by white familiesRhik SamadderSat 15 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere’s one you’ll like: a man comes home to find his wife handcuffed to the wall and his young children missing. They have been taken by child protection services due to the lack of a fridge in the house, which is treated as a sign of neglect. When he confronts law enforcement officials outside, they beat him to death. Decades later, one of the children, now adopted into a Jewish home in Montreal, goes looking for the family she lost, risking the collapse of her new life to do so. I never said it was a joke. Although it turns out there was a fridge, behind the house.Watching Little Bird (18 August, 9pm, Sky Atlantic), I was reminded that TV is capable of more than mere entertainment, something we lose sight of when we think of it as a purely profit-or loss-making enterprise. I felt the visceral anger and sadness of this story of a First Nations woman caught between cultures, robbed by forces beyond her control and stonewalled by the authorities. Set in Canada, the attitude, if not the events, feel shamefully familiar.Although fiction, the story is real. Canada’s colonial history includes the Sixties Scoop – the mass abduction of First Nations children, forcibly taken by welfare services and rehomed with white families. Their adoption papers were sealed, effectively giving them no contact with parents or clue as to their heritage. Little Bird’s six episodes examine the long shadow of this cultural genocide through one family. At the end of each episode we are reminded that there are more Indigenous children in the care system than ever before.Our self-elected detective is Esther Rosenblum, now in her 20s. Her only clue is a clipping of the newspaper advertisement placing her up for adoption. This is how she knows her real name: Bezhig Little Bird. Bezhig is Ojibwe for one – a fact with a cruel flipside, revealed later in her search. As for Little Bird, it’s a name that could signify rootlessness, fragility or the possibility of transcendence.View image in fullscreenNew life … Bezhig/Esther (Darla Contois) goes in search for her real family in Little Bird.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.Esther/Little Bird is punishingly self-reliant, being barely accepted by her Jewish in-laws, despite converting at a young age. She tracks down family living on reserves, who are surrounded by poverty but have each other. She is isolated by her relative privilege. Another family member abducted at the same time was taken in by a family who needed an indentured servant, and made to sleep in an outhouse.The show brilliantly dissects racism, from the sweeping and systemic to the petty and everyday. The Ojibwe men know any emotionalism or frustration with authority will be interpreted as aggression and brutally punished. Little Bird, a trained lawyer, is repeatedly told to calm down, act with decorum, while officials fob her off, oozing contempt. Any person of colour will wince with recognition when a case worker remarks: “You look so put together,” or her fiance’s mother tells her: “You’re one of the good ones.” (Unless they aren’t put together or one of the good ones, I suppose.)The show is, ironically, at its best when restrained, training a cool eye on the banality of injustice. We are not given access to the architects of brutal welfare policy but we do meet the staff who enact it. “You’re not going to be able to do this job if you can’t get past being nice,” an experienced child protection services officer tells Adele Halpern, a greenhorn struggling to suppress her own humanity. Adele’s attempt to be more of a bureaucratic bastard is heartbreaking – and hopefully temporary. I’ve not seen all the episodes yet, but there’s a chance she may be one of the good ones.Barrel of laughs? No. But Little Bird has dignity, tenderness and beauty. Filmed on location at Treaty 1 Territory in Manitoba, Esther’s suppressed memories of her stolen life are shot through with lushness as they return, though they aren’t all happy. The Indigenous Cree-Saulteaux actor Darla Contois gives a graceful, very moving performance as Little Bird, and the show cleaned up at the Canadian Screen Awards, winning 13 trophies. It would be easy for it to be lost in a crowded marketplace amid flashier, more commercial offerings. That would be further injustice. Watching it, you’ll be angry. And that’s OK.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Will Poulter on challenging stereotypes in new opioid drama: ‘Shame on us for stigmatizing people’ | Will Poulter | The Guardian
description: The British actor delivers his strongest performance to date in indie film Union County as a person struggling with substance abuse trying to turn his life around
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The British actor delivers his strongest performance to date in indie film Union County as a person struggling with substance abuse trying to turn his life around
Content: Will Poulter in Union County.Photograph: Oscilloscope Laboratories/APView image in fullscreenWill Poulter in Union County.Photograph: Oscilloscope Laboratories/APWill PoulterInterviewWill Poulter on challenging stereotypes in new opioid drama: ‘Shame on us for stigmatizing people’Owen MyersThe British actor delivers his strongest performance to date in indie film Union County as a person struggling with substance abuse trying to turn his life aroundSat 15 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery week, Annette Deao, a drug dependency counselor, sits in the county jail and offers incarcerated people in rural Ohio a chance at recovery. One bright day she meets Cody, a young man who shuffles towards the lectern and quietly says that he’s ready to give it a shot. “His self-respect is in the basement,” saidWill Poulter, the British actor who plays the character. “He doesn’t like or accept himself enough to embark on helping himself.”Union County review – an affecting Will Poulter lifts quiet addiction dramaRead moreDirected by Adam Meeks, anOhionative, Union County is a bruising yet poetic depiction of a real life drug recovery court in Bellefontaine, Ohio, where individuals join long-term treatment programs with daily sobriety testing. Though the film is led by Poulter and Noah Centineo as foster brothers taking steps to get clean, much of the supporting cast is made up of first-time actors who share their real – and often painful and non-linear – stories of recovery. The hybrid of narrative feature and documentary-esque elements combine in a deeply affecting watch that is anchored by Poulter’s natural-feeling approach to the role.“It was clear to me from the outset that Adam wasn’t interested in making a filmabouta community as he was in making it inwitha community,” Poulter said, speaking via Zoom a few days before Union County’s US release. “Top of mind was not interfering with the recovery process and not infringing on the path that the participants were walking. I think that’s the reason they were so generous.”Far too often, Hollywood gets its stories of addiction wrong, with surface-level treatment in misfires such asBeautiful Boy,Ben Is BackandHillbilly Elegy. After seeing Meeks’s contemplative 2020short filmof the same name, which also collaborated with Bellefontaine locals, Poulter felt sure that Union County would do justice to the subject. “In the representation of addiction on screen there is a tendency to focus on devastation and the negative side of things,” Poulter said. “What I appreciated about Adam’s approach was that it was more weighted on the success of the program. It has an over 50% success rate which is phenomenal – incomparable in some ways – so it was really about platforming that above all else.”Since breaking out as a child star in 2007 in British comedySon of Rambow, Poulter has traded teenage parts in centrist Hollywood fare such asWe’re The MillersandThe Maze Runnerfor subtle, sturdy work in auteur-driven projects such as Ari Aster’sMidsommar, Kathryn Bigelow’sDetroitand Alejandro G Iñárritu’sThe Revenantas well as receiving Emmy nominations for turns in TV showsDopesickandThe Bear. Poulter is undoubtedly dedicated to his work – in a trait which has seen him undergoing rigorous chef training for The Bear and an intense workout regimen for Marvel’sGuardians of The Galaxy Vol 3– but also has a taste for the unexpected. In the past year, he has canoodled with a Haim sister in the band’sAll Over Mevideo, played a stuck-up boutique manager inI Love Boostersand guest judged on RuPaul’s Drag Race vs The World.View image in fullscreenLionel Boyce and Poulter in The Bear.Photograph: Chuck Hodes/FX NetworksUnion County is the best showcase to date of Poulter’s ability to inhabit a character’s skin. At the start of the film Cody is broken down, near mute and blinking heavily as if he’s still trying to comprehend how he ended up here. You can imagine another actor over-doing it, but there’s an unshowy confidence to Poulter’s performance that captures the the young man’s quiet pride: he may live out of his car, but spends evenings hand washing his clothes and drying them on a line rigged between trees.With Meeks’s precise instinct for detail, Union County is grounded enough to make its flickers of hope feel earned. Most memorable of the first-time actors is Daeo, whose kind but firm counsellor becomes a parental figure to Cody as he gets back on track. “When Annette says ‘I’m really proud of you,’ it’s the first time he’s ever heard that in his life,” said Poulter.“There are plenty of people in their mid-20s who have never had that kind of affirmation or support,” he went on. “And yet we hold them to the same standard as people who have been told they are loved on a regular basis. That’s shame on us for stigmatizing people in that position.”Filming the movie sounds almost unbearably heavy. “It was emotional,” the actor said. “I don’t know how Annette does the work on a daily basis. As an actor I was simulating these experiences and I went home every night, whereas the real participants are in an 18-month program and the work and recovery is never done. So however it was for me, it pales in comparison to what it was like for the real participants.”Despite promises by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the health secretary, a recent reportfoundthat the Trump administration has cut more than $1bn in federal funding to mental health and addiction programs. “Those kinds of rollbacks are devastating to me because I can’t detach myself from the idea that that is informed by a lot of harmful stigma and misinformation,” Poulter said. “The stigmatization of addicts is such that we don’t afford the compassion that we would to anyone dealing with a mental health issue to someone who has substance use disorder.“When people think about an addict using heroin, they don’t think about the teenager who was prescribed Oxycontin for an injury at the age of 14,” he continued. “They don’t think about the possibility they might have been in a relationship characterized by domestic violence. They don’t think about the eviction that forced somebody onto the street.”View image in fullscreenPoulter, Annette Deao, Adam Meeks and Noah Centineo at the New York premiere of Union County on 12 August 2026.Photograph: Dave Allocca/Starpix/ShutterstockPoulter has often spoken up about political causes and publicly supportsPalestineas well asmigrantandLGBTQ+rights. Does he think that the current US administration has twisted priorities? “This isn’t me trying to sort of dodge a political question, but I am not educated enough on the latest here in America to answer that,” he said. “But I do know that there is so much misunderstanding, and I’d like to think that our film will hopefully move people to think differently about substance use disorder.”Mutants assemble: what does the future hold for the X-Men?Read moreThe actor said he aims to “maintain a balance” between mainstream films and artier fare. A few days before we talked, reports circulated that he was set to star in Rapture, a medieval body-horror from director Jordan Tannahill about the “deep, passionate relationship” that develops between monks played by Poulter and Heartstopper’sKit Connor. I am devastated to learn that the project is on pause. “I got whispers of the same thing, but I’m not working on that at the moment,” he said. “I really hope I can work with Jordan in the future; he’s so talented.” His upcoming TV roles sound no less intriguing: the Netflix hostage drama Rabbit, Rabbit alongside Adam Driver and Regina Hall, and the Apple TV dramedy Beat The Reaper.There’s one role that Poulter doesn’t mention: his rumored return to the Marvel cinematic universe. With December’sAvengers: Doomsdaypromising to be a fresh start to the franchise, will we be seeing more of his Adam Warlock character soon? “Do you know what? I have no idea,” he said. “As you probably know, even if I did know I couldn’t tell you. I genuinely have no information on that, but obviously I’d be honored to come back.”His blockbuster future may be under embargo, but Poulter is unequivocal about the kind of movies that are closest to his heart. “I love independent film more than anything,” he said. Earlier this month, he embarked on a road trip with Meeks and Deao to screen Union County at small movie theaters in Ohio. “Going to local independent cinemas in towns like Akron and Dayton, I’m reminded of just how sacred those spaces are,” he said. “I want to maintain a relationship to independent film as long as independent film is happy to have me.”Union County is out in the US now with UK and Australia releases to followExplore more on these topicsWill PoulterMarvelDrama filmsOhioDrugsOpioids crisisinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Their Strength Through Joy conversation is killing me’: Samuel Beckett’s German diaries | Samuel Beckett | The Guardian
description: Published for the first time this month, the Irish writer’s record of his months in pre-war Germany is a fascinating insight into his understanding of, and unease with, Nazism
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Published for the first time this month, the Irish writer’s record of his months in pre-war Germany is a fascinating insight into his understanding of, and unease with, Nazism
Content: ‘They’ll need to fight soon (or burst)‘ … crowds at Pariser Platz, Berlin, on the city’s 700th anniversary in 1937.Photograph: ullstein bild Dtl./Ullstein bild/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘They’ll need to fight soon (or burst)‘ … crowds at Pariser Platz, Berlin, on the city’s 700th anniversary in 1937.Photograph: ullstein bild Dtl./Ullstein bild/Getty ImagesSamuel Beckett‘Their Strength Through Joy conversation is killing me’: Samuel Beckett’s German diariesPublished for the first time this month, the Irish writer’s record of his months in pre-war Germany is a fascinating insight into his understanding of, and unease with, NazismKate ConnollySat 15 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWar was not yet on the immediate horizon whenSamuel Beckettvisited the German city of Hamburg in October 1936, but after watching the apoplexy that Adolf Hitler’s braying induced in ordinary Germans, the Irish playwright was certain that peace could not last. “They’ll need to fight soon (or burst),” he noted in his diary on 6 October.View image in fullscreenSamuel Beckett as a young man.Photograph: Estate of Samuel Beckett c/o Rosica Colin Limited, LondonThe six notebooks that Beckett compiled during his six-month journey across Germany between late September 1936 and April 1937, published for the first time by German publisherSuhrkamp on 20 Augustthis year, put paid to a commonly held view of the author of Waiting for Godot as a poet of pure pessimism, interested in despair and stasis but unconcerned by real-life politics.On the basis of letters and diary extracts, critics of the past concluded that the 1969 Nobel Prize winner travelled acrossGermanyin a state of self-absorption, without paying attention to the rise of totalitarianism. But the notebooks in their entirety show that Beckett was studying National Socialist resentment in close detail.He noticed changes in fashion, such as the predominance of the “Hitler coat”, and collected the “holy phrases” of the Nazi movement in lists:Führer(“leader”),Bewegung(“movement”),Blut und Boden(“blood and soil”), andFreiheit und Ehre(“freedom and honour”), even if they repulsed him.Ihre Kraft durch Freude Unterhaltung macht mich fertig, he noted in German on1 November 1936: “Their Strength Through Joy conversation is killing me.”For now Beckett, who would join the French resistance in 1940, kept his disgust mostly private, merely taking pleasure in subtle parodies of totalitarian behaviour, by “(sticking) the wrong arm out” when invited to give the Nazi salute.View image in fullscreen‘Very dubious at the moment’ … Samuel Beckett’s 1936 notebook.Photograph: Laura Bennetto“He was aware that his diaries could have been confiscated,” said the notebooks’ co-editor Mark Nixon, a professor of modern literature and Beckett studies at the University of Reading. “He has to be careful as he has to get out of Germany with them. Maybe he could have been more explicit had this danger not hung over him. But they do clearly form a rebellion against Nazi rationalising discourse.”Beckett’s tour of some 30 German towns and cities, including Hamburg, Berlin, Dresden and Munich, was motivated by a desire to view works of art and to improve his language skills. An interest in German – his third language after English and French – was probably influenced by lengthy visits between 1928 and 1932 to his cousin and sweetheart Peggy Sinclair and her family, who lived in Kassel.The curiosity about German language and culture was reminiscent of the American English writer Christopher Isherwood, who, asked how he documented Germany between 1929 and 1933, said: “I am a camera with its shutter open, quite passive, recording not thinking.”Beckett’s observed the country’s descent into totalitarianism in an already depressed state of mind. Peggy had died in Germany of tuberculosis in May 1933, his father of a heart attack the following month. The remaining Sinclairs, of Jewish descent, had been forced to flee Germany in 1936.By the time he set out for Cuxhaven, Beckett had two years of psychoanalysis behind him, and his diaries reflect deep anguish, psychosomatic complaints, medical ailments, bodily functions, financial woes and angst over his writer’s block. At times, it is hard to separate his own problems from the darkening political situation around him.Bald fange ich wirklich an zu kotzen. Oder fahr heim(“soon I’ll really start to puke. Or I’ll go home”)he writes on 15 January, 1937.View image in fullscreenThis 1931 portrait by Karl Leyhausen depicts Peggy Sinclair, Samuel Beckett’s cousin, who died in 1933.Photograph: piemags/Alamy“Beckett writes what he sees, that’s the value of him,” Nixon said. “At the same time the diaries are an important part of the journey of Beckett becoming Beckett. In the diaries he keeps telling himself to be more minimal, which is the Beckett we know, who strips everything away that doesn’t matter.”The writer’s subsequent move to France and involvement with the French resistance can be seen as a reaction to what he witnessed in Nazi Germany, Nixon believes. “He was an eye witness to totalitarianism,” he said. “His literature is very clearly based on this experience.”Filled with tiny, hard-to-decipher right-leaning handwriting, the 545 pages of the German diaries were found in the cellar of his Paris flat after his death in 1989 by his nephew Edward Beckett, who has worked with the editors Nixon and Oliver Lubrich to bring the 120,000 words to publication.They are, Nixon says, Beckett’s own personal witness statement, and were not meant for publication. Some entries reveal an unsavoury side to the revered modernist master, including misogynistic remarks and accounts of brothel visits.“Their value as a historical document is in large part due to the fact that he never edited them. The reason it’s ethically OK to be publishing them is that he didn’t destroy them like he did other things.”While Suhrkamp’s bilingual edition, translated by Gaby Hartel, is tailored to political historical interest, an English-language edition, expected to be published next April, will concentrate more on the place of the diaries in Beckett’s literary development. Rights have been acquired by China, France and Italy among other countries.Samuel Beckett: German Diaries (German and English version) is published bySuhrkamp on 20 AugustExplore more on these topicsSamuel BeckettAutobiography and memoirGermanyNazismEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Flamenc Oh!! review – frills, flirting and fierce footwork in breezy Spanish comedy | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Can you dance flamenco to Eye of the Tiger? Of course, says the company Yllana, in a flamboyant celebration of breaking down barriers
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Can you dance flamenco to Eye of the Tiger? Of course, says the company Yllana, in a flamboyant celebration of breaking down barriers
Content: A panto quality … Flamenc Oh!!Photograph: Pablo LorenteView image in fullscreenA panto quality … Flamenc Oh!!Photograph: Pablo LorenteEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewFlamenc Oh!! review – frills, flirting and fierce footwork in breezy Spanish comedyAssembly Hall, EdinburghCan you dance flamenco to Eye of the Tiger? Of course, says the company Yllana, in a flamboyant celebration of breaking down barriersLyndsey WinshipSat 15 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou don’t need to know anything about flamenco to enjoy Flamenc Oh!! That overuse of exclamation marks gives you an idea of the subtlety of this fun/silly dance-comedy by Spanish companyYllana, based on flamenco’s battle between tradition and modernity (which is a real thing in the flamenco world, with its division between purists and progressives).Here is our patriarch with his straight spine and authoritarian streak, banning all music other than flamenco from his family. There’s mother and daughter in polka dots and frills, the son forever trying (and failing) to impress his dad, and their hunk of a cousin who has returned from his travels with some new guitar chords and a love of the blues, ready to upset the status quo.View image in fullscreenStrong women … Flamenc Oh!!Photograph: Pablo LorenteThe show has a panto quality, with broad humour, winks to the crowd, audience singalongs and the injection of popular songs, from Eye of the Tiger to Purple Rain. Fast-fingered guitaristLuis Gallois really very good, riffing on Gershwin in a flamenco version of Summertime. (He’s also good at smouldering glances, tossing his long hair and comedically flirting with the audience.) Anyway, surprise, surprise, it turns out that yes, you can dance flamenco to rock music, and no, flamenco men don’t all have to be macho, and maybe a womancancarry the family flame.Boys Don’t Dance review – jump back to the 80s to celebrate the power of popRead moreThe flamenco itself is proper. The show is co-produced with Sadler’s Wells, home of London’s annualFlamenco festival. The cast are professional dancers (plus singer David Bastidas), and Anabel Moreno, especially, has verve and stagey panache. The choreography leans on virtuoso flourishes, bursts oftaconeoamplified to emphasise each volley of beats. The hour flies by and the jokes wear thin, but it’s all good humoured and done with heart. The takeaways: break down barriers, embrace difference, be our true selves, clap along together and swish your skirts while you’re at it. Olé!AtAssembly Rooms, Edinburgh, until 30 August. Then atPeacock theatre, London, 30 September-10 OctoberAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026DanceFlamencoEdinburgh festivalComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)TheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Foot Is Not an Appropriate Prize for the Tombola review – a fateful day at the fete | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Daniel McVey merrily recruits the audience for a fun hour of cosy crime that bleeds into cosmic horror
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: Daniel McVey merrily recruits the audience for a fun hour of cosy crime that bleeds into cosmic horror
Content: Gentle poking at Little England … Daniel McVey in A Foot Is Not an Appropriate Prize for the Tombola at Pleasance Courtyard.Photograph: Graeme BraidwoodView image in fullscreenGentle poking at Little England … Daniel McVey in A Foot Is Not an Appropriate Prize for the Tombola at Pleasance Courtyard.Photograph: Graeme BraidwoodEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewA Foot Is Not an Appropriate Prize for the Tombola review – a fateful day at the fetePleasance Courtyard, EdinburghDaniel McVey merrily recruits the audience for a fun hour of cosy crime that bleeds into cosmic horrorTim JonzeSat 15 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith a title like that, perhaps it’s no surprise that this afternoon’s show is sold out. Who wouldn’t want to find out how a stray limb ended up in a village fete’s raffle?Writer, performer and director Daniel McVey greets us as his drag character Lydia, a woman who rules over local festivities with a strict schedule – and a firm grip on the tombola. Audience members are encouraged to get up and have a go, and not just that: they’re also cast in McVey’s play as glove puppeteers, actors and – gasp! – suspects in a terrible murder.You see, the titular foot found in the titular tombola has caused shockwaves through the village. Who committed this murder – if it even is a murder? A list of Cluedo-esque suspects is pinned to the tombola stand: Dr Sage, Miss Lemon etc.This cosy crime becomes somewhat less cosy when a strand of cosmic horror enters the fray. Is the strange, multi-eyed presence spotted hovering in the sky responsible for the severed foot? Or is it all just a mass hallucination?During this charming, interactive play we get to partake in singalongs (“We all knit and crochet”), flag waving and even a little faux-democracy. There’s some gentle poking at Little England and our monied, law-making elites that could be developed a little more fully. But then, as Lydia reminds us, there is a crime to solve.Joseph Morpurgo: Highlander 70 review – a dork’s last day at school is one to rememberRead moreSuperb prizes are on offer for those that have a go at the tombola – a Susan Boyle CD is swiped early, a bag of hair clips later on, all taken home by the lucky winners. Miss Lemon – Lydia’s arch nemesis with whom she has an entertaining feud – receives a prize designed to play havoc with her lactose intolerance.The fete schedule on Lydia’s clipboard is actually a script and, while McVey inhabits his drag persona with aplomb, the magic is slightly undone by the fact so much dialogue is clearly being read from it. Still, there are twists and turns as we journey onwards, and the play’s finale suggests McVey has far more bizarre things in his brain than a mere disembodied foot.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalDragFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Charlene Kaye: Diversity Shredder review – killer riffs slay toxic music industry | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: This is a fun and feverish journey, with well-crafted comedy and screaming guitar, through the star’s career so far
Author: Arusa Qureshi
Headline: This is a fun and feverish journey, with well-crafted comedy and screaming guitar, through the star’s career so far
Content: Magnetic … Charlene Kaye.Photograph: Luci StansfieldView image in fullscreenMagnetic … Charlene Kaye.Photograph: Luci StansfieldEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewCharlene Kaye: Diversity Shredder review – killer riffs slay toxic music industryGilded Balloon Teviot, EdinburghThis is a fun and feverish journey, with well-crafted comedy and screaming guitar, through the star’s career so farArusa QureshiSat 15 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn an industry that claims to be inclusive, it’s so easy to feel tokenised. For musician and comedian Charlene Kaye, it has been an uphill battle feeling like the token queer Asian female guitar player, in demand to cater to people’s otherwise superficial concern around diversity, as well as their attempts at being perceived as politically conscious. But if you’re booked and busy, and genuinely skilled at what you do, does it matter if the requests come in through slightly nefarious means?Diversity Shredder is a fun and feverish romp through Kaye’s journey of finding her artistic voice, and what it means to be an Asian American musician in the context of a very broken and unbalanced capitalist system. Using well-crafted, multi-genre musical comedy along with her masterful guitar skills, Kaye reflects on the mental gymnastics at play when you’re a person of colour trying to navigate a career in music, when all people really seem to want is Cassandra from Wayne’s World.Flamenc Oh!! review – frills, flirting and fierce footwork in breezy Spanish comedyRead moreKaye has built a global following via Instagram and TikTok with videos in which she parodies popular music trends and genres such as K-pop, and chart-topping stars from Taylor Swift to Ed Sheeran. Going viral on social media doesn’t automatically translate to physical stage presence but as a musician who has consistently toured, playing solo and with multiple bands, her aura is magnetic and only amplified by her natural, conversational humour and unbridled sass.A large screen on stage displays obnoxiously written emails from prospective collaborators – from a fresh-faced Soundcloud rapper, to a monotonous folk singer-songwriter – as well as clips of the few examples of “Asian music” that exist in the western pop canon. Think the Vapors’ Turning Japanese, David Bowie’s China Girl, and the massively problematic Asian Girlz by LA band Day Above Ground.There’s a lot of material packed into this hour, largely because Kaye has such a hefty and high-quality bank of content. At times, it could do with some breathing room to allow for Kaye’s witty lyricism and uncompromising punchlines to land. Still, Diversity Shredder is a potent and unflinching critique of the stereotypes that box people in. In the end, she just wants to chart her own course. And my God, does she know how to shred.AtGilded Balloon Teviot, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsMusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Good With Faces review – mesmerising power struggle will have you sitting uncomfortably | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Every comment sparks suspicion in Oisín Kearney’s bold and unnerving play about a meeting between a mother and a social worker
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Every comment sparks suspicion in Oisín Kearney’s bold and unnerving play about a meeting between a mother and a social worker
Content: Comments left to curdle … Patrick McBrearty and Clodagh Mooney Duggan in Good With Faces.Photograph: Larissa Pinkham/View image in fullscreenComments left to curdle … Patrick McBrearty and Clodagh Mooney Duggan in Good With Faces.Photograph: Larissa Pinkham/Edinburgh festival 2026ReviewGood With Faces review – mesmerising power struggle will have you sitting uncomfortablySummerhall, EdinburghEvery comment sparks suspicion in Oisín Kearney’s bold play about a meeting between a mother and a social workerChris WiegandSat 15 Aug 2026 04.28 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 04.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you book a seat for Good With Faces you might only use the edge of it. This is a hugely assured psychological thriller, performed with just the right precision and edge. It is written and directed by Oisín Kearney, whose collaborations withMichael Patrickincluded the 2018 fringe hitMy Left Nut, which transferred to TV – this could easily do the same.I’d advise watching it without knowing anything else first. The two-hander opens with social worker Hegarty (Patrick McBrearty) training his video camera on newly single mother Garrick (Clodagh Mooney Duggan) in her hastily tidied living room, with children’s toys swept under the sofa. Garrick’s son has a bruise, which has led to this referral. It’s a matter of procedure, a discussion “for internal use”, Hegarty assures her, in an opening exchange where every comment sparks suspicion and even the correct pronunciation of bourbon biscuit is scrutinised.As it transpires that Hegarty already knows the answers to the questions he is asking, Garrick begins to crack – but she swiftly turns the tables so he is left scrabbling for explanations. Offsetting Katie Richardson’s discordant sound design are pregnant pauses as seemingly casual comments and assumptions are left to curdle, or moments of dark comedy turn into terror.The Real Kyle McCarren review – musical eulogy to lost bandmate strikes a chordRead moreMuch as the choice of each word could send the drama spinning in a new direction, the slightest physical behaviour may lose each the upper hand. Hegarty jokingly (and inappropriately) suggests she trust-falls into his arms to help things along; she touches his leg – or is she just brushing away a crumb? – when he shows her family snaps on his phone, only to give away more than he’d like.Never didactic, Kearney raises the pressures of parenting and care work in a considered examination of blurred professional and personal lives impacted by a harsh economic climate; it has something in common withYou and Me (and Whoever Comes Next)at Summerhall. Using a web of motifs, he gives the most mundane images – a glass of milk, a few nail clippings – an unnerving meaning. A bold and engrossing hour of shifting sands with an awful lot to say about blame, shame and many shades of abuse.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreCare workersSocial careEdinburgh festivalSummerhallChildrenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Secondhand booksellers in UK and Ireland suspect AI firms behind ‘strange’ bulk orders | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Development comes after Anthropic was found to have spent millions on books to scan for ‘data acquisition’
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Development comes after Anthropic was found to have spent millions on books to scan for ‘data acquisition’
Content: ‘My theory is that it’s masses and masses of AI money’: Stuart and Mary Manley, the co-owners of Barter Books in Alnwick, Northumberland.Photograph: suppliedView image in fullscreen‘My theory is that it’s masses and masses of AI money’: Stuart and Mary Manley, the co-owners of Barter Books in Alnwick, Northumberland.Photograph: suppliedAI (artificial intelligence)Secondhand booksellers in UK and Ireland suspect AI firms behind ‘strange’ bulk ordersDevelopment comes after Anthropic was found to have spent millions on books to scan for ‘data acquisition’Dan MilmoGlobal technology editorSat 15 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSecondhand booksellers in the UK and Ireland are reporting a flurry of bulk orders from mystery buyers, amid speculation AI companies are acquiring the tomes for their data.Bookshops contacted by the Guardian say they have been receiving orders from buyers in the US, Canada, continental Europe and the UK. The increase has been replicated around the world, with booksellers in the US, Australia and Europe also reporting unusual orders.Stuart Manley, the co-owner of Barter Books in Alnwick, Northumberland, said the orders, which began arriving three months ago, were unusual because they did not follow the typical pattern of being grouped into themes such as sport or motoring.“It’s definitely a strange combination of books,” said Manley. “Normally a book order is on a theme but this is all over the place.”A recent order included requests for an Estonian translation of John le Carré’s The Mission Song, a copy of Anne Brontë’s Agnes Grey from a specific imprint and the October 1983 edition of Warship, a monthly magazine. Manley said he had sold “hundreds” of random books to three buyers for a total of about £4,000.Jim Shaughnessy, the owner of MW Books in Claregalway, Ireland, said his business had been receiving large, varied orders since May.“They are sporadic, presumably machine-driven and have little in terms of thematic currency; books on agricultural implements in 18th century Africa through to biographies of 1950s racing car drivers,” he said. “Personally, I don’t see we have the right to dictate what any customer does with their purchases but it is more than curious to see what’s being selected.”David Gower-Spence, the owner of BookLovers of Bath, said he had received a rush of orders between May and July for about 200 books from buyers who have also been cited by other sellers contacted by the Guardian for this article.One, the Canada-based Zoom Books, which has featured in other media reports, describes itself as “North America’s leading book recycling company”. Zoom has been contacted for comment by the Guardian.“It was overwhelming for a while and I’m relatively well organised,” said Gower-Spence.One UK-based secondhand bookseller, speaking on condition of anonymity, said some random orders could come from different buyers but be delivered to the same address. “The aliases behind these orders are very opaque even to experienced booksellers,” the source said.One delivery postcode seen by the Guardian and used by different buyers points to a group of freight warehouses near Heathrow airport.The bookseller, who has received orders for 6,000 books from similar buyers since January worth thousands of pounds, said the buyers were paying “top whack” and were not seeking a discount despite requesting titles in bulk.“It’s disrupting the secondhand bookselling business because this isn’t typical for the trade,” the bookseller said. “It appears to be either a human or a machine dipping into the sandbox of secondhand books and what they are buying makes no sense in terms of the wider trends in the market.”The Guardian reported this month thatAustralian booksellers had also received a burst of orders, with one saying the sudden scale of demand was “driving me nuts”.The spate of orders has fuelled speculation among booksellers that AI companies are acquiring the books to scan their contents before pulping them.Manley said: “My theory is that it’s masses and masses of AI money being squandered.”Massachusetts teen accused of killing mother and brother used ChatGPTRead moreThe Washington Post revealed this year thatAnthropic, a leading AI company and developer of the Claude chatbot, had spent tens of millions of dollars acquiring books and slicing off their spines so their contents could be scanned before the books were sent for recycling.Anthropic said: “Claude is trained on a mix of publicly available web data, commercially acquired datasets, and data we generate ourselves. Sourcing books is a widely used approach for training large language models across the AI industry. None of our data acquisition programs buy and destroy rare or antiquarian books.”Last month, the tech news site 404 Media reported that a books database was telling booksellers “the world’s best AI training data is sitting on a shelf”, adding that books published before 2022 were ideal material for AI companies because their text was unpolluted by material that could have been generated by chatbots. The database in question, ISBNdb, said the report wasbased on a webpagethat was a “test of market interest” and had since been taken down.AI tools such as chatbots are “trained” on vast amounts of data to help them generate responses, a requirement that has set tech companies searching for fresh sources of material to build new models. Secondhand books, some of them published decades before ChatGPT exploded on to the scene and not available online, could be a source of fresh data.One post on an online forum for booksellers, seen by the Guardian, said: “Shame these are all destined for AI training, and will therefore get the covers stripped and ultimately end up being pulped.”Other posts expressed puzzlement at the erratic orders, while some questioned whether they could be intended for AI training when requests included books available for nothing in the public online domain such as Gulliver’s Travels, published in 1726.Orders are typically placed through book marketplaces including Biblio and the Amazon-owned AbeBooks. Biblio and AbeBooks have been contacted by the Guardian for comment.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingAmazonAnthropicInternetE-commerceRetail industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Picasso print stolen from Milwaukee art gallery in 2018 found by landlord while cleaning apartment | Milwaukee | The Guardian
description: Torero print, one of 30 known to exist signed by Picasso, was stolen from Bill DeLind’s gallery in 2018
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Torero print, one of 30 known to exist signed by Picasso, was stolen from Bill DeLind’s gallery in 2018
Content: Printouts of a photo of the Pablo Picasso etching on a table in DeLind Fine Art Appraisals in Milwaukee.Photograph: Laura Bargfeld/APView image in fullscreenPrintouts of a photo of the Pablo Picasso etching on a table in DeLind Fine Art Appraisals in Milwaukee.Photograph: Laura Bargfeld/APMilwaukeePicasso print stolen from Milwaukee art gallery in 2018 found by landlord while cleaning apartmentTorero print, one of 30 known to exist signed by Picasso, was stolen from Bill DeLind’s gallery in 2018Associated PressFri 14 Aug 2026 21.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill DeLind thought the Picasso print that was stolen from hisMilwaukeegallery in 2018 was gone forever. But then police called last week and asked him to look at an artwork that a local landlord found while cleaning out a vacant apartment.DeLind immediately recognized the stolen Torero print, one of 30 known to exist signed by Picasso.“I was overwhelmed,” DeLind said Friday. “I was at a loss for words. It was an overwhelming moment for me.”The sticker from his DeLind Fine Art Appraisals was still on the back of the framed print, just as it had been placed there in 2018.“It was indeed mine,” DeLind said. “It came back full circle.”Tim Dertz, a Milwaukee landlord,told WISN-TVthat he found the print while cleaning out an apartment of someone who had been evicted.“It was kind of in a weird spot hanging on a wall,” Dertz told theWisconsinABC affiliate. “It looked like it had been there for a long, long time because it had tons of dust across the top of it.”Dertz said he showed it to an antique dealer friend who recognized it as a Picasso and said it appeared to be the oneDeLind reported stolen in 2018. Dertz handed it over to police, who then contacted DeLind.“When they called me, I was in disbelief,” DeLind said.View image in fullscreenBill DeLind pointing to where a Pablo Picasso sketch was hanging when it stolen from his shop in 2018.Photograph: Laura Bargfeld/APThe Milwaukee police department said in an email on Friday that the statute of limitations for theft and property crimes is generally six years but the case remains under investigation. Caroline Clancy, a spokesperson for the FBI in Milwaukee, declined to comment.The year it was stolen the piece was appraised at between $35,000 and $50,000, DeLind said. He guessed that the value hasn’t changed much since then, but now given its story it may be worth closer to $50,000.The artwork remains in possession of Milwaukee police while the client who had commissioned it for sale with his art gallery works it out with his insurance company, DeLind said.DeLind said his former business partner, who died in February, was distraught over the theft in 2018 and called police every year on the anniversary of the crime asking that they publicize it again in the hope the Picasso could be found.“He would have been over the moon about this,” DeLind said. “It was special to him.”Explore more on these topicsMilwaukeePablo PicassoArt theftWisconsinnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Greatest Showman musical to come alive on the West End stage in 2027 | Stage | The Guardian
description: Disney production ran in Bristol earlier this year and its stars Oliver Tompsett and Samantha Barks will resume their roles at Theatre Royal Drury Lane
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Disney production ran in Bristol earlier this year and its stars Oliver Tompsett and Samantha Barks will resume their roles at Theatre Royal Drury Lane
Content: Oliver Tompsett and Samantha Barks will star in The Greatest Showman.Photograph: Sebastian NevolsView image in fullscreenOliver Tompsett and Samantha Barks will star in The Greatest Showman.Photograph: Sebastian NevolsStageThe Greatest Showman musical to come alive on the West End stage in 2027Disney production ran in Bristol earlier this year and its stars Oliver Tompsett and Samantha Barks will resume their roles at Theatre Royal Drury LaneChris WiegandFri 14 Aug 2026 23.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 23.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Greatest Showman, the 2017 Hugh Jackman film with a chart-topping soundtrack, is to bestaged in the West End next spring. After a sellout eight-week run at Bristol Hippodrome earlier this year, the Disney musical will arrive at the Theatre Royal Drury Lane, currently home to Disney’s Hercules.Its Bristol stars, Oliver Tompsett and Samantha Barks, will resume their respective roles as circus entrepreneur PT Barnum and his wife, Charity. Barks previously starred at Drury Lane as Elsa in Disney’sstage version of Frozen. Also returning from the Bristol production are Ben Joyce (as Barnum’s associate Phillip Carlyle), Vajèn van den Bosch (as opera singer Jenny Lind, known as the “Swedish nightingale”) and Malinda Parris (as the “bearded lady” Lettie Lutz).Oh what a circus! The Greatest Showman hits the stage as a high-flying, hammer-juggling, banger-filled spectacularRead moreThe stage version includes This Is Me, Never Enough and all of the other songs from the film, composed by Benj Pasek and Justin Paul. The duo have also written a handful of new songs. The production, which uses circus and magic tricks and features an aerial routine for Rewrite the Stars, follows roughly the same story as the screenplay – although in Bristol several of the “curiosities” recruited by Barnum for his ensemble differed from their screen equivalents. “We have created characters who are vulnerable and who represent the idea of otherness in a handful of different ways,” said Anne Quart, executive producer at Disney Theatrical Group, earlier this year.Quart and her colleague Andrew Flatt describedThe Greatest Showmanas “fearless in its emotion: open-hearted, exuberant and unapologetically joyous, celebrating those considered outsiders and dreamers”. The show has a book by Tim Federle and is directed by Casey Nicholaw (a Tony winner for The Book of Mormon).Another musical inspired by The Greatest Showman, entitledCome Alive!after one of the film’s numbers, has been running at the Empress Museum in London for two years. Its plot is different to the film yet it features the original songs. Come Alive! is currently booking until spring.Explore more on these topicsStageMusicals (Stage)The Greatest ShowmanMusicals (Film)Walt Disney CompanyWest EndTheatrenewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a gripping new thriller about the fall of Kabul | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: How the US abandonment of the Afghan capital destroyed lives. Plus: celebrating Paul Simon’s legendary Graceland album at the Proms. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: How the US abandonment of the Afghan capital destroyed lives. Plus: celebrating Paul Simon’s legendary Graceland album at the Proms. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: A tragic and shameful train of events … Kabul on BBC Four.Photograph: BBC/© Cinétévé - 24 25 Films - France Télévisions/Domniki MitropoulouView image in fullscreenA tragic and shameful train of events … Kabul on BBC Four.Photograph: BBC/© Cinétévé - 24 25 Films - France Télévisions/Domniki MitropoulouTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a gripping new thriller about the fall of KabulHow the US abandonment of the Afghan capital destroyed lives. Plus: celebrating Paul Simon’s legendary Graceland album at the Proms. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Priya ElanandSimon WardellSat 15 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKabul9pm, BBC FourWhen Joe Biden decided it was “time to end America’s longest war”, he set in motion a tragic and shameful train of events, dramatised in this gripping thriller. As Americans withdrew from Kabul the Taliban moved in, which meant hell for women, dissidents and anyone who had collaborated with the occupiers. Through the eyes of the Nazany family – trying to decide whether to stay or flee – Kabul illuminates the human dilemmas behind the geopolitics.Phil HarrisonCelebrating Graceland at the Proms7.30pm, BBC TwoA barely believable 40 years have passed since the release of Paul Simon’s remarkable album Graceland. As befitting their prominence on the original record, South African choral group Ladysmith Black Mambazo will be at the heart of the action at this Royal Albert Hall concert. They’re joined by Laura Mvula and James Bay.PHBettany Hughes’ Lost Worlds: Dawn of Civilisations8pm, Channel 4Historian Hughes concludes her journey across ancient Anatolia with a whistlestop tour of Neolithic sites. Amid the ruins of Karahantepe, she marvels at life-size human statues dating back 12,000 years, before travelling to Gordion to untangle some knotty myths about King Midas.Graeme VirtueGhosts US8.40pm, BBC ThreeView image in fullscreenThrilling scares … Ghosts US on BBC Three.Photograph: Bertrand Calmeau/BBC/CBS ©2024 CBS Broadcasting Inc. All Rights Reserved.Four back-to-back episodes open the fifth series of this American reimagining of the hit comedy – including a Halloween special involving an Egyptian ghost who is accidentally summoned. It’s zippy enough, with the spoilt Hetty, camp Issac and ditzy Flower being as watchable as their UK counterparts – even if the main couple are no match for Charlotte Ritchie and Kiell Smith-Bynoe.Priya ElanConcorde Crash: Days That Shocked the World10pm, Channel 4The 2000 Concorde crash in Paris wasn’t just a tragedy for the 113 people who lost their lives. It also marked the end of an era in terms of supersonic passenger flight. This fascinating one-off documentary explores the circumstances around the crash and asks if it could have been prevented.PHThe Staircase11pm, ITV1If you didn’t know it was based on a celebrated true-crime documentary, the revelations in this tense family drama might seem implausible. But after a lengthy trial, novelist Michael Peterson (Colin Firth) has finally been jailed for the death of his wife Kathleen. Will it give his shattered clan closure? (Short answer: no.)Graeme VirtueFilm choiceSignal One (Jonathan Sobol, 2026), 3.05pm, 10.20pm, Sky Cinema PremiereOne for fans of Denis Villeneuve’s film Arrival and the Netflix thriller 3 Body Problem, Jonathan Sobol’s science-fiction puzzler also digs into the complexities of first contact with extraterrestrials. Dennis Quaid’s tech billionaire Sam lures computer genius Annika (Isabelle Fuhrman) to his Caribbean island, where David Thewlis’s physicist Perry is on the verge of communicating with aliens. But how do you talk to them? And are they friendly or hostile? A sharp mystery in which scientific hubris vies with humanity.Simon WardellThe Batman (Matt Reeves, 2022), 9pm, ITV2View image in fullscreenBrooding … Zoe Kravitz and Robert Pattinson in The Batman on ITV2.Photograph: Jonathan Olley/APProbably the most brooding Batman on record, Robert Pattinson’s masked vigilante barely raises his voice above a whisper or his hopes above the despairing in Matt Reeves’s wonderfully dark take on the urban hero. In a crime-sodden Gotham, the murder of the mayor by a killer with a penchant for riddles plunges Bruce Wayne and his alter ego into a reckoning with widespread corruption and his own legacy. Zoë Kravitz, as the cat-like Selina Kyle, and Colin Farrell, unrecognisable as the Penguin, provide the zing as our implacable do-gooder battles chaos.SWLive sportAthletics: European Championships, 10am, BBC OneThe penultimate day sees Georgia Hunter Bell and Laura Muir in the 1500m heats from the Alexander Stadium, Birmingham.Championship Football: Sheffield Utd v Birmingham, 5.15pm, Sky Sports Main EventOn Sun, Watford v Southampton is at 12.30pm, followed by Burnley v West Ham at 3.45pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightPaul SimonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 20 of the best cabins, campsites and hotels in Europe’s mountains, lakes and forests | Europe holidays | The Guardian
description: From a 500-year-old inn in the Italian Dolomites to a log cabin in Finland’s lake district, these boltholes offer a tranquil getaway
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From a 500-year-old inn in the Italian Dolomites to a log cabin in Finland’s lake district, these boltholes offer a tranquil getaway
Content: Rifugio Val di Togno in northern Italy.View image in fullscreenRifugio Val di Togno in northern Italy.Top 20sEurope holidays20 of the best cabins, campsites and hotels in Europe’s mountains, lakes and forestsFrom a 500-year-old inn in the Italian Dolomites to a log cabin in Finland’s lake district, these boltholes offer a tranquil and restorative getawayFiona KerrSat 15 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the mountains …A remote refuge in northern ItalyIt’s not easy to get toRifugio Val di Togno,at 1,317 meters (4,320ft). The dirt road from the nearest town winds for 4 miles through 27 hairpins and is best done in a four-wheel drive, or it’s a solid two-hour hike from the tiny hamlet of Carnale. But as managers Luna Lybeer and Wout Allegaert say: “We offer guests nothing so they can get away from everything.” Although you can hardly describe this beautifully renovated mountain hideout as “nothing”. Every room looks down the valley, whether through a porthole-like round window or huge floor-to-ceiling sliding doors. Breakfast, lunch (or a picnic to take on a hike), afternoon snack,aperitivoand a two-course dinner are included too – delicious vegetarian meals made using produce from the couple’s garden, or foraged nearby, along with homemade kombucha, sourdough and gnocchi.Doubles from£298 all-inclusive(three-night minimum),rifugiovalditogno.comAn Austrian train station turned B&BBuilt in 1910, the old station at Lermoos in Austria’s Tirol had stood empty for years before Johann Ehmann and his wife Cleo Weber bought it in 2019. “We were fascinated by it and contacted Austrian Railways regularly for more than five years asking if it was for sale,” says Ehmann. Now the couple have converted the classic Alpine building at the foot of Zugspitze (Germany’s highest peak) intoLermooser, a design B&B. The eight rooms range from a cosy bunk bed “cabin” to the “team XL” with three single beds and a double in a row. There’s a communal kitchen and a kiosk downstairs for coffee, pastries and homemade soups. The train still stops right outside, and hikes up to the Tuftl Alm viewpoint, and to Seebensee and Drachensee, start right from the door.Doubles from £106 B&B,lermooser.comA historic wilderness hotel in NorwayView image in fullscreen‘Røisheim, a time capsule of a turf-roofed hotel.’In summer, the sun doesn’t set until 11pm atRøisheim, which sits on the fringes of Jotunheimen national park in southern Norway. That means all the more time to go on blue ice glacier walks and swim in mountain lakes, cycle over the Sognefjellet pass or tackle Galdhøpiggen, Norway’s tallest mountain at 2,469 metres (8,100ft). The first recorded ascent of Galdhøpiggen in 1850 started from Røisheim and the trail still leads from the courtyard of the hotel, although most hikers now choose quicker routes starting from nearby Spiterstulen. Røisheim, a time capsule of a turf-roofed hotel, has been welcoming mountain-lovers since 1858 and many of the rooms are faithfully preserved with timber-clad walls, carved wooden beds and barrel-like tubs.Doubles from £243 B&B,roisheim.noAlpine apartments in BavariaView image in fullscreenAn apartment at Karls Mittenwald.Photograph: Jessica Lerchenmüller“We didn’t choose Mittenwald because we wanted to open a hotel, we chose it because we wanted to live somewhere that summer still feels like summer,” says Anne-Sophie Trinkgeld, who recently openedKarls Mittenwaldin this pretty small town near the Austrian border with her husband Dario. Mittenwald came out top in their search for the best combination of climate, outdoor activities and accessibility in the Alps – it’s surrounded by mountains but just 40 minutes from Innsbruck. The couple turned the former bakery into 11 thoughtfully designed one- and two-bedroom apartments with a cafe downstairs serving breakfast spreads and homemade cakes. Just the fuel for days spent swimming in the clear waters of Lautersee, cycling to the source of the Isar River through theKarwendel nature parkor hiking to Germany’s highest brewery, Karwendelbräu.Apartments from £145 a night,karls-mittenwald.deAn eco-campsite in the Austrian TirolView image in fullscreenGerhardhof on the Mieming Sun PlateauNearly 1,000 metres (3,280 ft) above sea level, the wide Mieming Sun Plateau is known for its mild microclimate and looping hikes through pine forests and Alpine meadows. Josef Volgger grew up on a farm here,Gerhardhof, which his parents also ran as a small guesthouse. Now Volgger, along with two business partners, has transformed Gerhardhof into a sustainability-minded campsite with grey water recycling, wood-chip heating and solar energy, as well as a naturally filtered swimming pond. You’ll still see Josef’s mother Edith in the bakery, turning out apple strudel, and there is a restaurant for dinners of wiener schnitzel andKäsespätzle(an Alpine mac and cheese).Pitches from £38 a night,gerhardhof.comA 500-year-old inn in the Italian DolomitesView image in fullscreenOver its five centuries in the South Tirolean town of Lana, the building that now houses1477 Reichhalterhas had many incarnations, including a butcher, bakery, sawmill, stable and tavern. Since 2018 it has been a restaurant with eight bedrooms dressed in mid-century furniture. Room number 4, Helmsdorf, has a balcony with views of the Vigiljoch mountain and Braunsberg Castle (you can borrow a bike to explore further), while Schönmüller is another favourite for its raw plaster walls and tiledstubestove. Downstairs, tables spill on to the pedestrianised street from the restaurant, which dishes up a delicious beef tartare and house salad made with homemade pickled vegetables and whatever’s in season from the kitchen garden at sister hotel Villa Arnica.Doubles from £170 B&B,1477reichhalter.comA Bauhaus guesthouse in Italy’s South TirolFor 40 years, Johanna Fink ran her family’s Alpine hotelBriolwith simple efficiency: sheets air-drying on the line, guests summoned to dinner by cowbell at precisely 7pm. Recently, her children Victoria and Valentin von Klebelsberg have taken over, but Briol remains charmingly the same. The main house was renovated in 1928 by artist Hubert Lanzinger inmodernist Bauhaus style– the bedrooms have no heating (there is a hot-water bottle service), guests share a bathroom and there are no TVs, wifi or pictures on the walls. But with views like this, from a mountain meadow high above Barbiano and the Eisack valley, the lack of distraction is very welcome, and hiking trails fan out from the doorstep.Doubles from £255 half-board,briol.itBy the lake …A houseboat on a Swedish lakeView image in fullscreen‘It’s all about the lake’ at Stugbaat and its five houseboats on Lake Lelång.Photograph: Beyond Oceans MediaStugbaatis a collection of five houseboats that bob around the huge Lake Lelång in Dalsland. Each floats on an aluminium or stainless steel pontoon, and comes with a little motorboat for towing the tiny house to a quiet corner or pootling ashore to explore. On dry land, there are mountains to climb (Egersknatten), berries and chanterelles to forage in the forest, a straw museum in Bengtsfors and a microbrewery in Torrskog. But, really, it’s all about the lake: fish from or dive off the wooden deck that surrounds the cabin or take out the paddleboard included with each booking. You can hire a kayak, check out the floating sauna, or simply drop anchor and do nothing.From £233 a night (two-night minimum), sleeps 4,stugbaat.seBack-to-nature cabins in SwedenView image in fullscreenLife is off-grid at Naturbyn on Lake Eldan.Thomas Peterson started with just one log cabin, which he handbuilt on a section of pine and spruce forest on the shores of Lake Eldan in Värmland. Then he built another, and one up in the treetops, and one floating on the water. There are now seven atNaturbyn, all off-grid (no wifi or electricity, just wood-burning stoves and paraffin lamps), all with views of the lake and some with grass roofs dotted with tiny wild strawberries. This being Sweden, there’s a sauna on the lakeshore. Beyond that, borrow a canoe, forage in the forest, watch for elk among the trees, catch a pike for supper or count shooting stars across the inky sky.Cabins from £160 a night, sleeps 2,naturbyn.seA waterfront hotel in JutlandView image in fullscreenNy Hattenæs on the shores of Brassø Lake.In the heart of the Danish Lake District on the Jutland peninsula, the 19th-century mill town of Silkeborg is known as Denmark’s outdoor capital. Just south of Silkeborg, the waterfront hotelNy Hattenæshas sat on the forested shore of Brassø Lake since 1896 when it opened as a summer boarding house. It is now open year-round, but summer is still the loveliest time to stay, when days are long, the lake is filled with people swimming, paddleboarding and canoeing, and the terrace at Ny Hattenæs is the perfect place to catch the lingering twilight. Revamped in 2022 by the trio of siblings behind Danish design houseSociety of Lifestyle, the 14 bedrooms are filled with House Doctor furniture and the bathrooms stocked with Meraki natural products. Room number 7 is the plum pick, with a large balcony overlooking the water.Doubles from £205 B&B,nyhattenaes.comA new-gen hotel in BavariaLess than an hour’s drive south of Munich, Tegernsee is where city folk flock in the summer to drink in leafy beer gardens, tuck intoknödeldumplings in farmhouse restaurants and boat on the lake. Lederhosen and dirndls are still a regular sight in some parts here, but the recently opened hotelBlyb, in the quiet village of Gmund am Tegernsee, is as far from the usual Bavarian cliches as you can get. The villa dates back to 1892, and while it still has original stucco paintings and ornate wooden balconies, they’ve been updated with crisp monochrome decor, a restaurant from the team behind the hip Munich spotMural, an outdoor yoga deck and events that might include a doner kebab and DJ pop-up or intimate unplugged gigs in the library.Doubles from £112 room-only,blyb.coLakeside cabins in a German biosphere reserveBerlin school friends Julian Trautwein, Johann Ahlers and Christopher Eilers founded Raus in 2021 with the simple idea of getting city-dwellers like themselves out into nature. They started with a handful of sustainably built cabins near German cities and this year have added their 100th.Lodge am Seetakes the Raus concept and turns it into a little cabin resort, with 17 huts by a lake in the Unesco Elbe River Landscape Biosphere Reserve, between Berlin and Hamburg. The area is known for its quiet cycle paths, but the water is just as attractive, and there are free paddleboards to borrow, canoe hire nearby and sea eagles, storks and cranes to spot above the wetlands.Cabins from £126a night, sleep 2,raus.lifeskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLog cabins in Finland’s vast LakelandView image in fullscreenThe Sahanlahti Resort ‘has sleek modern villas that come with wraparound terraces’Finnish Lakelandis Europe’s largest lake district, a watery labyrinth of thousands of lakes, rivers and channels. Its biggest body of water, Lake Saimaa, is like an inland archipelago of nearly 14,000 forest-covered islands. In summer, Finns flock here to lakeside log cabins (known as amökki), which are an essential part of Finnish culture. On the site of a historic sawmill on Saimaa’s rippling shoreline,SahanlahtiResortembodiesmökkitradition old and new, with timeless red-painted wooden cabins (some with their own saunas) and sleek modern villas that come with wraparound terraces. You may even spot a Saimaa ringed seal, one of the world’s rarest.Cabins from £93 a night, sleep 4,sahanlahtiresort.fiAn adults-only hideout in the Austrian AlpsView image in fullscreenJust outside the medieval town of Kitzbühel, Schwarzsee is known for its mineral-rich peat waters (its name means black lake), which are some of the warmest in the Alps, reaching 27C in summer. On a hillside above the lake,Seebichlis another black beauty, its darkly painted wooden balconies spilling over with flowers. Brothers Max and Sebastian Witzmann, whose grandfather bought Seebichl in the 1950s, have created an artsy take on a traditional Alpine hotel, with bright orange Eames chairs rather than classic carved-wood Tirolean ones and contemporary art on the walls instead of antlers. And if Schwarzsee or the heated pool in the garden at Seebichl get too balmy, hike up to the nearbySintersbach Waterfallfor a chillier dip.Doubles from £170 B&B,hotel-seebichl.atIn the forest …A-frame cabins in the Slovenian AlpsView image in fullscreen‘A peaceful base for exploring the surrounding Savinja valley.’Photograph: Mamoot/Andrej LamutFamed for its emerald green water, theSavinja riverruns from the Rinka Falls at the head of the pristine Logar valley in northern Slovenia down through forested gorges in the Slovenian Alps. Along its banks,Forest Camping Mozirjeis a peaceful base for exploring the surrounding Savinja valley. Tents and campervans pitch up in meadows among the trees. For those allergic to pegging in a ground sheet, there are bell tents and A-frame-shaped wooden “forest beds” built from local timber. Campers swap hiking tips and debate rafting versus canyoning over dinner at communal tables in the well-stocked covered kitchen. Afterwards, gather around one of the campfires or kick back in a hammock next to the little outdoor library.Pitches from £15plus £14per adult. Forest Beds from £84,campingmozirje.comA design hotel in the Black ForestView image in fullscreenArtbau Designhotel and its treetop views.Photograph: Maris MezulisGermany’s Black Forest (Schwarzwald) is named for the canopy of conifers so dense it blocks out much of the sunlight. It’s a mysterious place, often linked to the dark fairytales of the Brothers Grimm, although the siblings actually collected and wrote their folktales farther north around the city of Kassel. It is easy to imagine Hansel and Gretel or Little Red Riding Hood trotting down the trails, although you’re more likely to encounter German families or a hilltop castle. In the Black Forest town of Waldkirch, famous for the production of church and fairground organs,Artbau Designhotelis a sharply modern riposte to all that fairytale tweeness, with concrete walls and steel tables softened by Moroccan textiles and balconies that look out to the treetops.Doubles from £115 room-only,artbau-designhotel.deA forest sauna in LatviaView image in fullscreen‘The glass cabin bedrooms … looking out across wildflower meadows by day and up to star-filled skies after dark.’Photograph: Stikla istabaDeep in a pine forest near theGauja national park,Ziedlejasis dedicated to the Latvian tradition ofpirts– steamy wood-fired bathhouses heated to about 65C. There are three here: the glass pirts beside the swimming pond, the smoke pirts under the grey fir trees and the wool pirts with walls made from sheep’s wool (which releases skin-soothing lanolin). Sessions last around four hours, guided by a pirts master (pirtnieks),who takes guests through the ritual, which includes “whisking” (tapping and brushing) bodies with bundled sticks, herbal scrubs, massage and alternating hot and cold water. The glass cabin bedrooms are just as restorative, looking out across wildflower meadows by day and up to star-filled skies after dark.Cabins from £110 a night, sleeps 2,ziedlejas.lvFamily-friendly huts and camping in the French AlpsView image in fullscreenThe Huttopia Bozel en Vanois campsite.Photograph: Manu ReybozHuttopia has dozens of nature-immersed campsites all over France (and a handful farther afield). There’s a formula – tree-shaded spots often beside lakes and rivers, pre-pitched safari tents if you don’t fancy BYO, a wood-fired pizza restaurant for the evening – and it works, with families returning year after year. Set among pine and fir trees on the banks of the Doron de Bozel river,Huttopia Bozel en Vanoiseis at the gateway to the Vanoise national park near the Italian border, which is criss-crossed with hiking trails and home to ibex, marmots and chamois. Closer still is the lake beach – a five-minute walk – or canyoning on the Doron de Bozel; while back at camp kids can join the forest-school-like Petits Trappeurs or hang with new friends at after-dinner magic shows and open-air film screenings.Nature pitch from £20, Trappeurwood and canvas tent from £146 a night,huttopia.comTiny houses in a Swedish forest full of wildlifeView image in fullscreenAn off-grid cabin at InforestThe only alarm clock at the four off-grid cabins that make upInforest,2½ hours north-east of Gothenburg, is the sound of robins, blackbirds and chaffinches, perhaps joined in their dawn chorus by the odd woodpecker or cuckoo. Each solar-powered tiny house here is a kilometre apart, so your only neighbours will be the roe deer, hares and the odd moose roaming among the hectares of pine, spruce and birch trees. Almost 70% of Sweden is covered in forest and the right of public access, orallemansrätten, means you can walk or bike in every direction. For a little more action, head to the perfectly preserved wooden town of Hjo on the edge of Lake Vättern, just 4 miles away, for a sauna on the harbour or to sail on the steamship Trafik before scurrying back into the woods.Cabins from £155 a night, sleep 2-4,inforest.seModernist treehouses on a farm in SwedenView image in fullscreenSuites on stilts at Trakt Forest Hotel.Photograph: James Silverman PhotographyIn the summer of 2022, this family farm in Småland opened five striking suites on stilts among the treetops of the surrounding pine forest. This spring,Trakt Forest Hoteladded seven bedrooms in its historic Erik’s House farmstead, the design more rattan headboards, crocheted cushions and views of cows grazing than the angular minimalism and secluded stillness of the treehouses. There is a restaurant, Traktköket, in a nearby log cabin and much of the food is grown on the farm or sourced locally. Outside, there’s a little sauna hut beside the farm pond, with a wood-fired bath squirrelled away deeper in the forest. The team can prepare afika(coffee break) backpack with coffee, cake and a sandwich to take out on a hike further into the wilderness.Doubles from £184 B&B,traktforesthotel.comSome of the areas mentioned above have been affected by wildfires this summer.
